entries.title: Ezekiel 1:1 "in the thirtieth year"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:1 "in the thirtieth year" This seems to relate to the age of the prophet (because Ezek. 1:2-3 are a parenthesis, possibly by an editor, to clear up any misunderstanding of Ezek. 1:1. The two dates [i.e. Ezek. 1:1 and Ezek. 1:2-3] refer to the same time). This theory goes back to Origen. Thirty years of age was the time that priests began their ministry in the temple (cf. Num. 4:3, 23, 30, 39, 43, 47). However, they began their training five years earlier (cf. Num. 8:23-25). Their length of service was to age fifty. This fits the length of Ezekiel's prophetic ministry (cf. Ezek. 40:1). Ezekiel understood this vision as his call to the prophetic ministry.

The Aramaic translation, called Targums, suggests the thirty years date from the discovery of "the book of the law" during the restoration of the temple in the eighteenth year of King Josiah (cf. 2 Kgs. 22:1-13).

The JPSOA footnote says "We do not know the 30th year of what."

▣ "on the fifth day of the fourth month" See Introduction, Date, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE CALENDARS

▣ "by the river Chebar" We know from archeological discoveries that this was a man-made irrigation canal from the Euphrates River, making a loop from near the city of Babylon, through the city of Nippur (cf. Ps. 137:1) and on to Erech (in all, about 60 miles).

▣ "among the exiles" Notice how different 8th century prophets were sent to different groups.

  1. Ezekiel's' specific ministry was to the covenant people who were in exile, primarily those of Judea, but also the Northern Ten Tribes.
  2. Jeremiah's ministry was to those left in Palestine.
  3. Daniel's ministry was to the royal court of Nebuchadnezzar II in the capital of Babylon.

▣ "the heavens were opened" The VERB (BDB 834, KB 986, Niphal PERFECT) denotes YHWH revealing Himself to Ezekiel. This phrase is parallel to "the windows of heaven were opened."

  1. for judgment, Gen. 7:11; 8:2; Isa. 24:18
    1. flood of water (see SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS)
    2. no water
  2. for agricultural blessings, 2 Kgs. 7:2,19; Mal. 3:10
  3. here, for revelatory vision (see SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION)

In ancient cosmology reality is described as

  1. heaven above (sun and moon, stars, God's throne, i.e. the three heavens; (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN and SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN)
  2. heaven above the earth (as a dome with windows; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH)
  3. the earth (dwelling place of physical life)
  4. Sheol (the place of the dead, see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEAD, WHERE ARE THEY [Sheol/Hades, Gehenna, Tartarus]), I. B.

▣ "I saw visions of God" There is a paradox in the Bible between those who claim to have seen God and the specific statements that no one can see God and live (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CAN HUMANS SEE GOD AND LIVE?). Apparently it is possible to see visions of Deity, but not to gaze intently on His form and especially His face (compare Exod. 24:11,12; Num. 12:8; Isaiah 6; Revelation 4 with Exod. 33: 20-23; John 1:18; 6:46; 1 Tim. 6:16; 1 John 4:12).

The word "vision" (BDB 909 I) is first used in Gen. 46:2, where it is parallel with "in visions of the night," which may imply

  1. a dream (cf. Gen. 15:12; 20:3,6; 31:10,11,24; 37:6,8,9,10.20)
  2. a special trance

In Num. 12:6 it relates to God's call to prophets (cf. 1 Sam. 3:15; Dan. 10:16; Ezek. 1:1; 8:3; 40:2). It is inferior to His face-to-face revelations to Moses (cf. Num. 12:8; Deut. 34:10). Still, it was divine revelation. These words are not Ezekiel's words, nor or the visions his imagination. YHWH is revealing His personal presence with the exiles!

It is also interesting that the very same Hebrew letters also mean "sight" or "appearance." This meaning is far more common than "vision." A few times the two meanings, "vision" and "appearance," overlap (i.e. Ezek. 8:4; 11:24; 43:3 [thrice]; Dan. 8:16,27; 9:23; 10:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Ezekiel Introduction
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
INTRODUCTION TO EZEKIEL

  1. NAME OF THE BOOK

    1. It is named after its chief spokesman, the prophet and priest (from Zadok), Ezekiel.

    2. His name (BDB 306, KB 406) meant "God strengthens," "may God make strong," or even possibly, "God is strong."

  2. CANONIZATION

    1. This book had difficulty being accepted into the Jewish yearly cycles of liturgy because
      1. Ezekiel's temple and procedures are different from those of Moses (i.e. compare Num. 28:11 with Ezek. 46:6)
      2. the vivid visionary language, especially Ezek. 1, 8, and 10
      3. the glory of YHWH and His Spirit leaves Jerusalem and moves to the exiles in Babylon (i.e. Ezek. 10:1-2,18-22; 11:22-25)

    2. Rabbi Hananiah ben Hezekiah of the rabbinical school of Shammai (the conservative school), is said to have used 300 jars of oil (i.e. staying up late) in order to reconcile Ezekiel with Moses (cf. Shabb. 14b; Menahuth 45a; Hagigah 13a).

    3. Jewish tradition said that when Elijah returned before the coming of Messiah (cf. Mal. 3:1; 4:5), he would solve the contradictions between Ezekiel's temple and Moses' tabernacle (cf. Menah 45a).

  3. GENRE

    1. This book contains many genres
      1. apocalyptic (Ezekiel 1; 8-10; 38-39; and possibly 40-48; see SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE)
      2. prophecy (Ezekiel 37, esp. vv. 4,9,12; see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT])
      3. parables (Ezek. 17:2; 20:49; 24:3)
      4. lament poetry (Ezek. 19; 26:17-18; 27:4-9,25-36; 28:2-23; 30:2-19; 31:2-9; 37:2-8,12-15; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY)
      5. dramatic symbols (Ezekiel 4-5; 12; 24)
      6. allegory (Ezekiel 16; 23)
      7. visions (Ezekiel 1-3; 8-11; 40-48; see SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION)

    2. Ezekiel composed most of his messages in written form. They were not given orally, as were Isaiah's and Jeremiah's. They are very structured.

  4. AUTHORSHIP

    1. The authorship of the book has never been doubted. The entire book, except for Ezek. 1:2-3, is written in the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR (autobiographical, cf. Ezek. 4:14; 9:8; 11:13). However, much of the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR is direct speech from YHWH.

    2. Jewish tradition (i.e. Talmud), Baba Bathra 15a, said, "the men of the Great Synagogue wrote Ezekiel and the Twelve." As we have seen in other books the word "wrote" means edited or compiled.

    3. Josephus' The Antiquities of the Jews, 10.5.1, said that Ezekiel wrote two books. This may refer to the characteristic structure of many of the Hebrew prophets because their books easily divide into two halves
      1. Isaiah 1-39 & 40-66
      2. Daniel 1-6 & 7-12
      3. Zechariah 1-8 & 9-14
      4. Ezekiel 1-32 & 33-48

        In the first part the historical setting is the author's day. In the second part of the book the setting is the future. This may be the reason why Josephus stated he wrote two books.

    4. It is written from Babylon (cf. Ezek. 1:1; 3:11,15; 11:24), but Ezekiel is taken to Jerusalem several times in visions (cf. Ezek. 8:3; 11:1; 40-48).

    5. All we know about the prophet Ezekiel is from his book. He is not mentioned anywhere else in the OT.
      1. he was born about 623 B.C. in Jerusalem
      2. he was a priest of the line of Zadok, Ezek. 1:3
      3. he was married but had no children, Ezek. 24:16-18
      4. he was taken captive when he was twenty-five years old in 597 B.C. by Nebuchadnezzar II along with King Jehoiachin, Ezek. 1:1; 33:21; 1 Kgs. 24:14-16
      5. he was exiled to a Jewish settlement not far from the city of Nippur on a man-made irrigation canal, Chebar, Ezek. 1:1,3, called Tel-Abib, Ezek. 3:15
      6. he preached at least twenty-two years, Ezek. 1:1-2; 29:17
      7. he was a strong but compassionate prophet, Ezek. 9:8; 11:13; 24:16

    6. His priestly training deeply affects his visions. He is particularly interested in the evil of the current temple (chapters 8-11) and the purity of the new temple (chapters 40-48).

  5. DATE

    1. He was born about 623 B.C. in Jerusalem.

    2. Ezekiel is one of the seventh century prophets: Jeremiah, Daniel, Nahum, Habakkuk and Zephaniah.

    3. During the period of the rise of Neo-Babylonian power under Nabopolassar and the crown prince Nebuchadnezzar II, God spoke through these prophets in different localities.
      1. Daniel was taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar II in 605 B.C. He was exiled to the palace in Babylon, Dan. 1:1.
      2. Ezekiel was taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar II in 597 B.C. along with 8,000 to 10,000 craftsmen, soldiers, and King Jehoiachin and his family, 2 Kgs. 24:14-16. They were settled in a refugee camp by the Canal Chebar.
      3. Jeremiah remained in Jerusalem until the death of Gedaliah (cf. 582 B.C.), the Babylonian appointed governor.
        SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

    4. Ezekiel dates his prophecies (which influenced Haggai [cf. Haggai 1:1,15; 2:1,10,20] and Zechariah [Zech. 1:1; 7:1]). These dates show that the book is not in chronological order. However, if you isolate the oracles against the surrounding nations (i.e. Ezekiel 25-32) the rest are in a chronological sequence.
      Day Month   Years of Jehoiachin's exile
      1. a vision, Ezek. 1:1 5 4 30 (?)
      2. a vision, Ezek. 1:2 5 4 5 (593 B.C.)
      3. a word from YHWH 12 4 5 (593 B.C.)
      4. a vision, Ezek. 8:1 5 6 6 (592 B.C.)
      5. elder's questions, Ezek. 20:1 10 5 7 (591 B.C.)
      6. siege of Jerusalem began, Ezek. 24:1 (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1) 10 10 9 (588 B.C.)
      7. oracle against Tyre, Ezek. 26:1 1 ? 11 (586 B.C.)
      8. oracle against Egypt, Ezek. 29:1 12 10 10 (587 B.C.)
      9. oracle against Egypt, Ezek. 29:17 1 1 27 (571 B.C.)
      10. oracle against Egypt, Ezek. 30:20 7 1 11 (586 B.C.)
      11. oracle against Egypt, Ezek. 31:1 1 3 11 (586 B.C.)
      12. oracle against Egypt, Ezek. 32:1 1 12 12 (585 B.C.)
      13. oracle against Egypt, Ezek. 32:17 15 (12 from 32:1) 12 (585 B.C.)
      14. fall of Jerusalem, Ezek. 33:21 5 10 12 (585 B.C.)
      15. a vision of new Jerusalem, Ezek. 40:1 10 1 25 (573 B.C.)

    5. HISTORICAL SETTING

      SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

      SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

    6. LITERARY UNITS

      1. Ezekiel's prophecies can be divided into two radically different messages.
        1. Before the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. his sermons were characterized by a call for repentance (i.e. Ezek. 14:6,18) because of the coming judgment of God (Ezekiel 1-32).
        2. After the fall of Jerusalem his sermons (for the most part) turned to hope, restoration, and forgiveness (Ezekiel 33-48).

      2. Brief Outline
        1. His call to ministry, Ezekiel 1-3
        2. The sinfulness of the Covenant People and the fall of Jerusalem, Ezekiel 4-24
        3. God's judgment on the surrounding nations, Ezekiel 25-32
        4. God's promise of restoration of His people, city, and temple, Ezekiel 33-37
        5. Apocalyptic invasion from the north, Ezekiel 38-39
        6. A vision of the restored temple, Ezekiel 40-48

  6. MAIN TRUTHS

    1. The covenant people were suffering because of their own sin, not YHWH's weakness.

    2. Covenant faith has both a corporate and individual aspect. The New Covenant mentioned in Jer. 31:31-34 is basically individual, as are chapters 18 and 33. The New Covenant was also guaranteed by God's action (cf. Ezekiel 36-37). This is the same balance between God's sovereignty and humanity's covenental responsibilities expressed in the NT.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE
      SPECIAL TOPIC: PREDESTINATION vs. HUMAN FREE WILL
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

    3. God is faithful to the seed of Abraham (Gen. 12:1-3) and David (2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17). The Covenant will be reestablished (cf. Ezekiel 37; 40-48). Exile was an act of love (i.e. disciplining parent).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

    4. The problems for the covenant people are not over, Ezekiel 38-39 (cf. Daniel 7-12). There is an ongoing struggle between the people of God and fallen humanity (Psalm 2).

entries.title: Ezekiel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
EZEKIEL 1

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS*

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
  The Call of Ezekiel
(1:1-3:27)		 Ezekiel's First Vision of God
(1:1-7:27)
The Vision of Four Figures Ezekiel's Vision of God Superscription God's Throne Introduction
1:1-3 1:1-3 1:1-3 1:1-3 1:1-3
The Throne Chariot Vision The Vision of the Chariot of Yahweh
1:4-14 1:4-14 1:4-14 1:4-9 1:4-12
1:10-12
1:13-14 1:13-14

* Although they are not inspired, paragraph divisions are the key to understanding and following the original author's intent. Each modern translation has divided and summarized the paragraphs. Every paragraph has one central topic, truth, or thought. Each version encapsulates that topic in its own distinct way. As you read the text, ask yourself which translation fits your understanding of the subject and verse divisions.

In every chapter we must read the Bible first and try to identify its subjects (paragraphs), then compare our understanding with the modern versions. Only when we understand the original author's intent by following his logic and presentation can we truly understand the Bible. Only the original author is inspired—readers have no right to change or modify the message. Bible readers do have the responsibility of applying the inspired truth to their day and their lives.

Note that all technical terms and abbreviations are explained fully in the following Special Topics:
Abbreviations, Hebrew Grammar, and Glossary.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Ezekiel 1-3 is a literary unit which functions in several major ways.
    1. Ezekiel's initial vision of YHWH in Babylon
    2. Ezekiel's sense of YHWH's call to the prophetic ministry
    3. The images and visions continue in Ezek. 8
    4. The holiness of God, symbolized in the portable throne chariot (the imagery of the Ark and a chariot are linked in 1 Chr. 28:18) and its surprising appearance apart from the temple in Jerusalem

  2. YHWH still wants a holy people to reflect Himself to the nations (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36)! This revelatory people will be those taken into exile, not the ones left in Judah. Israelites have always put too much emphasis on Jerusalem, as Stephen's sermon in Acts 7 shows.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2 All of the book of Ezekiel is in the FIRST PERSON except Ezek. 1:2,3, which seem to be a later scribal or editorial addition to explain the date of Ezek. 1:1. Note the parenthesis in NASB.

It must be admitted that moderns do not know when, who, or how the OT books were produced. It is a faith assumption and biblical claim that they are uniquely from God (inspiration) through selected human instruments (authors, editors, and scribes).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

Verse 2 reflects 2 Kgs. 24:14, which makes the date either 592 or 593 B.C. Ezekiel was exiled when he was 25 years old, but did not begin his ministry until five years later.

▣ "King Jehoiachin" See SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:3 "the word of the Lord came"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3 "the word of the Lord came" This is the repeated formula (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 3:16; 6:1; 7:1) denoting four divine revelations. It remains uncertain how the revelation came.

  1. verbal
  2. imagery
  3. main truths and Ezekiel chooses the genre

But what is sure, it was YHWH's revelation, not Ezekiel's.

▣ "to Ezekiel the priest" Ezekiel was from the priestly line of Zadok (cf. 2 Sam. 8:17; 15:24-36), while Jeremiah was from the priestly line of Abiathar (cf. 1 Sam. 22:20-23; 2 Sam. 8:17; 15:24-36), who was exiled to his home village of Anathoth by Solomon (cf. 1 Kgs. 2:26-27,35).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVITICAL PRIESTS

▣ "son of Buzi" This person (BDB 100, KB 115 II) is mentioned only here in the OT. It seems to be related to the Hebrew root meaning

  1. despise (BDB 100 I)
  2. contempt (BDB 100 II)
  3. a proper name (uncertain meaning)
    1. second son of Nahor, Abrahams' brother, Gen. 22:21, possibly related to a tribe of Arabia mentioned in Jer. 25:23
    2. a person of the tribe of Gad, 1 Chr. 5:14

The very fact that nothing else is known about Buzi implies that he was well known to the original recipients.

▣ "the Chaldeans" Herodotus (450 B.C.), Hist. I, uses this term to refer to

  1. an ethnic group (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:1-4; Dan. 5:30)
  2. as well as a priestly class (cf. Dan. 2:2; 3:8; 4:7; 5:7,11)
  3. this usage goes back to Cyrus II
  4. even before this, Assyrian records used the term (BDB 505) in an ethnic sense (cf. R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 1113)

Also read the good discussion of the possibility of a confusion of two similar terms (i.e. Kal-du vs. Kasdu) in The Expositors Bible Commentary, vol. 7, pp. 14-15 or Robert Dick Wilson, Studies in the Book of Daniel, series 1.

Because Gen. 11:28 states that Ur of the Chaldeans was the home of Terah and his family, Chaldeans may have been ethnically Semitic (i.e. same racial group as the Hebrews).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "the hand of the Lord came upon him" This is an anthropomorphic phrase used often for God's presence, power, and inspiration (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 3:14,22; 8:1; 33:22; 37:1; 40:1; 1 Kgs. 18:46; 2 Kgs. 3:15; Isa. 8:11; Jer. 15:17).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (anthropomorphic language)

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:4 "a storm wind coming from the north"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:4 "a storm wind coming from the north" YHWH is sometimes identified with a storm (i.e. Sinai, cf. Exodus 19). The north is often used in the OT imagery for impending judgment (i.e. invasion, cf. Jer. 1:12-14; 4:6; 6:1). But here it is a symbol of acceptance and renewal. YHWH Himself is coming to be with the exiles (in Isa. 14:13 a northern mountain is God's dwelling; see full exegetical note there).

▣ "a great cloud with fire flashing fourth continually" This would have reminded Ezekiel and his readers of Exod. 19:9,16,18, the inauguration of the Mosaic covenant when YHWH visits Mt. Sinai/Horeb and gives the Ten Words to Moses (and, the rabbis say, the oral law).

The literal phrase is "and fire taking hold of itself." This exact phrase is also found in Exod. 9:24 (i.e. BDB 77 and BDB 542, KB 534, Hithpael PARTICIPLE) used of one of the Egyptian plagues.

All of the prophets focus on the Mosaic Covenant. They judge Israel in light of her disobedience (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 28; 30:1,15,19' see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT]) to its commands. Ezekiel will contrast

  1. the current temple practices (cf. Ezekiel 8-11) with a future temple (cf. Ezekiel 40-48)
  2. current shepherds (i.e. leaders) with a future leader (cf. Ezekiel 33)

His readers had no other categories to relate to a restoration by YHWH than this one! The New Covenant (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:27-36) and its focus on individual faith and faithfulness (i.e. Ezekiel 18; 33) would be a shocking revelation which would have seemed to depreciate both the Mosaic Covenant and Israelite corporality!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOREB

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOCATION OF MT. SINAI

▣ "something like glowing metal" Throughout the book of Ezekiel his visions are described in terms "like" (BDB 198) or "similar to." It is obvious that Ezekiel is doing the best that he can in describing that which is not normative.

Notice the different phrases used to describe this vision.

  1. bright light or brightness (BDB 618 I) around it
  2. glowing or gleaming metal in the midst of it
    1. "amber" ‒ LXX, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA
    2. "bronze" ‒ TEV
    3. "brass" ‒ NEB, REB
    4. "electrum" (mixture of gold and silver) ‒ LXX, Vulgate

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

▣
NASB, NRSV, LXX  "fire flashing forth"
NKJV  "raging fire engulfing itself"
REB  "flashes of fire"
NJB, Peshitta  "flashing fire"
TEV  "lightning was flashing"

The MT has "fire taking hold of itself." The only other place this phrase occurs in the Hebrew Bible is Exod. 9:24. It seems to refer to lightning in a thunder storm.

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:5 "the four living beings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:5 "the four living beings" It is surprising that the MT has these "living beings" in the FEMININE PLURAL form. Usually, in this context, they are referred to in the MASCULINE PLURAL. These throne creatures are first described in Exod. 25:18-22; 37:7-9 and even to refer to Cherubim. It is uncertain if there are two Cherubim (i.e. two on the mercy seat of the ark) or four (two at each end of the ark and two on the lid). This same confusion can be seen in Solomon's temple (cf. 1 Kgs. 6:23-28; 2 Chr. 3:10-14). Jewish tradition has four and is the origin of the four of this vision.

I have always held to only two (on the lid) from the book of Exodus, with Solomon expanding the size of everything in the tabernacle when he built the temple in Jerusalem (cf. 1 Kings 6). By the way, Ezekiel felt the same freedom (or revelation) to expand and change the temple further in chapters 40-48.

Just a note on the term "cherub" (BDB 500). Several possible sources.

  1. Akkadian, lesser spiritual being
  2. Assyrian
    1. "to be gracious"
    2. ADJECTIVE, "great" or "mighty"
    3. similar to the name of the winged bulls on the gates of Nineveh
  3. BDB mentions possibility of "thunder cloud" (Ps. 18:11)

They are described again in Ezek. 10. They are the origin of the living creatures of Rev. 4:6-8. Their description changes from time to time, but it is obvious that they are the same group of angelic creatures (i.e. throne guardians). Ezekiel recognizes them as Cherubim in Ezekiel 10, but not here in Ezekiel 1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHERUBIM

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ARK OF THE COVENANT

1:7
NASB  "feet were like a calf's hoof"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "the soles of their feet were like the
  soles of calves' feet"
TEV  "they had hoofs like those of a bull"
NJB, REB  "they had hooves like calves"
JPSOA  "the feet of each were like a single
  calf's hoof"

This is the only place this detail is mentioned. The Hebrew term "feet" is really "soles" (BDB 496 #3).

Remember this is imagery! It is a vision! Accuracy and detail are not the issue, but the overall effect. YHWH is coming and the heavenly court with Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

▣ "burnished bronze" This metallic imagery (BDB 887 and BDB 638 I) describes heavenly beings.

  1. here the Cherubim
  2. the powerful angel in Dan. 10:6
  3. glorified Jesus in Rev. 1:15; 2:18

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:8 "wings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:8 "wings" There are several angelic creatures who are said to have wings.

  1. the Cherubim over the Ark of the Covenant, Exod. 25:20; 37:9; 1 Kgs. 6:24,27; 8:6,7; 2 Chr. 3:11-13; 5:7,8
  2. the Seraphim of Isaiah's heavenly throne room vision, Isa. 6:2
  3. the living creatures of Ezekiel's vision (i.e. called Cherubim in Ezek. 10:1), Ezek. 1:8,24
  4. the female angels of Zechariah's vision, Zech. 5:9
  5. even used as imagery for YHWH's special care (i.e. female bird, cf. Matt. 23:37), Ruth 2:12; Ps. 17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 61:4; 63:7; 91:4 (also see Gen. 1:2; Exod. 19:4; Deut. 32:11)
  6. imagery of John in Revelation (cf. Rev. 4:8; 9:9 from Ezekiel)
  7. regular angels do not have wings in OT or NT

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:9 "their wings touched one another, their faces did not turn as they moved"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:9 "their wings touched one another, their faces did not turn as they moved" This is a vision of the mobile throne chariot of God. This imagery may go back to David's Psalm of praise in 2 Sam. 22:11. The living creature's wings and the wheels formed a hollow square with burning coals in its midst and over it all a blue ice-crystal canopy (cf. Ezek. 1:22, in Rev. 4:6 it is the floor).

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:10 "all four had the face of the lion"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:10 "all four had the face of the lion" The two Cherubim (BDB 500, KB 497) are described in Exod. 25:20 as having one face that faced the middle of the Mercy Seat. In Revelation 4 each one had a separate face similar to the description here. The early church fathers tried to ascribe these different faces to the different gospel writers: Matthew, the lion; Mark, the ox; Luke, the man; John, the eagle. It is best to stay somewhat neutral on specific interpretations of these visions. Obviously it refers to some type of angelic order, which is very closely identified as guardians of "the" Throne of God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHERUBIM

SPECIAL TOPIC: MERCY SEAT

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:11 "and two covering their bodies"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:11 "and two covering their bodies" Without trying to read too much into this phrase, there are several ways to take it.

  1. sense of modesty (cf. Isa. 6:2, where "feet" may be a euphemism referring to the male sexual organs, cf. Ruth 3; 1 Sam. 24:3; see SPECIAL TOPIC: "the sons of God" in GENESIS 6)
  2. sense of preparation for action
  3. in Isaiah 6 and Rev. 4:8 they had six wings.

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:12 "the spirit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:12 "the spirit" This verse must be interpreted in light of Ezek. 1:20 and 21, which seem to imply the spirit of the four living creatures themselves (cf. Ezek. 1:21c). However, it must be admitted that the language of Ezek. 1:12 implies a separate personal will (i.e. God in the imagery of His Spirit [i.e. Gen. 1:2]).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:13 This verse tries to describe something that is occurring in the midst of the box formed by the Cherubim wings, the wheels, and the crystal covering. Whatever it was, it was below the throne (cf. Ezek. 1:26). Notice the parallelism, which attempts to describe the indescribable.

  1. burning coals of fire
  2. torches darting back and forth among the living beings
  3. bright fire
  4. lightening flashing from it

One wonders how Ezek. 1:14 is related to Ezek. 1:13. The Peshitta, NKJV, and REB translate Ezek. 1:13 as if it describes the living creatures themselves and not the coals of fire (LXX, NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB). The answer to this confusion is rectified by JPSOA, which puts a full stop after the first phrase of Ezek. 1:13, thereby relating it to the living creatures of Ezek. 1:12.

I assume Ezek. 1:13 does not describe the Cherubim, but is a sacrificial image going back to the tabernacle. It is uncertain if it refers to

  1. coals on the altar of incense, which were used to make good smelling smoke which veiled the view of YHWH, who dwelt between the wings of the Cherubim over the Ark of the Covenant (cf. Exod. 30:1-10; 37:5-28)
  2. the sacrificial altar (cf. Exod. 27:1-8; 38:1-7) at the front of the entrance to the tabernacle/temple where sacrifices (cf. Leviticus 1-7) were brought and given to the priests.

These sacrifices allowed sinful humans to approach a holy God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ARK OF THE COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALTAR OF SACRIFICE

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALTAR OF INCENSE

▣ "lightning" I take this opportunity to discuss the accommodation used by God to communicate His true revelation to a particular historical/geographical people. There are several items that especially fit into an ANE setting (i.e. multi-faced animals, spiritual guardians, and lightning). YHWH chooses imagery that His people have seen in other religions, but now they apply to Him.

  1. The three heavens described by Babylonians as made of gem stones (NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 164).
  2. Lightning is a common weapon in the hand of Canaanite gods, which are usually depicted on mountains (cf. Ezek. 1:4, "north," cf. Isa. 14:13).
  3. The multi-faced angelic guardians are also common in Mesopotamia (and Egypt), where they guard the entrance of temples and palaces (cf. IVP, Bible Background Commentary, p. 690).

YHWH often takes the names of foreign deities to describe Himself.

  1. King of Kings
  2. winged disk (sun)
  3. God of heaven
  4. Lord of Lords

In this way He shows that He is the only true God. The only universal God of creation and redemption. We must be careful as moderns

  1. not to make the images literal
  2. not to assume cultural borrowing has theological significance of the reality to the false gods of the nations
  3. that biblical images are just that—images attempting to convey spiritual reality! History is theologically affected and theology is historically/culturally affected. This is how human communication works. We move from the concrete to the figurative and from the known to the new reality!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:14 The question again has to do with the referent. It is

  1. the living creatures, Peshitta, NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB
  2. the central fire, JPSOA

It seems to me that Ezek. 1:5-12,14 describe the living creatures, but Ezek. 1:13 describes a central fire (cf. Ezek. 10:2,7; Isa. 6:6; Rev. 8:5). But the issue cannot be definitively solved. The MT (JPSOA) implies that it all refers to the living creatures.

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:15-19 "full of eyes round about"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:15-19 "full of eyes round about" These wheels were beside the angelic beings (Ezek. 1:15). There seems to be a wheel within a wheel at right angles to each other (Ezek. 1:16), which symbolized immediate mobility in any direction (cf. Ezek. 1:17; 10:11).

The eyes around each wheel symbolizes the omniscience of God (cf. Ezek. 10:12). From Babylonian literature "eyes" on wheels referred to jewels (cf. The IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 691). In Ezek. 1:19 the chariot throne rises from the earth that shows it is not earthbound (cf. Ezek. 10:16-17).

Ezekiel tries to describe the wheels.

  1. eight wheels
  2. two beside each cherub
  3. made of beryl (BDB 1076, cf. Ezek. 10:9; Exod. 28:20; 39:13; Song of Songs 5:14; Dan. 10:6)
  4. full of eyes (from Rev. 10:12 and Rev. 4:6,8 there were also eyes on the living creatures)
  5. all of them were alike (Ezek. 1:16)

The God of creation and covenant is not limited to the Promised Land! He goes and knows!

In Daniel's vision of heaven the Ancient of Days (i.e. YHWH) is also connected to fiery wheels (cf. Dan. 7:9) and angels (Dan. 7:10).

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:20-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:20-21 See note at Ezek. 1:12. The word "spirit" (BDB 924) is being used in two senses.

  1. YHWH (i.e. in imagery of "spirit," Ezek. 1:12,20)
  2. the living creatures (Ezek. 1:21)

"Spirit," in this context, is a way of expressing life/personality/being.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:22 "something like an expanse"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:22 "something like an expanse" The Hebrew word means "that which is beat out" and usually refers to a concave, shallow dish (BDB 956, cf. Gen. 1:6; see John H. Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, pp. 168-169, 174). Here it seems to be a reference to the dome of the earth or the sky (i.e. "over the heads," cf. Dan. 12:3; Exod. 24:10). It separated the waters above from the waters below. Its color was crystal, like ice (BDB 901), which implies a crystal blueness (see Rev. 4:6 for a foundation of the same color).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

▣ "awesome" This term (BDB 431, KB 432, Niphal PARTICIPLE) is used in several ways (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 532).

  1. fear during the wilderness wanderings of Israel, Deut. 1:19; 8:15
  2. YHWH's redemptive acts during this exodus period, Deut. 10:21; 2 Sam. 7:23; 1 Chr. 17:21; Ps. 66:3,5; 106:22
  3. YHWH's name, Deut. 28:58; Ps. 99:3; 119:9; Mal. 1:4
  4. YHWH's presence, Jdg. 13:6; Job 37:22; Isa. 64:3; Ezek. 1:22
  5. eschatological redemptive acts, Joel 2:11,31; Mal. 4:5

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:24 This verse is an attempt to describe the sound of the chariot moving (i.e. the living creatures' wings)

  1. like the sound of abundant waters (cf. Ezek. 43:2)
  2. like the voice (i.e. thunder, BDB 876) of the Almighty (cf. Rev. 1:15; 14:2; 19:6) or angel (cf. Dan. 10:6)
  3. like a sound of tumult (BDB 242), like the sound of an army camp (i.e. "host," BDB 334, cf. Jer. 11:16)

The implication is that the voice of God directs their movement (cf. Ezek. 1:25).

▣ "the Almighty" This is the term Shaddai (BDB 994, KB 1420, cf. Num. 24:4,16; Ruth 1:20,21; Ps. 91:1; Isa. 13:6; Ezek. 1:24; Joel 1:15). Usually it is combined with El (the general name for deity in the Ancient Near East, probably from the root "to be strong"). Shaddai's etymology is uncertain. Some scholars suggest

  1. the all-sufficient One
  2. the self-sufficient One
  3. the compassionate One (same consonants in Arabic mean a woman's breast, BDB 994)
  4. rain-giver (NEB)
  5. high (mountain) God
  6. mighty or violent

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ALMIGHTY (Shaddai)

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:26 "a throne"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:26 "a throne" It is described

  1. above the expanse (i.e. crystal dome, cf. Ezek. 10:1)
  2. color was "sapphire" or "lapis lazuli" (BDB 705, cf. Exod. 24:10; 28:18; 39:11; Job 28:6,16; Isa. 54:11). Notice Ezekiel's descriptions of colors come from his training as a priest. These were the colors of the tabernacle and priestly garments.
  3. usually YHWH's throne is in heaven (cf. Ps. 11:4; 103:19; Isa. 66:1) and the earth is His footstool (i.e. between the wings of the Cherubim over the Ark).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE SACRED COLORS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

▣ "high up was a figure" The throne's occupant is described.

1. appearance as a man, Ezek. 1:26

2. his loins and above like glowing metal, Ezek. 1:27 (cf. Ezek. 1:4; 8:2)

3. below loins like fire, Ezek. 1:27

4. radiance around him (like a rainbow), Ezek. 1:28

5. like the glory of YHWH, Ezek. 1:28

As in Isaiah 6, YHWH is depicted as a human person, but He Himself (i.e. face) cannot be described! He is the awesome, holy one, who only accommodates His glorious appearance to humans (cf. Exod. 24:10-11; Dan. 7:9). However, Israelites usually believed that to see God meant death (see notes online at Exod. 33:17-23; Isa. 6:5). Often this seeing of God is related to "the Angel of the Lord" (cf. Gen. 16:7,13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANGEL OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: CAN HUMANS SEE GOD AND LIVE?

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:27 "radiance"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:27 "radiance" This term (BDB 618, lit. "brightness") is often used to describe God and His presence (theophany).

  1. by David, 2 Sam. 22:13
  2. to an eschatological Israel, Isa. 4:5
  3. YHWH's portable throne chariot, Ezek. 1:4,13
  4. of YHWH Himself, Ezek. 1:27,28; 3:23; 10:4

▣ "fire" See SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

entries.title: Ezekiel 1:28 "the rainbow"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:28 "the rainbow" This seems to represent the grace and mercy of YHWH as expressed in the sign to Noah (cf. Gen. 9:13-17). God's purpose of a covenant people will not change, as He does not change (cf. Mal. 3:6; James 1:17)!

▣ "the glory of the Lord" This "glory" (BDB 458) is the theme of Ezekiel (19 times, mostly in chapters 10 and 43). This is also a major theme in Isaiah (38 times). In many ways it is theologically parallel to "holy" (BDB 872) as in Exod. 29:43; Lev. 10:3 and especially Isa. 6:3. These terms stand for YHWH's uniqueness and majesty! His personal presence is overwhelming and awe inspiring (El Shaddai). He is the God of creation (Elohim) and redemption (YHWH). He is the ever-living, only-living source of life.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (kabod, OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C., D.

▣ "I fell on my face" This is often what occurs in the presence of the divine or His representative (cf. Ezek. 1:28; 3:23; 43:3; 44:4; Gen. 17:3,17; Dan. 2:46; 8:17; Rev. 1:17).

Paul House, Old Testament Theology, p. 329, compares this with

  1. Moses' reluctance to serve (cf. Exodus 3-4)
  2. Isaiah's sense of personal and corporate sinfulness (cf. Isa. 6:5)
  3. Jeremiah's personal depreciation (cf. Jer. 1:6-10)

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What exactly did Ezekiel see and why?
  2. Why is the description of the Cherubim different from that in Ezekiel 10?
  3. How does Ezekiel 10 relate to Ezekiel 1?

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:1 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:1 "Son of man" This is literally "ben-Adam" (BDB 119 CONSTRUCT BDB 9). This is used often in Ezekiel as a way of referring to Ezekiel as a human being (93 times, cf. Ps. 8:4). In Ezekiel it is the way YHWH addresses Ezekiel. This same phrase is found in Ps. 8:4 in parallel with "man" (i.e. Enosh, BDB 60 and Adam, BDB 9).

In Dan. 7:13 this term takes on divine characteristics as one likened to "a son of man" coming before the Ancient of Days (i.e. Deity) riding on the clouds of heaven. Daniel 7:13 is the background for Jesus' use of this term for himself, which combines humanity and deity (i.e. 1 John 4:1-3). The phrase had no nationalistic or militaristic rabbinical overtones.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ YHWH addresses Ezekiel.

  1. "stand on your feet" (BDB 763, KB 840, Qal IMPERATIVE)
  2. "I may speak with you" (BDB 180, KB 210, Piel IMPERFECT, but used in a COHORTATIVE sense [cf. Ezek. 2:2])

Notice the personal (cf. Ezek. 1:26) God of glory (cf. Ezek. 1:28) addresses Ezekiel! This is one of the major themes of this book (the personal presence of YHWH in Babylon). Also note a mere human, a fallen human, part of a rebellious people, is addressed face to face, standing before the holy presence. This says something of the dignity of humanity made in the image and likeness of God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27).

entries.title: Ezekiel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
EZEKIEL 2

The Prophet's Call Ezekiel Sent to Rebellious Israel

(1:28b-3:15)		 The Vision of the Scroll
(2:1-3:15)
1:28b-2:5 1:28b-2:7 1:28b-2:5
2:1-7 2:1-8
2:6-8 2:6-7
2:8-10 2:8-10 2:8-10
2:9-10 2:9-10

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:2 "the Spirit entered me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:2 "the Spirit entered me" It is not certain if we are speaking of the Holy Spirit or, more probably, simply personal imagery parallel to "the hand of the Lord" from Ezek. 1:3 (cf. Ezek. 3:14; 33:22; 37:1; 40:1). A non-human life force (ruah, BDB 924) entered me (i.e. divine wind or breath, cf. Ezek. 37:9,14). The term "spirit" has no ARTICLE in Hebrew (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT).

Ezekiel's call to the prophetic ministry is signaled in several characteristic phrases.

  1. "spirit/Spirit entered me" (cf. 1 Chr. 15:1; 20:14; 24:20; Isa. 61:1; Joel 2:28)
  2. "I am sending you" (cf. Ezek. 2:3, 4)
  3. "Thus says the Lord God"
  4. "do not fear them"
  5. "you shall speak My words to them"
  6. "eat the scroll," Ezek. 2:8-3:3
  7. "go to the house of Israel and speak with My words to them," Ezek. 3:4,11
  8. "spirit/Spirit lifted me up" (cf. Ezek. 8:3; 11:1,24)

For a good brief discussion of ruah (BDB 924) see Norman Siraith, The Distinctive Ideas of the Old Testament, pp. 143-158.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:3 "I am sending you to the sons of Israel, to a rebellious people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:3 "I am sending you to the sons of Israel, to a rebellious people" The phrase "sons of Israel" in the book of Ezekiel is sometimes used for the Northern Ten Tribes, but most often it is used for all of the covenant people.

The term "rebellious" is a Qal PARTICIPLE (BDB 597, KB 632). It is followed by a Qal PERFECT of the same VERB (lit., rebels who rebel). Their personal and continual rebellion is directed against the covenant God (i.e. "Me"). This is what their fathers, grandfathers, and great grandfathers also did.

To this terrible characterization is added another term for rebellion ("transgressed," BDB 833, KB 981, Qal PERFECT). This is defined as "a rebellious nation" (cf. Exod. 32:9; 33:3,5; 34:9; Deut. 9:6,7,13; 10:16; 31:27; 2 Chr. 30:8; Acts 7:51).

The term "people" (BDB 156) is the term goim, which is often used contemptuously by the Israelites of the pagan Gentile nations. It is PLURAL, which probably refers to Israel and Judah. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1048, says rabbinic commentators think it refers to Judah and Benjamin. This was purposeful sarcasm.

2:4
NASB, TEV, NJB, REB  "stubborn"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "impudent"
JPSOA  "brazen of face"

This was originally an agricultural phrase referring to unruly oxen. Literally it means "hard of neck" or "stiff-necked" (BDB 904, cf. Exod. 32:9; 33:3,5; 34:9; Deuteronomy 6; 7; 13; 24; 27; 10:16; 31:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

NASB, NJB, REB  "obstinate"
NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, Peshitta  "stubborn"
TEV  "do not respect me"

The second term (BDB 305 CONSTRUCT BDB 524, lit. "strong of heart"), in this context, implies a hardness toward God and His revealed will (cf. Ezek. 3:7).  What a striking series of descriptive phrases characterizing the covenant people.

▣ "Lord God" This is "adonai – YHWH," which is a characteristic title of God in the book of Ezekiel. It comes from the term Adon, which is the Hebrew term for "master-lord" (BDB 10, KB 12) and the Covenant name for God, YHWH, from the Hebrew VERB "to be" (BDB 217, KB 394).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:5 "a rebellious house"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:5 "a rebellious house" This descriptive phrase (BDB 108 CONSTRUCT BDB 598) is used often in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 2:5,6,8; 3:9,26,27; 12:2 [twice],3,9,25; 17:12; 24:3; also note 44:6). Moses also saw this propensity in Israel (cf. Deut. 31:27, also note Neh. 9:17), as did Samuel (cf. 1 Sam. 15:23) and Isaiah (cf. Isa. 30:9).

YHWH seems to have chosen a people who were notoriously stiff-necked and rebellious for the theological purpose of demonstrating His long-suffering covenant faithfulness, even amidst their inability to faithful obedience! YHWH did not choose the family of Abraham because of anything special in them, but to reveal His own character (i.e. Deut. 7:7,8; Isaiah 48; Jer. 7:24-26; 11:7-8). The OT is not primarily about Israel, but about YHWH!

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "whether they listen or not" This is a recurrent theme (cf. Ezek. 2:5,7; 3:11,27). This is parallel to Isa. 6:9-10.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣ "they will know that a prophet has been among them" God chose to reveal His future actions in order that

  1. the people are responsible for their rebellious acts (cf. Ezek. 2:6-7; note Josh. 24:19-28)
  2. He is revealed as the only true God (i.e. predictive prophecy, cf. Jer. 28:9; Ezek. 33:33)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:6 There is a series of commands from YHWH to Ezekiel.

  1. "neither fear," BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense and repeated three times (cf. Jer. 1:8)
  2. "nor be dismayed," BDB 369, KB 365, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense, cf. Josh. 10:25; Jer. 17:18

The reason Ezekiel is not to be afraid is YHWH's presence and promises (i.e. Deut. 31:8; Josh. 1:9; 1 Chr. 22:11-13; 28:20).

God uses several images to describe the reaction to Ezekiel's words by the rebellious house.

  1. thistles (BDB 709, KB 768, lit. "rebel," only here in the Hebrew Bible)
  2. thorns (BDB 699, KB 756, cf. Ezek. 28:24)
  3. scorpions (BDB 875, KB 875, cf. Deut. 8:15)

Numbers 1 and 2 are found only in Ezekiel. Israel did not want to hear from God. They wanted the covenant blessings, but not the covenant requirements and consequences (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28)!

Just a note to those of us who minister to God's people—they will not always appreciate or advocate our ministry (i.e. Moses and Israel). We must remember who we serve and why! It is possible that the thorns, thistles, and scorpions (possibly another thorny bush) refer to a hedge of God's protection around the prophet and his God-given message.

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:7 "whether they listen or not"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:7 "whether they listen or not" This is repeated from Ezek. 2:5 and again in Ezek. 3:11. The same concept is repeated in Ezek. 3:27. God will reveal Himself to His covenant people, even if they refuse to hear (cf. Isa. 6:9-13). This is because

  1. He has an eternal redemptive purpose that involves Israel
  2. of His love for the Patriarchs
  3. of His character, bound to His promises

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:8 "do not be rebellious like the rebellious house"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:8 "do not be rebellious like the rebellious house" Like Ezek. 2:6, Ezek. 2:8 has a series of commands from YHWH to Ezekiel.

  1. "listen," BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal JUSSIVE
  2. "do not be rebellious," BDB 224, KB 243, Qal JUSSIVE
  3. "open your mouth," BDB 822, KB 953, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. "eat," BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERATIVE

Ezekiel's obedience constitutes his acceptance of YHWH's call to be His spokesperson. It is analogous to

  1. the Seraph touching Isaiah's lips with a coal from the heavenly altar (i.e. Isa. 6:6-7; also note Jer. 1:9)
  2. Jeremiah's eating a scroll (cf. Jer. 15:16)
  3. John's vision in which an angel gives him a scroll to eat (cf. Rev. 10:8-11)

Obviously eating the scroll is imagery for receiving God's message and passing it on.

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:9 "a hand was extended to me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:9 "a hand was extended to me" The text is ambiguous as to whose hand was extended and from where. It could be from the throne itself, but more likely, an attending angel, as in Isaiah 6.

▣ "a scroll" This would refer to a piece of papyrus rolled up (BDB 706). It symbolized the message of God (cf. Isa. 29:11-12; 30:8; Jer. 25:13; 30:2; 36:2,4; Dan. 12:4).

Notice how the message of judgment on this scroll is described.

  1. lamentations (BDB 884)
  2. mourning (BDB 211)
  3. woe (BDB 223)

entries.title: Ezekiel 2:10 "It was written on the front and the back"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:10 "It was written on the front and the back" It was highly unusual for either papyrus (i.e. hard to write against the grain) or parchment (i.e. part of message can be worn off) to be written on both sides. This seems to be imagery reflecting God's entire message of judgment (cf. Rev. 5:1). Once Jerusalem is destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's army, Ezekiel begins to proclaim restoration in YHWH's name (i.e. Ezekiel 36-37; 40-48).

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:1 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:1 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ Chapter 3 closes out the literary unit of chapters 1-3, which is Ezekiel's call to the prophetic ministry. This call involves YHWH addressing him in several commands.

  1. "eat," Ezek. 3:1 (twice), BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERATIVE (see note at Ezek. 2:8)
  2. "go" (lit. "walk"), Ezek. 3:1,4,11, BDB 229, KB 241, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "speak," Ezek. 3:1, BDB 180, KB 210 Piel IMPERATIVE (Piel PERFECT with waw in Ezek. 3:4)
  4. "feed" (lit. "cause to eat," cf. Ezek. 3:2), Ezek. 3:3, BDB 37, KB 46, Hiphil JUSSIVE (Qal stem in Ezek. 3:2,3; 4:9,10 [twice],12,13,14,16; 5:10 [twice])
  5. "come," Ezek. 3:4,11,24, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. "take into your heart," Ezek. 3:10, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE
  7. "listen closely," Ezek. 3:10, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE
  8. "get up," Ezek. 3:22, BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE
  9. "go out," Ezek. 3:22, BDB 422, KB 425, Qal IMPERATIVE
  10. "shut yourself up in your house," Ezek. 3:24, BDB 688, KB 742, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  11. "let him hear," Ezek. 3:27, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERFECT used in aJUSSIVE sense
  12. "let him refuse" (lit. "cease"), Ezek. 3:27, BDB 292, KB 292, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:3 "Then I ate it, and it was sweet as honey to my mouth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:3 "Then I ate it, and it was sweet as honey to my mouth" This conveys the thought that YHWH's word is significant and meaningful even when it is a message of judgment (cf. Ps. 19:10; 119:103; Jer. 15:16; Rev. 10:9, 10). That the Holy Creator God would be involved with sinful humanity is amazing! God's judgment is really a sign of His parental discipline (cf. Heb. 12:5-13).

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:4, 5 "the house of Israel. . .a people of unintelligible speech or difficult language"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:4, 5 "the house of Israel. . .a people of unintelligible speech or difficult language" Ezekiel's primary ministry was to the covenant people in exile. God was not sending him to a foreign people, as He did Daniel. However, the irony of Ezek. 3:7 is that they (foreign nations with strange languages) would be willing to listen, but Israel would not.

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:7 "the whole house of Israel is stubborn and obstinate"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:7 "the whole house of Israel is stubborn and obstinate" See note at Ezek. 2:4. They will not listen to Moses or the Prophets (i.e. 20:8; Isa. 6:9-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:8,9 "hard. . .harder"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:8,9 "hard. . .harder" This word (BDB 305) is a play on the name of Ezekiel (BDB 306), which means "to harden or strengthen." God will equip Ezekiel to face head on the rebellious house of Israel (cf. Ezek. 2:5-6; 3:9,26-27; 12:2-3; 44:6).

3:9
NASB  "emery"
NKJV, JPSOA, REB, Peshitta  "adamant stone"
NRSV  "the hardest stone"
TEV  "as firm as rock"
NJB  "a diamond"

This Hebrew root (BDB 1038) has several meanings.

  1. thorns, briars, only in Isaiah (cf. Ezek. 5:6; 7:23,24,25; 9:18; 10:17; 27:4; 32:13)
  2. adamant, flint (i.e. hard stone), Jer. 17:1; Ezek. 3:9; Zech. 7:12
  3. person's name, 1 Chr. 24:24
  4. place name, Josh. 15:48; Jdg. 10:1,2

Context determines meaning! Only #2 fits. Which hard stone is being referenced is uncertain.

▣ "Do not be afraid of them or be dismayed before them" See note at Ezek. 2:6.

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:10 What an insight into how inspiration worked in this case. The prophet had to listen (i.e. eat the scroll, cf. Ezek. 2:8), receive (i.e. comprehend), and then speak the message to the exiled tribes in Babylon.

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:11 "go to the exiles"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:11 "go to the exiles" This is the specific group that Ezekiel is commissioned to speak YHWH's message to, the exiled tribes in Babylon.

 ▣ "whether they listen or not" Some will respond, but others will not (note the parable of the soils, Matt. 13:1-15; Mark 4:1-12; Luke 8:4-10). There has always been a spiritual divide within national Israel. Some are covenant people by lineage only, but others are trusting, obeying, and heart-felt covenant followers!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:12 "the Spirit lifted me up"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:12 "the Spirit lifted me up" There is some doubt about to whom "spirit" refers in Ezek. 1:12,20,21 (there is no DEFINITE ARTICLE), but here and in Ezek. 2:2 it obviously refers to the active presence of God. It may be true that a full-blown Trinitarian understanding of God is absent from the OT. There are still texts (such as this one) that point toward a plurality in God (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY, II.).

There are several places in Ezekiel where this phrase is used implying that it is a literary way of introducing revelation (cf. Ezek. 2:2; 3:12,14,24; 8:3; 11:1,24; 37:1; 43:5). Ezekiel is receiving active, personal revelation in the form of visions and words.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY, II. C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

NASB  "a great rumbling"
NKJV  "a thunderous voice"
NRSV  "the sound of loud rumbling"
TEV  "the loud roar of a voice"
NJB  "a great vibrating sound"
JPSOA  "a great roaring sound"
LXX  "the voice as of a great earthquake"
REB  "a fierce rushing sound"
Peshitta  "a great rushing"

This NOUN (BDB 950, KB 1272) can refer to

  1. the sound of an earthquake, 1 Kgs. 19:11-12; Ezek. 38:19; Amos 1:1; Zech. 14:5
  2. the context of a loud voice, Isa. 29:6
  3. the sound of military action
    1. warriors, Isa. 9:4
    2. war chariots, Jer. 10:22; 47:3
    3. war horses, Job 39:24
  4. the shaking of persons, Ezek. 12:18
  5. the VERB is used often of divine comings for judgment or blessing

In this context (cf. Ezek. 3:13) it was the sound of YHWH's throne chariot lifting up and moving. Somehow the "lifting up" of the Spirit is equated with the lifting up of the throne chariot (cf. Ezek. 1:12,20-21). With the sound of the movement of the throne chariot was a vocal statement of the attending angelic being, "Blessed by the glory of the Lord in/from His place." This is similar to the Seraphim of Isa. 6:3.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta  "blessed by the glory of the
  Lord in His place"
NRSV, REB  "the glory of the Lord rose
  from its place"
TEV  "Praise the glory of the Lord
  in heaven above"
JPSOA (footnote emendation)  "as the Presence of the Lord
  rose from where it stood"

The UBS Text Project, pp. 7-8, notes a manuscript variant between

  1. the MT ‒ ברון כבוד יהוה
  2. the NRSV, REB, JPSOA (footnote) ‒ ברום כבוד יהוה

The 2nd option comes from the context, but not the Hebrew wording. The UBS Text Project gives the 1st option an "A" rating (high probability). But, the Jewish Study Bible, p. 1049, asserts option #2 says, "the proposed emendation is almost certainly correct."

Ezekiel heard a sound (vv. 12-13) and saw an event, just before the Spirit carried him away.

▣ "glory" SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (kabod, OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:14 "and I went embittered in rage of my spirit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:14 "and I went embittered in rage of my spirit" This is a very difficult phrase. It has been translated in one of two ways:

  1. Ezekiel is upset at having to give a hard message which will be rejected
  2. Ezekiel was filled with the righteous indignation of God at the sin of the Jewish nation (cf. Jer. 6:11)

I think theory 2 fits the context much better.

▣ "the hand of the Lord" Notice the different ways the presence of YHWH is alluded to.

  1. direct speech, Ezek. 3:1,4,16,24,27
  2. the Spirit, Ezek. 3:12,14,24
  3. the glory of the Lord, Ezek. 3:12,23 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY [OT])
  4. the hand of the Lord, Ezek. 3:14,22 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND)

The anthropomorphic imagery denotes the reception of divine revelation (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 3:14,22; 8:1; 33:22; 37:1; 40:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (anthropomorphism).

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:15 "Tel-abib"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:15 "Tel-abib" This is also the name of one of the Canaanite months, which was the month of the Exodus/Passover. Here it is a settlement by the Grand Canal close to the city of Nippur.

The Hebrew word abib (BDB 1) means "green ears of grain." "Tel" (BDB 1068) means "mound."

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE CALENDARS

NASB  "I sat there seven days where they were living,
 causing consternation among them"
NKJV, Peshitta  "I sat where they sat, and remained there
 astonished among them seven days"
NRSV, JPSOA  "I sat there among them, stunned for seven
  days"
TEV  "I came. . .and for seven days I stayed there,
 overcome by what I had seen and heard"
NJB  "I came. . .and there I stayed with them
 in a stupor for seven days"
LXX  "I sat there seven days, conversant in the
  midst of them"

The Hebrew VERB (BDB 1030, KB 1563, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) means "appalled," "awestruck," "devastated." But to whom does it refer?

  1. Ezekiel (i.e. the vision itself), NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, JPSOA
  2. the exiled Israelites of Tel-abib (i.e. the message of Ezekiel), LXX, NASB

Just an added thought. The time of "seven days" may be related to a designated "ordination" period for priests (cf. Exod. 29:35-37; Lev. 8:33-35); if so, then option #1 above seems best, but it does not explain the VERB.

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:17 "I have appointed you a watchman"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:17 "I have appointed you a watchman" This is expanded in Ezekiel 33. It is a concept used often in the prophets (cf. Isa. 56:10; Jer. 6: 17; Hosea 9:8). Remember the prophets functioned as YHWH's covenant enforcers for the Mosaic covenant. Israel's obedience determined her destiny. The prophets reminded Israel of the consequences of disobedience (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). How the people responded to the prophets' message (i.e. repentance or hardness) determined their future.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:18 "You shall surely die"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:18 "You shall surely die" This is a Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and a Qal IMPERFECT of the same VERB (BDB 559, KB 562), which denotes emphasis. In this setting it refers to physical death. This same phrase occurs in Gen. 2:17! Disobedience has consequences in time and eternity!

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?

▣ "but his blood I will require at your hand" Being called to serve God is a great honor, but it also carries great responsibilities. If I know God's message and do not speak, it brings spiritual consequences, as does ignoring the message once given (cf. Ezek. 3:20; 33:6,8).

The term "blood" (BDB 196) is imagery of death. The ancients knew that as the blood flowed away, so too, life. Therefore, the life was in the blood (cf. Gen. 9:5-6; Lev. 17:11,14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BLOOD

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:18-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:18-19 This is a major theological truth of both Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which deals with individual responsibility for spiritual choices. The full theological discussion is in Ezekiel 18 and 33.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:20 "a righteous man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:20 "a righteous man" See SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "I place an obstacle before him" God tests all those who belong to Him (cf. Gen. 22:1; Exod. 15:25; 16:4; 20:20; Deut. 8:2,16; 13:3; Jdg. 2:22; 2 Chr. 32:31; Matt. 4:1; Heb. 12:5-13).

Ezekiel uses the imagery of a stone or obstacle placed on the road (i.e. life's path) as a way of denoting judgment (cf. Jer. 6:21). The fact that God tests humans demands that humans have a God-given "free will" (cf. Gen. 1:26-27). If there is no personal responsibility there can be no ethical consequences! The interpersonal relationship desired by God of His human creatures demands a free will.

Ezekiel also emphasizes an individual aspect to faith and obedience that is unique in the prophets who usually address national Israel (cf. Ezek. 3:20-21; 14:12-20; 18:5-32; 33:12-20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD TESTS HIS PEOPLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:22 "The hand of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:22 "The hand of the Lord" See notes at Ezek. 3:14.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ This is similar to Ezek. 2:1. YHWH is initiating contact and preparing to communicate revelation.

  1. "Arise," BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "Go out," BDB 422, KB 425, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "I will speak to you," BDB 180, KB 210, Piel IMPERFECT

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:23 "I got up and went out on the plain and behold the glory of the Lord was standing there"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:23 "I got up and went out on the plain and behold the glory of the Lord was standing there" This experience was a major theological revelation. God's glory and presence were not limited to Palestine or the temple (i.e. Acts 7). The exiles needed to know this. He is the God of all the earth, of all creation!

  1. that God had not abandoned them
  2. that God was not limited to the Holy Land

Notice how "glory" is personified as "standing." The term "glory" stands for the personal presence of YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (kabod, OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:24 "The Spirit then entered me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:24 "The Spirit then entered me" This is the same "spirit" that controlled the living being of chapter 1 (cf. Ezek. 1:12,20-21). It is the same "spirit" that entered Ezekiel and caused him to stand in Ezek. 2:1-2. It is a way of referring to God Himself. Notice "He spoke with me" and the obvious antecedent is "the Spirit."

The Spirit of God is active in the OT in equipping humans to perform divine tasks or assignments.

  1. design and building of the tabernacle, Exod. 31:3; 35:31
  2. military deliverers, Jdg. 6:34; 11:29; 13:25; 14:6,19; 15:14
  3. political leaders, 1 Sam. 10:10; 11:6; 16:13; 2 Sam. 23:2
  4. prophets, 1 Kgs. 18:12,46; 2 Kgs. 2:16; Ezek. 2:2; 3:12,14,24; 8:3; 11:24; 37:1; 43:5; Micah 3:5
  5. Messiah, Isa. 11:2; 42:1; 61:1; Luke 4:18-19; see SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

▣ "Go, shut yourself up in your house" Notice how specific God's message is. Ezekiel is claiming that his dramatic acts are direct commands from YHWH.

  1. "go," BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "be shut up," BDB 688, KB 742, Niphal IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:25 The question is, who does the PRONOUN "they" refer to?

  1. other exiles
  2. the Babylonian army besieging Jerusalem (cf. Ezek. 4:8)

Whatever the exact meaning, it is clear from the context that there will be opposition to Ezekiel's message (cf. Ezek. 3:26-27). Ezekiel is declaring the complete destruction of Jerusalem and the temple and the exile, which was not a popular message (i.e. Jeremiah's message).

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:26 "I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:26 "I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth" In context this is highly unusual, since God is commanding him to tell the message, but it may communicate the truth that the prophet is only to speak when God speaks. There will be a specific content and time to speak (cf. Ezek. 24:27; 33:22). This reference to a divine silence is seen again in Ezek. 24:27: 29:21; 33:22.

entries.title: Ezekiel 3:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:27 This verse concludes with two commands.

  1. "let him hear," BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  2. "let him refuse" (lit. "cease"), BDB 292, KB 292, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:1 "son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:1 "son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

YHWH commands the prophet to do several dramatic acts of judgment which depict the fall of Jerusalem. Because of Ezek. 3:25, these dramatic acts were probably performed in front of his house, in public view.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "Get yourself a brick" BDB 527 says that this refers to a tile, not a brick, but the lexicon KB 518 says it was a sun-baked brick (larger in size than modern bricks), probably of white clay. It is uncertain if it was soft clay, which was normally used for writing, or baked clay with an outline of the city scratched into it.

  1. get a brick, Ezek. 4:1, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE
    1. set it before you
    2. inscribe (outline of the city of Jerusalem) on it
    3. build siege wall, ramps, camps around the brick
    4. place battering rams (i.e. another Qal IMPERATIVE)
  2. get an iron plate, Ezek. 4:3, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE (used as a divider)
  3. lie on your side, Ezek. 4:4, BDB 1011, KB 1486, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. take (food items), BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE
  5. take (sharp sword and cut off hair and beard), Ezek. 5:1, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

The entire context (i.e. chaps. 4-5 is a literary unit) is one sustained dramatic act foreshadowing the siege and fall of Jerusalem.

These dramatic prophetic acts of Ezekiel occurred exactly four years before the siege of Jerusalem by Neo-Babylon, which resulted in the total destruction of the city (i.e. 586 B.C.). Chapters 4 and 5 contain a series of silent, dramatic acts related to God's enforced silence of Ezek. 3:26.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:2 "siege-wall"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:2 "siege-wall" This (BDB 189, KB 220) was a series of siege towers that were built to put the archers of the invaders on level with the ramparts of the city (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1; Jer. 52:4; Ezek. 4:2; 17:17; 21:27; 26:8).

▣ "raise up a ramp" This was an earthen ramp (BDB 700, KB 757, cf. 2 Sam. 20:15; Jer. 32:24; 33:4) where the ramming instruments (BDB 503, cf. Ezek. 4:2; 21:27) could be brought against the walls of the city (e.g. the Roman ramp at Masada).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIEGE MOUNDS

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:3 "an iron plate"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:3 "an iron plate" This (BDB 290) is used in Lev. 2:5; 6:21 for a small, concave plate for the baking of bread. In context it seems to relate to God setting His face against His own people and not hearing their cries for help (i.e. His prophet/priest is silent, cf. Ezek. 3:25-27).

▣ "this is a sign to the house of Israel" Signs (BDB 16) were God's way to show His people that He was in control of history. Ezekiel uses this phrase often (cf. Ezek. 4:3; 12:6,11; 24:24). Ezekiel's God-given signs were a dramatic way to communicate with the exiled community. It is uncertain if all of these signs were literally acted out or were literary in nature. The truth and trustworthiness of God's message remains the same either way. One wonders how Ezek. 4:8 could be literal or related to Ezek. 3:25.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:4 God commands the prophet to lie (BDB 1011, KB 1486, Qal IMPERATIVE) on his left side to bear (BDB 669, KB 724, lit. "to carry," Qal IMPERFECT) the sin of Israel. Apparently this is a function of the priesthood (cf. Num. 18:1). The VERB implies the carrying away of sin, like the scapegoat in the ceremony of Leviticus 16, the Day of Atonement. However, Ezekiel's actions do not cause God to spare Jerusalem, but judge it (cf. Ezek. 4:7). Ezekiel's acts show the extent of the people's rebellion (i.e. longevity).

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:5 "three hundred and ninety days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:5 "three hundred and ninety days" Ezekiel is told to lie on his side to show the sin of both Israel (Ezek. 4:4-5) and Judah (Ezek. 4:6). It is obvious here that "the house of Israel" means the Northern Ten Tribes only.

There has been much difficulty concerning "390 days." The Septuagint has "190 days" and this may be closer to the original number because the difference in time between Ezek. 1:2 and 8:1 is only 14 months, which seems not to leave enough time for 430 days of silent witness (i.e. 390 for Israel and 40 for Judah).

It is possible that the combined numbers (i.e. 390 + 40) equals Israel's time in Egypt plus the wilderness wanderings (cf. Gen. 15:13; Exod. 12:40; Acts 7:6; Gal. 3:17). Therefore, it might be a way of referring to the beginning of Israel as a people (i.e. Abraham - Moses). If so, it symbolized that they had always been a sinful, rebellious, stiff-necked people (cf. Ezek. 2:3-4,7,8).

We as moderns must remember that the ancients used certain numbers in symbolic ways. Often these are round numbers (cf. John J. Davis, Biblical Numerology).

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:6 "forty days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:6 "forty days" The number forty in the Bible is often a long period of indefinite time. Why this different number applies to Judah is uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:7 "with your arm bared"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:7 "with your arm bared" This was imagery for God's effective action against Jerusalem.

God's arm/hand can be for good or woe.

  1. positive, Exod. 6:6; 15:16; Deut. 4:34; 5:15; 7:19; 2 Chr. 32:8; Ps. 98:1; Isa. 52:10; Jer. 32:17-18
  2. negative, Jer. 6:12; 21:5; 27:5-6; Ezek. 20:33-34; 30:24-25

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:8 "I will put ropes on you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:8 "I will put ropes on you" This same imagery is used in Ezek. 3:25. God directs the prophet's words and actions to communicate His message to His people.

It seems from Ezek. 3:25 that the prophet was limited to his home. The elders had to go there to see him (cf. Ezek. 8:1; 14:1; 20:1). He was also allowed to communicate either by a message or a dramatic act only if God directed him.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:9-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:9-17 The dramatic action of Ezekiel lying on his side was only part of the symbolism; what he ate and drank and how much he ate and drank also had significance (cf. Ezek. 4:16-17). The siege would cause famine in Jerusalem.

  1. A food shortage required that the people eat a combination of grains, some of which were not normally eaten.
  2. It meant less water per day.
  3. There would be no wood or oil to cook with. Animal dung would be the only source of fuel

Cow dung was and still is (i.e. India) often used as fuel.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:10 "twenty shekels a day by weight"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:10 "twenty shekels a day by weight" This would equal about 8-10 ounces of bread. This amount is too small for a healthy diet.

▣ "from time to time" This is a Hebrew idiom which means at a set time each day (cf. Ezek. 4:11; 1 Chr. 9:25).

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:11 "a sixth part of a hin by measure"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:11 "a sixth part of a hin by measure" This would be a little under a pint, according to rabbinical commentators. Ezekiel would lose weight and strength on this diet, which mimicked a siege situation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES (Metrology)

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:13 Using dung as a cooking fuel would make the inhabitants of Jerusalem ceremonially unclean. It would be a symbol of the Levitically unclean food they would be forced to eat as exiles in a foreign land (cf. Dan. 1:8; Hosea 9:3-4).

▣ "I shall banish them" This VERB (BDB 623, KB 673, Hiphil IMPERFECT) describes YHWH's sending the covenant people out of the Promised Land (cf. Jer. 8:3; 16:15; 24:9; 27:10,15). However, if they repent, YHWH will restore them (cf. Deut. 30:1,4; Jer. 23:3,8; 29:14; 32:37; 46:28).

Ezekiel presents YHWH's message of the destruction and exile of Jerusalem until it happens and then his message changes to one of a divine restoration (cf. chaps. 33-48).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:14 "I have never eaten what died of itself or was torn by beasts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:14 "I have never eaten what died of itself or was torn by beasts" This relates to Ezekiel's squeamishness ("I have never been defiled," BDB 379, KB 375, Pual PARTICIPLE) about the uncleanness involved in this symbolic act. The human dung was the primary issue (cf. Ezek. 4:12), but he expands his affirmation of his faithfulness to the Mosaic Law in Ezek. 4:14. He would be referring to animals that had not been properly killed and bled (cf. Exod. 22:31; Lev. 17:11-16; Deut. 12:16). God responds to the prophet's squeamishness and allows cow dung (BDB 861, only here in the OT) to be substituted for fuel in Ezek. 4:15.

The MT has "nephesh," translated "I." See notes online at Gen. 35:18 and Lev. 17:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:16 "the staff of bread"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:16 "the staff of bread" This unusual imagery uses "staff" in the sense of supply (cf. Lev. 26:26; Ps. 105:16; Isa. 3:1; Ezek. 4:16-17; 5:16; 14:13).

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:17 "waste away in their iniquity"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:17 "waste away in their iniquity" The VERB (BDB 596, KB 628, Niphal PERFECT with waw) means

  1. fester, Ps. 38:5
  2. rot, Zech. 14:12 (three times)
  3. wear away or dissolve, Isa. 34:4

It is used three times in Ezekiel describing YHWH's judgment on His people (cf. Ezek. 4:17; 24:23; 33:10). The choice of this term by Ezekiel may go back to Lev. 26:39, where it is used twice. Ezekiel, as a trained priest, drew much of his vocabulary from Leviticus.

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 5:1 "son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:1 "son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "take a sharp sword" The VERB (BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE) is a command. The normal instrument for shaving was a "razor" (BDB 1074, cf. Num. 6:5; 8:7). However, here a "sword" (BDB 352, Ezek. 5:1,2 [twice], 12 [twice], 17) is used. It was a symbol of the coming judgment (cf. Ezek. 6:3,8, 11,12; 7:15). This same judgment is alluded to in Isa. 7:20, using the word "razor." Shaving the hair and beard was a sign of shame (cf. 2 Sam. 10:4). The sword was a symbol of death and devastation. Judah would reap a divine judgment for her sins (i.e. Nebuchadnezzar's army).

▣ "scales for weighing" This is a Hebrew CONSTRUCT (BDB 24 and 1054). Scales were used in weighing the purchase of agricultural items. When used in an unfair way it became an idiom of exploitation and unfairness (cf. Deut. 25:13-16; Prov. 11:1). In contrast, God's scales (i.e. of justice) were fair and reliable. Judah was weighed by YHWH and found wanting! Judah deserved both

  1. shame (i.e. sword for shaving)
  2. judgment (i.e. scales for weighing)
