FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:2 "Son of man" This phrase is a literary marker of a new topic or new revelation. See note at Ezek. 2:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "make known" The VERB (BDB 393, KB 390, Hiphil IMPERATIVE) means "to announce." The Niphal stem is often used of making YHWH known (cf. Ezek. 20:5,9; 38:23; 35:11) and also in the Hiphil (cf. Ezek. 39:7). However, in this context it means declaring to Jerusalem her "abominations." YHWH made Himself and His will clear to His people, but they would not draw near to Him and follow Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:3 "origin"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:3 "origin" This term (BDB 468) occurs only three times in the OT and are all in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 16:3; 21:30; 29:14). The etymology is uncertain.

  1. The same letters can mean "a kind of weapon" (cf. Gen. 49:5).
  2. Some scholars think the meaning is related to the VERB (BDB 468 II) "dig" or "hew" (cf. Ps. 22:16).
  3. Others think it is from BDB 500 II, "to get by trade" or "purchase."

▣ "Your origin and your birth are from the land of the Canaanite" This could be understood in several senses.

  1. This explains the source of their idolatrous tendencies
  2. They were not a people until YHWH chose them and delivered them from Egypt
    1. from the land of Canaan (idolatrous tendencies)
    2. father was an Amorite, Ezek. 16:45
    3. mother was a Hittite, Ezek. 16:45
  3. refers exclusively to the physical city of Salem, Jebus, and later Jerusalem

The term "father" may refer to tribal ancestors (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 219) and not Abraham, who is called "a wandering Aramean" in Deut. 26:5. This verse is figurative, meaning that Judah's parents were non-Israelite. This was revealed by their idolatrous actions. This is not a text on genealogy, but on idolatry! Israel was unfaithful from the very beginning (cf. Deut. 32:5; Isa. 1:2-3; Jer. 7:24-26; 11:7-8; Ezek. 2:6-8; 3:9,26; 12:2-3; 16:3,45; Hosea 6:7; 9:10; 11:1-4; 13:4-6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MORIAH, SALEM, JEBUS, ZION, JERUSALEM

▣ "Canaanite" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE, C. #8

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:4 "washed with water for cleansing"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 16:4 "washed with water for cleansing" The word "cleansing" (BDB 606, KB 650) is found only here and its meaning is unknown.

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:4-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:4-5 These verses describe, in birthing symbolism, Israel's predicament at birth without YHWH's help.

  1. the umbilical cord was not cut
  2. they were not washed with water for cleansing
  3. they were not rubbed with salt
  4. they were not wrapped in cloths (this was meant to protect the limbs, the opposite of squirming, cf. Ezek. 16:6)
  5. no eye looked on them with pity
  6. there was no compassion on them
  7. they were thrown out into the open field (female babies were sometimes abandoned in the Ancient Near East)

Israel was neglected and abandoned by all! None of the traditional birthing rites were observed! Death was certain!

Numbers 1-4 detail practices of Arab groups, which are still present in Palestine today. It would have been the expected procedures for a "wanted" child.

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:5 "abhorred"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:5 "abhorred" This NOUN (BDB 172) appears only here in the OT. However, the VERB is used in Ezek. 16:45 (BDB 171, KB 199, Qal PARTICIPLE and Qal PERFECT) twice. It denotes something hated because it is unclean (i.e. dung or spoilage).

Much of Ezekiel's terminology is drawn from Leviticus 26. In this chapter this word is used of both Israel and YHWH.

  1. Israel
    1. they abhorred YHWH's commandments, Ezek. 16:15
    2. they abhorred YHWH's commandments, Ezek. 16:43
  2. YHWH
    1. YHWH will not abhor them, Ezek. 16:11
    2. YHWH abhors them because of their idolatry, Ezek. 16:30
    3. YHWH abhors them because of their covenant disobedience, Ezek. 16:44

Leviticus 26 is parallel to Deut. 28:15-68.

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:6-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:6-14 This describes YHWH's loving acts toward Israel.

  1. saw her predicament and commanded life (two Qal IMPERATIVES, BDB 310, KB 309), Ezek. 16:6
  2. made her numerous, like the plants of the field, Ezek. 16:7
  3. Israel grew like a young woman to maturity (full height, full breasts, long hair or pubic hair), but was uncared for (i.e. naked and bare). YHWH proposed to her and made promises to her (i.e. marriage covenant), Ezek. 16:7-8
    1. bathed with water, Ezek. 16:9
    2. anointed with oil, Ezek. 16:9
    3. clothed, Ezek. 16:10
    4. put shoes on her feet, Ezek. 16:10
    5. wrapped in fine shawl, Ezek. 16:10
    6. gave jewelry, Ezek. 16:11-13a
    7. gave good food, Ezek. 16:13b
  4. her beauty was renowned because of YHWH's care and gifts, Ezek. 16:14

She was nothing, yea despised, until YHWH chose her, cared for her, and married her (i.e. "swore," BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal IMPERFECT).

16:6
NASB, TEV  "squirming"
NKJV  "struggling"
NRSV  "flailing about"
NJB, REB, NET  "kicking"
Peshitta, JPSOA  "wallowing"
LXX  "polluted"

The term (BDB 100, KB 115, Hithpolel PARTICIPLE) normally means "to tread down" or "trample," but in the Hithpolel stem (here and v. 22) it seems to refer to the random movement of an infant's limbs.

16:7
NASB  "numerous"
NKJV  "thrive"
NRSV, LXX  "grow up"
TEV, NJB, JPSOA  "grow"
Peshitta  "multiply"

"A myriad" (BDB 914) literally refers to ten thousand, but it is often used in a figurative sense (i.e. Gen. 24:60; Ps. 3:6; Song of Songs 5:10).

▣ "You grew up" (BDB 915, KB 1176, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) means "become a numerous people" (i.e. Gen. 1:28; 9:1-7; Exod. 1:10,12,20; Deut. 6:3; 8:1; 30:16).

  1. BDB suggests that here it means "grow great" or "grow strong," from an Aramean root (NASB, Peshitta)
  2. KB suggests "grow up" for the meaning here (NRSV, TEV, NJB, LXX)
  3. It is a word play on "numerous" (רבה, BDB 915), which means "myriad" (רבבה, BDB 914), found at the beginning of v. 7
NASB  "reached the age for fine ornaments"
NKJV  "became very beautiful"
NRSV, REB  "arrived at full womanhood"
TEV  "became a young woman"
NJB  "reached marriageable age"
JPSOA  "your tiime for love had arrived"
Peshitta  "your had reached marriage age"

This is literally "with ornament of ornaments" (BDB 725 CONSTRUCT BDB 725). This phrase and the next two mean she had reached an age to be married (RSV, NEB).

The UBS Text Project, p. 40, gives two translation options based on textual variants.

  1. "to the beauty of beauties" (lit. "jewellery" doubled, BDB 725, KB 791 II)
  2. "in the time of menstruations" (emendation)
  3. JPSOA footnote, "meaning of Hebrew uncertain"
NASB  "I spread My skirt over you"
NKJV, LXX  "I spread My wing over you"
NRSV  "I spread the edge of my cloak over you"
TEV  "I covered your naked body with my cloak"
NJB  "I spread my cloak over you"
JPSOA  "I spread My robe over you"
Peshitta  "I spread my hand over you"
REB  "I spread the shirt of my robe over you"

This was a gesture of proposal (cf. Ruth 3:9) or an idiom for marriage (cf. Deut. 22:30).

The term "skirt" (BDB 489) literally means "wing," but here it refers to the corner of one's robe (cf. Deut. 22:12; Ezek. 5:3).

The prophets often used the intimate covenant of marriage as imagery for the relationship between YHWH and His covenant people (cf. Isa. 66:7-14; Jeremiah 2-3; Ezekiel 16; 23; Hosea 1-3; Zeph. 3:14-20).

▣ "entered into a covenant with you" See SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:9 This describes what the prospective husband (YHWH) did for His wife-to-be.

  1. bath of cleansing, still done before the wedding rite
  2. blood washed off, this refers to her menstrual period, denoting she is of marriageable age and not pregnant (this may also be implied in Ezek. 16:7)
  3. anointed with oil, preparation for the wedding feast

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:10 "embroidered cloth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:10 "embroidered cloth" This term (BDB 955) is used several times in Ezekiel of expensive multi-colored or embroidered cloth (cf. Ezek. 16:10,13,18; 26:16; 27:7,16,24). It is used in Ezek. 17:3 to describe a multi-colored great eagle.

NASB  "porpoise skin"
NKJV  "badger skin"
NRSV, NJB, NET  "fine leather"
TEV  "of the best leather"
REB  "dugong-hide"
JPSOA  "dolphin leather"

The term (BDB 1065, KB 1720 I) refers to a type of animal skin. Exactly which animal is uncertain.

  1. dolphin, Arabic (JPSOA, NASB in Exod. 25:5)
  2. sheep, conjecture
  3. leather, Egyptian (NRSV, NJB, NET, "fine leather," KB's best guess)
  4. seal, NASB, Exod. 35:23

Elsewhere, this term is used for the construction of the tabernacle (cf. Exod. 25:5; 26:14; 35:7,23; 36:19; 39:34; Num. 4:6,8). The best choices seem to be #1 or #4, both found in the Red Sea in large numbers having skins large enough to make durable sheeting for the tabernacle.

▣ "fine linen" The etymology of this word (BDB 1058, KB 1663 III, B) is uncertain (JPSOA). Most scholars relate it to an Egyptian word for fine woven linen JPSOA.

  1. for fine garments, Gen. 41:42; Prov. 31:22
  2. for sails, Ezek. 16:10,13; 27:7
  3. for priestly garments, Exod. 28:5,39
  4. for hangings in the tabernacle, Exod. 27:9,16,18; 38:9,16,18
  5. for curtains in the tabernacle, Exod. 26:1,31,36; 36:8,35,37

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:12-13a
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:12-13a This is a list of jewelry expressing YHWH's love and care for Israel.

  1. ornaments, Ezek. 16:11, BDB 725
  2. bracelets, Ezek. 16:11, BDB 855
  3. chain (necklace), Ezek. 16:11, BDB 914, cf. Gen. 41:42
  4. ring in your nose, Ezek. 16:12, BDB 633, cf. Gen. 24:47; Isa. 3:21
  5. earrings, Ezek. 16:12, BDB 722, cf. Num. 31:50
  6. crown of beauty, Ezek. 16:12, BDB 742
  7. adorned with gold and silver, Ezek. 16:13

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:13 "exceedingly beautiful"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:13 "exceedingly beautiful" The ADVERB "exceedingly" comes from a repetition of BDB 547, cf. Ezek. 9:9; Gen. 17:2,6,20; Exod. 1:7.

▣ "advanced to royalty" This orphan child (i.e. Israel) is elevated to the royal family status, both by adoption and marriage.

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:14 "it was perfect"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:14 "it was perfect" This ADJECTIVE (BDB 483) is used in the sense of wholeness or an entire state of completion. It is used

  1. of the report of Jerusalem's beauty, 16:14; Ps. 50:2; Lam. 2:15
  2. of the King of Tyre, 27:3; 28:12

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:15 "you trusted in your beauty"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:15 "you trusted in your beauty" This VERB (BDB 105, KB 120, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) basically meant "trust" or "rely upon." In this context it denotes Judah's reliance on fertility idolatry (cf. Ps. 115:4-8; 135:15-18; Isa. 42:17; Jer. 13:25; 48:7).

▣ "played the harlot" This VERB (BDB 275, KB 275, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) means "commit fornication." Idolatry is imagery for sexual unfaithfulness (cf. Ezek. 16:28; 23:30; Jer. 3:1). Israel and Judah were married to YHWH (cf. Ezek. 16:8), but they pursued the gods of Egypt, Canaan, Assyria, and Babylon. This could have been done in one of two ways.

  1. official governmental relations (i.e. treaties) which were done in the name of these national gods (cf. Ezek. 16:26,28; 23:5,7; Isa. 23:17)
  2. the worship of these foreign gods (cf. chapter 8; Exod. 34:15-16; Lev. 20:5; Deut. 31:16)

This sexual (marriage, cf. Hosea 1-3; Eph. 5:21-31) imagery is used because of the personal nature of faith. Marriage is often used as a way of referring to intimacy. Faith is a spiritual intimacy! YHWH takes human commitment (i.e. free will) seriously.

See a brief discussion of prostitution in the ANE in IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 702.

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:16-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:16-21 The apostasy of Jerusalem took Judah's beauty and wealth given to her by YHWH (cf. Ezek. 16:10-14) and turned it into pagan shrines and worship practices.

  1. decorated shrines ("high places," cf. Ezek. 16:24,31,39) of multi-colored cloth, given by YHWH, used as a place to commit adultery
  2. made idols with ornaments and jewels given by YHWH, Ezek. 16:17
  3. offered YHWH's oil and incense, Ezek. 16:18
  4. offered YHWH's food, Ezek. 16:19
  5. offered the fruit of the womb (i.e. children, Ezek. 16:36), which YHWH had bestowed, Ezek. 16:20-22.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:17 "made for yourself male images"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:17 "made for yourself male images" These could refer to phallic statues (i.e. Ba'al) or jewelry. The gold and silver were YHWH's gifts to His bride (Israel). They turned these gifts into fertility idols (like the golden calf of Exodus 32), just as they turned the beautiful clothing given by YHWH into mats and blankets on which to fornicate (cf. Ezek. 16:16).

They took other clothing (Ezek. 16:18) and dressed up their images and took YHWH's oil, incense, and food and offered it to these lifeless fertility idols (cf. Ezek. 16:18-19).

They were so caught up in their commitment and superstition that they sacrificed their own children to Molech to insure the fertility of land, cattle, and the human population (cf. Ezek. 16:20-21; 20:26,31; 23:37).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:19 "a soothing aroma"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:19 "a soothing aroma" This is an idiomatic way of referring to an accepted sacrifice. Again Ezekiel is influenced by Leviticus 26, where this terminology is used in a threat (cf. Lev. 26:30-31). Ezekiel uses this idiom mostly in connection with pagan idolatries (cf. Ezek. 6:13; 16:19; 20:28), however, Ezek. 20:41 is a future-oriented exception (i.e. the Messianic temple).

SPECIAL TOPIC: A SOOTHING AROMA

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:22 "you did not remember the days of your youth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:22 "you did not remember the days of your youth" The VERB "remember" (BDB 269, KB 219, Qal PERFECT) occurs twice. Jerusalem's idolatries are more egregious because

  1. she was chosen by YHWH
  2. she was blessed by YHWH
  3. she was married to YHWH

It was a violation of love as well as law!

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:23 "(Woe, woe to you!' declares the Lord God)"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:23 "(Woe, woe to you!' declares the Lord God)" This INTERJECTION (BDB 17) implies "grief and despair to you" (cf. Ezek. 24:6,9). It is used mostly by Jeremiah (cf. Ezek. 4:13,31; 6:4; 10:19; 13:27; 15:10; 45:3; 48:46). There are consequences of human choices! Infidelity brings a sharp response from a faithful, loving God! Judgment is painful for Judah and for YHWH!

16:24
NASB, NKJV  "a shrine. . .a high place"
NRSV  "a platform. . .a lofty place"
TEV  "places to worship"
NJB  "a mound. . .a high place"
REB  "a couch. . .a shrine"
Peshitta  "a house of idols. . .altars"
JPSOA  "an eminence. . .your mound"
LXX  "a house of fornication. . .a public place"

These two terms denote a raised platform.

  1. "shrine," BDB 146, literally "mound" (in this sense only in this chapter, Ezek. 16:24,31,39)
  2. "high place," BDB 928, in this chapter (Ezek. 16:24,25,31,39) are the only occurrences of this term in the sense of a manmade, raised platform. It is used in 1 Sam. 22:6 as a natural height. These same Hebrew letters (BDB 941 II) form the VERB "to deal treacherously" (in Piel stem). This might be a wordplay.
    1. מרום ‒ "high place"
    2. מרמה ‒ "deal treacherously"

Fertility worship was usually performed on hills, but Israel and Judah moved the worship onto man-made platforms in every town square.

16:25
NASB, LXX, JPSOA  "you spread your legs"
NRSV, TEV  "you offered yourself"
NRSV  "offering yourself"
NJB  "opening your legs"
REB  "offering your body"
Peshitta  "exposed yourself"

The VERB (BDB 832, KB 979, Piel IMPERFECT) is used as a female sexual position euphemism (i.e. "feet," BDB 919, KB 1148) to refer to genitalia (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 1048).

  1. male, Exod. 4:25; Jdg. 3:24; Ruth 3:4,7; 1 Sam. 24:3; Isa. 7:20
  2. female, Deut. 28:57; Ezek. 16:25
  3. possibly angels (Seraphim), Isa. 6:2 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: "Sons of God" in Genesis 6
16:26
NASB, NKJV, TEV, REB  "your lustful neighbors"
NRSV  "your very fleshly neighbors"
NJB  "your big-membered neighbors"
LXX  "great in flesh"
Peshitta  "who have large male organs"
JPSOA  "the lustful Egyptians"
NET  "sexually aroused neighbors"

The Hebrew construct (BDB 152 CONSTRUCT 142) literally means "great of flesh," which in this context, would refer to aroused male genitalia (i.e. of animals, cf. Ezek. 23:20).

▣ "to make Me angry" The VERB (BDB 494, KB 491, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is often used of the covenant community provoking YHWH by covenant infidelity, 8:17; Jdg. 2:12; 1 Kgs. 14:9,15; 16:33; 22:54; 2 Kgs. 17:11; 23:19; Isa. 65:3; Jer. 7:18-19; 11:17; 32:29,32; 44:3. This is where the imagery of YHWH as "jealous" begins (cf. Deut. 32:16,21)! Idolatry is a violation of faithful love. It is personal and purposeful! Notice these emotional words.

  1. wrath, Ezek. 16:38,42; (BDB 404)
  2. jealousy, Ezek. 16:38,42 (BDB 888)
  3. enraged, Ezek. 16:43 (BDB 919, KB 1182)

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEALOUS/ZEALOUS

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:23-29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:23-29 This is a list of the nations with which Judea made political alliances and, thereby, introduced their gods into its culture.

  1. Egypt, Ezek. 16:26
  2. Philistia, Ezek. 16:27
  3. Assyria, Ezek. 16:28
  4. Babylon, Ezek. 16:29

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:27 "I have stretched out My hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:27 "I have stretched out My hand" This is an idiom for action.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "who are ashamed of your lewd conduct" Even the pagans were ashamed (i.e. "humiliated," BDB 483, KB 480, Niphal PARTICIPLE) by Judah's idolatry, cf. Ezek. 16:57; 5:14-15; 22:4. Instead of being a light to the nations Judah was a stumbling block.

The term "lewd" (BDB 273) is a term used several times in Leviticus to denote improper sexual partners (cf. Lev. 18:17; 19:29; 22:11). This lewdness would result in exile from the Promised Land (cf. Lev. 18:24-30; 20:22-23). Ezekiel uses this priestly terminology (i.e. he was a priest of the line of Zadok) to shock Judah about her sins (cf. Ezek. 16:27,43,58; 22:9,11; 23:21,27,29,35,44,48[twice],49; 24:13; see NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 1113).

16:29
NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB, NET  "merchants"
NKJV, REB, JPSOA  "traders"

This term "merchants" (BDB 488 II) is related to the term Canaan or Canaanite (BDB 488 II, LXX, Peshitta). Its basic meaning was "trader" (cf. Ezek. 17:4 [BDB 488 II]; Zeph. 1:11 [BDB 489 II]; Zech. 14:21 [BDB 489 II]). However, in the OT it has a negative connotation because of the idolatries of the ten tribes of Canaan. When God's people act like unfair traders, they are characterized as Canaanites (cf. Hosea 12:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:30-34
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:30-34 Judah was so desperate for political alliances that she pursued the surrounding nations for help. She never felt secure (i.e. "never satisfied," cf. Ezek. 16:28,29). She was an unusual harlot in that she paid to be loved (cf. Ezek. 16:41, i.e. protected)! This is possibly a reference to Tiglath-pileser III being bribed by King Ahaz in 2 Kgs. 16:8.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA, #19

16:30
NASB  "How languishing in your heart"
NKJV  "How degenerate is your heart"
NRSV, JPSOA, NET  "How sick is your heart"
RSV  "how lovesick is your heart"
REB  "How you anger me!"
NJB  "How simple-minded you are"
JPSOA (footnote)  "How furious I was with you"
  (revocalization of "heart" with
  Akkadian root)

This is the only occurrence of this VERB (BDB 51, KB 63, Qal PARTICIPLE) in the Qal stem in the MT. Its basic meaning is "weak," implying weak-willed. The NASB translates this as "languishing." The UBS Text Project, p. 42, gives this an "A" rating. But some say this does not fit the context of the next phrase. Some early copies of the Hebrew Bible were found in a hidden room behind the shelves that contained the Scripture scrolls in the synagogue of Cairo, Egypt. These copies have "How inflamed was your heart," which fits the context much better and may be the source of the Septuagint and Vulgate translations of "how strong" (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 426).

KB (63 II) asserts there is another use of this root in the Qal stem that means "hot with fever."

NASB  "a bold-faced harlot"
NKJV  "a brazen harlot"
NRSV  "a brazen whore"
TEV  "a shameless prostitute"
NJB  "a professional prostitute"
REB  "headstrong harlot"
JPSOA  "self-willed whore"
Peshitta  "a whore and a rebellious woman"
NET  "arrogant prostitute"

The ADJECTIVE (BDB 1020) is used only here in this sense. The term's basic meaning is "domineering" (cf. Gen. 42:6). The sense of "hard headed" or "hard hearted" is found in Jer. 3:3.

16:33
NASB, NRSV, JPSOA  "your gifts"
NKJV, LXX  "your payments"
REB, NJB, TEV  "presents"
Peshitta  "you pay a price"
NET  "receive payment"

There are two roots translated "gift."

  1. BDB 622, KB 673, נדה ‒ an Arabian root only in Ezek. 16:33 for gift or payment
  2. BDB 673 I, KB 674 II, נדן
    1. BDB, an Assyrian loan word only in Exek. 16:33
    2. KB, an Akkadian root denoting a marriage dowry or the cost of a prostitute

Judah was the prostitute but she paid lovers (i.e. political alliances) for protection!

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:37 "I shall gather"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:37 "I shall gather" This VERB (BDB 867, KB 1062, Piel PARTICIPLE and Piel PERFECT with waw) is used twice in this verse. It is YHWH who brings the mercenary Neo-Babylonian army into Judah (Ezek. 16:40). All of Judah's political alliances are useless. Most of the surrounding nations are now part of the Neo-Babylonian army under Nebuchadnezzar II.

The theological tragedy is that this word is often used of YHWH gathering His people as a flock from exile (cf. Isa. 40:11; Jer. 31:10; Ezek. 34:13; 37:21)but here, because Judah would not repent, her enemies are gathered to attack her!

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:39 "into the hands"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:39 "into the hands" See SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "and will leave you naked and bare" The innocent imagery of Ezek. 16:7 has now been replaced with the violent treatment by the invaders sent by YHWH to punish His unfaithful bride (Ezek. 16:48).

The rabbis developed this contrast between a time of innocence and a time of responsibility by their theological concept of the two yetzers ("intents"). Until the age of knowledge and commitment (i.e. Bar Mitzvah, males, age 13 or Bat Mitvah, females, age 12) children were not responsible for keeping the Law, but after study and vows, they were responsible.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE AGE OF ACCOUNTABILITY

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:40
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:40 This verse makes clear that it is YHWH behind the judgment. Two judgments are mentioned.

  1. stoning was a way for the community to remove evil from its midst
    1. worship of Molech by child sacrifice, Lev. 20:2 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH)
    2. mediums, Lev. 20:27 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC)
    3. blasphemer, Lev. 24:23
    4. false prophets, Deut. 13:5
    5. idolaters, Deut. 13:9; 17:5 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY)
    6. rebellious son, Deut. 21:21
    7. adultery or fornication, Deut. 22:21 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ADULTERY)
    8. rape, Deut. 22:24
  2. death by the sword to idolatrous cities, Deut. 13:15

SPECIAL TOPIC: STONE TO DEATH

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEATH PENALTY IN ISRAEL

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:42
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:42 This is the first note of hope (cf. Ezek. 16:60-63). YHWH's jealousy will pass!

  1. I shall calm My fury, BDB 628, KB 679, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
  2. My jealousy will depart, BDB 693, KB 747, Qal PERFECT with waw
  3. I shall be pacified, BDB 1052, KB 1641, Qal PERFECT
  4. I will no more be angry, BDB 494, KB 491, Qal IMPERFECT

This is similar to Ezek. 5:13!

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:43 "you have not remembered"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 16:43 "you have not remembered" This VERB (BDB 269, KB 269, Qal PERFECT) is a recurrent theme (cf. Ezek. 16:22,43; 23:19). Judah's violation of YHWH's love was very painful for Him! He chose them but they chose idols!

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:44 "like mother, like daughter"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 16:44 "like mother, like daughter" This denotes that the children take on the characteristics of the families in which they are raised (note Exod. 20:5; Deut. 5:9).

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:44-59
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 16:44-59 This is another parable in a series of parables (i.e. Ezekiel chapters 15-18).

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:46
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:46 This verse specifies that Ezekiel is talking about three sinful capital cities that experienced the judgment of God.

  1. Samaria (i.e. Israel), taken captive for her unfaithfulness by Assyria in 722 B.C.
  2. Sodom (and Gomorrah), destroyed for their wickedness in Genesis 18
  3. Jerusalem (i.e. Judah), who has been (i.e. 605, 597 B.C.) and would be, taken captive (i.e. 586 B.C.) by Neo-Babylon (even another exile in 582 B.C.)

This comparison is very similar to chapter 23 (Oholah/Samaria and Oholibah/Jerusalem). Also note Jer. 3:6-10,11.

▣ "and her daughters" This phrase (cf. Ezek. 16:49,55,57,61) refers to the surrounding villages, socially and economically connected to these large walled cities.

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:49
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:49 In Genesis 19 Sodom is described as a city of sexual deviation (i.e. homosexuality) and is destroyed by God. But here, she is later condemned for her lack of care for the poor and needy. She could help, but she would not! YHWH cares for the poor, alien, outcast, orphaned, and socially disenfranchised (cf. Deut. 10:18; 14:29; 24:17-22; 26:13; 27:19)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOMOSEXUALITY

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:50 "abominations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 16:50 "abominations" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION (OT) and SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:51-52
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:51-52 Judah's sins were even more egregious than the other two! Judah should have known better

  1. because of the judgments of God that befell the other two (i.e. Sodom and Samaria)
  2. because of the presence of the temple in Jerusalem with its leadership

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:52
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:52 There is a series of IMPERATIVES of judgment.

  1. bear your disgrace, BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. be ashamed, BDB 101, KB 116, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. #1 is repeated

Jerusalem's sins are so base that they make Sodom and Samaria appear righteous (cf. Ezek. 16:54b)!

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:55 "daughters"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:55 "daughters" See full notes at Jer. 46:11 and Amos 5:2.

16:57
NASB, NJB, Peshitta  "Edom"
NKJV, LXX  "Syria"
NRSV, REB, JPSOA, Vulgate, NET  "Aram"
TEV  "Edomites"

The Masoretic Hebrew text has a similar word "Aram" (BDB 74, ארם, which denotes Syria), as do the Septuagint and Vulgate, but some Hebrew manuscripts and the old Syriac and the Peshitta have "Edom" (BDB 10, אדם), which fits the context better, but "Aram" is the best textual option (UBS Text Project, p. 48, "B" rating).

The Rotherham's Emphasized Bible, in a footnote, p. 801, mentions that some MSS have "daughters of men" (Adam, אדם, BDB 9, instead of Aram).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:59 "you who have despised the oath by breaking the covenant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:59 "you who have despised the oath by breaking the covenant" These are serious charges!

  1. "despised," BDB 102, KB 117, Qal PERFECT, cf. Ezek. 17:16,18,19; Isa. 24:5
  2. "breaking," BDB 830, KB 924, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

Covenants were confirmed by a sacrifice (i.e. cutting an animal) and an oath of obedience to its obligations. In the Ancient Near East, breaking an oath (BDB 46)/covenant (BDB 136) resulted in the curses and negative consequences spelled out in the covenant (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). Israel had reaped these curses and now Judah!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: HITTITE (SUZERAIN) TREATIES

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:60 "I will establish an everlasting covenant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:60 "I will establish an everlasting covenant" This is surprising because the Mosaic covenant was meant to be perpetual. However, it was also conditional on human obedience (as well as a circumcized heart, cf. Lev. 26:41; Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4; 9:25-26; Rom. 2:28-29). It was the inability for obedience on the part of fallen mankind (cf. Genesis 3; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND), even covenant people, that necessitated a "new" different approach. The "new" covenant would be based on divine performance (cf. Isaiah 53 and Ezek. 36:22-36). It would provide internal motivation for obedience (cf. Jer. 31:31-34). The contrast can be seen by comparing Ezek. 18:30-32 with Ezek. 36:26-27.

God still wants a righteous people who will reflect His character to the nations, but now the focus has shifted from human performance-based covenant to a divine performance-based covenant. Gratitude and family love replace the wages of a hireling! We serve and obey because we are already accepted! Obedience is not what makes us accepted, but the evidence that we have been accepted (cf. Eph. 1:4; 2:8-10; James 2:14-26). The goal for new covenant believers is Christlikeness!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 16:60-63
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:60-63 YHWH will remember His covenant and restore His people (cf. Gen. 17:7,19; Lev. 26:11,44-45; Deut. 4:31) because of His eternal plan of redemption (SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

Notice the reciprocal actions

  1. God's sovereign choices (notice the number of "I's" like Ezek. 36:22-36).
    1. "I will remember My covenant with you," Ezek. 16:60, BDB 269, KB 209, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Lev. 26:42,45
    2. "I will establish an everlasting covenant with you," Ezek. 16:60, BDB 877, KB 1086, Hiphil PERFECT with waw. This is referring to the "new covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34, which is described in Ezek. 36:22-38
    3. "when I have forgiven you for all that you have done," Ezek. 16:63, BDB 497, KB 493, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  2. the covenant people's actions
    1. you will remember your ways, Ezek. 16:62,63; 20:43; 36:31
    2. you will be ashamed, Ezek. 16:62,63; 36:32

Both divine initiative and human repentance are required for covenant!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

entries.title: Ezekiel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
EZEKIEL 17

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
Parable of Two Eagles and A Vine The Eagles and the Vine The Allegory of the Eagles The Parable of the Eagles and the Vine The Allegory of the Eagle
17:1-6 17:1-10 17:1-10 17:1-6 17:1-10
(3b-6) (3b-8) (3b-6)
17:7-10 (7-8) 17:7-8 (7-8)
(9-10) (9-10) 17:9-10 (9-10)
Zedekiah's Rebellion The Parable Is Explained
17:11-21 17:11-21 17:11-21 17:11-15 17:11
17:12-18
17:16-18
17:19-21 17:19-21
Israel Exalted at Last Allegory of the Cedar God's Promise of Hope
17:22-24 17:22-24 17:22-24 17:22-24 17:22-24

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This is a riddle/parable of
    1. Neo-Babylon, Nebuchaddnezzar II (605-562 B.C.) ‒ a great eagle, vv. 3-6,12
    2. Egypt, either Pharaoh Psammetichus II (Psamtik), who reigned from 593-588 or Pharaoh Apries (Hophea), who reigned from 588-569 ‒ another great eagle, vv. 7-8
    3. the vine, the Faith remnant ‒ a twig, a branch, vv. 22-24
      SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

  2. The historical context is Nebuchadnezzar II's exile of Josiah's son, Jehoiachin and the appointment of Josiah's third son, Zedekiah, as vassal king. In turn, Zedekiah approached Egypt for a military alliance (cf. 2 Kgs. 24-28; 2 Chr. 36; Jer. 52). As a result, Neo-Babylon's army invaded again.

  3. There is a future hope in
    1. Cyrus II's victory over Neo-Babylon (notice Isa. 44:45; 45:1). Persia let all captured national people groups return home. Mostly, Judah returned to a small province surrounding Jerusalem under Zerubbable and Joshua.
    2. There are clear hints in the text that this passage may have an ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, the true Davidic Messiah (cf. Isa. 11; Jer. 23:5-6)

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:2 This verse has two parallel IMPERATIVES.

  1. "propound a riddle," BDB 295, KB 309, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jdg. 14:12-19
  2. "speak a parable," BDB 605 II, KB 648 I, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 12:23; 16:44; 17:2; 18:2; 20:49; 24:3

The term "riddle" (BDB 295, note the relation of the VERB, BDB 295, and NOUN, BDB 295) means a statement that needs to have some information hinted at or supplied to be understood (cf. Prov. 1:6).

The term "parable" (BDB 605 II, note the relation of the VERB, BDB 605 II, and NOUN, BDB 605 II) implies a brief poetic structure, possibly a proverb which uses comparison as a way to illustrate truth. Ezekiel often used well known cultural proverbs.

Ezekiel has been using highly figurative language to convince the exiles of the just and sure judgment of Jerusalem.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERPRETING PARABLES

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:3 "a great eagle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:3 "a great eagle" The imaginary bird (eagle or vulture, a large bird of prey) is described as

  1. "great," BDB 152
  2. "great wings," BDB 152 CONSTRUCT BDB 489
  3. "long pinions," BDB 74 CONSTRUCT BDB 7
  4. "rich in plumage," BDB 570 CONSTRUCT BDB 663
  5. "of many colors," BDB 955

This is a description of the large mercenary and conscripted army of Neo-Babylon who captured Jerusalem in 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C. In this context it is the 597 B.C. exile (i.e. "took the top of the cedar") in which Ezekiel and thousands of other craftsmen and leaders were taken to Babylon (cf. Ezek. 17:12-13; 2 Kgs. 24:24,15).

▣ "Lebanon" This is imagery referring to Judah. Possibly

  1. It is used because the parable will involve tall cedars and Lebanon was famous for hers (cf. Ezek. 31:3).
  2. Solomon's palace was paneled and beamed with cedars from Lebanon (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:1-3). The remodeled palace was called "The House of the Forest of Lebanon" (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:2; 10:17,21; 2 Chr. 9:16).
▣
NASB, NRSV, JPSOA, TEV, NJB, NET  "top"
NKJV  "the highest branch"
REB  "the very top"
Peshitta  "the choicest branch"
LXX  "the choice branches"

This term (BDB 856, KB 1035) is found only in Ezekiel (i.e. Ezek. 17:3,22; 31:3,10,14). Its etymology is unknown. The meaning is derived from the context.

  1. Neo-Babylon ‒ Ezek. 17:3
  2. Messianic ‒ Ezek. 17:22 (cf. Isa. 11)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: BRANCH OF THE LORD
    SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE
  3. Assyria ‒ Ezek. 31:3,10

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:4 The destination of exiled Judean society is described as

  1. "to a land of trade," BDB 488 II (e.g. Ezek. 16:15-20)
  2. "a city of traders," BDB 746, and BDB 940, KB 1237, Qal PARTICIPLE

Back in Ezek. 12:13 Chaldea is the resettled destination of the Judean exiles (cf. Ezek. 1:3). The term "Chaldea" (BDB 505) may be related to the term "Canaanite" (BDB 489, or "merchants" in Ezek. 16:29, where they appear together).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:5 This is a description of the relatively easy treatment of the first exiles. They were settled by a canal and given limited autonomy.

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:5 "land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:5 "land" The MT has "the seed of the land." This would refer to the exiled Davidic seed, Jehoiachin (v. 12, cf. Ezek. 1:2). But the JPSOA, in a footnote, suggests an emendation to "cedar."

  1. land, ארץ (BDB 75)
  2. cedar, ארז (BDB 72)

Both make sense in this context and refer to transplanted and restored Judean captives (esp. their Davidic leader).

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "placed it beside abundant waters"
NRSV, LXX  "a plant by abundant waters"
REB  "a shoot beside abundant waters"
NJB  "by the side of a generous stream"
JPSOA  "planted it. . .beside abundant waters"

The problem is the Hebrew CONSONANTS (word), קח (BDB 881 brief note), which does not exist. Therefore, most translations supply the VERB "place" or "set" (BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERFECT with waw, לקח).

NASB, REB, JPSOA, NET  "like a willow"
NKJV, NJB  "like a willow tree"
NRSV  "like a willow twig"
TEV  "young plant"

This term (BDB 861) is found only here in the OT. It seems to be of onomatopoeic origin from the Arabic term for "rustling." Context implies an easily germinating tree twig (cf. Ezek. 17:22).

The two ancient translations translate this last line differently.

  1. LXX ‒ "he set it in a conspicuous place"
  2. Peshitta ‒ "and set a watchman over it"

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:6 This verse describes the low growth of the remaining Judeans in Judea. They were still in the Promised Land, but were very weak as a vassal nation (cf. Ezek. 17:13-14).

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:7 "another eagle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:7 "another eagle" The first eagle referred to Nebuchadnezzar II. This refers to Egypt (cf. Ezek. 17:15). Judah looked to Egypt for military aid and protection (i.e. Jeremiah 37).

The MT has "one" but the LXX has "another." This is another example of Hebrew CONSONANTS "R" and "D" being confused.

  1. "one" ‒ אחד (MT)
  2. "another" ‒ אחר (LXX, JPSOA, Peshitta)

The UBS Text Project, p. 49, mentions that this same "d" ‒ "r" confusion occurs in Ezek. 11:19; 19:5; 34:23; 37:16.

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:8 There is a series of Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS. They describe in this verse (1) how King Zedekiah believed that an alliance with Egypt would help Judah or (2) a repeat of Ezek. 17:5, illustrating that there was no need for Zedekiah to rebel and seek help from Egypt

  1. that it might yield branches
  2. that it might bear fruit
  3. that it might become a splendid vine

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:9-10 These are parallel and describe Judah's attempt to seek help from Egypt, but YHWH will not allow it.

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:9 "leaves"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:9 "leaves" This term (BDB 383) normally refers to the prey of a lion, killed and torn apart (cf. Ezek. 19:3,6; 22:25,27). Only here does it refer to plucked leaves (although the same CONSONANTS with different VOWELS refer to plucked olive leaves in Gen. 8:11).

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:10 "completely wither"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:10 "completely wither" This is an emphatic grammatical construction that uses the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 386, KB 384) together. The VERB is used twice in Ezek. 17:9 and twice in Ezek. 17:10.

▣ "the east wind" This CONSTRUCT (BDB 924 and BDB 870) is used as an active representation of God's power (ruah) to accomplish His purposes. The east wind is associated with judgments and the west wind with blessings.

  1. the Lord directed an east wind. . .brought the locusts, Exod. 13:10
  2. the Lord swept the sea back by a strong east wind, Exod. 14:21; 15:10
  3. with the east wind, Thou does break the ships of Tarshish, Ps. 48:7
  4. like an east wind I will scatter them (Israel) before the enemy, Jer. 18:17
  5. completely wither as soon as the east wind strikes it (Judah), Ezek. 17:10
  6. the east wind dried up its (Israel) fruit, Ezek. 19:12
  7. the east wind has broken you (Tyre), Ezek. 27:26
  8. an east wind will come. . .his (Israel) spring will be dried up, Hosea 13:15
  9. God appointed a scorching east wind, Jonah 4:8
  10. an east wind is implied in Job 1:19 and Jer. 4:11

The west wind is mentioned once in Exod. 10:19 and implied in Num. 11:31. Rain would come from a northwesterly direction.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:11-12 "saying, Say. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:11-12 "saying, Say. . ." This is a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 55, KB 65), repeated for emphasis. YHWH is speaking to Judah through His prophet.

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:11-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:11-21 This is the interpretation of the imagery of Ezek. 17:1-10 about the two great eagles.

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:12 "the rebellious house"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:12 "the rebellious house" This is a characteristic phrase of Ezekiel referring to Judah (cf. Ezek. 2:5,6,8; 3:9,26,27; 12:2 [twice],3,9,25; 17:12; 24:3). Moses first called the covenant people rebellious (BDB 598) in Deut. 9:7; 31:27.

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

▣ "the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, took its king and princes, and brought them to him in Babylon" This exile is recorded in 2 Kings 24. The date would be 597 B.C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:13 The new Neo-Babylonian puppet king was Jehoiachin's uncle, Mattaniah, whose name was changed to Zedekiah (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:17; 2 Chr. 36:10). He made a loyalty oath to Neo-Babylon (v. 16), which he later broke seeking help from Egypt (v. 15).

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:14 Nebuchadnezzar II was hoping that the partial deportation would teach Judah a lesson and keep them a vassal nation (i.e. paying tribute, cf. Jeremiah 27), but it did not work (cf. Ezek. 17:16).

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:15 "But he rebelled"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:15 "But he rebelled" See 2 Kgs. 24:20, where Zedekiah, King of Judah, rebelled

  1. against the prophecy of Jeremiah (cf. Jeremiah 27 and 37)
  2. by breaking his pledge to Nebuchadnezzar II, which he had taken in YHWH's name (cf. Ezek. 17:18; 2 Chr. 36:13)
  3. his disobedience was also an affront to YHWH (v. 19)

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:16 "in Babylon he shall die"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:16 "in Babylon he shall die" See Jeremiah 52:11.

17:18
NASB, NJB  "he pledged"
NKJV, NRSV  "gave his hand"
Peshitta, TEV  "oath"
LXX  "oath-making"
JPSOA, NET  "promise"

The imagery for giving an oath (BDB 46) was "he gave his hand" (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT). The giving of one's hand denoted

  1. friendship, 2 Kgs. 10:15
  2. pledge/oath, 1 Chr. 29:24; 2 Chr. 30:8; Ezra 10:19; Lam. 5:6; Ezek. 17:18
  3. allowing one to do something, Exod. 10:25
  4. giving power to, 2 Sam. 16:8
  5. entrusting to, 2 Chr. 34:16
  6. giving authority to, Gen. 39:4,8,22

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND (illustrated from Ezekiel)

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:19 This verse relates to Zedekiah's oath to Nebuchandezzar II (cf. Ezek. 17:13,14). It was made in YHWH's name.

  1. "As I live" ‒ This is a wordplay on the covenant name for Judah's God, YHWH, cf. Num. 14:21,28; Isa. 45:23; 49:18
  2. "My oath" ‒ BDB 46, cf. Deut. 29:14. This refers to YHWH's covenant promises which, when violated, become "a curse," cf. Deut. 29:19
  3. "which he despised"
    1. Judah, 16:59
    2. Zedekiah, 17:16,18,19
  4. My covenant

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:20 This is mentioned earlier in Ezek. 12:13 and is documented in 2 Kgs. 25:7; Jer. 39:7; 52:11.

17:21
NASB  "choice men"
NKJV  "all his fugitives"
NRSV, NJB  "his pick of his troops"
TEV  "his best soldiers"
REB  "picked troops"
JPSOA  "fugitives"
Peshitta  "noble men"
LXX  "his remnant"
NET  "all the fugitives"

The MT has "his fugitives (BDB 138), which is found only here in the OT. It is related to the VERB "flee" (BDB 137, KB 156). The UBS Text Project, p. 50, mentions "his places" of refuge" (Qere), but gives it a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

The UBS Text Project suggests another root (BDB 103), "chosen."

  1. םברחיו (Qere) ‒ "his places of refuge"
  2.  םבחריו ‒ "his chosen troops"

This verse may refer to Zedekiah and his bodyguard trying to escape Jerusalem, but were captured. The king was blinded and exiled, his men killed. If this is true, then both options above fit the context.

▣ "the survivors will be scattered to every wind" See note at Ezek. 5:10.

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:22 "young twigs a tender one"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:22 "young twigs a tender one" The imagery of a newly planted twig begins in vv. 1-6, referring to Judah in exile. However, here the imagery is repeated of a future national hope in Canaan. This hope is a returning Davidic seed.

The concept of a "shoot," "stem," or "branch" (cf. Isa. 11:1) becomes a Messianic symbol of the restoration of the Davidic seed (cf. 2 Samuel 9; Psalm 89).

The Branch (cf. Isa. 4:2; 11:1; 53:2; Jer. 23:5; 33:15; Zech. 3:8; 6:12; Acts 13:23; Rom. 15:12) becomes the hope of all mankind for YHWH to fulfill His promises to Israel and to the nations! Remember Gen. 3:15 is a promise to humanity made in YHWH's image, not Israel!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BRANCH OF THE LORD (Messianic title)

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO OT COVENANT PROMISES SEEM SO DIFFERENT FROM NT COVENANT PROMISES?

▣ "on a high and lofty mountain" This refers to the supremacy of YHWH's universal rule (cf. Micah 5:5) through His people (cf. Isa. 2:2-4; Micah 4:1-4).

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:22-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 17:22-23 Again, at the end of a judgment oracle there is hope for a future for YHWH's covenant people (cf. Ezek. 16:60-63).

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:23 "birds of every kind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:23 "birds of every kind" This is a universal element (i.e. ANE's "cosmic tree"), as is the phrase, "all the trees of the field" in Ezek. 17:24. Isaiah captures this same planting imagery that reaches all the world in Isa. 27:6. YHWH has an eternal redemptive plan for all the sons and daughters of Adam, not just Jacob's children!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Ezekiel 17:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:24 YHWH describes His control of His creation in a series of plant imagery.

  1. I bring down the high tree
  2. I exalt the low tree (i.e. here)
  3. I dry up the green tree
  4. I make the dry tree flourish

Examples of #1,3 would be Egypt in Ezekiel 31 and Neo-Babylon in Daniel 4. An example of #2,4 would be the promises to restore Israel/Judah (Ezek. 16:60-63; 17:24). In the NT the mustard seed and resulting large bush become the symbol of a universal cosmic tree (cf. Matt. 13:31-32; Mark 4:30-32; Luke 13:18-19. Also note Dan. 4:12,21), which is the kingdom of our God and His Christ!

The final statement, "I am the Lord; I have spoken, and I will perform it," is a key theological statement (i.e. Isa. 55:9-11). Humans can depend on God's word, both His judgments and His promises! He is the creator and controller of all life! History/time are in His hands (cf. Ezek. 12:25,28; 22:14; Isa. 14:24; 55:11)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: TREES
