READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:2 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

Special Topic: Son of Man

▣ "set your face toward Jerusalem" This is judgment imagery. Notice it says, "the land of Israel," but it denotes Judah. Israel is already in exile in Assyria. See note at Ezek. 20:41.

▣ Notice the negative parallelism.

  1. Set your face toward (BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE)
  2. Speak against (lit. "preach," BDB 642, KB 694, Hiphil IMPERATIVE)
  3. Prophesy against (BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE)

This exactly matches Ezek. 20:46. YHWH's judgment against His own disobedient people is described by the personification of His sharp (BDB 292) and polished (BDB 598) sword.

His sword will strike

  1. the capital with its political leaders
  2. the mountain/hilltop sanctuaries of Ba'al and Asherah
  3. the entire Promised Land

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:3 "sword"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:3 "sword" This is one of the most graphic chapters in all of the Bible on the judgment of YHWH. YHWH's sword (BDB 352, cf. Ezek. 21:3,4, 5,9,2,14,15,19; Isa. 31:8; 34:6; 66:16) is personified and His attitude of judgment is heightened. In Ezek. 20:49 (MT 21:5) the leadership in exile said, "Don't speak to us in parables anymore," so Ezekiel graphically described the judgment of YHWH on Jerusalem and Judah (cf. Jer. 12:12).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:3-4 "cut off from you the righteous and the wicked"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:3-4 "cut off from you the righteous and the wicked" In Ezek. 20:47 the same groups are described as green and dry trees. YHWH's judgment on those left in Judah will affect both the faithful and unfaithful (see Special Topic: Biblical Faith is Corporate). The Septuagint changes the term "righteous" to the term "unrighteous" because they think this verse violates the truth presented in Ezek. 14:20; 18:lff; 33:lff (see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 315-316). Isaiah 57:1-2 struggles with this issue and gives an after-life answer.

Special Topic: Septuagint

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:5 "Thus all flesh will know that I, the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:5 "Thus all flesh will know that I, the Lord" This "all flesh" (cf. Ezek. 20:48; 21:4,5) emphasis can be seen in two aspects.

  1. all humans, Num. 16:22; 27:16; Ezek. 20:48 (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27, possibly eschatological)
  2. all Judah, Ezek. 21:4,5; Jer. 12:12 (immediate context)

YHWH cares about His namesake among the nations (cf. Ezek. 36:22-38). The seed of Abraham was YHWH's instrument to reach the nations (i.e. Gen. 12:3).

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ "It will not return to its sheath again" This is an idiom for YHWH's judgment that cannot be stopped (cf. Jer. 23:20). It seems to contrast Ezek. 21:30. This is literary hyperbole. Judgment was sure (cf. Ezek. 21:7)! Those left in Jerusalem did not believe judgment was truly coming, not to Jerusalem, not to the temple, not to them! They misunderstood YHWH's longsuffering, patient endurance.

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:6 "groan with breaking heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:6 "groan with breaking heart" This VERB (BDB 58, KB 70) is used twice.

  1. Niphal IMPERATIVE (command)
  2. Niphal IMPERFECT (continuing action)

This VERB denotes a deep distress caused by physical or emotional pain (i.e. Lam. 1:8,22). In Ezek. 9:4 it is used to describe the guilt feelings connected to true repentance (note Jer. 13:17).

"Heart" is literally "loins" (BDB 608). This was the seat of strength (i.e. the largest muscle in the body is the thigh). It is a Hebrew idiom (cf. Ezek. 21:12; Job 40:16; Ps. 66:11; Isa. 21:3; Nahum 2:10). Verse 6 describes another symbolic drama dictated by YHWH for the purpose of reaching exiled Judah.

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:7 Note the reason for groaning was the arrival of YHWH's sword.

  1. every heart will melt
  2. every hand will be feeble
  3. all hands will be feeble
  4. every spirit will faint
  5. all knees will be weak as water (i.e. possibly referring to urinating on oneself in fear)

This description of utter fear and desperation is used to describe YHWH's judgment on the pagan nations.

  1. Canaan, Josh. 2:11; 5:1
  2. Babylon, Isa. 13:7; Jer. 50:43
  3. Egypt, Isa. 19:1
  4. Assyria, Nah. 2:10
  5. Syria, Jer. 49:24
  6. on the wicked, Ezek. 7:17

But now on Judah (i.e. Lev. 26 and Deut. 28 are a reality).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:9 The urgency of the message is stressed, as it was in Ezek. 21:2. This verse has

  1. two IMPERTIVES
    1. "prophesy," BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE
    2. "say," BDB 55, KB 65, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "say" repeated several times
    1. "saying," Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, Ezek. 21:8
    2. "say," Qal PERFECT, Ezek. 21:9
    3. "say," Qal PERFECT, Ezek. 21:9
    4. "say," Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 21:9

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:10 It is often hard to tell the difference between "elevated prose" and poetry.

  1. NASB has Ezek. 21:9b-10a as poetry
  2. NKJV has Ezek. 21:9b-11,12,13,14-15,16,17,26-27, 28b-29,30-32 as poetry
  3. NRSV has Ezek. 21:9b-12,14-17,25-27,28b-32 as poetry
  4. TEV has Ezek. 21:9b-13,28b as poetry

▣ "polished to flash like lightening" This is a Hebrew idiom of both speed and turning many directions (i.e. Nah. 2:3-4).

NASB  "Or shall we rejoice, the rod of My son despising
  every tree"
NKJV  "It despises the scepter of My son, as it does
  all wood"
NRSV  "How can we make merry? You have despised the
  rod, and all discipline"
TEV  "There can be no rejoicing, for my people have
  disregarded every warning and punishment"
LXX  ready for slaughter, slay, set at naught, despise
  every tree"
Peshitta  "and it is sharpened to cut off the family of my son;
  and to reject every other branch"
REB  "(Look, the rod is brandished, my son, to defy
  all wooden idols)"
JPSOA  "How can we rejoice? My son, it scorns the rod
  and every stick"

Obviously the Hebrew text is in disarray (note the differences in the translations, ancient and modern).

  1. The mentioning of the word "rod" (BDB 986) in Ezek. 21:10,13 can refer to
    1. a rod of correction by a parent (cf. Prov. 10:13; 22:15)
    2. a rod for correction by a community (cf. Prov. 19:29; 26:3)
    3. a staff of a shepherd
    4. a scepter of a king
    5. a club of a shepherd (Ps. 23:4)
    6. a means of divine punishment (Ezek. 21:10)
      Here in Ezek. 21:10, it may refer to
      1. Zedekiah's impotence in protecting Judah from Neo-Babylonian invasion, in which every Judean left in the land will be affected (i.e. "despising every tree," cf. Ezek. 20:47; 21:3-4)
      2. a future leader from the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49:10); alluded to in Ezek. 21:27
  2. These verses are related in the people's concept that the ancient promises of YHWH for a special leader (i.e. "My son"), presented in Gen. 49:10 (cf. Targums, cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 4, pp. 1267-8), would be fulfilled instead of judgment.
  3. The phrase "every tree" somehow refers to the total judgment of Ezek. 20:47.
  4. In context it seems best to see the object of the FEMININE VERB "despise," Ezek. 21:10,13, to refer to "the sword" of YHWH. The Jerusalemites disregarded the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel's messages of judgment, but in reality the continuous Davidic line of kings from David (cf. 2 Samuel 7) would be stopped. Zedekiah would be the last. However, one would come in the future (cf. Ezek. 21:26b; 27b).
  5. UBS Text Project, p. 62, suggests the translation, "or shoud we rejoice (that) 'the scepter of my son (i.e. of King Zedekiah) looks down upon all (other) scrptors."

YHWH states that nothing at this point could stop His judgment from falling on Jerusalem, who had despised His prophetic messages.

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:11 "the slayer"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:11 "the slayer" This term (BDB 246, KB 255, Qal PARTICIPLE) denotes the invading mercenary army of Neo-Babylon. It is used of the judgment on Tyre in Ezek. 28:9. It is also used in Jeremiah's description of Judah's destruction (i.e. Jer. 4:27-31).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:12 Three IMPERATIVES related to mourning are mentioned in this verse.

  1. "Cry out," BDB 277, KB 277, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 9:8; 11:13; 27:30; Isa. 14:31; Jer. 25:34; 48:20
  2. "Wail" or "howl," BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 30:2; Isa. 14:31; 49:3; Jer. 25:34; 47:2; 48:20,21; Hosea 7:14; Zech. 11:2
  3. "Strike," BDB 706, KB 765, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 31:19

The theme of total slaughter continues as "against My people" is paralleled with "against the officials of Israel" (cf. Ezek. 21:25; 22:6).

▣ "strike your thigh" The thigh (BDB 437) was the largest muscle in the body. To strike one's thigh was imagery for

  1. incapacitation
  2. pain (cf. Jer. 31:19)
21:13
NASB  "For there is a testing; and what if even the rod which
  despises will be no more"
NKJV  "Because it is a testing and what if the sword despises
  even the scepter"
NRSV  "For consider: What! If you despise the rod, will it not
  happen"
TEV  "I am testing my people, and if they refuse to repent,
  all these things will happen to them"
TEV  "I am testing my people, and if they refuse to repent,
  all these things will happen to them"
NJB  "for this will be an ordeal"
LXX  "and what if even the tribe be rejected"
JPSOA  "Consider: How shall it fail to happen, seeing that it
  even scorns the rod"

This may refer to the life and exile of King Zedekiah. He despised YHWH's leadership, now he is rejected as leader. But one of David's line will be king again in the future (Ezek. 21:26b, 27b; 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17). This may parallel Ezek. 21:10.

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:14 This verse also has several commands from YHWH to Ezekiel.

  1. prophesy, BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  2. "clap your hands," BDB 645, KB 697, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  3. "let the sword be doubled," BDB 495, KB 493, Niphal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense. Doubled is imagery for a complete and total destruction.

▣ "clap your hands together" This physical gesture of clapping the hands denotes several different emotions.

  1. affirmation, 2 Kgs. 11:12
  2. anger, Num. 24:10; Ezek. 21:14
  3. contempt/mockery, Job 27:23; 34:37 (possibly 36:18); Lam. 2:15; Ezek. 6:11; 25:3,6
  4. pledge/oath, Prov. 11:21; Ezek. 21:17
  5. joy, Ps. 47:1; 98:8; Isa. 55:12

If you look these up you will see there is some overlap in these categories and the exact emotion meant is often uncertain.

Special Topic: Hand

NASB, NRSV  "surrounds them"
NKJV  "enters their private chambers"
NJB  "threatening them from every side"
REB  "whirling about them"

This VERB (BDB 293, KB 293, Qal PARTICIPLE) occurs only here in the OT. Its basic meaning in the cognate languages is

  1. encompass
  2. room, chamber
  3. In Sirah 51:10, it means "to enter" (i.e. "a penetrating sword," cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 28).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:15 This is the filfillment of Ezek. 21:7. See note there.

▣ "many fall at all their gates" The gates would be the key defensive positions. Resistance was futile!

NASB, Peshitta  "the glittering sword"
NKJV  "made bright"
NRSV  "the point of the sword"
TEV, REB  "that flashes like lightning"
NJB  "polished to flash like lightning"
JPSOA  "from its sheath"
LXX  "for glittering"

The UBS Text Project, p. 63, suggests three possible meanings of this abvbiguous Hebrew phrase.

  1. the threat of the sword
  2. the unsheathing of the sword
  3. the glittering of the sword

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:16 This verse has four Hiphil IMPERATIVES, FEMININE SINGULAR. This is another personification of YHWH's sword. It is addressed in several IMPERATIVES.

  1. NASB ‒ "show yourself sharp"
    NKJV ‒ "swords at the ready!"
    TEV ‒ "you sharp sword!"
    REB ‒ "be sharpened"
    LXX ‒ "sharpen thyself"
    The MT has a root, אחד (KB 29), that is unknown. Most translations emend it to חדד (BDB 292). KB 291 lists several stem connotations:
    1. Qal ‒ to be quick
    2. Hiphil ‒ to sharpen
    3. Hophal ‒ to be sharpened
    4. Hithpael ‒ to prove oneself sharp
      The UBS Text Project, p. 64, gives a "C" rating to "join (in an attack)" directed to the sword.
  2. "Go to the right," BDB 412, KB 415, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  3. "Set yourself," BDB 962, KB 1321, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  4. "Go to the left," BDB 970, KB 1332, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:17 YHWH brings the deserved judgment and He also stops it at His discretion (cf. Ezek. 5:13; 16:42; 24:13)! Judah's fall and exile are not the result of the power of the invading army (cf. Ezek. 21:19-27).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:19-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:19-20 This is another acted-out parable at YHWH's command (BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE). Apparently Ezekiel drew a map ("mark," "make," "appoint," BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE) in the ground. At the fork in the road, one sign ("cut down," "cut out," "inscribe," "prepare a wooden sign" [BDB 388], BDB 135, KB 153, Piel INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE, twice; in other TENSES this is the term for YHWH creating in Genesis 1).

  1. One sign at the fork pointed to Riblah, the capital of Ammon.
  2. The other sign at the fork pointed to Jerusalem, the capital of Judah. Ammon had also rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Jer. 27:1-3).
  3. Both of these capitals deserved and received YHWH's judgment by means of Neo-Babylon (Ezek. 21:22)!

Ezekiel is mimicking what Nebuchadnezzar, a pagan, superstitious king would do as he approached the fork in the road. One would lead down the right side of the Jordan River and one down the left. Eventually, both capitals fell. The thrust of the acted out parable was that YHWH would lead him to act on His behalf, not diviners but the Divine One!

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:21 This verse describes three Babylonian means of knowing the will of the gods by divination.

  1. putting the names on arrows and drawing one out (or spinning the quiver until one fell out) of the quiver or throwing arrows on the ground and analyzing their patterns
  2. consulting the household idols or ancestral spirits by prayer and incense (i.e. teraphim, cf. Gen. 31:19ff; see Special Topic: Teraphim)
  3. examining a sheep's liver for signs (i.e. color, shape, deformities; see Special Topic: Divination)

God is asserting that even by means of pagan divination He will bring judgment on Jerusalem. God used this divination for His own purposes. He uses even evil to accomplish His purposes (i.e. the witch of Endor, 1 Samuel 28 and Balaam, Numbers 22-24)!

Special Topic: Magic

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:22 This verse has a series of INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS that describes the Babylonian commander's (possibly Nebuchadnezzar himself) orders (fulfills Ezek. 4:2)

  1. to set battering rams
  2. to open the mouth for slaughter (possibly, "war cry," which would form a four-part chiasm with #1,2,3,4; see Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry)
  3. to lift up the voice with a battle cry
  4. to set battering rams against the gates
  5. to cast up mounds
  6. to build a siege wall

For a good brief discussion of siege techniques see Roland de Vaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 236-240.

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:23 This describes the reaction of the people of Jerusalem (cf. TEV). They think they are safe because of their political alliances (i.e. with Neo-Babylon or Egypt).

The "he" can refer to

  1. Ezekiel speaking for YHWH
  2. YHWH Himself
  3. the king of Neo-Babylon

Jerusalem is being judged because of her continuing covenant disobedience. Their God is now fighting against them!

▣ "they have sworn solemn oaths" This is the Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE and the NOUN of the same root (BDB 989, KB 1396) for emphasis. The Septuagint omits this phrase altogether. However, it may refer to the political alliance that Judah had with Babylon (cf. Ezek. 17:13; 2 Chr. 36:13).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:24 YHWH states that Judah's

  1. iniquity (BDB 730) will be remembered (BDB 269, KB 269, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
  2. transgressions (BDB 833) will be uncovered (BDB 162, KB 191, Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
  3. sins (BDB 305) will appear (BDB 906, KB 1157, Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
  4. people have come to remembrance (BDB 269, KB 269, Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
  5. people will be sieged (BDB 1074, KB 1779, Niphal IMPERFECT)

The three words used to describe rebellion against YHWH (i.e. iniquity, transgressions, and sins) appear together in several texts (cf. Exod. 34:7; Lev. 16:21; Job 13:23; Ps. 32:5; Isa. 59:12; Dan. 9:24). They form a summary triad.

Special Topic: Sin in the OT

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:25-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:25-26 Notice the different ways of referring to Zedekiah (Neo-Babylon's puppet king of Josiah's line).

  1. O slain (NKJV, "O profane")
  2. wicked one
  3. prince of Israel

Notice what will happen to him when his day (i.e. in the time of the iniquity of the end) has come.

  1. remove the turban ‒ BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  2. take off the crown ‒ BDB 926, KB 1202, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    (Here, "turban" (BDB 857) and "crown" (BDB 742) are parallel. This is surprising because in every other place the turban is for a priest. In many texts the office of king and High Priest are co-leaders [cf. Psalm 110; Zech. 3, 4; 6:12-13; Heb. 4:14-5:10; 6:13-7:28]).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:26b, 27b
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:26b, 27b These two concluding remarks seem Messianic (cf. E. W. Hengstenberg, Christology of the Old Testament, pp. 683-687). In context Ezek. 21:26b refers to Neo-Babylon, but when Ezek. 21:27b is brought in it appears to refer to Gen. 49:10 (i.e. Shiloh), see

  1. F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, p. 7
  2. Gleason Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 107-108
  3. These two taken together would describe Jesus as a humble one (cf. Zech. 9:9) and of the line of David (cf. Ezek. 34:23-24; 37:24,25; Jer. 30:9; Hosea 3:5).

It is surely possible that this refers to Nebuchadnezzar II as YHWH's instrument of judgment on Judah, as Cyrus II is later YHWH's instrument of release from exile and then restoration (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:1). As a Christian I must be careful of my biases which desire to read the full New Testament revelation back into the Old Covenant in too many places (e.g. Christ in the tabernacle). He is surely in the OT, but not on every page. Here (1) the royal line is the issue and a prediction of a future restoration is possible and also (2) the repeated use of the phrase "whose day has come in the time of the punishment of the end" in Ezek. 21:25 and 29 implies an eschatological setting.

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:27 "A ruin, a ruin, a ruin"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:27 "A ruin, a ruin, a ruin" A threefold repetition is a Hebrew idiom expressing the superlative degree (cf. Isa. 6:3; Jer. 7:4). It possibly links to Ezek. 21:14. The interpretive issue is to whom or what does the FEMININE form refer?

  1. the sword of the Lord
  2. the turban, crown, symbol of Davidic reign

Does this verse refer to the future fall of Babylon (v. 30) or to Zedekiah and Judah?

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:28-32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:28-32 This prophecy ("prophesy," BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERTIVE) is against the land of Ammon (cf. Ezek. 21:20). It is for one of two possible reasons:

  1. It possibly relates to Ammon taking advantage, possibly even some participation in the fall, of Judah (as Edom did in chapter 35).
  2. God's sure justice on the iniquity of Ammon.

The flow of thought could be outlined as follows:

  1. Ammon, mentioned in Ezek. 21:20, will also be destroyed, Ezek. 21:28 (cf. Ezek. 25:1-7).
  2. This is happening because
    1. of their reproach (cf. Ezek. 36:15; Zeph. 2:8-10)
    2. of their false prophets' messages from their divinations, Ezek. 21:29 (i.e. Ezek. 21:30a; see Special Topic: Diviner)
    3. they are wicked murderers, Ezek. 21:29
    4. their time has come, Ezek. 21:29
  3. How YHWH will judge (Ezek. 21:30) is specified in Ezek. 21:31-32.
    1. I shall pour out My indignation on you, Ezek. 21:31
    2. I shall blow on you with the fire of My wrath, Ezek. 21:31
    3. I shall give you into the hand of brutal men, skilled in destruction, Ezek. 21:31
    4. you will be fuel for the fire, Ezek. 21:32
    5. your blood will be in the midst of the land, Ezek. 21:32
    6. you will not be remembered, Ezek. 21:32

Another possible way to interpret these last three verses is to see them as referring to Neo-Babylon (i.e. YHWH's sword), not Ammon (see Encyclopaedia Judaica, vol. 6, p. 1086). This would make sense of Ezek. 21:30a, "return it to its sheath." Neo-Babylon's judgment was in the future. YHWH used her to judge His people (and other surrounding nations), but in return they were responsible for their own sin. Cyrus II would be YHWH's sword to destroy them (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:1).

entries.title: Ezekiel 21:31 "into the hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:31  "into the hand" See Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
EZEKIEL 22

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
The Sins of Israel Sins of Jerusalem Oracles of Judgment The Crimes of Jerusalem The Crimes of Jerusalem
22:1-5 22:1-5 22:1-5 22:1-12 22:1-5
22:6-12 22:6-12 22:6-12 22:6-12
22:13-16 22:13-16 22:13-16 22:13-16 22:13-16
Israel In the Furnace God's Refining Furnace
22:17-22 22:17-22 22:17-22 22:17-22 22:17-22
Israel's Wicked Leaders The Sins of Israel's Leaders
22:23-31 22:23-31 22:23-31 22:23-31 22:23-31

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:2 "Then the word of the Lord came to me saying"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:2 "Then the word of the Lord came to me saying" See note at Ezek. 21:1.

▣ "son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

▣ "will you judge, will you judge" The repetition of the VERB (BDB 1047, KB 1622, Qal IMPERFECT SINGULAR) is for emphasis (cf. Ezek. 20:4). Ezekiel acted as both prosecutor and judge on YHWH's behalf (cf. Ezek. 23:36). He lays out the charges and the consequences, then because of no intercessor or repentance (cf. Ezek. 22:30-31) they are implemented (i.e. 586 B.C.)!

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "the bloody city"
TEV  "the city that is full of
  murderers"
NJB  "blood-stained city"
JPSOA, Rotherham  "the city of bloodshed"
LXX  "the city of streams of blood"
REB  "the murderous city"

Jerusalem was bloody in two senses.

  1. murder, injustice (vv. 3b, 4a, 9a, cf. 2 Kgs. 21:6)
  2. idolatrous sacrifices (vv. 3c, 4b, 9b)

This is the key CONSTRUCT (BDB 746, 196) used throughout this chapter (cf. Ezek. 22:2 [twice], 3,4,6,9,12,13). It is used of Nineveh in Nahum 3:1. Some think it is used of Jerusalem because of

  1. the worship of Molech (cf. Ezek. 16:21; 20:26,31; 23:37)
  2. the killing of the righteous (cf. Ezek. 22:25)

It is historically possible that Nebuchadnezzar's initial raid in 588 B.C. caused the population of the area to seek refuge in the walled city of Jerusalem, but instead of refuge they found exploitation and death by their own countrymen!

In 586 B.C. the city and temple were destroyed by Neo-Babylon's army and the populace who escaped the sword were exiled to Babylon.

▣ "cause her to know" See SPECIAL TOPIC: Know (using mostly Deuteronomy as a paradigm)

▣ "abomination" See Special Topic: Abomination.

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:3 "for defilement"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:3 "for defilement" This VERB (BDB 379, KB 375, Qal INFINITIVE) means to become unclean because of her creation of and association with foreign pagan idols (cf. Ezek. 22:4).

This defilement (Qal PERFECT in Ezek. 22:4, i.e. uncleanness) is also described in Ezek. 22:4. Ezekiel, being a priest, was well trained in the laws of Leviticus.

  1. I have made you a reproach (BDB 357) to the nations, cf. Ezek. 5:14,15; 16:57
  2. I have made you a mocking (BDB 887) to all lands, cf. VERB (Hithpael IMPERFECT) in Ezek. 22:5 (Hithpael only 3 times in the OT, 2 Kgs. 2:23; Hab. 1:10; and Piel only once, Ezek. 16:31).
  3. you of ill repute (BDB 1027, lit. "infamous one," Ezek. 22:5

There is a parallelism among

  1. the nations, Ezek. 22:4
  2. all the lands, Ezek. 22:4
  3. those who are near. . .far, Ezek. 22:5

All people will be affected by Judah's sin (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6)! Judah's actions affect the way the world understands YHWH. The same is true as to the way the church's sin and false teachers confuse the world about Jesus!

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:4 "thus you have brought your day near"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:4 "thus you have brought your day near" YHWH asserts that their sin has hastened the day of their judgment (e.g. 2 Pet. 3:12)!

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:5 "you of ill repute, full of turmoil"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:5 "you of ill repute, full of turmoil" These are two characterizations of Judah.

  1. "of ill repute" is literally a Hebrew CONSTRUCT (BDB 379, 1027) "polluted name." They are considered ceremonially unclean and thereby cannot approach YHWH.
  2. "full of turmoil" is literally a Hebrew CONSTRUCT (BDB 912, 223), "full of confusion," which is a "Holy War" term (cf. Exod. 14:24; 23:27; Deut. 7:23). The tragedy is that now YHWH fights against His polluted people (cf. Deut. 28:20)! Isaiah 22:5 describes an eschatological scene (cf. Ezek. 7:5-9, esp. Ezek. 22:7).

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:6-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:6-12 First, Ezekiel lists (PERFECT TENSE) the settled rebellious attitude of Judah's political leaders, especially the kings in violation of the Mosaic Covenant.

  1. shed blood, Ezek. 22:6
  2. treated fathers and mothers lightly, Ezek. 22:7
  3. oppressed the alien, fatherless, and widows, Ezek. 22:7 (cf. Jer. 7:6; 22:3)

Then he lists the sins of Judah (cf. Jer. 7:5-11; Isa. 1).

  1. despised YHWH's holy things, Ezek. 22:8
  2. profaned YHWH's sabbaths, cf. Ezek. 20:13,16,21,24; 23:38
  3. lied (i.e. slandered, cf. Lev. 19:16), Ezek. 22:9
  4. worshiped idols (i.e. shed blood and eaten at mountain shrines, fertility worship, cf. Ezek. 18:6,11), Ezek. 22:9
    1. committed acts of lewdness, Ezek. 22:9
    2. uncovered their father's nakedness (sexual contact with mother or another of his father's wives, cf. Leviticus 18), Ezek. 22:10
    3. sex with women during menstrual period (cf. Lev. 18:19), Ezek. 22:10
    4. sex with neighbor's wife (cf. Lev. 18:20; 20:10), Ezek. 22:11
    5. lewdly defiled his daughter-in-law (cf. Lev. 20:12), Ezek. 22:11
    6. humbled his sister (or half sister), his father's daughter, in a sexual sense (cf. Lev. 20:17), Ezek. 22:11
  5. took money to commit murder (cf. Deut. 27:25), Ezek. 22:12
  6. loaned money with interest (cf. Ezek. 18:13; Lev. 25:36,37; Deut. 23:19,20; Prov. 28:8), Ezek. 22:12
  7. took advantage of neighbors, Ezek. 22:12
  8. forgot YHWH (cf. Ezek. 23:35; Deut. 6:12; 8:11,14; Isa. 17:10; Jer. 3:21; 13:25; Hosea 2:15; 8:14; 13:6), Ezek. 22:12 (also 23:35)

The Mosaic Covenant and common decency had been lost to Canaanite fertility worship. Ezekiel tries to embarrass Judah by using shocking language related to their fertility worship (cf. Ezek. 16:27; 43; 58; 22:9,11; 23:21,27,29,35,44,48,49; 24:13)!

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:7 "treated their father and mother lightly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:7 "treated their father and mother lightly" See Exod. 20:12; 21:17; Lev. 20:9; and Deut. 27:16.

Special Topic: Honor Father and Mother

▣ "the widow" See Exod. 22:22-24 and Deut. 24:17; 27:19.

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:9 "slanderous men"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:9 "slanderous men" See Lev. 19:16.

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:10 "uncover their fathers' nakedness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:10 "uncover their fathers' nakedness" This seems to refer to sexual intercourse with a father's former wife, stepmother, or concubine (cf. Lev. 18:7, 8; 20:11; Deut. 22:30; 27:20).

Special Topic: Abomination

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:13 "I strike my hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:13 "I strike my hand" See note at Ezek. 21:14.

Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:14 This is an allusion to Ezek. 21:7.

▣ "I, the Lord, have spoken and will act" This is a recurrent theme of Ezekiel which emphasizes

  1. YHWH's control of world events
  2. the fact that YHWH's word can be trusted and depended on (i.e. Isa. 55:9-11)
  3. the fact that judgment is coming, repentance (i.e. conditional covenant) is no longer possible

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:15 The threat of removal from the Promised Land for covenant disobedience goes back to Lev. 26:33 and Deut. 4:27; 28:64; 29:28. YHWH removed the Canaanites from Canaan because of their sins (cf. Gen. 15:12-21), now He will remove Judah. He is no respecter of persons, shows no favoritism!

The VERBS "scatter" (BDB 806, KB 918, Hiphil PERFECT with waw; cf. Ezek. 12:15; 20:23,24) and "disperse" (BDB 279, KB 280,Piel PERFECT with waw; cf. Ezek. 5:10,12; 6:8; 12:15; 20:23; 36:19) are most often used of Israel's and Judah's exiles, but they are also used of YHWH's judgment on Egypt, 29:12,13; 30:23,26. Egypt was the source of idolatry (cf. Ezek. 23:27,48). YHWH must cleanse His people of this pollution.

The same VERBS are used to describe YHWH's fighting on Israel's behalf (i.e. Num. 10:35), but now He fights against them because they have become abominations like the ten Canaanite tribes. They must be removed from YHWH's land, which they are polluting!

Special Topic: Pre-Israelite Inhabitants of Palestine)

YHWH's purpose in the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles was the purification of His people! YHWH wants a righteous people who reflect His character to a lost world so that they may know Him and come to Him!

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

22:16
NASB, ASV  "you will proface yourself"
NKJV  "you shall defile yourself"
NRSV, RSV  "I shall be profaned through you"
NJB  "through your own fault, you will be profaned"
JB  "I shall be dishonoured by you"
LXX  "I will take possession of thee"
Peshitta  "I will chastise you"
REB  "I shall sift you"
JPSOA  "you shall be dishonored"
NIV  "when you have been defiled"

The MT has "you," but several ancient versions (LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate) change this to "I." The second part of the verse lends support for the MT, but Ezek. 22:26 tends to support the versions. The UBS Hebrew OT Project, p. 71, gives "I" a "C" rating (considerable doubt). If "I" is correct, YHWH's people's sinning brought shame to Him!

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:17-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:17-22 This is imagery from ancient metallurgy. YHWH calls Jerusalem a mixture of metals, which made them absolutely useless (cf. Jer. 6:27-30). The mixture was the Mosaic Covenant with Egyptian idolatry and Canaanite idolatry. YHWH would melt them so as to remove the useless metals (cf. Isa. 1:22,25).

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:21 As so often Ezekiel uses terms normally reserved for a positive connotation in a shockingly negative way. In this verse "gather" (BDB 488, KB 484, Piel PERFECT with waw) is used in a judgment sense, but usually it refers to a gathering of Israelites from among the nations where they have been exiled (cf. Ezek. 39:28; Ps. 147:2).

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:24 "is not cleansed or rained on"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:24 "is not cleansed or rained on" This is a very difficult verse. Some think it refers to (1) no human tending and no divine rain or (2) no cleansing rain. For sure God's judgment has fallen and no moisture came (sign of judgment in Deuteronomy).

Special Topic: Waters

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:25-28 "There is a conspiracy of the prophets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:25-28 "There is a conspiracy of the prophets" The Septuagint has "whose princes" (cf. NRSV, NJB, REB) because the prophets are mentioned in Ezek. 22:28. This paragraph is a condemnation of all of Judean society (cf. Zeph. 3:3-4).

  1. the political leaders (LXX has "princes"), Ezek. 22:25, repeated in Ezek. 22:28
    1. acted like ravenous lions (cf. Ezek. 19:3,6; see Special Topic: Lions in the OT)
    2. devoured lives
      (1)  took treasure and precious things
      (2)  killed many (i.e. made widows)
  2. the priests, Ezek. 22:26
    1. have done violence to YHWH's law
    2. profaned YHWH's holy things
      (1)  made no distinction between holy and profane, cf.
        Lev. 10:10; 11:47; 20:25
      (2)  have not taught the difference between unclean and
        clean (Special Topic: Food Laws)
    3. hid their eyes from YHWH's sabbaths (Special Topic: Sabbath (OT)
  3. the prophets, Ezek. 22:28
    1. have smeared whitewash, cf. Ezek. 13:10,11,12,14,15 (twice)
    2. saw false visions, cf. Ezek. 13:6,7,9,23
    3. divining lies (see Special Topic: Divination)
  4. the people, Ezek. 22:29 (cf. Ezek. 18:7,12,16; Jer. 22:3)
    1. practiced oppression
    2. committed robbery
      (1) wronged the poor and needy
      (2) oppressed the alien/sojourner

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:29 "The people of the land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:29 "The people of the land" This term originally (and here) meant "landed owners with full rights as citizens" (cf. Ezek. 12:19; 45:16,22; 46:3), but after the Exile it referred to the poorest people of the land (cf. the use in the NT).

Special Topic: The People of the Land

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:30 This is such a shocking verse, which mirrors Isa. 59:16; 63:5 and Jer. 5:1. There was no one! What was YHWH looking for? Someone to

  1. build up the wall, cf. Ezek. 13:5; Ps. 106:23
  2. stand in the gap (intercede in prayer on behalf of Judah as Moses and Samuel had, cf. Jer. 15:1, which is similar to Ezek. 14:14,20; 33:1-6)

It is surprising that Ezekiel himself did not fulfill this text, but remember the setting is Jerusalem, not the exiles in Babylon. But then Jeremiah was in Jerusalem, why did he not fulfill this search? The verse is a literary hyperbole. It is not meant to be taken literally. It is for shock value only! There were some righteous people in Jerusalem (cf. Ezek. 20:47; 21:4).

The good news is that YHWH seeks intercessors! He wants to be convinced to withhold judgment. He wants to forgive, but no one interceded and people did not repent!

Special Topic: Intercessory Prayer

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:31 See notes at Ezek. 7:3,8,9; 9:10; 16:43. We reap what we sow! See full note at Gal. 6:7-10.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 22:32-34
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:32-34 This is a poem about "the cup" (BDB 468) of judgment mentioned in Ezek. 23:31.

  1. description of the cup
    1. your sister's cup, Ezek. 23:32,33
    2. deep and wide
    3. cup of horror and desolation, Ezek. 23:33
    4. contains much
  2. description of its event
    1. you will be laughed (BDB 850) at and held in derision (BDB 541)
    2. You will be filled with drunkenness and sorrow
    3. you will drink it and drain it (i.e. experience every last drop of YHWH's judgment)
    4. you will gnaw its pieces and tear your breasts

This imagery of a cup of judgment is recurrent in Scripture, see Ps. 75:8; Isa. 51:17,22; Jer. 25:15,16,27,28; also Matt. 20:22; 26:39,42; Mark 14:36; Luke 22:42; 2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:13.

23:34
NASB  "then you will gnaw its fragments"
NKJV  "you shall break its shards"
NRSV, JPSOA, REB  "you shall gnaw its shards"
TEV  "with its broken pieces"
NJB, NET  "then you will break it in pieces"
LXX  "I will take away her feasts and her
  new moons"
Peshitta, RSV  "you shall cut off your hair"
NIV  "you shall dash it to pieces"

It is obvious from the Septuagint and Peshitta that the ancient versions were confused by this line of poetry. In context it seems that one of two options seems logical.

  1. the large cup of judgment is drunk to the last drop (i.e. full measure)
  2. it is an idiom of regret, as is the next line, "tear your breasts" (i.e. once offered to foreign lovers, v. 21), possibly the broken pieces are used to mutilate her erotic regions (cf. Ezek. 23:3,8,21)

The UBS Hebrew OT Project, p. 75, gives "and you will chew on its broken pieces" a "B" rating (some doubt).

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Ezekiel 23 is a series of judgment oracles
    1. similar in subject matter to Ezek. 16
    2. similar in genre to "the sword oracles" of Ezek. 21

  2. YHWH's reasons for judging His own people are laid out in the allegory of two faithless sisters. This literary form is not meant to support
    1. polygamy
    2. marrying sisters

      It is for shock value. It is designed to be disgusting. It is ironic tragedy, but with a hopeful outcome.

      1. YHWH found and took special marvelous care of national Israel
      2. Israel, as a whole, was repeatedly unfaithful
      3. YHWH will restore her (e.g. Hosea 1-3)

  3. Ezek. 23:35 is theologically significant, as is the PERSONAL PRONOUN'S repeated use in Ezek. 23:36-45.

  4. The term "Israel" can refer to
    1. the title of the seed of Abraham that went to Egypt during the famine under Jacob, but was turned into slave labor by a later Egyptian dynasty that did not know Joseph.
    2. the Northern Kingdom, which split off from the United Kingdom in 922 B.C. This new nation of Abraham's seed took the collective title, "Israel," for themselves.
    3. Only context can tell which group is being referred to.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:2 The NKJV sees most of the chapter as poetry.

  1. Ezek. 23:2-4
  2. Ezek. 23:5-8
  3. Ezek. 23:9-10
  4. Ezek. 23:12-16
  5. Ezek. 23:17-18
  6. Ezek. 23:19-21
  7. Ezek. 23:22b-24e
  8. Ezek. 23:24f-27
  9. Ezek. 23:32-35
  10. Ezek. 23:35

Most other modern English translations only view Ezek. 23:32-34 as poetry. It is hard to distinguish elevated, emotional, figurative prose from poetry.

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:3 "bosom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:3 "bosom" This term (BDB 186) occurs uniquely in this chapter (i.e. Ezek. 23:3,8,21 [with emendation]) and possibly in Prov. 5:19. The other Hebrew word for "breasts" (BDB 994) is also found in Ezek. 23:3,21, and often in Song of Songs.

It seems unusual to have the term "virgin" (BDB 144) in this context because this refers to the wives of YHWH figuratively bearing His children (cf. Ezek. 23:4, 37). NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 782, says that this refers to "reputable" and not "wanton" women.

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:4 "Oholah and Oholibah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:4 "Oholah and Oholibah" Their Hebrew names are a play on the Hebrew word for "tent" (BDB 14). This is an allegory similar to chapter 16 based on Israel's and Judah's infidelity to the covenant (i.e. marriage vow) with YHWH. Oholah (BDB 14, lit. "her tent," which may be an allusion to pagan tent-shrines or to false temples at Dan and Bethel) stands for the capital of Israel, Samaria. Oholibah (BDB 14, lit. "my tent is in her," i.e. temple) stands for the capital of Judah, Jerusalem.

Notice how their disobedience is characterized.

  1. played the harlot in Egypt, Ezek. 23:3
  2. played the harlot in their youth
    1. breasts pressed, Ezek. 23:3
    2. virgin bosom handled, Ezek. 23:3
  3. they were wed to YHWH and bore children, Ezek. 23:4

Israel's idolatry in Egypt is a recurrent theme unique to Ezekiel, see Ezek. 16:26; 20:4-17. The judgment of Egypt is described in Ezek. 29:1-32:21.

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:5-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:5-8 This describes the acts of Oholah (Samaria).

  1. played the harlot (BDB 275, KB 275, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) while married (lit. "under me" BDB 1065,1,c) to YHWH (cf. Isa. 54:5-6; Jer. 3:1,20; Hosea 2:2 and note 2:16), Ezek. 23:5
  2. lusted (BDB 721, KB 783, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) after other lovers, Ezek. 23:5
  3. lusted especially after Assyria, Ezek. 23:5,7,9
    1. leader dressed in purple, Ezek. 23:6
    2. governor and officials, Ezek. 23:6
    3. desirable young men, Ezek. 23:6
    4. riding on horses, Ezek. 23:6
    5. the choicest men of Assyria, Ezek. 23:7
  4. accepted their gods (idols) and defiled herself (BDB 379, KB 375, Niphal PERFECT), Ezek. 23:7
  5. harlot from her youth (i.e. Egypt), Ezek. 23:8 (see note at Ezek. 23:4)
  6. "they poured out their lusts," Ezek. 23:8, cf. Ezek. 16:15; this refers to the desire for political alliances, but these attempts at security involved the ritual acknowledgment of their national idols

For "mine," which is lit. "under me."

Special Topic: Anthropomorphic Language to Describe Deity

23:5
NASB, NJB, LXX, Peshitta  "her neighbors"
NKJV  "the neighboring"
NRSV, JPSOA, NIV, NET  "warriors"
REB  "officers"

This Hebrew term (BDB 898) usually means "come near," "approach" and can be used for bringing an offering. It is only in this context (i.e. Ezek. 23:5,12 [i.e. "the ones near"]) that it can mean "warlike" or "warrior" (from an Akkadian root). It is also possible that it refers to a governmental official (i.e. one who is near the king) or the military officers described in Ezek. 23:6.

▣ "her lovers" In context this refers to political alliances, but this also involved the acknowledgment of their gods, which led to idolatrous practices with the fertility gods (cf. Hosea 11:7, 8:9; 12:1).

23:6
NASB, NKJV, NJB, TEV  "purple"
NRSV, REB, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "blue"

The MT has BDB 1067, which calls it "violet," connected to

  1. the tabernacle hangings, Exod. 25:4; 26:1; 28:33; 35:25
  2. the tabernacle cords, Exod. 26:4; 28:28,37; 36:11; 39:21,22,31
  3. priest's ephod, Exod. 28:31
  4. tassels on Israel's men's robes, Num. 15:38
  5. Persian hangings in Shusham, Esth. 1:6
  6. dyed fabric, Ezek. 23:6; 27:24; Jeremiah 9

This color was obtained from murex snails harvested in large numbers by the Phoenicians (cf. Ezek. 27:7). In this context it would refer to high ranking givernment officials, possibly military (i.e. JPSOA footnote).

Special Topic: ANE Sacred Colors

▣ "governors and officials" In context this refers to political alliances, but this also involved the acknowledgment of their gods, which led to idolatrous practices with the fertility gods (cf. Hosea 11:7,8,9; 12:1).

  1. "governor" ‒ BDB 808, NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 602, notes that this term referred to the chief local Assyrian official when Israel was a vassal region after the fall of Samaria in 722 B.C. by Shalmaneser V and Sargon II.
  2. "officials" ‒ BDB 688, cf. Ezek. 23:6,12, this would denote the chief local Assyrian official when Israel became a province in 841 B.C. under Shalmaneser III.

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:9-10 YHWH's response to His unfaithful wife Oholah.

  1. I gave her into the hands of her lovers
  2. They uncovered her nakedness
  3. They took her children (i.e. exile)
  4. They killed many inhabitants of Israel (i.e. invasion in 724 B.C., Samaria fell in 722 B.C.)
  5. He made her a byword among women
  6. Assyria became the "rod" (cf. Isa. 8:7; 10:5) of YHWH's anger and judgment

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 23:11 Judah should have learned from the excesses of her northern sister, but she did not. This description relates to the Syro-Ephraimatic War (cf. 2 Kings 16:8; Isa. 7:7-9).

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:11-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:11-17 These verses describe the acts of Oholibah (Jerusalem).

  1. more corrupt in her lusts than her sister, Ezek. 23:11
  2. more harlotries than her sister, Ezek. 23:11
  3. lusted after Assyrian (possibly related to 2 Kgs. 15:17-22; 17:1-6) officials, Ezek. 23:12
    1. governors, officials
      (1)  magnificently dressed
      (2)  riding on horses (or riding in chariots)
      (3)  desirable young men
    2. "The Assyrians were famous for their rich and costly apparel. The expression ‘Assyrian garments' became synonymous with elegant and expensive clothing," James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, pp. 307-308.
  4. defiled herself, Ezek. 23:13
    1. Babylonian and/or Assyrian men portrayed on the wall, Ezek. 23:13-14
      (1)  girded with bells, Ezek. 23:15
      (2)  flowing turbans
      (3)  looking like Babylonian officers, Ezek. 23:15
    2. sent messengers to Chaldea (Babylon, cf. 2 Kings 16; 20:11-19), Ezek. 23:16
    3. Babylon came, Ezek. 23:17
      (1)  to her bed of love
      (2)  they defiled her with harlotry
      (3)  uncovered her nakedness
  5. her soul became disgusted with them, Ezek. 23:17c,22,28, their rich and costly apparel.

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:14 "portrayed on the wall"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:14 "portrayed on the wall" These wall paintings, carvings, and inlays (BDB 348, KB 347, Pual PARTICIPLE) are the source of much of the historical and cultural information moderns possess about the culture of Mesopotamia and Egypt. Ezekiel uses this VERB to describe

  1. the idolatry of the temple, Ezek. 8:10
  2. the glory of the Neo-Babylonian officers and soldiers, Ezek. 23:14

▣ "with vermilion" This (BDB 1059, KB 1666) refers to a red pigment used for wall painting cf. Jer. 22:14, here of Neo-Babylonian soldiers' outfits. The pigment came from one of two sources.

  1. a certain insect
  2. Egyptian ochre from Sinopis
23:15
NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB, JPSOA, NET  "officers"
NKJV  "captains"
LXX  "princely appearance"
Peshitta  "handsome men to
  look at"

This term (BDB 1026, KB 1544 or 1545) means "the third one" and refers to

  1. the third person in a war chariot, cf. Exod. 14:7
    1. one to drive
    2. one to shield
    3. one to fight
  2. a high court official, cf. 2 Kgs. 7:2,17,19;10:25; 15:25
  3. a military officer, cf. 2 Sam. 23:8; 2 Kgs. 9:25; Ezek. 23:15,23

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:18 The FIRST PERSON PRONOUN (used twice) is the term Nephesh.

Special Topic: Nephesh

23:20
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "paramours"
TEV  "oversexed men"
NJB  "big-membered"
NET, NIV Interlinear  "genitals"
Peshitta  "male organs"
REB  "members"
JPSOA  "for concubinage"

The MT has "concubine" (BDB 811, but it is MASCULINE), which in context seems not to balance the second phrase well. Though it is crude to modern standards Ezekiel is suggesting

  1. large penis
  2. strong ejaculation

The NET translation captures the sense well — "She lusted after their genitals — they were as large as those of donkeys and their seminal emission was as strong as that of horses." This sexual imagery is meant to shock and nauseate God's people about their idolatry (i.e. foreign alliances). Often the sexual imagery is also literal because the fertility gods of the Ancient Near East are the national gods.

NASB, NKJV  "issue of horses"
NRSV  "emission of stallions"
NJB  "ejaculating as violently as stallions"
LXX  "members of horses"
Peshitta  "whose privates are like those of horses"
JPSOA  "whose organs were like those of stallions"

This term (BDB 281) refers either to a sexually aroused male organ or a powerful ejaculation. It occurs only here in the Bible, but similar allusions are made to Israel acting in idolatrous ways as animals long for reproduction (i.e. Jer. 2:24; 14:6).

23:21
NASB  "handled your bosom"
NKJV, REB  "pressed your bosom"
NRSV, Peshitta  "fondled your bosom"
TEV  "played with your breasts"
NJB, JPSOA  "handle your nipples"

The MT has "for the sake of, למען, but the UBS Text Project, p. 73, suggests an emendation to למעך, which means "to press," to which it gives a "C" rating. The translation committee thought it was the best of two bad choices.

Ezekiel is referring to national Israel during the Egyptian bondage. Her sexual idolatry was nothing new (cf., vv. 3,8)! ANE fertility worship was pervasive.

The human desire and need to reproduce is God-given (cf. Gen. 1:28; 9:1,7), but for long term societal stability and human family happiness, He put some needed guidelines!

Special Topic: Human Sexuality

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:18-21,22-35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:18-21,22-35 YHWH's response to His unfaithful wife Oholibah.

  1. YHWH became disgusted (BDB 429, KB 431, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) with her, as with her sister, Ezek. 23:18, cf. Jer. 6:8
  2. The repeated reasons for YHWH's disgust.
    1. uncovered her harlotries, Ezek. 23:18
    2. uncovered her nakedness, Ezek. 23:18
    3. multiplied her harlotries, Ezek. 23:19
    4. remembered the days of her youth (i.e. idolatry in Egypt), Ezek. 23:19
    5. lusted after their Egyptian paramours, Ezek. 23:20-21 (this may refer to Judah seeking help from Egypt against Neo-Babylon, who was her supposed ally, cf. 2 Kgs. 24:1-7)
  3. YHWH arouses (BDB 734, KB 802, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) her lovers against her, Ezek. 23:22
    1. a large mercenary army of Neo-Babylon will attack them from every side, Ezek. 23:23
    2. description of their weaponry, Ezek. 23:24
    3. treat Jerusalem according to their customs (i.e. slaughter and exile), Ezek. 23:24
  4. YHWH sets His jealousy (BDB 888) against them, Ezek. 23:25
  5. YHWH sets His wrath (BDB 404) against them, Ezek. 23:25
  6. Wrath described in vivid terms, Ezek. 23:25-27
    1. remove your nose
    2. remove your ears
    3. death by the sword
    4. death by fire
    5. take their wealth
      (1)  children
      (2)  clothes, cf. Ezek. 23:29; 16:39
      (3)  jewels from Egypt, cf. Ezek. 16:39
  7. YHWH will deal with them in hatred (BDB 971), Ezek. 23:29
    1. take property (i.e. that which they have worked for all their lives, CONSTRUCT BDB 481, 388, cf. Deut. 28:33; Jer. 20:5) and leave them naked and bare, Ezek. 23:29, cf. Ezek. 16:39. Nakedness was part of the curses of Deuteronomy (cf. Ezek. 28:48).
    2. because of their idolatry, Ezek. 23:30
    3. because they walked in the way of their sister, Ezek. 23:31
    4. because they forgot YHWH and cast Him behind their back, they now face the judgment, Ezek. 23:35 (i.e. lived as if there were no covenant and no YHWH)

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:22 "from whom you were alienated"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:22 "from whom you were alienated" This refers to Ezek. 23:17c and is repeated in Ezek. 23:28. This phrase (BDB 668, KB 722, Qal PERFECT and BDB 659) occurs only here and in Ezek. 23:28 in the entire OT. A related phrase occurs in Ezek. 23:17,18. This refers to the emotional results of a faithless relationship. Judah was unfaithful (idolatry) throughout her history. Finally YHWH had enough and abrogated the covenant relationship! But He would restart it.

  1. the post-exilic return (cf. Ezra-Nehemiah)
  2. the new covenant (i.e. NT, cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36)

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:23 Judah became a Neo-Babylonian vassal in 605 B.C., when General Nebuchadnezzar II (later king) invaded. This did not stop the rebellion so he invaded again in 597 and 586 (destruction of the temple and Jerusalem). At this point Judah became a province. Even then Nebuchadnezzar II had to send an invasion in 582 because of the assassination of his appointed governor Gedaliah (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:22-24).

▣ "Chaldeans, Pekod and Shoa and Koa" These refer to Armenian tribes in the eastern part of Babylon (cf. Jer. 50:21). This whole verse implies that the Neo-Babylonian army was made up of mercenary troops including the remnant of the Assyrian army. The IVP Bible Background Commentary suggests that these roots mean "punishment," "war cry," and "shriek" (p. 709).

NASB, NKJV, NRSV TEV  "Pekod and Shoa and Koa"
NJB, REB, JPSOA  "Pod, Lod, and Koa"
Rotherham footnote  "officer and noble and man of
  wealth"
  1. Pekod ‒ BDB 824, KB 958 can mean
    1. "commissioner," "deputy," or "overseer"
    2. KB 959, "Aramaean tribe"
  2. Shoa ‒ BDB 1003 III, nomads of eastern Mesopotamia, KB 144 I, "leader," "chief," "master"
  3. Koa ‒ BDB 880 and KB 1085 suggest similar meaning to Shoa (above)

It is uncertain if these NOUNS refer to

  1. tribal groups
  2. leadership groups
  3. war cries (see IVP Bible Background Commentary, OT, p. 709)

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:24 This is a list of all the military equipment arrayed against besieged Jerusalem.

  1.  mobile weaponry
    1. NASB, "weapons"
      NRSV, TEV, NJB, "from the north" (from LXX, cf. Ezek. 26:7)
      JPSOA, "fleets," BDB 246, KB 254, meaning uncertain; it is found only here in the OT
    2. "chariots," BDB 939, KB 1233 cf. Isa. 2:7; 22:18 (UBS Text Project, p. 74, rates it as "D")
    3. "wagons" (lit. "wheels," BDB 165, KB 190 I, possibly related to the vision of chaps. 1 and 10). Used in Isa. 5:28 and Jer. 47:3 for war chariot wheels
  2. fully equipped infantry
    1. "buckler," BDB 857 III, KB 1037 II, full body shield, cf. Ezek. 26:8; 38:4; Jer. 46:3
    2. "shield," BDB 171, KB 545, small personal shield, cf. Ezek. 38:4,5; 39:9; Jer. 46:3,9
    3. "helmet," BDB 875, KB 1081, loan word used only twice in the OT, cf. Ezek. 27:10; 38:5; 1 Sam. 17:38; Jer. 46:6

All of Assyria's arsenal of weaponry was arrayed against God's special city, now abandoned by Him!

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:25 "I will set My jealousy against you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:25 "I will set My jealousy against you" The VERB "set" or "direct" (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT with waw) is a common VERB (e.g. Ezek. 23:7,9,24,25,28,31,42,46,49).

"My jealousy" (BDB 888) is a way of referring to the monotheistic character of YHWH (cf. Exod. 8:10; 9:14; Deut. 4:35,39; 5:7; 32:39; 33:26; 1 Sam. 2:2; 2 Sam. 7:22; Isa. 43:9-11; 45:21-22; 46:9; Jer. 2:11; 5:7,10; Rom. 3:30; 1 Cor. 8:4,6; 1 Tim. 2:5; James 2:19).

Special Topic: Jealousy, Zeal

▣ "They will remove your nose and your ears" These were the places where women wore jewelry. This violent removal of jewelry was practiced in the Ancient Near East as punishment of adulteresses (i.e. Middle Assyrian Law Code).

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:28 "into the hands"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 23:28 "into the hands" See Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:31 "her cup into your hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:31 "her cup into your hand" This is a biblical imagery for one's destiny. It can be positive (cf. Ps. 23:5) or negative (cf. Ps. 75:8; Isa. 51:17-22; Jer. 25:15-29; Lam. 4:21; Hab. 2:16). In many ways Judah was more responsible for her sin because

  1. she saw what happened to Samaria, but did not change
  2. she had the temple, priests, and Davidic rulers (i.e. Rom. 9:4)

Special Topic: Cup

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:35 Amazingly the people of God have knowingly, purposefully turned away from Him (cf. Genesis 3). Oh, the tragedy.

  1. forgotten Me, BDB 1013, KB 1489, Qal PERFECT, cf. Ezek. 22:12; Ps.106:21; Isa. 17:10; Jer. 3:21; Hosea 2:13; 8:14; 13:6
  2. cast Me behind your back, BDB 1020, KB 1527, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw (i.e. modern idiom, "out of sight, out of mind"), cf. 1 Kgs. 14:9; Ps. 50:17; Jer. 2:27; 32:33

Notice the number of times in this context where phrases containing a PRONOUN denoting YHWH are used.

  1. they have forgotten Me, Ezek. 23:25
  2. they have cast Me behind their back, Ezek. 23:35
  3. (killed children) whom they bore to Me, Ezek. 23:37
  4. they have done this to Me, Ezek. 23:38
  5. they have defiled My sanctuary, Ezek. 23:38
  6. they have profaned My sabbath, Ezek. 23:38,39
  7. they practiced idolatry in My house, Ezek. 23:39
  8. they used His incense and oil to impress foreigners at a special meal, Ezek. 23:41

Sin is rebellion against a personal God! This is a fulfillment of Deut. 31:16.

The goal of humanity is fellowship with our Creator. Nothing in the world can take His place. The essence of sin is "self." Salvation is freedom from the tyranny of self-focused living and the restoration of the image and likeness of God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27), which allows an intimate, daily fellowship with God (e.g. Gen. 3:8).

Because humans turn away from God they bear (BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE) the full consequences of their deeds.

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:36
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 23:36 As Ezekiel was commanded to act as judge (BDB 616, KB 665, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, lit. "declare") in Ezek. 20:4 (twice) and 22:2 (twice), now again (compare Jer. 1:10).

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:36-45
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:36-45 The two sister's sins are enumerated again.

  1. committed adultery, Ezek. 23:37 (see Special Topic: Adultery)
  2. committed murder, Ezek. 23:37 (see Special Topic: Murder)
  3. committed idolatry, Ezek. 23:37 (see Special Topic: Idolatry)
  4. defiled My sanctuary, Ezek. 23:38
  5. defiled My sabbaths, Ezek. 23:38 (see Special Topic: Sabbath)
  6. sacrificed children, Ezek. 23:39 (see Special Topic: Molech)
  7. played the harlot with foreigners (i.e. political alliances), Ezek. 23:40-44

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:37 "their sons, whom they bore to me, to pass through the fire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:37 "their sons, whom they bore to me, to pass through the fire" This idiomatic language refers to the redemption of the firstborn found in Exodus 13. But these idolatrous Jerusalemites were sacrificing their children to Molech (see cf. Ezek. 23:39; 16:20,36), not presenting them to YHWH.

Special Topic: Molech

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:38
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:38 The accusation against God's people acting inappropriately in their worship of YHWH is recurrent.

  1. defiled (BDB 379, KB 375, Piel PERFECT) His sanctuary, cf. Ezek. 5:11; 7:20
  2. profaned (BDB 320, KB 319, Piel PERFECT) His sabbaths, cf. Ezek. 20:13,16,21,24; 22:8

YHWH took these actions personally as an attack on Himself (cf. Ezek. 23:38a).

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:40
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:40 Israel and Judah decorated themselves for the idolatrous meals (cf. Ezek. 23:41) with foreign gods (i.e. political alliances).

  1. bathed, BDB 934
  2. painted their eyes, cf. 2 Kgs. 9:30; Jer. 4:30 (usually black or blue around the eyes to highlight them)
  3. decorated themselves with ornaments, BDB 725, cf. Ezek. 16:13-16; Isa. 3:18-23

Verse 42b seems to describe presents brought by the foreign officials.

  1. bracelets, BDB 855, cf. Ezek. 16:11,12; Gen. 24:22,30,47; Isa. 3:19
  2. crowns, BDB 742, this action may be mimicking YHWH's actions in Ezek. 16:9-14. The crown can refer to royalty or a wedding crown (cf. Song of Songs 3:11)

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:42-43
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:42-43 These verses are difficult to translate and, therefore, difficult to interpret. The context helps, but does not reveal the specifics related to the lovers of Ezek. 23:42.

The ADJECTIVE "worn out" (BDB 115) is meant to express that Judah is an experienced prostitute, as a matter of fact, a prostitute used so often that she has become unattractive.

The MT Hebrew text offers a suggested change (i.e. Qere, "what is read") to a VERB (BDB 275, KB 275, Qal IMPERFECT). The original unchanged text was "Will they commit adultery with her now, and she with them?" The emended text reads "Will they now commit adultery with her when she is thus?"

23:42
NASB, NRSV  "drunkards" (Ketiv)
NKJV, REB  "Sabeans" (Qere)
TEV, NJB, JPSOA  "a crowd of men"
Peshitta  "men who had come from Sheba"

The MT has the hapax legomenon, "drunkards," סובאים, BDB 685 from the VERB (BDB 684, KB 738). Masoretic scholars change (Qere) it to "Sabeans" סבאים (BDB 685, cf. Isa. 45:14), which is similar. Sheba (שׁבא, BDB 985, cf. Ezek. 27:22,23; 38:13) is an ancestor of the Sabeans (i.e. raiders, cf. Gen. 25:3), who lived in southwest Arabia.

The word is missing from the LXX. The UBS Text Project, p. 76, supports this with a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:43
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 23:43 See note at Ezek. 23:42-43.

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:44 "they went in to"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:44 "they went in to" This is a Hebrew idiom for sexual intercourse (e.g. Gen. 6:4; 24:67; 38:2,8, 9,16,18; 39:14; Deut. 22:13).

Special Topic: OT Euphemisms for Sexual Activity

23:45
NASB  "But they, righteous men, will judge them"
NKJV  "But righteous men will judge them"
NRSV  "But righteous judges shall declare them"
TEV  "Righteous men will condemn them"
NJB  "All the same, there are upright me who will
  judge them"

This is the use of "righteous" (BDB 843) as "fair." This does not refer to people who know and follow YHWH. In context it refers to YHWH's instruments of judgment, Assyria and Neo-Babylon, and that His judgment on Israel and Judah was deserved!

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:46-49
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:46-49 These verses list the consequences of their acts.

  1. invasion, Ezek. 23:46
  2. given over to terror (cf. Deut. 28:25) and plunder (in the sense of shame, cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 632), Ezek. 23:46
  3. many/most killed, Ezek. 23:47
    1. by stones
    2. by swords
    3. by fire
  4. idolaters cut off, Ezek. 23:48
  5. idolaters judged, Ezek. 23:49

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:47 "stone them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:47 "stone them" This was the punishment for adultery (cf. Lev. 20:10; Deut. 21:21). It is also mentioned in Ezekiel's parallel allegory (cf. Ezek. 16:40).

Special Topic: The Death Penalty in Israel

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:48
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 23:48 This verse uses "women" as imagery for all of God's people. "Admonish" (lit. "discipline," BDB 415, KB 418, Nithpael PERFECT with waw) is often used of YHWH's judgment on the disobedience of His covenant people (cf. Lev. 26:18,28; Ps. 6:1; 38:1; 39:11; 118:18; Jer. 31:8).

entries.title: Ezekiel 23:49 "you will bear the penalty of worshiping your idols"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:49 "you will bear the penalty of worshiping your idols" The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) is the common VERB "give."

  1. required (Ezek. 9:10; 23:9)
  2. punish (Ezek. 7:4,9)

Special Topic: Consequences of Idolatry

Special Topic: Idolatry

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:1 This is the fourth date (cf. Ezek. 1:2; 8:1; 20:1) listed in Ezekiel. Surprisingly one would expect another date at chapter 25, which starts the judgment context on the nations. This may mean chapters 24 and 25 are a literary unit.

This dates the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1; Jer. 39:1; 52:4). It was begun on January 15, 588 B.C. (NET Bible). The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 710, calculates the date as Jan. 5, 587 B.C. It took until 586 B.C. for the city to fall. Remember, there are two ways to count the reign of kings in the ANE.

In a book of prophecy the question of final revision always comes into play. Did Ezekiel know the exact date of the siege and later fall of Jerusalem? Of course he could; he was a prophet of YHWH. YHWH often used this predictive quality to encourage His people that He was in control of history. However, it is also surely possible, without distracting from the power of YHWH or the foresight of His prophets, to see these dates as literary. These books were, at some point, the collected and arranged prophecies of Ezekiel. Literary design does not diminish prophetic predictions!

Special Topic: Inspiration

Special Topic: The Bible (its uniqueness and inspiration)
