READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:2 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

▣ "write" The MT has "write" (BDB 507, KB 503) as a Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE , but the Masoretic scholars suggested it be read (Qere) as a Qal IMPERATIVE (same kind of problem as in Ezek. 24:10).

There are many IMPERATIVES in this chapter (cf. Ezek. 24:2,3 [three], 4,5 [two], 6,10 [two], 11,17[two], 21. Most of them occur in the poetic section (i.e. Ezek. 24:3b-5, 6-13) and are directed to the rebellious house (i.e. Judah).

Special Topic: Masoretic Text

▣ "the name of the day, this very day" Judgment on Jerusalem was not a future prediction, but a terrible reality (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28)!

▣ "has laid siege" The VERB (BDB 701, KB 759, Qal PERFECT) is literally "lean on," but is used here as an idiom of a city being besieged (Jerusalem's siege is begun, cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1; Jer. 39:1; 52:4).

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:3 "speak a parable"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:3 "speak a parable" This (BDB 605, KB 647) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. See note at Ezek. 12:22,23; 17:2; 18:2, 3; 20:49. Ezekiel used several poems to communicate YHWH's messages.

  1. poem of Judah as a ruined vine, Ezek. 19
  2. poem of the sharp, bright, swift sword of judgment, Ezek. 21:9-10
  3. poem of the large cup of drunkenness, Ezek. 23:32-34
  4. poem of the corrupted, large, bronze (cf. Ezek. 24:11) cooking pot, Ezek. 24:3-13
  5. poems about the fall of Tyre, Ezek. 26:17-18; 27:3-9,25-36; 28:2-19
  6. poems about the fall of Egypt, Ezek. 29:3-7; 30:2-19; 31:2-9; 32:2-8,12-15

▣ "to the rebellious house" This (BDB 598, cf. Ezek. 2:5,6,8; 3:9,26,27; 12:2[twice],3,9,25; 17:12; Isa. 30:9) is a derogatory way of referring to faithless Judah (cf. Ezek. 2:6,8).

The idiom is repeated with the PARTICIPLE of the VERB (BDB 597, KB 632) in Ezek. 2:3 (also note the use of the parallel terms

  1. BDB 833, KB 981 in Isa. 1:2
  2. BDB 710 in Isa. 30:1

Judah's stubborn rebellion (cf. Deut. 9:5-6,13; 10:16; 31:27) has been continual and purposeful! I think YHWH chose Israel with all her weaknesses to clearly reveal His faithfulness in the stark light of their unfaithfulness! If YHWH can continue to love, forgive, and use Israel, then there is a great hope for all of Adam's children, based solely on the unchanging, merciful, gracious character of YHWH!

Special Topic: Stubbornness

Special Topic: Characteristics of Israel's God

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ This chapter is based on Jeremiah's parable about a boiling pot (cf. Jer. 1:13, 14).

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:3-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:3-5 This first poetic stanza has several commands from YHWH which set the stage for the parable/proverb.

  1. put on the pot, BDB 1046, KB 1636, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:3
  2. put it on, BDB 1046, KB 1636, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:3
  3. pour, BDB 427, KB 428, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:3
  4. put (lit. gather), BDB 62, KB 74, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:4
  5. fill, BDB 569, KB 583, Piel IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:4
  6. pile, BDB 189, KB 217, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:5
  7. boil, BDB 958, KB 1299, Piel IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:5

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:4-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:4-5 The very best pieces of the very best of the flock were put in the pot. Who does this refer to?

  1. the royal, priestly, and civic leaders who remained in Jerusalem, cf. Jer. 39:6; 52:10,24-27
  2. national Israel herself when YHWH found her in the wilderness, Ezek. 16:4-14

In this context of the citizens of Jerusalem seeing themselves as the "lucky ones," "spared ones," "better ones" than those taken into exile, this phrase may well refer to all of them! However, they will be destroyed and YHWH will choose to work with and restore the early exiles! This was shocking to the arrogant, sinful Judeans still in Jerusalem and Judah.

24:5
NASB, TEV, NJB, REB  "wood"
NKJV  "fuel bones"
LXX, Peshitta  "bones"
JPSOA  "the cuts"

The MT has "bones" (BDB 782, v. 4), but "wood" or "logs" (BDB 781, v. 10) fits the context better.

  1. the bones ‒ העצמים
  2. the logs ‒ העצים

However, the UBS Text Project, p. 78, thinks "bones" (BDB782) is original (an "A" rating). "Bones" appears again at the end of v. 5.

▣ "Make it boil vigorously" This is the VERB (BDB 958, KB 1299, Piel IMPERATIVE) and the NOUN of the same root for intensity (i.e. "vigorously").

This is paralleled with "seethe" (BDB 143, KB 164, Qal PERFECT). The cooking is imagery for YHWH's complete judgment.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:6 "Woe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:6 "Woe" This INTERJECTION (BDB 17, cf. Ezek. 24:9) expresses deep emotion often connected to judgment (cf. Ezek. 16:23; Jer. 4:13; 6:4; 10:19; 13:27; 15:10; Hosea 7:13).

▣ "the bloody city" See note at Ezek. 22:2.

NASB, NRSV  "rust"
NKJV, JPSOA  "scum" (i.e. left at the bottom of the pit)
TEV  "corroded"
NJB  "rusty"
REB  "green with corrosion"
LXX  "blight," "rust," or "scum"
Peshitta  "is set on the fire" (from v. 5)

This Hebrew word is uncertain ((BDB 316, KB 315). It is found only in this chapter in the OT. The same trilateral root means "rust" in Arabic. YHWH had tried to cleanse His people over and over again, but their sin was too deep (i.e. Genesis 3; see Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind).

▣ "Without making a choice" This VERB (lit. "fall," BDB 656, KB 709, Qal PERFECT) was used of casting lots to know YHWH's will.

  1. dividing the Promised Land among the tribes, Num. 34:2; Josh. 13:6; 23:4; Ezek. 45:1
  2. dividing the duties in the temple, 1 Chr. 24:31; 26:13,14
  3. determining who would supply wood for the new sacrificial system, Neh. 10:34
  4. determining who would live in the rebuilt Jerusalem, Neh. 11:1
  5. determining the guilty party, Jonah 1:7

This phrase seems to imply that death would come indiscriminately to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:7 This refers to the openness and flagrant nature (i.e. "places it on a bare rock," i.e. in the sight of all) of Judah's sin. This refers to:

  1. an allusion to a priestly act of draining the blood from sacrificial animals and putting it on the appropriate places (Leviticus 1-7). The remainder was poured out at the base of the altar of sacrifice (see Special Topic: Altar of Sacrifice)
  2. the proper slaughter of wild animals to be consumed (cf. Lev. 17:13; Deut. 12:16; see Special Topic: Food Laws).

▣ "To cover it with dust" This seems to refer to the blood of their victims (cf. Lev. 17:13).

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 24:8 As Judah flagrantly sinned for all to see, now YHWH will judge her for all to see (cf. Deut. 29:24-28; Jer. 16:10; 22:8,9).

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:9-10 This is a reflection of Ezek. 24:3b-5. The pot of judgment is boiling and Judah is in it!

Verses 10-11 have a series of commands related to the boiling pot.

  1. heap, BDB 915, KB 1176, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 24:5b, 9c
  2. kindle, BDB 196, KB 223, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 24:5c
  3. boil, BDB 1070, KB 1752, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    1. (John J. Owens, Analytical Keys to the Old Testament, vol. 4, p. 572, calls it a Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    2. Beall, Banks, Smith, Old Testament Parsing Guide, p. 619, calls it a Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
    3. Benjamin Davidson, Analytical Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon of the Old Testament, p. 231, gives both options).
  4. mix, BDB 955, KB 1289, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (Owens) or INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE (Beall, Banks, Smith) or either (Davidson)
  5. set, BDB 763, KB 840, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:11

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:10 The fully cooked meat will be poured into the fire and completely destroyed.

NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "and mix in the spices"
TEV  "boil away the broth"
LXX  "and the liquor boiled away"
REB  "pour out all the broth" (JPSOA footnote)
JPSOA  "and stew it completely"

The MT is reflected in JPSOA (UBS Hebrew OT Text Project, p. 79, gives it a "B" rating). The possible emendations are reflected in TEV, REB, LXX.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:11 The empty pot (cf. Ezek. 24:11) is set on the hot coals and the remaining scum (or "rust, v. 6") will be completely burned up and removed (i.e. ritual cleansing). Verse 12 either

  1. describes YHWH's continual attempts to cleanse His people
  2. even with all of this burning (i.e. Ezek. 24:10-11), Judah is not yet clean (cf. Ezek. 24:12-13)

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:12 "She has wearied Me with toil"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:12 "She has wearied Me with toil" This refers to YHWH's attempt to bring Judah to repentance. He made a great and continuous effort to bring her back to Himself. This phrase is difficult to understand because

  1. the MASCULINE PLURAL NOUN "toil" (BDB 20) is unusual and found only here in the OT
  2. the VERB has no OBJECT
  3. the LXX omits it

therefore, some scholars see it as an addition.

Notice how the JPSOA translates these three poetic lines:

"It has frustrated all efforts,
Its thick scum will not leave it‒
Into the fire with its scum!"

The "it" would refer to the copper cooking pot.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:13 "lewdness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:13 "lewdness" This term (BDB 273) describes Judah's idolatry, of which they refuse to give up and respond appropriately to YHWH's warnings. It is often associated with inappropriate sexual activity (cf. Ezek. 16:27,43,58; 22:9,11; 23:21,27,29,35,44,48 [twice],49; 24:13).

▣ "Until I have spent My wrath on you" The VERB (lit. "cease activity," BDB 628, KB 679, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) denotes that at some point YHWH's wrath will be appeased and brought to an end (cf. Ezek. 5:13; 16:42; 21:17).

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:14 YHWH's word (prophetic predictions of judgment) is sure! He has tried again and again to get His people to repent (cf. Ezek. 24:12-13). Notice the number of "I's" in the English translation (6). Therefore, He will not (i.e. Jer. 13:14)

  1. relent, BDB 828, KB 970, Qal IMPERFECT
  2. pity, BDB 299, KB 298, Qal IMPERFECT
  3. be sorry, BDB 636, KB 688, Niphal IMPERFECT

He will judge Judah according to her ways and deeds (cf. Ezek. 7:3,8,27; 18:30; 36:19). This is figurative language for YHWH's refusal to forgive (cf. Ezek. 8:18)! Only judgment remains!

NASB, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta  "I will judge you"
NKJV  "they will judge you"
TEV, JPSOA  "you will be punished"
NJB, REB  "you will be judged"

The MT is reflected in the NKJV. However, there is a series of "I's" in v. 14. The UBS Text Project, p. 81, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 24:15 The NASB 1995 Update starts a new paragraph at Ezek. 24:15; NASB 1970 does so at v. 16.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:16-17 "the desire of your eyes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:16-17 "the desire of your eyes" This shows the tenderness of Ezekiel toward his wife. This also is the imagery used in verses 16-24 to describe the unbelievable pain of the people of Judah when Jerusalem fell.

In Ezekiel's pain he is told to

  1. not mourn, BDB 704, KB 763, Qal IMPERFECT, negated
  2. not weep, BDB 113, KB 129, Qal IMPERFECT, negated
  3. no tears shall run down, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERFECT, negated, because this phrase
    1. is left out of the LXX
    2. does not fit the parallelism
    3. is redundant with #2, many scholars think it is an addition

This is similar to YHWH's message about grieving to Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 16:5).

Just a personal note, it is always hard for me, being a modern western person, to not be affected as an interpreter by my culture's overemphasis on the rights and value of the individual. Most societies in the world are tribal or clan-focused. It bothers me when

  1. Job's children die
  2. David's child dies
  3. Jeremiah is told not to marry
  4. YHWH takes Ezekiel's wife

My mind screams to me "Are not these affected individuals as important to God as the biblical characters? Does not God love and care for them? Do not His promises cover them?" Do you hear the twenty-first century American in me?

God has a universal plan. This world is affected by sin. This life is only the beginning of an eternal relationship! Yes, God loves and cares for individuals, but He has bigger and better plans for all humanity. This is not the world God intended it to be!

Theologically I know that the OT attributes all causality to God as a way of affirming monotheism! He, and only He, is in control. Individuals get hurt, die, both by natural causes and by the hand of evil, manipulative people. Yet God's promises are still sure! He does care for each, but also for all (cf. 2 Cor. 5:21)! The book by Hannah Whithall Smith, The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life, has really helped me in this area.

Special Topic: One Causality

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:17 This is a series of Hebrew cultural images describing mourning rites (cf. Jer. 16:5-13). Ezekiel was not allowed to mourn ("be silent," BDB 198, KB 266, Qal IMPERATIVE) for the death of his own wife. The things he was expected to do, he was told to do the opposite.

  1. put on your hat
  2. put on your shoes
  3. do not cover your mouth
  4. do not eat mourner's bread

Ezekiel's grief (i.e. Ezek. 24:22) over the loss of his wife parallels YHWH's grief over the loss of His wife (i.e. Judah). However, Judah's judgment was appropriate! Grieving over them would imply that the judgment was not deserved, appropriate, and necessary (e.g. Lev. 10:1-7 in Nadab and Abihu's death).

Special Topic: Grieving Rites

NASB, LXX Targums, Vulgate  "the bread of men"
NKJV  "man's bread of sorrow"
NRSV  "the bread of mourners"
NJB  "the usual food"
REB  "the bread of sorrow"
JPSOA  "the bread of comforters"

The MT has "the bread of men" (v. 22). The UBS Text Project, p. 81, gives this a "B" rating (some doubt). The Peshitta, translated by George M. Lamsa, has a good footnote, p. 852, "In the East mourners do not bake break or cook. Food is brought to them by their sympathetic neighbors." This cultural act is alluded to in Jer. 16:7.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:21 Notice the parallel phrases YHWH uses to describe Judah's feelings toward the temple.

  1. the pride of your power
  2. the desire of your eyes
  3. the delight of your soul

Judah had substituted devotion to a building for their devotion to YHWH (e.g. Jer. 7). This is always a problem for religiously oriented people! The goal is fellowship with God (cf. Ps. 42:1-2; 63:1; 143:6). It is an orientation of the heart, not a physical place to worship, or human performance.

Special Topic: Lifted Up

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:23 "you will rot away in your iniquities"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 24:23 "you will rot away in your iniquities" This VERB (BDB 596, KB 628, Niphal PERFECT with waw) is used several times by Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 4:17; 33:10) and may reflect Lev. 26:39. Jeremiah's and Ezekiel's condemnations of both Israel and Judah reflect the terminology of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Remember, both of them were from priestly families.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:24 Notice the direct speech of YHWH where Ezekiel is mentioned by name. The prophet himself is a sign (cf. Ezek. 24:27; 12:11).

YHWH addresses Ezekiel directly in Ezek. 24:25-27. We, as later readers of the OT, know more about the man Ezekiel from this chapter than from any other OT prophet. We sense his love for his wife and his people. We feel his pain over Judean sin and incalcitrance!

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:25 Notice the list of things the Judeans trusted in and longed for.

  1. their stronghold (i.e. Jerusalem)
  2. the joy of their pride (i.e. the temple, see Jeremiah's temple sermon in Jer. 7)
  3. the desire of their eyes (i.e. the temple)
  4. their heart's delight (i.e. their idols)
  5. their children (i.e. exile or death)

See not at 24:21.

entries.title: Ezekiel 24:27 "On that day your mouth will be opened"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:27 "On that day your mouth will be opened" Originally, after the vision of Ezekiel in chapter 1, God told the prophet that he would be unable to speak at times (cf. Ezek. 3:26). Therefore, these opening chapters of Ezekiel deal quite often with symbolic action. However, after the Fall of Jerusalem, the prophet's mouth was opened (cf. Ezek. 3:27; 33:22) and his message changed from doom/judgment to forgiveness/restoration! Now he could preach hope, restoration, and the renewal of covenant promises.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What is the unifying theme of Ezek. 20 through 24?
  2. Describe the worship of the god Molech.
  3. Define divination and list its numerous forms found in the OT (cf. Deuteronomy 18).
  4. Why is the marriage relationship such a good analogy to the covenant relationship?

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:1 "And the word of the Lord came to me saying. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 25:1 "And the word of the Lord came to me saying. . ." This is the characteristic literary marker that a new oracle is beginning. It is surprising that a date does not appear here, as it does in Ezek. 26:1 and 24:1. This causes the interpreter to ask if chapters 24-25 form a literary unit. From content it seems that these chapters form a unit of pronouncements regarding YHWH's coming judgment on the surrounding nations.

entries.title: Ezekiel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
EZEKIEL 25

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO CHAPTERS 25-32

  1. There is a subject unity (judgment on these nations) to these chapters, but not a genre uniformity. Also note the different dates.
    1. 9th year, 10 month, 10th day, Ezek. 24:1 (may cover chapter 25)
    2. 11th year, 1st month , 1st day , Ezek. 26:1
    3. 10th year, 10th month, 12th day, Ezek. 29:1
    4. 27th year, 1st month, 1st day, Ezek. 29:17
    5. 11th year, 1st month, 7th day, Ezek. 30:20
    6. 11thth year, 3rd month, 1st day, Ezek. 31:1
    7. 12th year, 12th month, 1st day, Ezek. 32:1
    8. 12th year, 12th month, 15th day, Ezek. 32:17

      This clearly demonstrates that the literary unit (Ezek. 25-32) was an edited collection. By whom and when is uncertain.

  2. The oracles against the nations (see D.) are characteristic of Hebrew Prophetic Literature.
    1. Isaiah 13-21, 23, 24
    2. Jeremiah 46-51
    3. Ezekiel 25-32, 35, 38-39
    4. Amos 1-2
    5. Joel 3:1-16
    6. Zephaniah 2:1-3:5

  3. Nations to Be Judged by YHWH

  4. The nations listed in chapter 25 tried to get Judah to rebel against Neo-Babylon (cf. Jeremiah 27), but in the end, they benefitted, even participated in, Judah's fall (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:1-2).

  5. Theological Issues
    1. The judgment oracles on surrounding nations and world powers of the Ancient Near East (ANE) accentuate the power, glory, and uniqueness of Israel's God (i.e. monotheism; see Special Topic: Monotheism).
    2. They show that YHWH has a larger purpose for a repentant Judah. Ezekiel's prophesies of a restored, glorified temple was a way of asserting a future hope and purpose for Israel (i.e. the Messiah). The first temple became corrupt (cf. Ezek. 8-10) and YHWH left, but a future temple is promised (Ezek. 40-48).
    3. The messages of doom on the pagan nations were Ezekiel's first message of hope for God's exiled people after the exiles heard of Jerusalem's demise (cf. Ezek. 24:25-27).
    4. The book of Jonah is also a condemnation of a foreign oppressor nation (i.e. Assyria). Yet, it functioned theologically as YHWH's willingness to accept the repentance of the pagan nations (i.e. Isa. 19:23,24-25). The reality of Gen. 12:3 is being fulfilled!
      Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:2 "set your face toward"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:2 "set your face toward" This IMPERATIVE (BDB 967, KB 1321, Qal IMPERTAIVE) is a standard idiom of judgment (cf. Ezek. 15:7; Lev. 20:5; 26:17; Jer. 21:10; 44:11; Amos 9:4). See note at Ezek. 6:2; also note Ezek. 13:17; 20:46; 21:2; 25:2; 28:21; 29:2; 35:2; 38:2.

▣ "Ammon" All three trans-Jordan nations were relatives of Israel, Edom through Esau (cf. Gen. 36:1) and Ammon and Moab through Lot (cf. Gen. 19:37-38).

Ammon was located south of the Jabbok River and another boundary somewhere north of the Arnon River.

Special Topic: Ammon

▣ "prophesy" This is a second IMPERATIVE (BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 4:7; 6:2; 11:4; 13:2,17; 21:2,7; 25:2; 28:21; 29:2; 34:2; 35:2; 36:6; 38:2; 39:1). After the fall of Jerusalem, Ezekiel now proclaims YHWH's judgment on the surrounding nations who supported or maybe were directly involved in Jerusalem's demise (cf. Jer. 49:1-6; Amos 1:13-15; Zeph. 2:8-9).

  1. Herodutus specifically mentions Nebuchadnezzar's devastation of the trans-jordan area in 582 B.C.
  2. Josephus mentions that it occurred five years after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:3 "Hear"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:3 "Hear" This is the third opening IMPERATIVE (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE) in this section. One wonders if any of these nations ever heard these prophecies. They were addressed to them, but obviously they were directed toward the exiles. They demonstrate that

  1. YHWH is a universal God
  2. YHWH is no respecter of persons
  3. YHWH will punish sin
  4. YHWH's word does come to pass
  5. YHWH's ultimate will will be accomplished

Special Topic: Listen/Hear (Shema)

▣ "Aha" This INTERJECTION expresses the joy of the Ammonites (cf. Ps. 35:21,25; 40:15-16; Isa. 44:16; Ezek. 25:3; 26:2; 36:2), which is defined in Ezek. 25:6. They rejoiced over

  1. the sanctuary being profaned
  2. the land of Israel made desolate
  3. the house of Judah sent into exile

They may have participated in this exile (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:1-2).

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:4 "I am going to give you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:4 "I am going to give you" The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PARTICIPLE, in Ezek. 25:10 Qal PERFECT with waw) is used in Ezek. 11:15 (Niphal PERFECT) of Canaan being given to YHWH's covenant people, but because of their sin, the land will now be given to "the sons of the east." This is similar to Canaan originally being taken away from the ten nations and given to Israel (cf. Gen. 15:12-21).

▣ "the sons of the east" This phrase occurs several times with several possible meanings.

  1. warriors, Ezek. 25:10; Jdg. 6:3,33
  2. wisemen, 1 Kgs. 4:30
  3. future relatives (i.e. Syria), Gen. 29:1
  4. nomadic Arabs from northern Arabia (Jer. 49:28)

Here it refers to Neo-Babylon, which is beyond Syria. Ezekiel has predicted that YHWH will judge His people with an "east wind" (cf. Ezek. 17:10; 19:12; note Isa. 27:8).

Special Topic: East Wind

▣ "they will eat your fruit and drink your milk" This phrase is similar to Deut. 28:33, which describes Israel's fate if she does not keep YHWH's covenant (cf. Isa. 1:7).

These terms are normally a prayer of thanksgiving (i.e. Ps. 128:2; Isa. 3:10), but here it is a curse.

Special Topic: Keep

Special Topic: Covenant

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:5 "Rabbah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:5 "Rabbah" This is the capital of Ammon located on the Wadi Amman, which becomes the Jabbok River. This water source was the key to the city's continuity. It is the capital of the nation of Jordan today, Amman.

▣ "a pasture for camel. . .a resting place for flocks" This is a way of predicting the nation's depopulation, only nomadic herdsmen will be there for short periods (cf. Isa. 27:10).

The term "resting place" (BDB 918) is found only here and in Zeph. 2:5 where it is used of wild beasts. This judged place was so dry that it could only be used for grazing at certain brief times of the year.

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:6 The physical gestures of "clapping hands" and "stomping feet" can be understood as a way of expressing joy or approval (cf. Ezek. 6:11; Nahum 3:19). In this context Ammon rejoiced at Judah's demise (and may have participated in it, cf. 2 Kgs. 24:1-2).

Special Topic: Clap Your Hands

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:7 "I have stretched out My hand against you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:7 "I have stretched out My hand against you" This is another idiom of judgment (cf. Exod. 7:5; 15:6,12; Isa. 5:25; 9:12,17,21; 10:4; 14:27; 23:11; Jer. 6:12; 15:6; 51:25; Ezek. 6:14; 14:13; 20:33,34; 25:7,13; 35:3; Zeph. 1:4; 2:13).

Special Topic: Hand

Special Topic: Anthropomorphic Language to Describe Deity

▣ "I shall give you for spoil to the nations" Spoil (BDB 103) refers to the property of conquered nations, including even their own people (i.e. Num. 31:32-40). This term is found several times in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 25:7; 26:5; 29:19; 36:4; 38:12,13).

The MT has a word that is unknown. This has been emended by changing one consonant.

  1. "spoil" ‒ בז (BDB 103; Qere)
  2. from ‒ בג (BDB 93)

Notice the things YHWH says He will do to Ammon.

  1. stretched out His hand against them
  2. gave them for spoil to the nations
  3. cut them off from the peoples
  4. made them perish from the lands
  5. destroyed them (cf. Ezek. 25:10)

Ammon will be no more! This is surprising in light of Jer. 49:6 (and Moab's restoration in Jer. 48:47). This may have an eschatological orientation or simply a poetic hyperbole.

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:8-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:8-11 This chapter addresses

  1. Ammon, Ezek. 25:1-7
  2. Moab, Ezek. 25:8-11
  3. Edom, Ezek. 25:12-14
  4. Philistia, Ezek. 25:15-17

▣ "Moab" This is another trans-Jordan country from Lot's incestuous children by his own daughters (cf. Genesis 19). There are several prophecies against Moab (cf. Num. 21:27-30; Isaiah 15-16; Jeremiah 48; Amos 2:1-3; Zeph. 2:8-11). Moab's boundaries are from the Arnon River to the Brook Zered.

Special Topic: Moab

▣ "Seir" This (BDB 973) refers to a mountain range running parallel to the Arabah (see The Zondervan Pictorial Encyclopedia of the Bible, vol. 5, pp. 329-330). It was originally the homeland of Horite settlers (cf. Gen. 36:20-30), but they were defeated by Esau (cf. Deut. 2:12,22). Therefore, "Seir," "Mount Seir," became ways of referring to Edomites (cf. 2 Chr. 20:10; 25:11). Edom is located south of the Brook Zered and extends down the eastern side of the Arabah.

Special Topic: Edom and Israel

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:8 "the house of Judah is like all the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:8 "the house of Judah is like all the nations" This statement, in one sense, was surely true. Judah had taken up the Canaanite religion. In another sense the phrase depreciates Judah's unique relationship with YHWH (i.e. Gen. 12:1-3; Exod. 19:4-5). These trans-jordan relative nations saw nothing different, unique, or respectable in Judah or her God.

It is also possible that Marduk (i.e. chief god of Babylon) was seen as being stronger than the gods of the nations which were conquered. It was Judah's military defeat that precipitated the accusations and slurs.

Special Topic: Marduk

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:9 "Beth-jeshimoth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:9 "Beth-jeshimoth" This Moabite city was located on the eastern side of the Jordan in the ancient tribal allocation of Reuben (cf. Josh. 12:3; 13:20). The name means "place of the desert" (BDB 111).

▣ "Baal-meon" This Moabite city was also located in the ancient tribal allocation of Reuben (cf. Num. 32:28; Josh. 13:17; also note Jer. 48:23). Note it carries the name of the Canaanite male fertility deity.

▣ "Kiriathaim" This is also a Moabite town in the tribal allocation of Reuben (cf. Num. 32:37; Josh. 13:19), located on the tableland. It is also mentioned in YHWH's judgment on Moab in Jer. 48:1.

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:10 "Ammon may not be remembered among the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 25:10 "Ammon may not be remembered among the nations" The VERB (BDB 269, KB 269, Niphal IMPERFECT) is also used of Ammon in Ezek. 21:32. Ammon will exist no more as a nation. Israel will return to its land, but Ammon will not (the same is true of Edom).

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:12 Edom acted against the house of Judah (cf. Ps. 137:7; Lam. 4:21-22; Obad. 1:10-14) by

  1. taking vengeance (BDB 667, KB 721, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) plus the related NOUN, BDB 668). This action caused great guilt (Qal IMPERFECT VERB plus INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root, BDB 79, KB 95, which is a grammatical way to show intensity).
  2. avenging themselves (BDB 667, KB 721, Niphal PERFECT)

Also they apparently took the opportunity of the collapse of the Judean state to annex part of her land (cf. R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 844).

Special Topic: Edom and Israel

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:13 "Teman"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:13 "Teman" This is the Hebrew word for "south," "south wind" (BDB 412). It originally designated a grandson of Esau (cf. Gen. 36:11). It came to refer to

  1. the northern part of the nation of Edom (cf. Obad. 1:9; Hab. 3:3)
  2. a city (cf. Jer. 49:7,20; Amos 1:12)
  3. In this context it represents a region because it is contrasted with Dedam to designate the whole nation (similar to the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba").

▣ "Dedan" This refers to a southern region in northwestern Arabia (cf. Gen. 10:7; 25:3). The Arab inhabitants became identified with Edom (cf. Jer. 49:8). As an area it extended down the eastern side of the Gulf of Aqaba.

The exact locations of Teman and Dedan are uncertain and whether they refer to a city or a region in this context is uncertain.

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:13-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:13-14 YHWH will respond in vengeance (BDB 668).

  1. stretch out His hand against them
  2. cut off man and beast
  3. lay it waste
  4. fall by the sword

This violation of Edom against Judah and her God (cf. Ezek. 25:8) was taken very personally by YHWH.

  1. My vengeance, twice (BDB 668)
  2. My people
  3. My anger
  4. My wrath

Note how many prophecies are against Edom (cf. Isa. 34:5-17; 63:1-6; Jer. 49:7-22; Ezek. 25:12-14; 35:1-15; Lam. 4:21-22; Amos 1:11-12; Mal. 1:2-4).

Special Topic: Edom and Israel

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:14 "by the hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 25:14 "by the hand" See Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:15 "Philistines"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:15 "Philistines" The Philistines were apparently Greeks from the Aegean Islands. They were the only group of people in this part of the world who were uncircumcised. They were apparently a mercenary force who tried to attack Egypt in the twelfth century B.C. but were defeated. They then settled on the southern coast of Palestine. They had five major city-states which are delineated in Jos.13:3: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. They were a major military problem throughout the period of the judges and even throughout the reign of Saul and David. The name "Palestine" comes from the word "Philistine."

Special Topic: Philistines

▣ "have acted" This verse describes Philistia's actions against YHWH's people (cf. Joel 3:4-8).

  1. acted in revenge
  2. took vengeance
  3. displayed scorn of soul
  4. destroyed with everlasting enmity (cf. Ezek. 35:5)

Wow! What strong language!

entries.title: Ezekiel 25:16 "Cherethites"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
25:16 "Cherethites" This name is of uncertain origin (BDB 504). Two principles of hermeneutics can help here.

  1. In context they are parallel to Philistines. They could be a synonymous name or a specific group who were assimilated. The Philistines were possibly Aegean people (sea peoples). The Cherethites were possibly from Crete (because of)
    1. Amos 9:7
    2. the similarity of the root consonants
    3. the LXX translation)
  2. Parallel passages link them to the Philistines (i.e. Pelethites, cf. 2 Sam. 8:18; 15:18; 20:7,23; 1 Kgs. 1:38,44; 1 Chr. 18:17; Zeph. 2:5).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What is the theological significance of the literary unit of Ezekiel 25-32?
  2. Why does Ezekiel mention the small surrounding nations first?
  3. Who are the Cherethites of Ezek. 25:16?
  4. What is the significance of the phrase "they will know that I am the Lord," Ezek. 25:17?

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:1 Ezekiel dates his prophecies (cf. Ezek. 1:1; 8:1; 20:1; 26:1; 29:1,17; 30:20; 31:1; 32:1,17; 33:21). Surprisingly, the month is not named here. His book is not in chronological sequence, which implies an editor. It must be admitted that moderns do not know how, who, or when the OT was complied and edited in its current form.

Ezekiel 26:1 through 28:19 forms a literary unit denoting Phoenicia's judgment and total destruction. See note at Ezek. 26:11! The subdivisions are identified by the literary marker "the word of the Lord came to me saying" (cf. Ezek. 26:1; 27:1; 28:1,11).

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:2 "the gateway of the peoples is broken"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:2 "the gateway of the peoples is broken" There are two ways of understanding this phrase.

  1. It has to do with Phoenicia's territorial expansion because of Judah's destruction of Neo-Babylon (notice the last phrase of v. 2).
  2. Jerusalem is located on a major international highway between the powerful nation of Egypt and the powerful nations of Syria, Anatolia, and Mesopotamia. Because of her strategic location, Judah charged a tax on all of the caravans who passed this way. Tyre, also a commercial center, was glad that one more middleman was eliminated.
  3. It relates to the use of the phrase in Isa. 62:10, which denotes Jerusalem, and particularly the temple, as a universal access (i.e. highway) to the worship of YHWH.

▣ "I shall be filled" This VERB (BDB 569, KB 583, Niphal COHORTATIVE) expresses the joy of the Phoenicians at the demise of Judah ("she is laid waste," BDB 351, KB 349, Hophal PERFECT). The VERB stem implies it was permanent.

▣ "because Tyre has said" Chapters 26-28 form a literary unit of judgment (a funeral dirge, cf. Ezek. 19:1-14; 26:17-18; 27:2-9,25-36; 28:12-19; 32:2-8) against the Phoenician maritime cities of Tyre and Sidon (cf. Isa. 24; Jer. 47:4).

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:3 These nations who gloated over Judah's fall were judged by YHWH (e.g. Micah 4:11).

▣ "as the sea brings up its waves" This is a play on the fact that Tyre was an island fortress. Most of the city was located on the mainland, but the citadel was located on a rocky island about one-quarter mile off shore. During ancient times it proved to be one of the most impregnable fortresses in the Near East.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:4 This is another reference to the island fortress (cf. Ezek. 26:17). The city was finally captured by Alexander the Great in 332 B.C.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:5 This curse is repeated in Ezek. 26:14. There were two types of fishing nets used.

  1. casting nets, 12:13; 32:3
  2. dragnets, 26:5,14; 47:10

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:6 "her daughters who are on the mainland"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:6 "her daughters who are on the mainland" This refers to the part of the city which surrounded the harbor. Only the walled citadel was on the island. It was the walls of the houses and buildings that Alexander used to build a causeway to the islands (cf. Ezek. 26:12).

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:7 "I will bring upon Tyre"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:7 "I will bring upon Tyre" Notice the actions of Neo-Babylon's army are controlled by YHWH. Nebuchadnezzar II is His instrument.

Flavius Josephus mentions that Nebuchadnezzar II seized the island fortress for 13 years (586-573 B.C.) without taking it, but that a treaty was made in which the royal family was exiled but not the king himself (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 712).

▣ "from the north" This compass direction became a proverb (e.g. Jer. 4:6; 6:1,22; 10:22; 13:20; 15:12; 46:20, 24) for evil because this was the only land route for invasion from the Fertile Crescent empires (i.e. Assyria in Isa. 14:31; Neo-Babylon in Jer. 1:13-15).

▣ "Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon" This Neo-Babylon king's name is spelled in two ways.

  1. Nebuchadnezzar ‒ 2 Kgs. 24:1,10,11; 25:1,8,22; 1 Chr. 6:15; 2 Chr. 36:6,7,10,13; Ezra 1:7; 2:1; 5:12,14; 6:5; Neh. 7:6; twenty-seven times in Daniel
  2. Nebuchadrezzar ‒ thirty-seven times in Jeremiah, four in Ezekiel

▣ "kings of kings" This title reflects the conquests of the Neo-Babylon Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Jer. 27:6-7; Dan. 2:37). It was also later used of Artaxerxes, the Persian king in Ezra 7:12. It came to be a title for the Messiah (cf. 1 Tim. 6:15; Rev. 19:16). A similar title was used of YHWH in Deut. 10:17 and I Enoch 9:4. It is a phrase that emphasizes sovereignty!

Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

▣ "a great army" The Neo-Babylonian army grew by including the defeated armies into their ranks as mercenaries.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:8 "siege walls against you, cast up a mound"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:8 "siege walls against you, cast up a mound" This may refer to two separate siege tactics or just to one (cf. 2 Sam. 20:15; 2 Kgs. 19:32; Isa. 37:33; Jer. 6:6; Ezek. 4:2; 17:17; 21:22; 26:8). These ramps allowed soldiers and siege machines (i.e. battering ram, BDB 867) to approach the stone walls of a city in order to loosen the lower foundation stones and cause the wall to fall.

▣ "raise up a large shield against you" This is a technical term (BDB 857, cf. 1 Kgs. 10:16) for what was known as "the roof" of the siege machines, which was raised as a shield to protect the attacking soldiers from those defenders on the walls of citadels. We know that Nebuchadnezzar II began this siege in 587 B.C., and it lasted until 574 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar never defeated the main citadel (cf. Ezek. 29:18), but it apparently surrendered. There is no record of the city's capture in the Babylonian chronicles.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:9 Nebuchadnezzar's siege machines never reached the island citadel of Tyre, but Alexander's did in 332 B.C.

▣ "blow of his battering rams" This is a rare term (BDB 562 II). In Num. 34:11 it is translated "border" (KB 568 or "to run along beside"), but that meaning does not fit this text in Ezekiel.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:10 Neo-Babylon learned the use of cavalry and chariot warfare from the Assyrians (i.e. Jer. 6:23).

Special Topic: Chariots

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:11 Some would read these words and assert that the Bible is in error at this point. We must remember that prophecy is hyperbolic literary genre. The books that have really helped me in my understanding of both prophecy and apocalyptic literature are

  1. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic
  2. G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible

▣ "your strong pillars" From the Greek historian, Heroditus (II. 44), we understand there were two famous obelisks in the city of Tyre. One was gold and the other was emerald and they were dedicated to the god Melqart ("King of the City"), probably another name for Ba'al, the fertility god of Canaan. The worship of this god was brought into Israel by Jezebel (cf. 1 Kgs. 16:21-32).

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:11-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:11-12 There is a switch from the PRONOUN "he" (Ezek. 26:11) to "they" (Ezek. 26:12) in these verses. Some have assumed a theological significance that this refers to subsequent besiegers of Tyre, like Alexander the Great, to whom the city fell in 332 B.C. See Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 276-278.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:13 This is an idiomatic way of asserting their society will cease (i.e. Isa. 23:16; 24:8,9). Tyre may have been renowned for her musicians (cf. Isa. 23:16).

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:14 "a place for the spreading of nets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:14 "a place for the spreading of nets" The citadel will be so completely destroyed that it will only be good for is drying fishermen's nets (cf. Ezek. 26:5). This was historically fulfilled in Alexander's conquest.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:15 "groan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:15 "groan" This VERB (BDB 60, KB 72) occurs three times in Ezekiel.

  1. 9:4, those who sigh and groan over Judah's sins
  2. 24:17, Ezekiel groans quietly over the death of his wife
  3. 26:15, the dying of Tyre groan loudly at their approaching death (cf. Job 24:12; Jer. 51:52; Ezek. 30:24). It occurs only one other time in the OT, Jer. 51:52. The NOUN (BDB 60) occurs in Ps. 12:5; 79:11; 102:20; Mal. 2:13.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:16 "they will sit on the ground"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:16 "they will sit on the ground" This is a sign of mourning (e.g. Lam. 2:10, esp. for a king, cf. Isa. 47:1).

Special Topic: Grieving Rites

▣ "trembling. . .tremble" This term (BDB 353, KB 350) denotes great fear. It is used twice (VERB and NOUN) in this verse. The ones trembling are the colonies which the Phoenicians had started all around the Mediterranean. These outposts of Phoenician culture were dependant on Tyre.

▣ "be appalled at you" This VERB (BDB 1030, KB 1563, Qal PERFECT with waw) denotes astonishment at YHWH's judgment (cf. Lev. 26:32; Job 17:8; Isa. 52:14; Jer. 50:13; Ezek. 26:16; 27:35; 28:19; 32:10; Dan. 8:27). This fear at the fall of a powerful commercial nation is used in Revelation 18.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:17 The questions about the first two lines of the lament are:

  1. are there two parallel VERBALS
    1. "perished"
    2. "ceased" (NET Bible)
  2. are there two parallel titles
    1. O inhabited one
    2. O renewed city
  3. or, is there one of each

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:17-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:17-18 This is a lamentation (BDB 884, cf. Ezek. 2:10; 19:1,14; 27:2,32; 32:2,16) in poetic form.

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:19 "the deep over you and the great waters"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:19 "the deep over you and the great waters" This refers to the chaotic waters of creation (cf. Gen. 1:2,6-7,9-10), which became known as Sheol or the holding place of the dead (i.e. "the pit," Ezek. 26:20; 31:16; Ps. 28:1; 30:3; 40:2; 88:4; 143:7; Prov. 1:12; Isa. 14:15; 38:18).

"The deep" is the Hebrew term tehom (BDB 1062 #3, KB 1690-91). A similar, but different, Hebrew root is personified as Tiamat in the Sumerian and Babylonian creation myths as the monster of chaos and the mother of the gods, wife of Apsu. She tried to kill all lesser gods that came forth from her.

Marduk killed her. Out of her body Marduk fashioned heaven and earth in the Babylonian Genesis account called Enuma Elish.

The Hebrews believed that water was the beginning element of creation (cf. Ps. 24:1; 104:6; 2 Pet. 3:5). It is never said to have been created. However, the Hebrew term is MASCULINE, not FEMININE and it is unrelated etymologically to Tiamat.

There are passages in the OT which describe YHWH in conflict with personified watery chaos (cf. Ps. 74:13-14; 89:9-10; 104:6-7; Isa. 51:9-10). However, these are always in poetical, metaphorical passages. Water is a crucial aspect of creation (cf. Ezek. 1:2b,6-7), but its creation is never mentioned.

Special Topic: The Dead, Where Are They?, I. B.

Special Topic: Ancient Near East Creation and Flood Myths

Special Topic: Waters

entries.title: Ezekiel 26:20 "I shall bring you down with those who go down to the pit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:20 "I shall bring you down with those who go down to the pit" This refers to Sheol, the holding place of the dead until judgment day. The rabbis speculated that it was divided into two sections—the righteous dead and the wicked dead.

This three-level worldview (earth for the living, below the earth for the dead, and heaven above, e.g. Ps. 139:8; Amos 9:2) was based on the burial practice of the Jews. The dead were buried, so they were in the ground (cf. Ezek. 31:14,16,18; 32:18,24). Smoke from the sacrifices and incense altars rose to God so heaven was up. This is metaphorical, not literal (e.g. Isa. 14:9-10). In reality Scripture reveals very little about the afterlife (heaven or hell), but focuses on choices, actions, and consequences of current reality!

Special Topic: The Dead, Where Are They?

NASB, NKJV  "I shall set glory in the land of the living"
NRSV  "or have a place in the land of the living"
TEV  "and take your place in the land of the
  living"
NJB  "or be restored to the land of the land
  of the living"
LXX  "nor rise (or stand) upon a land of life"
Peshitta  "and I will not cause your resurrection in the
  land of the living"
REB  "or take your place in the land of the living"

The MT has "and I will give beauty (BDB 840) in the land of the living," which does not make sense in this context, unless it is a statement of pride, like Ezek. 28:2,12. So, most modern English translations follow the Septuagint.

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter is part of a larger literary unit, 26:1-28:26. See note at 27:1.

  2. This chapter has two laments
    1. vv. 1-25
    2. vv. 26-36

  3. Ezekiel's knowledge of the trading centers and their known exports is absolutely amazing. This chapter forms one of the most detailed commercial chapters anywhere in ancient literature.
     Tyre was the transporter of goods, materials, and persons for the entire Mediterranian for hundreds of years. She grew wealthy and politically significant over time. In this period, after Neo-Babylon invasion, Tyre became the political and economic power of Canaan.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:2 "take up"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:2 "take up" This is a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 669, KB 724, cf. Ezek. 27:12; 19:1; 26:17).

▣ "lamentations" See note at Ezek. 26:17. See Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How To Read the Bible for All Its Worth, pp. 225-248.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:3 This chapter is an allegorical personification of Tyre as the beautiful and well-equipped merchant ship. A good title would be "The Flagship Tyre of the Materialistic Fleet."

▣ "I am perfect in beauty" This was the problem, the arrogance of the king of Tyre (cf. Ezek. 27:4,11; 28:2-5,15,17 and possibly Ezek. 26:20).

The JPSOA footnotes, p. 1093, suggest an emendation for the last line of poetry in v. 3, "O Tyre, you are a ship, Perfect in beauty" (also see NJB).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:5 Notice the poetic description of a sailing ship

  1. fir (juniper) from Senir, Ezek. 27:5
  2. cedar from Lebanon, Ezek. 27:5
  3. oaks from Bashan, Ezek. 27:6
  4. boxwood from Cyprus, Ezek. 27:6
  5. sails from Egypt, Ezek. 27:7
  6. awnings from Elishah (BDB 47), Ezek. 27:7
  7. rowers from Sidon and Arvad (BDB 71), Ezek. 27:8
  8. wise men from Tyre as pilots, Ezek. 27:8
  9. maintenance workers from Gebal (BDB 148), Ezek. 27:9

This ship was made of the best and most beautiful material and manned by the best possible crew.

▣ "Senir" This (BDB 972) is the Amorite term for Mount Hermon (cf. Deut. 3:9; 1 Chr. 5:23; Song of Songs 4:8).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:6 "of boxwood"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:6 "of boxwood" The MT reads "daughters of Ashurim," but by making the CONSTRUCT (BDB 123 and 81) into one word, "made with boxwood" (see UBS, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, p. 99). This tree is mentioned in Isa. 41:19; 60:13. A type of tree fits the context better than a place name.

27:7
NASB  "distinguishing mark"
NRSV  "ensign"
TEV  "easily recognized from afar"
NJB  "your flag"
REB, JPSOA  "that served you for sails"
Peshitta  "was made for your sails"

This term (BDB 651) normally stands for a military banner or sign. Here, it refers to a characteristic type of sail that denoted "the flagship of Tyre"!

▣ "purple" It was a very expensive dye made from the mollusk shell of Murex, which are found in abundance along this portion of the Phoenician coast.

Special Topic: ANE Sacred Colors

▣ "Elishnah" From Gen. 10:4 we learn this was a tribe of Javan (Greece, cf. 1 Chr. 1:7). It seems to refer to inhabitants of the Aegean Islands, possibly Cyprus. The NIV Study Bible (p. 1263) identifies it as a city on the east side of Cyprus, but this is speculation.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:8 "Arvad"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:8 "Arvad" This (BDB 71) is another off-shore fortified island about 100 miles north of Tyre inhabited by a Canaanite people group (cf. Gen. 10:18). It was a Phoenician aligned settlement (provided "powers" for the large Phoenician mercant ships, two sets on each side).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:9 "Gebal"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:9 "Gebal" This (BDB 148) is the modern city Byblos, which is located on the Mediterranean coast between Sidon and Arvad.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:10 "Persia and Lud and Put"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:10 "Persia and Lud and Put" These same countries had mercenaries in many armies (cf. Ezek. 30:5; 38:5; Jer. 46:9). Lud, in some translations, refers to North Africa and in others, to Asia Minor. Put, in the Septuagint, refers to the Libyans (i.e. North Africa), but from Gen. 10:6 it seems to be on the coast of Africa by the Red Sea. Some of these geographical sites can be identified with people from Genesis 10 who later become tribes, localities, and countries.

▣ "They hung shield and helmet in you" This was a type of standard decoration for military installations. Tyre used mercenaries who displayed their national military insignias (e.g. 1 Kgs. 10:16-17).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:10-25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:10-25 This section lists many nations. It is similar to Genesis 10. Some nations are listed as part of Tyre's military and some as her trading partners. It is somewhat hyperbolic to demonstrate Tyre's influence, power, and commercial reach.

  1. military
    1. Persia
    2. Lud
    3. Put
    4. Arvad
    5. Gammad
  2. trading partners
    1. Tarshish
      1. silver
      2. iron
      3. tin
      4. lead
    2. Javan, Tubal, and Meshech
      1. slaves
      2. bronze vessels
    3. Beth-togarmah
      1. horses
      2. mules
    4. Dedan and coastlands
      1. ivory
      2. ebony
    5. Syria (Aram)
      1. emeralds
      2. purple dye
      3. embroidered cloth
      4. fine linen
      5. coral
      6. rubies
    6. Judah and Israel
      1. wheat
      2. pannag (BDB 815, only here, some kind of food)
      3. honey
      4. olive oil
      5. balm/balsam resin
    7. Damascus
      1. wine
      2. white or reddish gray (BDB 856 construct 850) wool
    8. Vedan and Javan (spelled different from Ezek. 27:13)
      1. iron
      2. cassia spice
      3. calamus, aromatic reed ("sweet cane")
    9. Arabia and Kedar
      1. lambs
      2. rams
      3. goats
    10. Sheba and Raamah
      1. spices
      2. jewels
      3. gold
    11. Haran, Canneh, Eden, Sheba, Asshur, Chilmad
      1. blue cloths
      2. embroidered cloth
      3. carpets in many colors
      4. ropes

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:11 "Arvad"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:11 "Arvad" The place name "Arvad" (BDB 71) is mentioned in Gen. 10:18 (from Canaanite line, cf. 1 Chr. 1:16). It is a city located (as Tyre is) just off the coast on a small island in the northern area of Phoenician territory. See note at v. 7.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NET, LXX, Peshitta  "your army"
REB  "Cilicia"
NJB  "their army"
NRSV, JPSOA  "Helech"

The MT has "your army" (Helech). As a place name it is associatd with "Hilakku," a city in Cilicia (southeastern Turkey).

Some scholars see this as the same sity as "Hethlon" (cf. Ezek. 47:15; 48:1), which would be closer to Tyre.

NASB  "Gammadim"
NKJV, JPSOA  "Gammad"
NRSV, TEV  "Gamad"
NJB  "Gammadians"
Peshitta  "your army"
Targum of Jonathan  "Cappodocia"

This term (BDB 167, KB 196) is found only here. BDB assumes it means "valorous men," but the LXX and Peshitta assume "guardians" or "wall soldiers." It may be a place name referring to another coastal city near Arvad (NIV Study Bible, p. 1263).

The thrust of the phrase is that although Tyre had numerous mercenaries, she trusted the defense of her protective walls to her own soldiers (LXX, "your army was upon your walls").

▣ "they perfected your beauty" This is a repeated phrase. See note at Ezek. 27:4. It is significant because of its use in chapter 28 and even possibly Ezek. 26:20.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:12 "Tarshish"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:12 "Tarshish" It is surprising that this term (BDB 1077) appears to be a place name because it is also a person in Gen. 10:4. Several other persons from Genesis 10 are mentioned in this context (i.e. Elishah, Arvad). The term is used in several senses in Scripture.

  1. Persons
    1. grandson of Javan (Greece) and brother to Elishah in Gen. 10:4; 1 Chr. 1:7
    2. grandson of Benjamin in 1 Chr. 7:20
    3. one of the powerful seven princes of Persia in Esther 1:14
  2. Places
    1. Phoenician mining city in southern Spain on the Guadalquiver River (Tartessus)
    2. Phoenician colony in north Africa, Carthage (LXX translation of Ezek. 27:12)
    3. Phoenician colony in Indian Ceylon
    4. Phoenician colony on Sardina (city of Nora)
    5. an idiom for the end of the earth
  3. Things
    1. precious stones (cf. Exod. 28:20; 39:13; Ezek. 10:9; 28:13; Dan. 10:6; Rev. 21:20)
    2. special ships (cf. 1 Kgs. 10:22; 22:48; 2 Chr. 9:21; Ps. 48:7; Isa. 2:16; 23:1; 60:9)

Special Topic: Tarshish

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:13 "Javan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:13 "Javan" Because of the spelling "ionia" (BDB 402), most commentators refer it to Greece. It is spelled differently from the same word used in Ezek. 27:19 (BDB 402).

▣ "Tubal and Meshech" In Gen. 10:2 and 1 Chr. 1:5 these are listed as sons or descendants of Japheth, one of Noah's three sons.

  1. Gomer (his son Togarmah, cf. Ezek. 27:14; Gen. 10:3)
  2. Magog
  3. Madai
  4. Javan
  5. Tubal
  6. Meshech
  7. Tiras

The significance is that several of these are mentioned as tribes or peoples in Ezekiel 38-39 (i.e. #1,2,5,6). They were inhabitants of eastern Turkey (Anatolia). They are mentioned by

  1. Herodotus (3:94; 7:28)
  2. Josephus (Antiq. 1.6.1)

▣ "the lives of men" This refers to the slave trade (cf. Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:9, 10; Rev. 18:12).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:14 "Beth-togarmah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:14 "Beth-togarmah" From Gen. 10:3, we know that this was the name of a descendant of Japheth, one of the three sons of Gomer (1 Chr. 1:6). It is related to Gomer in Ezek. 38:6, where it is said to be "from the far north" (i.e. northern Anatolia or modern Turkey, or even farther north in Armenia).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:15 "Dedan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:15 "Dedan" This is a descendant of Ham (cf. Gen. 10:7; 1 Chr. 1:9) and a brother of Sheba (cf. Ezek. 38:13,14).

  1. The same group is mentioned in Ezek. 27:20 as an Arabian tribe (possibly related to a specific desert oasis close to Tema).
  2. The LXX changed it to Rhodes. This is supported by UBS Text Project, p. 89, but with a "C" rating.
  3. Because it is identified in context with "coast lands" (BDB 912). It is possible that it relates to a region north of Tyre known as "Danuna" in the Amarna letters (IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 713).

The UBS Text Project, p. 89, accepts the LXX, "Rhodians" (i.e. the island of Rhodes) as the original text (i.e. "C" rating). The REV and NRSV follow this.

  1. Dedanites (MT) ‒ בני דדן
  2. Rodanim (LXX) ‒ בני רדן
▣
NASB, NKJV, TEV  "Syria"
NRSV, REB, NJB, Peshitta  "Edom"
MT, JPSOA, NET  "Aram"

"Edom" is spelled אדם, while "Aram" is spelled ארם. As you can see the letters d and r are formed in similar ways and easily confused in copying. The MT has "Aram" (BDB 74), but the Hebrew translations "Aquila" and "Symmachus" have "Edom." Why Damascus is listed separately in Ezek. 27:18 is uncertain. Aram was a coalition of independent tribes/clans north of Palestine and west of Assyria. Damascus may have had special autonomy.

The UBS Text Project, p. 89, thinks "Edom" is original but only with a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

NASB, NKJV, TEV  "emeralds"
NRSV, JPSOA, NIV  "turquoise"
NJB, REB  "garnets"
JB, Josephus  "carbuncle"

This term (BDB 656) refers to some kind of precious stone (cf. Ezek. 28:13). It was one of the jewels in the High Priest's breastplate (cf. Exod. 28:13; 39:11).

▣ "rubies" This rare term (BDB 461) occurs only here and in Isa. 54:12. It may be related to the Aramaic root "to sparkle" or "a red-hot rod." Rubies were not common in this area of the world until a later date.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:17 Notice it says "Judah and the land of Israel." Judah was still (or until very recently) an existing nation, but Israel had been exiled by Assyria since 722 B.C. and was no longer a nation.

▣ "Minnith" This is a location (BDB 585) in Ammon (cf. Jdg. 11:33) which produced especially fine wheat.

NASB  "cakes"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "millet"
NJB, JPSOA  "pannag"
JB  "wax"
REB  "meal"

This term (BDB 815, KB 937) appears only here in the OT. In context it refers to some type of merchandise, probably food. In Akkadian the root means "pastry" or "cake."

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:18 "Helbon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:18 "Helbon" This (KB 316 II, i.e. "forest place") refers to a grape-growing area eleven miles north of Damascus. The modern name is Helbun.

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA  "white wool"
TEV  "Sahar"
NJB  "Zahar"
REB  "Suhar"
BDB  "reddish-grey"

The KB 1019 denotes the BDB meaning comes from Arabic root. It also notes that it can refer to a territory northwest of Damascus, called "es-Sahra."

27:19
NASB, NRSV, JPSOA  "Vedan"
NKJV, NJB, Peshitta  "Dan"
NIV  "Danites"

Both lexicons, BDB (255) and KB (259), assert the meaning as "uncertain."

  1. Some scholars think it is a place name near Medina, Arabia.
  2. Most assert a textual corruption.
  3. However, since it is linked to Javan (Greece) it may be another name for them (i.e. Homer and the History Channel video, "Decoding the Exodus").
  4. The Septuagint has "and wine from" instead of a name.

▣ "Uzal" This (LXX, "Asel") may be

  1. the capital of Yemen (BDB 23)
  2. a word for "yarn" (BDB 23)
  3. a city (Izalla) in Cilicia (IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 713).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:20-22 "Dedan, Arabia, Kedar, and Raamah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:20-22 "Dedan, Arabia, Kedar, and Raamah" These all refer to Arabian tribes.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:22 "Sheba and Raamah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:22 "Sheba and Raamah" These two trading partners are mentioned in

  1. Gen. 10:7, as descendants of Ham from Cush (cf. Isa. 43:3)
  2. Isa 60:6, with Midian and Ephah
  3. Ezek. 38:13, with Dedan

The AB suggests these people were from the southwest corner of the Arabian peninsula (p. 1171). Both Ps. 72:15 and Isa. 60:6 mention they traded in gold and frankincense (cf. Jer. 6:20). Ezekiel 27:22 mentions precious jewel stones as their wares.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:23 All of these locations are in Mesopotamia and most are associated with Assyria. The Jewish Study Bible asserts that the first three of these are all Syrian cities (p. 1094, cf. Gen. 12:4; 10:10; 2 Kgs. 19:12; Isa. 10:9; 37:12; Amos 1:5).

▣ "Asshur" Asshur (BDB 78) is a son of Shem (cf. Gen. 10:22; 1 Chr. 1:17). It becomes a region synonymous with Assyria. One of the national gods of Assyria is named Asshur. Asshur became the name of one of the capitals of Assyria.

▣ "Chilmad" This place (BDB 484) is unknown. The Targums revocalize the consonants and come up with "all Media" (REB and Kimchi; see Anchor Bible Dictionary, vol. 1, p. 908).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:24 "clothes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:24 "clothes" Another rare term possibly "clothes" (BDB 166). The NOUN is found only here and the VERB (i.e. "to wrap") only in 2 Kgs. 2:8. It refers to a large garment wrapped around the body (i.e. same meaning in Aramaic, Syrian, Arabic, and Persian, NIDOTTE, vol. 1., p. 865).

▣ "carpets of many colors" This phrase has two rare words.

  1. "Carpets" (BDB 170) possibly means chests (cf. NKJV). It is found only here and in Esther 3:9 and 4:7, where it is translated "treasury."
  2. The phrase "many colors" (BDB 140) occurs only here. In Arabic it denotes a rope made of two colors. The trilateral Semitic root means "to twist."
27:25
NASB, NKJV, TEV, NIV  "the carriers for your merchandise"
NRSV, NASB (margin)  "travelers for your trade"
NJB  "soiled in your business"
JPSOA  "in the service of your trade"
REB  "caravans of your imports"

The root (BDB 1003-1004, KB 1449-1452) has several meanings.

  1. to travel, to journey
  2. to behold, to regard
  3. (unknown, Ps. 92:12)
  4. head of cattle, bullock
  5. wall

Context determines meaning. In this context #1 fits best. There are no guarantees on exact meaning for roots that

  1. are rare
  2. are used in poetic texts
  3. are uncertain of the origin of the Semitic root

Even ancient cognate languages are unable to precisely define all Hebrew terms.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:26 "the east wind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:26 "the east wind" See note at Ezek. 17:10.

Special Topic: The East Wind

▣ "into great waters" Again this may refer to the chaotic waters of creation. Notice Ezek. 27:34 "broken by the seas in the depth of the waters." See note at Ezek. 26:3,19-21.

Special Topic: Waters

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:26-36
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:26-36 This starts the second poetic lament of chapter 27 (cf. Ezek. 27:3b-9). This lament first lists all of the people/groups mentioned in the first poem (those who built, manned the ships of Tyre and those who guarded the city). They will all be shipwrecked with the "great ship of Tyre." Then in Ezek. 27:30-32, these same groups mourn for Tyre's destruction (i.e. and their own).

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:30-32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:30-32 This is a series of mourning rites.

  1. cry bitterly, Ezek. 27:30,31,32
  2. put dust on their heads
  3. wallow in ashes
  4. pull out their hair
  5. put on sackcloth

Special Topic: Grieving Rites

27:32
NASB, TEV, JPSOA  "like her who is silent in the midst of the sea"
NKJV, NRSV, NAB  "destroyed in the midst of the sea"
NJB  "far out to sea"
Peshitta  "built in the midst of the sea"
  1. The Hebrew root דמה has several meanings (KB 225).
    1. to be like or resemble
    2. to be silent or still
    3. to cease to exist or be destroyed
  2. BDB 199 has "one silenced, brought to silence (destroyed)."
  3. Either option fits the context.
  4. UBS Text Project, p. 92, thinks option #2 is original.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:34
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:34 Tyre is lost in the depth (BDB 771) of the chaotic waters sent by YHWH. The ship, the contents, and all on board are lost!

Special Topic: Waters

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:35 Trembling takes hold of fearful people (cf. Ezek. 32:10; Job 18:20; also notice Exod. 15:14,15; Isa. 21:3; 33:13; Jer. 13:21). Note the parallel in Ezek. 26:16.

entries.title: Ezekiel 27:36 "The merchants among the people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:36 "The merchants among the people" Ezekiel's knowledge of the trading centers and their known exports is absolutely amazing. This chapter forms one of the most detailed commercial chapters anywhere in ancient literature.

Tyre was the transporter of goods, materials, and persons for the entire Mediterranean for hundreds of fyears. She grew wealthy and politcally significant over time. In this period after Neo-Babylon invasion, Tyre became the political and economic power of Canaan.

▣ "hiss at you" This (BDB 1056) is an audible gesture of astonishment (cf. Jer. 19:8; 49:17; 50:13). It also can be used of derision (cf. 2 Chr. 29:8; Jer. 25:9,18; 29:18; 51:37; Lam. 2:15; Micah 6:16). In context it is hard to make a distinction between astonishment and a sense of the appropriateness of what has happened.

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
