28:25-26 28:25-26 28:25-26 28:25-26 28:25-26

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Ezekiel 28 is part of a larger literary unit (i.e. Ezekiel 26-28), which denotes the fall of Phoenicia.

  2. Phoenicia, once a friend of Israel (i.e. supplied materials and artisans for the temple in Jerusalem), became a pagan empire exporting Ba'al worship to Israel (i.e. Jezebel, queen of the Israelite King Ahab, cf. 1 Kgs. 16:29-34; 18-19).

  3. Phoenicia (like Edom) was an immoral, pagan nation. Her pride and slave trade made her an example of human society functioning apart from God.

  4. For many years I saw this chapter and Isaiah 14 as referring to the origin of Satan, but in context this cannot be. It is true that human leaders and Satan share the problem of pride, arrogance, and rebellion. Because the descriptions from the Garden of Eden are also used of the person of chapter 28, it is obvious to me this was the only passage in the Bible that described the fall of Satan.
     But wait, this chapter is about the king of Tyre, as Isaiah 14 is about the king of Neo-Babylon. Yet, what about the Garden of Eden descriptions? The king of Tyre was not in the Garden of Eden; he was not a covering cherub!
     The answer to this quandary came home to me when I realized that Pharaoh is also described in Garden of Eden imagery in Ezekiel 31. Ezekiel uses Edenic imagery. Because I am a conservative Christian who honors and respects Scripture, without even thinking about it, I assumed that for it to be true it must be "literal." I have come to realize it is "literary." Here are the three books that have helped me deal with my American, twentieth century, conservative biases.
    1. How to Read the Bible For All Its Worth by Gordon Fee and Doug Stuart
    2. Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic by D. Brent Sandy
    3. The Language and Imagery of the Bible by G. B. Caird

Authorial intent, literary and historical context, and genre are the keys in interpreting the Bible!

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:2 "Son of man" See Special Topic: Son of Man

▣ "say to the leader of Tyre" At this time the leader of Tyre was Ittobaal, who had been the High Priest of Astarte and who assassinated the heir of Hiram I. Hiram's daughter was Jezebel, who was married to Ahab, king of Israel. Sennacherib appointed a later descendant, Ittobaal II (also known as Ethbaal II and Ithobalus II), king of Tyre (590-543 B.C.).

Tyre was the capital of the Phoenician empire. Tyrians were extremely arrogant because of their commercial prowess and their kings claimed to be descendants of the gods. This was also the claim of the Pharaohs of Egypt.

This section has caused great consternation to commentators. It seems to refer to a human king, but is described in supernatural terms (cf. Isa. 14:12-20). It is possible that Isaiah 14 refers to a military power that has gone beyond the bounds of pride and Ezekiel 28 refers to a commercial power that has gone beyond the bounds of pride (cf. Ezek. 28:2,9,16).

▣ "Because your heart is lifted up" See Special Topic: Heart

▣ "is lifted up" This VERB (BDB 146, KB 170, Qal PERFECT) can have two senses.

  1. positive
    1. God, Isa. 5:16
    2. Messiah, Isa. 52:13
    3. God's ways, Isa. 55:9
    4. God's true followers, 2 Chr. 17:6
  2. negative
    1. 2 Chr. 26:16; 32:25
    2. Ps. 131:1 (the psalmist asserts he is not)
    3. Prov. 18:12
    4. Isa. 3:16
    5. Jer. 13:15
    6. Ezek. 16:50; 28:2,5,17
    7. Zeph. 3:11
  3. the NOUN is also used of haughty people
    1. 2 Chr. 32:26
    2. Ps. 10:4
    3. Prov. 16:18
    4. Jer. 48:29
  4. as is the ADJECTIVE
    1. 1 Sam. 2:3
    2. Ps. 101:5; 138:6
    3. Prov. 16:5
    4. Eccl. 7:8
    5. Isa. 5:15

The major problem of mankind (and some angels) is pride (cf. Ezek. 16:49; 24:21; 27:3; 28:2-6,9,17; Gen. 3:5; Isa. 10:12; 14:13,14; 23:8-12; 25:11-12; Jer. 48:29-30; Daniel 2-4, esp. 4:29-30; Zeph. 2:8-11; 3:11; 1 Tim. 3:6). Notice the Proverbs that deal with this sin: 11:2; 13:10; 16:18; 29:23.

I think pride, arrogance, and self-centeredness are the epitome of the attitude of independence and self-achievement, which characterizes the fall of Genesis 3 (see Special Topic: The Fall). Salvation is a restoration of the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:26-27) from the original creation. Intimate fellowship with God, for which humans were created, is possible again, even now in a fallen world. The evidence that salvation/conversion has occurred is that the new creation is selfless, not self-centered. Selflessness is analogous to Christlikeness, which is God's irreducible will for every Christian!

▣ "I am a god" Also see Ezek. 28:6 and 9. This possibly reflects the kings of Tyre's (esp. Ittbaal II) claims that they were part god (i.e. El), like Hercules. Tyre's chief deity, Melqart (i.e. "king of the city") was called the Tyrian Hercules.

▣ "I sit in the seats of the gods" This phrase is parallel with the next one. It is possibly a reference to Poseidon or Neptune.

▣ "In the heart of the seas" Tyre's unique physical location was a source of security and pride.

▣ "Yet you are a man and not God" Because of this phrase, repeated three times for emphasis in Ezek. 28:4, 8, and 9, it is obvious that this refers to the political leader of Tyre as representative of the whole nation. This would not fit Satan at all! But it might fit the political leader of 2 Thess. 2:4 (i.e. the Man of Lawlessness, who I think refers to Nero; see my exegetical notes there).

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:3 "you are wiser than Daniel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:3 "you are wiser than Daniel" To whom does this refer? Daniel, who was a contemporary of Ezekiel in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar II, or to the famous Ugarit Danel of the Ugaritic Rash Shamra texts. See full note at Ezek. 14:14. When all is said and done, I still must go with Daniel of the Bible, but it is not an easy choice. The name "Daniel" here is spelled differently than the name "Daniel" in the biblical book. See note at BDB 193, #3 and #4.

There is an obvious purposeful literary allusion to Genesis 1-3 in this chapter. The wisdom of the tree of knowledge (cf. Gen. 2:9,17; 3:3,11) here denotes commercial skills (cf. Ezek. 28:3-5). It was a wisdom that destroyed!

Notice all the different terms used for human intelligence in Ezek. 28:3-10.

  1. wiser than Daniel, ADJECTIVE, BDB 314
  2. no secret hidden (cf. Dan. 8:26; 12:4,9)
  3. wisdom, BDB 315
  4. understanding, BDB 108
  5. great wisdom, BDB 913, 315
  6. the beauty of your wisdom, BDB 421, 315
  7. possibly "splendor" (BDB 422) is parallel to wisdom in Ezek. 28:7

Number 2 is obviously sarcasm (cf. E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech in the Bible, p. 810) or all are a series of self-descriptions.

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:3-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:3-5 JPSOA sees vv. 3-5 as a parenthetical insertion of the King of Tyre's self-assertion and YHWH's evaluation (vv. 2,6).

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:4 "wisdom. . .acquired riches"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:4 "wisdom. . .acquired riches" There seem to be three sources of the arrogance of the Tyrian people: (1) wisdom; (2) power and wealth; and (3) beauty (cf. Ezek. 28:5,17; 27:3,4,10-11,25).

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:7 "strangers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:7 "strangers" The term (BDB 266, KB 267, Qal PARTICIPLE) refers to foreign invaders (cf. Isa. 1:7; 25:2,5; 29:5; 61:5; Jer. 5:19; 30:8; 51:2,51; Lam. 5:2; Ezek. 7:21; 11:9; 16:32; 28:7,10; 30:12; 31:12) who worship foreign (i.e. "strange") gods (cf. Deut. 32:16; Isa. 17:10; Jer. 2:25; 3:13; 5:19).

▣ "most ruthless of nations" Here this (BDB 792, lit. "terror-striking") refers to the Neo-Babylonians (cf. Ezek. 30:11; 31:12; 32:12; Isa. 13:11). Nebuchadnezzar II besieged the island fortress for over a decade and destroyed the city on the mainland (cf. Ezek. 26:3-14; Hab. 1:6-8). Apparently the island fortress finally surrendered.

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:8 "the pit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:8 "the pit" See Special Topic: The Dead, Where Are They? (Sheol/Hades, Gehenna, Tartarus).

▣ "you will die the death of" This verse is referring to drowning (cf. Ezek. 27:27,34). Remember, Tyre is depicted as a beautiful, expensive cargo ship in chapter 27, which is destroyed by YHWH's east wind and sinks with all cargo and all hands.

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:9 "Will you still say"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:9 "Will you still say" The shocking claim to deity is emphasized in the Hebrew by a repetition of the Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the IMPERFECT VERB of the same root, "say" (BDB 55, KB 65).

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:10 "the death of the uncircumcised"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:10 "the death of the uncircumcised" Since all peoples of Canaan practiced circumcision, mostly at puberty, this must refer to something else (cf. Ezek. 31:18; 32:19,21).

  1. uncircumcised people were thought to be residents of the lowest part of the underworld (JPSOA footnote)
  2. a special category of the dead, like the unburied, possibly referring to children who died before puberty

The term "death" is PLURAL, which denotes an awful death.

Special Topic: Circumcision

▣ "‘For I have spoken!' declares the Lord God" God's word is sure (cf. Ezek. 5:17; 6:10; 12:25,28; 17:24; 21:32; 22:14; 24:14; 26:5,14; 30:12; 34:24; 36:36; 37:14; 39:5,8; Isa. 55:9-11)!

Special Topic: Lord (adon and kurios)

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:11 This is a new oracle, marked by the repeated literary marker "the word of the Lord came to me saying."

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:12 "lamentation"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:12 "lamentation" This is a funeral dirge, noted by a distinctive poetic beat. It is common in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 2:10; 19:1,14; 26:17; 27:2,32; 28:12; 32:2,16). See note at Ezek. 2:10.

▣ "the king of Tyre" This (BDB 572) is parallel to Ezek. 28:2, "leader" (lit. "prince," BDB 617 only here in Ezekiel; only once in Isa. 55:4 and Jer. 20:1).

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:13 "Eden" See Special Topic: Eden and John H. Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, pp. 124-125.

▣ "Every precious stone was your covering" This seems to be an allusion to the ephod (i.e. breastplate) of the High Priest (cf. Exod. 28:17,20; 39:10-14). Although the Masoretic Text lists only nine jewels, the Septuagint lists all twelve (sometimes the LXX reflects the more ancient text). The king of Trye is symbolized as

  1. priestly
  2. kingly
  3. wealthy

Special Topic: Septuagint

▣ "settings and sockets" The MT has "tambourines" (BDB 1074, KB 1772, both lexicons say this is a textual corruption).

Sockets (BDB 666, refers to a jeweler's work of boring a hole to mount a jewel, see KJ, NKJV, ASB, JB. The VERB means "piercing" or "boring").

▣ "On the day that you were created" It is assumed that the angelic realm was created (cf. Ezek. 28:15; Ps. 104:4; Heb. 1). Biblical faith is not an eternal dualism like Zoroastrianism, but the Bible is silent on when, how, and why of the origin of evil. The Bible focuses on the actions and motives of humans on this planet.

The two phrases "on the day that you were created" (cf. Ezek. 28:15) and "I placed you there" (cf. Ezek. 28:14) denote the authority and sovereignty of YHWH. Evil has no independent existence. Evil acts at YHWH's permission (cf. 1 Kgs. 22:19-28; Job 1-2; Zechariah 3).

Special Topic: Angels and Demons

Special Topic: The Demonic in the OT

▣
NASB, NKJV  "You were. . .cherub"
TEV  "angel to guard you"
NRSV  "with. . .cherub. . .you"
NET  "you there with. . .cherub"
JPSOA  "you as cherub"
Peshitta, LXX  "you were with. . .cherub"
REB  "cherub as your guardian"

The textual confusion among the translations is, does this phrase start with

  1. you ‒ את
  2. with ‒ את

I think the King of Tyre is being compared to Adam, who was at first guarded by a cherub, but later after he sinned, was expelled from God's presence by the same cherub.

The UBS Text Project, p. 94, thinks option #1 is original (i.e. "B" rating, some doubt).

▣ "the anointed cherub" This form of the NOUN, "anointed" (ממשׁח, BDB 603, KB 596 II) is found only here in the OT (normal form is משׁיח). Therefore, its meaning is uncertain. Here are some theories.

  1. cherub of expansion (BDB; REB, "towering")
  2. cherub that covereth (i.e. "sheltering," Peshitta; "shielding," JPSOA)
  3. cherub with far-reaching wings
  4. cherub of sparkling (i.e. "to illuminate," from Akkadian root, KB)

The LXX has "with the Cherubim," not one of them (see NET Bible footnote #2 and NRSV).

Cherubim are involved in several aspects of OT history.

  1. they guard the Garden of Eden after mankind's fall, Gen. 3:24
  2. they face inward on the Mercy Seat, the place of propitiation, Exod. 25:8; Ps. 80:1; 99; Isa. 37:16
  3. they form YHWH's throne chariot, 2 Sam. 22:13; Ps. 18:10; Ezek. 1, 10

The descriptions in Ezek. 1:5-28 and 10:15-20 are similar to Rev. 4:6-9. However, Revelation does seem to blend the description of the Cherubim with the Seraphim of Isaiah 6.

Special Topic: Cherubim

Special Topic: Seraphim

▣ "You were on the holy mountain of God" This is a different imagery from the Garden of Eden (Ezek. 28:13). This refers either to Mount Sinai (cf. Exodus 19-20; Ezek. 20:40) or to the mountain in the north where God dwells (cf. Ezek. 28:16; Ps. 48:2; Isa. 14:13-14, similar to Ugaritic Ba'al poetry). Note that Psalm 50:2 uses similar descriptions of Mt. Zion (i.e. "perfect in beauty," cf. Ezek. 28:12).

It was common in Ancient Near Eastern religious thought to view the gods as living on mountain tops (cf. Gilgamesh Epic). This is especially true for the Ugaritic Ba'al myth poems from Ras Shamra. The gods met and lived on a northern mountain called Saphon or Zaphon. Ba'al had a throne there built by Anath. The male god of Phoenician fertility worship was called Baal Saphon. This name has been found in Phoenician colonies around the Mediterranean. This northern mountain tradition (i.e. imagery is from the north pole, around which all the heavenly zodiac rotates), totally unrelated to Israel's holy Mt. Moriah (cf. Ezek. 20:40), seems to be the source of the imagery of both Isa. 14:13-15 and Ezek. 28:14,16. See Roland de Vaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 2, pp. 279-281.

▣ "the stones of fire" This (BDB 6 CONSTRUCT BDB 77) can be translated "glittering gems." Some commentators try to link these with the jewels of Ezek. 28:13, but that is a different literary setting. This fire may be associated with YHWH's personal presence (cf. Exod. 3:2; 13:21,22; 14:24; 19:18; 24:17; Deut. 1:33; 4:11,12,15,24,33,36; 9:3).

Special Topic: Shekinah

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:13-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:13-15 There seems to be a series of statements that go beyond the possibility of a mere human king.

  1. the seal of perfection, Ezek. 28:12
  2. full of wisdom and beauty, Ezek. 28:12
  3. in the Garden of Eden, Ezek. 28:13
  4. clothed with colored/gems, Ezek. 28:13
  5. an anointed cherub who covers, Ezek. 28:14,16
  6. in God's presence on God's mountain, Ezek. 28:14
  7. blameless, Ezek. 28:15

Could this be the first mention of Satan and his origin (see Origen, Tertullian, and Jerome)? All believers want more information about the origin and purpose of evil, see Special Topic: Personal Evil. However, this would be a strange context (i.e. God's judgment on surrounding nations) to be the only biblical revelation on this subject. Pride and arrogance are characteristics of this fallen reality. YHWH judges pride! Ezekiel uses hyperbolic language from the Garden of Eden, not only here related to the king of Tyre, but also in chapter 31, related to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. See Contextual Insights, D.

Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:15 "blameless"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:15 "blameless" This is a sacrificial term (BDB 1071) for "unblemished" (e.g. Ezek. 43:22). Here the term denotes an original innocence. Humans were not created sinful, but "good" (cf. Gen. 1:31). Evil was an invader into original creation (cf. Genesis 3). This phrase relates to Ezek. 28:12-13. We learn from

  1. Ezek. 28:17 that pride corrupted original innocence and wisdom (see note at Ezek. 28:3)
  2. Ezek. 28:18 that unfair and violent trade practices (cf. Ezek. 28:16) brought YHWH's judgment

Hyperbole and history are mixed together for powerful poetry.

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:16 "by the abundance of your trade"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:16 "by the abundance of your trade" Obviously this is a reference to the historical king of Tyre (cf. Ezek. 28:18).

▣ "Therefore I cast you as profane

From the mountain of God" Notice YHWH's sovereign judgment. The term "profane" (BDB 320, KB 319) means "polluted" and "defeated." This is a priestly word that Ezekiel uses often (32 times).

Note that this is not the same imagery (i.e. Garden of Eden) as Ezek. 28:13. This refers to a northern holy mountain. See full note at Ezek. 28:14.

NASB, NKJV, REB  "covering cherub"
NRSV, NIV  "the guardian cherub"
TEV  "the angel who guarded"
NJB  "guardian winged creature"
JPSOA  "shielding cherub"
LXX  "the cherub brought thee out"
Peshitta  "sheltering cherub"
NET  "the guardian cherub expelled you"

The FEMININE NOUN "covering" (BDB 697, KB 605) is found only here, "raiment" or "wrapping." The MASCULINE form means "covering" or "screen" (i.e. used of the screens of the tabernacle, cf. Exod. 22:16; 35:17; 38:18; 30:40; 40:8,33; Num. 3:26). In Exod. 25:20 it deontes the wings of the cherub over the Ark (i.e. acting as guards).

The term (BDB 697 I) also denotes the covering with YHWH's wings as imagery for protection. The cherubim protected the Garden of Eden in Gen. 3:24 or, more probably, protected the tree of life from Adam and Eve, lest they eat from it in the spiritual condition in which they find themselves (i.e. estrangement from God). So in this sense the cherub protects mankind from itself!

I must admit I am attracted to the Septuagint's understanding that the referent in this poetry is to Adam, who was escorted out of the Garden by a cherub (cf. James Moffatt translation and Edgar J. Goodspeed's translation of Ezek. 28:14, "I placed you with the guardian Cherubim on the holy hill of God"). See NET Bible footnote at v. 14, p. 1509, footnote #2.

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:17 "I cast you to the ground;
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:17 "I cast you to the ground;

 I put you before kings" This again stresses the sovereignty of YHWH (cf. Ezek. 28:18). The mention of kings may

  1. be an allusion to Ezek. 26:16 (Tyre's trading partners, cf. Ezek. 28:19)
  2. be an allusion to the multi-national mercenary army of Neo-Babylon

Number 1 fits the context best.

Also note that the first phrase could be translated "I cast you to the earth," implying a fall from heaven (i.e. God's mountain), but probably it is imagery for rejection.

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:18 "You profaned your sanctuaries"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:18 "You profaned your sanctuaries" The TEV has "You did such evil in buying and selling that your places of worship were corrupted." This is the only Bible text that uses "profane" in connection with a pagan sanctuary. One cannot separate life and worship!

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:20-24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:20-24 This is the judgment against Sidon, another Phoenician city linked with Tyre.

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:21 As Ezek. 28:2 starts out with a command "say" (BDB 55, KB 65,Qal IMPERATIVE), so too, this judgment starts with two commands.

  1. Set your face against, BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 6:2; 13:7; 15:7; 20:46; 21:2; 29:2; 35:2; 38:2
  2. Prophesy, BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 4:7; 11:4; 13:17; 25:2; 29:2; 34:2; 35:2; 36:6; 38:2; 39:1
28:22
NASB, NKJV, LXX, Peshitta  "I shall be glorified"
NRSV, JPSOA, NIV  "I will gain glory"
NJB, REB  "I will show My glory"

Ezekiel is all about the glory (paralleled with "My holiness") of YHWH! The glory is for the purpose of revelation. YHWH wants the people of Phoenicia to know Him. Judgment is an instrument of revelation (i.e. "I shall manifest My holiness in her," cf. Ezek. 28:25). He is always acting for the redemption of those created in His image and likeness!

Special Topic: Glory (kabod)

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:25,26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:25,26 The prophet again speaks of the hope of the restored people, the restored temple, and the restored covenant (cf. Ezek. 11:17-20; 20:40-44). After the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple, Ezekiel's message changed to one of restoration. He even illustrates the New Covenant concept in Ezek. 36:22-36. A new day is dawning!

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:25 "My servant Jacob"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:25 "My servant Jacob" See Special Topic: My Servant and Special Topic: Israel (the name)

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:26 "They will live in it securely. . .live securely"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:26 "They will live in it securely. . .live securely" This term "securely" (BDB 105) is repeated for emphasis. It reflects YHWH's earlier promises (cf. Lev. 25:18,19; 26:5; Ps. 4:8; Jer. 23:5-6; 32:37; Ezek. 34:25-28; 38:8,11,14; 39:26; Zech. 14:11).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why was God so angry at Tyre?
  2. Did Tyre ever fall to Nebuchadnezzar II?
  3. What is a cherub?
  4. Does the chapter describe the fall of Satan? Why or why not?

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:1 There is a series of dates mentioned in connection with this literary unit related to YHWH's judgment on Egypt (i.e. Ezek. 29:1-32:32). See note at Contextual Insights, B.

entries.title: Ezekiel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
EZEKIEL 29

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
  Oracles Against the Nations
(25:1-32:32)
Judgment of Egypt Proclamation Against Egypt Against Egypt Prophecy Against Egypt Against Egypt
29:1-7 29:1-7 29:1-7 29:1-6a 29:1-7
(3b-7) (3b-5) (3b-7) (3b-7)
(6-7) 29:6b-9a
29:8-9b 29:8-16 29:8-9b 29:8-16
29:9b-12
29:9c-12 29:9c-12
29:13-16 29:13-16 29:13-16
Babylonia Will Plunder Egypt King Nebuchadnezzar Will Conquer Egypt
29:17-20 29:17-20 29:17-20 29:17-20 29:17
29:18-20
29:21 29:21 29:21 29:21 29:21

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. The prophecies against Egypt run from Ezek. 29:1 through 32:32. Egypt was an active political influence during this period of Judean history. She tried to offer political security against Neo-Babylon. Egypt promised aid to Judah and Tyre; she promised more than she could perform (cf. Isa. 30:1-3; 31:1-3; Jer. 2:18,36; Lam. 4:17).

  2. The characteristic literary marker, "the word of the Lord came to me saying," occurs seven times in this literary unit. They mark off different prophecies.
    1. Ezek. 29:1 (587 B.C.)
    2. Ezek. 29:17 (571 B.C.)
    3. Ezek. 30:1
    4. Ezek. 30:20
    5. Ezek. 31:1
    6. Ezek. 32:1
    7. Ezek. 32:17
      All are dated except number 3, why is unknown.

  3. The first date (i.e. Ezek. 29:1) is about a year after Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem began. Apparently Egypt fielded her army against Nebuchadnezzar's forces (cf. Jer. 37:7), but quickly retreated. See Special Topic: Kings of Neo-Babylon

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:2 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

Special Topic: Son of Man

▣ "set your face against" See note at Ezek. 28:21.

▣ "set. . .prophesy. . .speak" These are all commands.

  1. "set," BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "prophesy," BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  3. "speak," Ezek. 29:3, BDB 180, KB 210, Piel IMPERATIVE

These are not Ezekiel's words nor his message!

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:3 "the Lord God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:3 "the Lord God" This is the recurrent title for Deity (i.e. Adonai YHWH), used so often in the book of Ezekiel.

Special Topic: Lord (adon and kurios)

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

▣ "Pharaoh" This (BDB 829, KB 971) is the characteristic title for Egyptian kings starting with the Eighteenth Dynasty. It means "the great house" (i.e. royal family).

▣ "That has said, ‘My Nile is mine, and I myself have made it'" As the king of Tyre claimed deity (cf. Ezek. 28:2,9), so too, the Pharaohs of Egypt (cf. Ezek. 29:9b). The name of the Pharaoh at that time was Hophra or Apries (589-570 B.C.). Herodotus mentions his claim to divine power in Hist. 2.169. The Nile and the sun were the chief deities of Egypt (i.e. depending on the city and the particular Pharaoh).

Special Topic: KIngs of Egypt

▣
NASB  "the great monster"
NKJV  "O great monster"
NRSV, LXX, Peshitta  "the great dragon"
REB  "you great monster"
NJB  "the great crocodile"
TEV  "you monster crocodile"
JPSOA  "mighty monster"

This term ("tanin," BDB 1072, KB 1764; "jackal" does not fit the context) means

  1. serpent, Exod. 7:9,1012; Deut. 32:33; Ps. 91:13; see Special Topic: The Serpent
  2. dragon, Neh. 2:13; Jer. 51:34; see Special Topic: The Great Red Dragon
  3. sea/river monster, Gen. 1:21; Job 7:12; Ps. 74:13; 148:7. It is parallel to Leviathan (cf. Psalm 74:13-14). It is used as a metaphor for Egypt in Isa. 27:1; 51:9,10; Ezek. 29:3; 32:2; see Special Topic: Leviathan

The two great river systems of the Ancient Near East were the cradles of civilization (i.e. the Nile and the Tigris/Euphrates).

Tanin (BDB 1072) is parallel with

  1. Leviathan, Ps. 74:13-14; Isa. 27:1
  2. Rahab, Ps. 89:9-10; Isa. 30:7; 51:9
  3. Bashan, Ps. 68:22; Amos 9:3 (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 87)

The context shows us that "serpent, dragon, sea-monster" (תנין, BDB 1072) is a better word choice than "jackal" (תן, BDB 1072, KB 1759, which is supported by the UBS Text Project, p. 95; though both meanings are philologically possible).

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:3-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:3-7 This is a poetic lamentation (i.e. funeral dirge).

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:4 "hook"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:4 "hook" This (BDB 296) can mean

  1. thorn or thistle, cf. 2 Kgs. 14:9; Prov. 26:9; Isa. 34:13; Hosea 9:6
  2. here, imageries for meat or fish hooks ‒ these were used (first by the Assyrians) to control and humiliate people being taken into exile/slavery (cf. Isa. 37:29; Ezek. 19:4,9; 29:4; 38:4).

▣ "the fish of your rivers cling to your scales" This refers to politically allied, but weaker, nations.

29:5
NASB, NKJV  "gathered"
NRSV, NJB, Peshitta  "buried"
TEV, JPSOA  "unburied"
NIV  "picked up"
REB  "none to give you burial"

The MT has "gathered" (BDB 867, KB 1062, Niphal IMPERFECT, which the UBS Text Project, p. 96, gives a "B" rating). "Buried" is found in some Hebrew manuscripts and the Aramaic Targums.

Proper burial (i.e. mummification and preservation) was a major requirement for happiness in the afterlife in Egyptian theology. Egyptian leaders were enamored with this issue (i.e. The Egyptian Book of the Dead). The great pyramids served this function as secure burial places for the elite.

The prophetic theme of animals and birds eating the fallen is common in Jeremiah (cf.Jer. 7:33; 9:22; 15:3; 16:4; 19:7; 34:20) and Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 29:5; 32:4; 33:27; 39:4,17-18). This seems to be a fulfillment of Deut. 28:26.

Notice the things that YHWH will do to Egypt, symbolized as a sea monster.

  1. cast forth into the wilderness
  2. along with all her supporters (v. 4)
  3. will fall in an open field
  4. will not be gathered
  5. will not be buried

Special Topic: Burial Practices

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:4-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:4-8 These verses describe what YHWH will do to the arrogant leaders of Egypt.

  1. I shall put hooks in your jaws, Ezek. 29:4
  2. I shall make fish cling to your scales, Ezek. 29:4 (twice)
  3. I shall bring you up out of the midst of your rivers, Ezek. 29:4
  4. I shall abandon you and all your fish to the wilderness, Ezek. 29:5
    1. fall in open field
    2. be gathered for food
      (1) beasts
      (2) birds
  5. I shall bring a sword upon you, Ezek. 29:6,11
    1. man
    2. beasts

Notice all the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR NOUNS. YHWH is the one and only true God. He alone can act in judgment. The mighty river beast is brought onto the land where he is helpless and will die. He will be eaten by the creatures of the wilderness.

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:6 "Then all the inhabitants of Egypt will know that I am the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:6 "Then all the inhabitants of Egypt will know that I am the Lord" This was the purpose of the ten plagues (each against an Egyptian deity, the same is true of the creation account of Genesis 1's condemnation of Babylonian astral deities). All humans are made in God's image and likeness (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27)! All were created for fellowship with God (i.e. Gen. 3:8)! Tragically in the OT, often it is judgment (cf. Ezek. 29:9-10) that reveals YHWH!

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ "they have been only a staff made of reed" This is imagery for weakness and inability (cf. Isa. 36:6). Egypt was a weak security partner (cf. Isa. 30:1-3; 31:1-3; Jer. 37:7).

29:7
NASB, NKJV  "you broke and made all their loins quake"
NRSV  "made all their legs unsteady"
Peshitta, JPSOA  "you would break, and make all their loins
  unsteady"
NJB, REB  "you broke, making all their limbs give way"
LXX  "thou wast utterly broken, and didst crush
  the loins of them all"

The MT has "you broke and you made to stand them all their loins." Most modern translations follow the Peshitta or Septuagint. The question is whether this phrase is sarcastic (God made them stand) or literal (God caused them to fall). The context is related to God's judgment on Egypt. Egypt promised help but was unable to provide it (i.e. 588 B.C., cf. Jer. 37:5-8).

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:8 YHWH will bring death and destruction to all Egypt, human and animal. Animals were common Egyptian gods. Their devastation would symbolize YHWH's power, as did the plagues of the Exodus.

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:9 "Then they will know that I am the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:9 "Then they will know that I am the Lord" This is a recurrent phrase (cf. Ezek. 6:14; 7:27; 12:20; 15:8; 29:9; 32:15; 33:29; 35:3,9,14). YHWH wanted to be revealed through Israel's abundance, moral standards, and theology, but because of her unfaithfulness, He is revealed through judgment, judgment on her and other idolatrous nations (i.e. Egypt).

Special Topic: Judge, Judgment, and Justice

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:10 "from Migdol to Syene"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:10 "from Migdol to Syene" The term "Migdol" (BDB 154) means "tower" or "fortress." In context this reference is to a location in the northeast delta region where Israelites were living (cf. Jer. 44:1; 46:14).

Syene (BDB 692) refers to a southern city on the border of Cush/Ethiopia, known today as Aswan. This same phrase is repeated in Ezek. 30:6 and functions for Egypt as the phrase "from Dan to Bethel" did for Palestine. It denotes the far reaches of the land and the mentioning of them together became an idiom for the whole land.

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:12 "forty years"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:12 "forty years" It denotes a long period of time, often a full generation.

Special Topic: Symbolic Numbers in Scripture, #7

▣ "scatter. . .dispense" These (BDB 806, KB 918, Hiphil PERFECT with waw; BDB 279, KB 280, Piel PERFECT with waw) are parallel and both refer to Judah's exile. When national armies were defeated their populace were regularly sold into slavery (cf. Jer. 49:32,36; 51:2). Egypt will be scattered (cf. Ezek. 29:12,13; 30:23,26).

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:13-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:13-16 YHWH will restore Egypt to their land (cf. Deut. 32:8), but they will not be a powerful nation.

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:14 "Pathros"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:14 "Pathros" This (BDB 837) refers to upper (i.e. southern region) Egypt, from Cairo to Aswan (cf. Gen. 10:14; Jer. 44:1,15).

▣ "they will be a lowly kingdom" Verse 15 continues this theme. The question is, does this refer to the period of

  1. Neo-Babylonian dominance; see note at 29:17-20 (i.e. the battle of Carchemish, 605 B.C.)
  2. Persian dominance by Cambyses in 525 B.C. (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 716)

Special Topic: KIngs of Egypt, D.

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:16 Israel will never again trust in Egypt for security (cf. Isa. 30:1-3; 31:1-3; 36:6 [note Ezek. 29:6]).

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:17-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:17-20 YHWH allowed Nebuchadnezzar II to capture Egypt (cf. Ezek. 30:10; Jer. 43:10,11; 46:13,26) and take its spoils as payment for his army, since they received nothing for their hard work (cf. Ezek. 29:18) at Tyre (i.e. thirteen-year siege, cf. Josephus, Antiq. 10.9.7).

It is possible that Pharaoh Hophra allied with Tyre and took away Tyre's treasures before Tyre surrendered to the army of Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 6, pp. 892-3).

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:18 This verse states that Nebuchadnezzar II did not take the island fortress (Greek historian Menander), but did capture and destroy the mainland city (cf. Ezek. 26:7-12). The problem is that Ezek. 26:14 implies that he did. Many commentators note that the PLURAL is used in Ezek. 26:7-17, but the SINGULAR in Ezek. 26:13-14, which

  1. implies that YHWH Himself will do it (note Ezek. 29:3-6)
  2. refers to Alexander the Great's destruction of the island fortress in 322 B.C.

▣ "every head was made bald" This was not a mourning rite, but imagery for heavy work (i.e. Nebuchadnezzar's siege and destruction of mainland Tyre). It is parallel to "every shoulder was rubbed bare."

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:20 As YHWH used Assyria to judge Israel (cf. Isa. 10:5), so now He uses Neo-Babylon to judge, not only Judah, but all the nations in the area. The figurative language used here sees it as a wage paid.

entries.title: Ezekiel 29:21 "I shall make a horn sprout for the house of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:21 "I shall make a horn sprout for the house of Israel" Animal horns were a symbol of power and strength. This refers to a national and Messianic restoration (cf. 1 Sam. 2:10; Ps. 132:17; Luke 1:69).

Special Topic: Messianic Era

▣ "I shall open your mouth" YHWH is in control of national and Messianic restoration as He is His prophet. Ezekiel's message was controlled by YHWH (cf. Ezek. 3:27; 24:27; 33:22).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:2 "prophesy"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:2 "prophesy" This VERB (BDB 612, KB 659) is a Niphal IMPERATIVE. It is used thirty-seven times in Ezekiel. The book is a series of messages from YHWH to Judah through Ezekiel. How or when or by whom they were gathered and combined is uncertain.

▣ "Thus says the Lord God" YHWH is the source of the message, not Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 25:3; Amos 1:3; 2:1).

▣ "Wail" This VERB (BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE) is common in

  1. Isaiah, 13:6; 14:31; 15:2,3; 16:7 (twice); 23:1,6,14; 52:5; 65:14
  2. Jeremiah, 4:8; 25:34; 47:2; 48:20,31,39; 49:3; 51:8
  3. Ezekiel (only twice), 21:12; 30:2
  4. Joel, 1:5,11,13

It denotes those who cry out like wounded animals at the judgment of God which has come upon them (i.e. "Wail, also for the day!" Ezek. 30:2-3).

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:3 "the day of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:3 "the day of the Lord" See note at Ezek. 7:19. This reference is to the immediate invasion of Neo-Babylon, not an eschatological orientation.

Special Topic: The Day of the Lord

▣ "It will be a day of clouds" The phrase is an idiom of gloom (i.e. sirocco east winds from the desert, cf. Ezek. 30:18; 32:7; 34:12), but it denotes more. The clouds are often the transportation of deity (e.g. Jer. 4:13; Dan. 7:13; Nah. 1:3).

Special Topic: Coming On the Clouds

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:4 "anguish"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:4 "anguish" This term (BDB 298) comes from "birth pains" (BDB 296). It describes the terrible pain, emotionally and physically, of God's judgment

  1. against Philistia, Exod. 15:14
  2. against unspecified foreign kings, Ps. 48:6
  3. against Babylon, Isa. 13:8; 21:3; Jer. 50:43
  4. against Israel, Jer. 6:24; 22:23
  5. against Lebanon, Jer. 22:23
  6. against Moab, Jer. 48:41
  7. against Edom, Jer. 49:22
  8. against Egypt, Ezek. 30:4,9
  9. against Assyria, Nahum 2:10

Special Topic: Birth Pains

▣ "Ethiopia" This is literally "Cush" (BDB 468). Cush controlled Egypt during the twenty-fifth dynasty (716-663 B.C.), but had since been overthrown. However, in Ezek. 30:4 and 9 "Cush" seems to be a designation for Egypt (cf. Isa. 20:4).

Special Topic: Kings of Egypt, I.

▣ "They take away her wealth" The term translated "wealth" (BDB 242) has several meanings.

  1. sound, murmur, roar of a crowd, Isa. 13:4; 17:12
  2. tumult, confusion, Isa. 33:3
  3. crowd, multitude, Ezek. 7:12,13; 23:42; 30:4; 39:11; Jer. 49:32
  4. abundance, Ps. 37:16; Eccl. 5:10; Isa. 60:5

Context must determine which fits best. Because of Ezek. 29:19 some choose #4, but 30:4 itself supports #3. Notice the same ambiguity in Ezek. 30:10.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:5 This verse refers to (1) mercenary soldiers (cf. Ezek. 30:8; 27:10) or (2) allies (i.e. "in league," Ezek. 30:5; and Ezek. 30:6,8).

  1. Ethiopia/Cush (BDB 468), cf. Ezek. 27:10; 38:5; Gen. 10:13
  2. Put/Libia (BDB 806), cf. Gen. 10:6; Jer. 46:9
  3. Lud/Lydia (BDB 530 [1] it is possible to link them with the northern Mediterranean, cf. Isa. 66:19 or [2] it is grammatically possible that all three denote Egypt)
  4. Arabia (Peshitta, BDB 787) or "mixed people" (LXX. NKJV, BDB 786), both have the same consonants
  5. Libya/Kub (see note below; BDB 464, cf. Gen. 10:13, another descendant of Ham living in northeast Africa)
  6. "the people of the land," this phrase refers to another people group, but which one is uncertain. Some commentators speculate that because the term "covenant"/berith is used it refers to Jews living in north Africa (i.e. Jer. 44:1).
NASB, TEV, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta  "all Arabia"
NKJV  "all the mingled people"
REB  "all the Arabs"
JPSOA  "all the mixed populations"
LXX  "all these mixed in"

This verse is describing the people groups connected to Egypt that will experience the judgment of YHWH. The Hebrew words

  1. mixed company ‒ ערב, BDB 786, cf. Jer. 25:20; 50:37
  2. Arabian ‒ ערבי, BB 787

are very similar. The UBS Text Project, p. 97, suggests option #1 with a "B" rating (some doubt). It is PLURAL and may refer to mercenary troops.

NASB, NRSV, REB, LXX  "Libya"
NKJV, Peshitta  "Chub"
TEV  "Kub"
NJB, JPSOA  "Cub"

The MT has כיב (BDB 464; TEV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta) but many translations emend it to לוב (BDB 530; LXX, NRSV, REB). The UBS Text Project, p. 98, gives the MT a "B" rating.

In the list of people groups allied with Egypt, Lud and Lydia are spelled similarly.

  1. Lud ‒ לוד (BDB 530)
  2. Lydia ‒ לוב (BDB 530)

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:6 "the pride of her power will come down"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:6 "the pride of her power will come down" This is the common thread between Tyre and Egypt (cf. Ezek. 28:2; 29:9b).

▣ "From Migdol to Syene" See note at Ezek. 29:10.

▣ "by the sword" YHWH sends the sword (cf. Ezek. 7:15). In this context, the sword is Nebuchadnezzar II's army (cf. Ezek. 21; 30:10-11).

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:8 Fire is often the imagery used to describe YHWH's judgment (cf. Ezek. 30:14,16; 5:4; 10:2,6-7; 15:4-7; 16:41; 19:12,14; 20:45-49; 21:31-32; 23:25,47; 24:10,12; 39:6).

Special Topic: Fire

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:9 Notice the words and phrases that refer to Egypt's day of judgment.

  1. "on that day"
  2. "on the day of Egypt"
  3. "it comes"

Special Topic: That Day

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB  "in ships"
LXX, RSV, NEB  "rushing"
Peshitta  "in haste"
JPSOA   —

The MT has "in ship" (BDB 850). The UBS Text Project, p. 98, suggests this reading over the LXX with a "B" rating (some doubt).

  1. in ship ‒ בצים (MT)
  2. hurrying ‒ אצים (LXX)

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:10 "hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:10 "hand" See Special Topic: Hand

▣ "Nebuchadnezzar" This is literally "Nebuchadressar." It is difficult to translate a foreign name into a new language. This Neo-Babylonian king's name was "Nabu-Kudurri-usur," which may mean

  1. "Nebo, protect the boundary"
  2. "Nebo, watch over my heir (i.e. eldest son)"
  3. "Nebo, protect the crown"
  4. "Nebo, protect against misfortune"

The OT spells the name in three ways.

  1. נבוכדנצר
  2. נבוכדנאצר
  3. נבוכדרער

Special Topic: Nebo

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:11 "The most ruthless of the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 30:11 "The most ruthless of the nations" This phrase describes the mercenary army of Nebuchadnezzar II, King of Neo-Babylon (cf. Ezek. 28:7; 31:12; 32:12; Hab. 1:6-8).

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:12 Notice the number of FIRST PERSON SINGULAR VERBS referring to YHWH's sovereignty.

  1. I will make, BDB 678, KB 733,Qal PERFECT with waw
  2. I will sell, BDB 569, KB 581, Qal PERFECT with waw
  3. I will make (lit. "I will bring desolation"), BDB 1030, KB 1563, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
  4. I, the Lord, have spoken, BDB 180, KB 210, Piel PERFECT

Number 2 is especially interesting because it uses a term normally reserved for YHWH's actions toward unfaithful Israel (cf. Deut. 32:30; Jdg. 2:14; 3:8; 4:2,9; 10:7; 1 Sam. 12:9). The usage here implies YHWH's ownership of all lands and all peoples (cf. Deut. 32:8).

"Sell" is imagery for giving a people group into the hand of another group. A nation loses its autonomy.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:13 "the idols"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:13 "the idols" There were several categories of idols (BDB 156) in Egypt.

  1. royal rulers (Pharaohs)
  2. animals
  3. half human, half animals
  4. fertility gods

Each city had their own chief god and/or goddess.

▣ "images" This (BDB 47) is parallel to "idols." Its basic meaning is uncertain, but the same root in Syriac means "weak," "feeble," "poor." It has the connotation of that which is insufficient or worthless. It is translated "idols" in Leviticus 19:4; 26:1; Psalm 96:5; 97:7; Isa. 2:8,18,20(twice); 10:10; 19:1,3; 31:7(twice); Hab. 2:18.

▣ "there will no longer be a prince in the land of Egypt" Apparently Neo-Babylon's conquest and exile completely removed all the royal family to Babylon. Pharoah Hophra was assassinated and a new dynasty started.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:13-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:13-19 Notice the list of Egyptian allies.

  1. Memphis, Ezek. 30:13,16, first known capital of Egypt named Menes after the first powerful king. Its chief deity was Ptah, the creator-god. The later name, Memphis, came from its association with the pyramid of Pepi I.
  2. Pathros, Ezek. 30:14, see note at Ezek. 29:14
  3. Zoan, Ezek. 30:14, also called Tanis and probably the Hyksos Avaris, later called Ramesses, the delta capital of Egypt in 21st and 22nd dynasties (i.e. the area where Jacob settled)
  4. Thebes, Ezek. 30:14,16, is the location of the valleys of the kings and temples of Amun. Today it is called Luxor, about 400 miles south of Cairo.
  5. Sin (LXX, Syene), Ezek. 30:15,16, a city is located in the delta. In Greek it is called Pelusium (i.e. city of mud). It guarded the highway to the north.
  6. On (LXX, Heliopolis), Ezek. 30:17, this city is close to Cairo in the delta region. In Greek it is called Heliopolis (i.e. city of the sun). It was one of the cities built by Hebrew slaves (cf. Exod. 1:11).
  7. Pi-beseth, Ezek. 30:17, later the capital of Egypt (22nd dynasty). It was named after the goddess Bastet (woman with cat head). It was made famous by Pharaoh Shishak.
  8. Tehaphnehes, Ezek. 30:18, in Jer. 43:7 it is spelled Tahpanhes. It is located on the highway going to Arabia in the eastern delta region.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:14 "Zoan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:14 "Zoan" This is a Hebrew form of the name of a famous ancient city (cf. Num. 13:22) in the eastern delta region that is known by several names.

  1. Avaris (Hyksos name)
  2. Pi-Ramesse (moved to a new location to the north which became Zoan, ABD, vol. 6, p. 1106)
  3. Tanis (later Greek name)

It was the northern capital of several Egyptian dynasties (i.e. Hyksos and Ramses II). It became the site of a revival temple to Amon (original temple was at Thebes).

It is mentioned in the OT in Num. 13:22; Isa. 19:11,13; 30:4; Ezek. 30:14, as well as Ps. 78:12,43.

30:15
NASB, NRSV, TEV  "Thebes"
NKJV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "No"
REB  "Noph"
LXX  "Memphis"

The MT has "No" (נא, BDB 609), which was later called Thebes. The NEB, REB have "Noph" (נף, BDB 592), which was also called "Memphis" (LXX).

The UBS Text Project, p. 98, gives "No" a "B" rating (some doubt). Both "No" and "Memphis" are mentioned in v. 16.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:16 "writhe in anguish"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:16 "writhe in anguish" This VERB (BDB 296, KB 297) is repeated to denote intensity (i.e. INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT and IMPERFECT VERB).

▣ "will be breached" This is a Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (BDB 131, KB 149). The TEV and NJB follow the Septuagint, which sees the breach as referring to the city's (i.e. Thebes) walls breaking and letting the Nile flood the city. The Septuagint (LXX) does not mention Memphis in the closing line of Ezek. 30:16.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:17-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:17-18 The NASB translates "they" (a FEMININE PLURAL ) of Ezek. 30:17b as "the women," while NKJV translates "they" as "these cities" (also FEMININE in Hebrew), as do NRSV and NJB. The TEV identified "they" as other people.

The NASB probably bases its understanding on the parallelism of Ezek. 30:18e.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:18 "the day will be dark"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:18 "the day will be dark" Most English translations change the MT's "shall be withheld" (BDB 362, חשׂך, JPSOA) to "will be darkened" (BDB 364, חשׁך, LXX, Peshitta).

▣ "the pride of her power will cease" Pride is a major spiritual problem for humans, angels, and nations. It is the essence of the self-centeredness of Genesis 3. It is always followed by divine judgment (e.g. Ezek. 28:2; 29:3; 32:12; 33:28; Isa. 14:13-14; 16:6; 25:11).

Special Topic: Lifted Up

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:20-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:20-26 This is a new revelation about YHWH's judgment on Egypt, which uses the idiom of "arm" in several ways. Arm is imagery for ability.

  1. I have broken the arm of Pharaoh, Ezek. 30:21,22. Pharaoh Hophra gave himself the title of "The Strong-Armed One." This is, therefore, powerful irony.
  2. It has not been bound up for healing, Ezek. 30:21
  3. Or wrapped with a bandage that it may be strong to hold the sword, Ezek. 30:21
  4. I will make the sword fall from his hands, Ezek. 30:22
  5. I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, Ezek. 30:24,25
  6. I will put My sword in his hand, Ezek. 30:24,25
  7. I will break the arms of Pharaoh, Jer. 48:25
  8. The arms of Pharaoh will fall, Jer. 37:5

Special Topic: Hand

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 31:1 See note at Ezek. 29:1. The date is 587 B.C.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:2-3 "say to Pharaoh. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:2-3 "say to Pharaoh. . ." The literary unit dealing with YHWH's judgment on Egypt began in chapter 29 and continues through chapter 32. Therefore, it is surprising to have "Assyria" addressed in Ezek. 31:3. Assyria is mentioned in Ezek. 32:22-33. There are two options.

  1. Pharaoh is to view YHWH's judgment on Assyria (i.e. a tall tree, cf. Isa. 2:13; 10:18-19) as an example of what will befall him and his nation (Jewish Study Bible, p. 1101 and NET Bible, p. 1512, #3).
  2. The Hebrew text, אשור (BDB 78), is corrupt and must be emended to
    1. "I will liken you to a cedar" (RSV), שור (BDB 1003 II, Qal IMPERFECT plus "cedar," BDB 72)
    2. a variant spelling of "cypress" (i.e. "box-wood," type of cedar, אשׁור, BDB 81, KB 1677, cf. Ezek. 27:6)

The UBS Text Project, p. 101, gives "Assyria, a cedar" an "A" rating.

  1. Assyria, אתור (BDB 78)
  2. a cedar, תאשׁור (BDB 81)

Another word for "cedar" appears after "Assyria" in the MT, which is spelled ארז (BDB 72), see 2,a, above.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:3-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:3-9 The nation (i.e. I think this whole context is about Egypt, not Assyria) is described as

  1. beautiful branches for shade
  2. very tall (i.e. MT, NKJV, Peshitta, "among thick boughs' LXX, NRSV, NET, "among the clouds")
  3. deep roots into good water
  4. watered other trees
  5. protection for many animals (i.e. nations)
  6. greater than the trees of Eden
  7. many branches

In essence this is the "global/cosmic tree" imagery (cf. Psalm 80; Daniel 4). Trees were places of special reverence and respect. They often served as holy sites (e.g. Gen. 35:4,8; Josh. 24:26; palm tree, Jdg. 4:5; oaks of Ophrah, cf. Jdg. 6:11,19; 1 Kgs. 13:14; 1 Chr. 10:12) and also sites of fertility worship (e.g. 1 Kgs. 14:23-24; Hosea 4:13). However, this cosmic tree symbolized a universal motif. It, of course, is a hyperbole in this context describing Egypt (see note at Ezek. 31:2-3). YHWH allows nations to rise and He causes nations to fall (i.e. Jer. 1:10; 18:2-9).

In YHWH's garden His trees continue to grow and bear fruit (cf. Ezek. 47:12; Rev. 22:2). Heaven is symbolized as a beautiful, fruitful garden (cf. Genesis 2 and Revelation 22).

Special Topic: Trees

Special Topic: Eden

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:4 "the deep"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:4 "the deep" This is the Hebrew term tehom (BDB 1062, KB 1690) personified (cf. v. 15). See full note online at Gen. 1:2, "the deep."

Special Topic: ANE Creation and Flood Myths

Special Topic: Waters

31:8
NASB, NJB, JPSOA   "cypresses"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV   "fir trees"
REB, NASB margin   "juniper"
LXX, NEB   "pines"

The UBS, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, pp. 162-163, identifies this (BDB 141) as an Aleppo pine, which is the largest conifer in the Mediterranean area. They can reach over 50' in height. Its wood is hard enough to use as building material (cf. 1 Kgs. 5:8,10; 6:15,34; 2 Chr. 2:8; Isa. 14:8; Ezek. 27:5; 31:8). It is used to characterize a nation in Hosea 14:8; Zech. 11:1-3.

NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "the plane trees"
NKJV  "the chestnut trees"
LXX  "silver firs"

The UBS, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, pp. 166-167, calls this a "plane tree." The Hebrew (BDB 790) root means "stripped" of bark (cf. Gen. 30:37). It is native to Palestine and grows near a water source. They are large and long-lived.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:9 "Eden"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:9 "Eden" Eden is a geographical location (i.e. in Ugaritic, "a plain") in Genesis 2-3 which contained a special garden planted and prepared by God for His highest creation (i.e. made in God's image and likeness, cf. Gen. 1:26-27), mankind (cf. Gen. 2:8).

The special garden is alluded to in Isa. 51:3; Ezek. 28:13; 31:9,16,18(twice); 36:35; and Joel 2:3.

Apparently the word means "abundance" from an Aramaic root. In Hebrew (BDB 727 III, 792 II) the root means "delight" or "pleasure." After Genesis the term is imagery for a well watered, fruitful place.

Special Topic: Eden

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:10 Again, like Tyre (i.e. Ezek. 28:2,17), Assyria (cf. Isa. 10:12), and Babylon (cf. Isa. 14:11-14; Dan. 4:30; 5:20-23), the sin which caused YHWH to act was pride, arrogance, hubris! It is the essence of self-centeredness. It is the fruit of Eden (see Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind). Maybe this is why Ezekiel uses the Garden of Eden imagery to characterize

  1. Tyre, Ezek. 28
  2. Egypt, Ezek. 31

 The word "greatness" or "magnify" (BDB 152) is most often used of YHWH (e.g. Deut. 3:24; 5:24; 9:26; 11:2; 32:3; Ezek. 38:23), but here it is used of human pride.

  1. Israel, Isa. 9:9
  2. Assyria, Isa. 10:12
  3. Egypt, Ezek. 31:2,7,8,18
  4. Edom, Ezek. 35:13
  5. Moab, Jer. 48:26,42
  6. the king, Dan. 11:36-37
31:11
NASB  "despot of the nations"
NKJV  "the most terrible of the nations"
LXX, NRSV, NJB, REB  "the presence of the nations"
TEV  "a foreign ruler"
JPSOA  "the mightiest of the nations"
Peshitta  "the mighty one of the nations"

The MT has a CONSTRUCT of BDB 18 and 156 ("a mighty one of the nations"). The key term (BDB 18, KB 40) means "leader," "chief," originally "ram." The same term is used of the tree in Ezek. 31:14 (cf. Isa. 1:27-31).

▣ "he will thoroughly deal with it" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 793, KB 889), which denotes intensity or completeness. This refers to YHWH's agent of judgment on Egypt.

▣ "I have driven it away" This same VERB (BDB 176, KB 204, Piel PERFECT) was used

  1. of Adam and Eve being driven from Eden (cf. Gen. 3:24)
  2. of Cain (cf. Gen. 4:14)
  3. of Egypt exiled from her homeland by YHWH

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:12 "alien tyrants of the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:12 "alien tyrants of the nations" This is the same phrase that is used in Ezek. 28:7; 30:11; 32:12 to refer to the army of Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Neo-Babylon.

▣ "all the peoples of the earth have gone down from its shade" This is typical prophetic hyperbole. Egypt did have many allies and many mercenaries in her army (cf. Ezek. 31:12-13).

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:14 The destruction of Assyria, Tyre, Egypt, and later Neo-Babylon itself should be a graphic warning to other prideful, power-hungry nations (cf. Ezek. 31:15-18). Death finally sends all fallen humans to their grave (i.e. "to the earth beneath. . .those who go down to the pit").

Special Topic: Where Are the Dead?

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:15-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:15-18 This paragraph mixes imageries.

  1. Sheol (i.e. "the deep"), Ezek. 31:15-18 (cf. Isa. 14:8-11; see Special Topic: Sheol, I. B.)
  2. Egypt as a river nation (i.e. "held back its rivers"), Ezek. 31:15
  3. Lebanon darkened, Ezek. 31:15
  4. all the trees of the field wilt away, Ezek. 31:15,16b

The trees of Eden and Lebanon are parallel and represent nations. There is a recurrent play on water in this paragraph.

  1. the deep, Ezek. 31:15
  2. rivers, Ezek. 31:15
  3. many waters
  4. drinkers of water (i.e. trees of Eden), Ezek. 31:16

Special Topic: Waters

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:16 "I made. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:16 "I made. . ." The NASB repeats this VERB twice, but in the MT it is two VERBS.

  1. BDB 950, KB 1271, Hiphil PERFECT
  2. BDB 432, KB 434, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, cf. Ezek. 26:20

Both of these VERBS show the sovereign actions of YHWH. He sets up nations; He humbles nations. All history is in His hand.

Notice the three "I" VERBS of Ezek. 31:15.

▣ "go down to the pit" This idiom is found in Ezek. 26:20; 32:18,24,29. It denotes Sheol, which refers to the holding place of the dead until judgment day (see Special Topic: Sheol, I. B.)

The question is, "Are there levels of Sheol?"

  1. Ezek. 26:20, "the lower parts of the earth"
  2. Ezek. 31:18, "in the midst of the uncircumcised"

The first is simply a parallel, but the second may denote a worse place (cf. Ezek. 28:10; 32:24,29,30).

Special Topic: Degrees of Rewards and Punishment

31:17
NASB  "those who were its strength"
NKJV  "those who were its strong arm"
NRSV, NET  "its allies" (cf. v. 6)
NJB  "its offspring"
REB  "those among the nations"
JPSOA  "its supporters"
LXX  "his seed"
Peshitta  "its posterity"

The MT has "and his arm" (BDB 283). The LXX, Peshitta, and NJB assume the same consonants but different vowels, "seed" (BDB282).

The UBS Text Project, p. 104, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "lived under its shade" See Special Topic: Shadow As a Metaphor for Protection and Care

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:18 The prophet is addressing Egypt in terms that described her greatness. Now he asks Egypt, are you a great tree also? YHWH will cut down Assyria, Egypt, and later Neo-Babylon.

▣ "the uncircumcised" See note at Ezek. 28:10.

Special Topic: Circumcision

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why did Ezekiel use metaphors from the Garden of Eden?
  2. What is the symbol of a cosmic tree?
  3. How do the metaphors of Ezek. 31 affect one's interpretation of Ezekiel 28?

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

Remember, Ezekiel 29-32 are several poems about the fall of Egypt.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:2 The four-chapter litany of judgment against Egypt continues (i.e. chapters 29-32).

▣ "take up a lamentation" A lamentation denoted a well known form of poetic meter ( BDB 884, cf. Ezek. 2:10; 19:1,14 [twice]; 26:17; 27:2,32; 28:12; 32:16; Jer. 9:10,20). This chapter, like 19:1; 27:2; 28:12, starts with a command for a funeral dirge ("take up," BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 7:29). Isaiah 14:4 has the same VERB in Qal PERFECT, but with "taunt" or "proverb" (BDB 605).

▣ "You compared yourself to a young lion of the nations" Again this is a reference to Pharaoh's pride and arrogance (cf. Ezek. 29:3; 30:6; 31:2-9,10; 32:12). He was not a lion, but a water creature.

Special Topic: Lions in the OT

NASB, NKJV, REB, Peshitta  "like the monster"
NRSV, JPSOA  "like a dragon"
TEV, NJB  "like a crocodile"
LXX  "like a serpent"

See full note at Ezek. 29:3. This may be an allusion to Canaanite mythology where Ba'al defeats Yam, or Babylonian mythology where Marduk defeats Tiamat. The OT alluded to these myths without acknowledging their reality (e.g. Isa. 27:1).

The UBS Text Project, p. 105, gives "crocodile" an "A" rating

Special Topic: The Serpent

Special Topic: Leviathan

Special Topic: The Great Red Dragon

Special Topic: ANE Creation and Flood Myths

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:3 In Ezek. 29:4 YHWH uses a hook, here a net (cf. Ezek. 12:13; 17:20). This is also described in mythological terms in Ps. 74:13-14. For the different types of mythology, see book #1 above, pp.219-242.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:3-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:3-7 The language of ANE cursing is dramatic hyperbole. It is difficult for literalistic westerners to understand this genre. A good brief chapter, "How does the language of destruction and blessing work?" in D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, pp. 75-102, has been helpful to me. I hope you will read it.

Two other books in this same area of a genre-related approach to biblical interpretation arre

  1. G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible
  2. Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:4 This same ignominious fate (i.e. unburied and eaten by animals) is described in Ezek. 29:5; 39:4. It reflects the curse of Deut. 28:26.

32:5
NASB "refuse"
NKJV "carcass"
Peshitta "dust"
TEV, JPSOA "rotting corpse"
NJB "corruption"
REB "worms that fed on it"

The REB assumes that the MT's "with your height," רמות (BDB 928, KB 1242) should be רממ (BDB 942, KB 1244 I, "be wormy," cf. Exod. 16:20). Some see a parallel to Isa. 14:11 to "maggots" רמה (BDB 942, KB 1241, see NET Bible).

32:6
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "flowing blood"
LXX  "dung"
NEB  "discharge"
JPSOA  "oozing blood"
TEV, NJB, REB, Peshitta  "blood"

The MT has two NOUNS.

  1. with your out flow ‒ BDB 847 (see NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 833)
  2. blood ‒ BDB 196

The first NOUN is found only here in all the OT.

Special Topic: Blood

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:7-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:7-8 As the Genesis creation account (Genesis 1) depreciates the astral deities of Babylon, these verses depreciate the astral deities of Egypt. The darkness shows YHWH's power over Ra, the sun god.

  1. "make dark," BDB 871, KB 1072 (Hiphil found only in Ezekiel, 3 times, cf. Ezek. 31:15)
    1. Hiphil PERFECT with waw, Ezek. 32:7
    2. Hiphil IMPERFECT, Ezek. 32:8
  2. "darkness," BDB 365 (cf. Gen. 1:2; Exod. 10:22; Amos 5:18,20)

Special Topic: Darkness, I.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:9-10 This is a common theme in these chapters (cf. Ezek. 32:16,19; 27:29-36; 28:19). YHWH's judgment on prideful Tyre and Egypt was meant to send a message to the nations (i.e. they will know that I am the Lord, e.g. Ezek. 32:15; 29:9; 33:29; 35:3,4,9,14).

32:9
NASB, NKJV, TEB, NJB, NET  "bring your destruction"
NRSV, LXX  "carry you captive"
REB  "bring your broken army"
JPSOA  "bring your shattered
  remnants"
Peshitta  "bring the news of your
  destruction"

The UBS Text Project, p. 106, gives the MT's "destruction" a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

  1. MT ‒ שׁבר, BDB 991 I, #4, KB 1402-1406 (i.e. break, fracture, crush)
  2. LXX ‒ שׁבי, BDB 985, #3 (i.e. captives)

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:10 "shall be horribly afraid"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:10 "shall be horribly afraid" This is the NOUN and VERB (Qal IMPERFECT) of the same root (BDB 972, KB 1343, cf. Ezek. 27:35; Jer. 2:12), which denotes the hair standing up in fear.

▣ "they shall tremble" This term (BDB 353, KB 350, Qal PERFECT with waw) denotes fear in YHWH"s coming and present judgment (cf. Ezek. 26:16,18; 30:9; note Heb. 10:31).

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:11 Nebuchadnezzar II was YHWH's instrument of judgment (cf. Ezek. 21:19), as Assyria had been (cf. Isa. 10:5) and Cyrus II will be (cf. Isa. 44:28; 45:7).

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:13 This could be another way of depreciating the gods of Egypt, as did the ten plagues in the Exodus.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:14 The waters of Egypt will be undisturbed (clear and settled) by any animal or human. No one will be left alive. This imagery for total destruction is found only here.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:16 The professional wailers and mourners (BDB 884, 1096 three times) would be from all the nations.

  1. those who were helped and protected by Egypt (Ezek. 32:18)
  2. those who were trading partners with Egypt

▣ "daughters of. . ." See full notes at Jer. 46:11 and Amos 5:2.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:17 Same year as v. 1 but different month.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:18-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:18-19 These verses contain four commands, two to Ezekiel, two to Egypt.

  1. wail, BDB 624, KB 675, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 32:18
  2. bring it down, BDB 432, KB 434, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 32:18
  3. go down, BDB 432, KB 434, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 32:19
  4. make your bed, BDB 1011, KB 1486, Hophal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 32:19

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:19 "with the uncircumcised"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:19 "with the uncircumcised" See full note at Ezek. 28:10. This is a recurrent curse (cf. Ezek. 28:10; 31:18; 32:19, 21,24,29,30; Jer. 9:25-26). It is possible that this is imagery for the lowest part of sheol (cf. vv. 21,24,29,30; 31:18).

Special Topic: Sheol

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:22-30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:22-30 This is a series of related paragraphs/strophes that list the dead in Sheol who greet new arrivals.

  1. Assyria ‒ Ezek. 32:22-23
  2. Elam ‒ Ezek. 32:24-25
  3. Anatolia ‒ Ezek. 32:26-28
  4. Edom ‒ Ezek. 32:29
  5. Syrians and Aramenians ‒ Ezek. 32:30
  6. Egypt ‒ Ezek. 32:31-32

In many ways this is similar to the imagery of Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28. The dead rejoice when the powerful join them in Sheol and become their equals!

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:23 "whose graves are set in the remotest parts of the pit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:23 "whose graves are set in the remotest parts of the pit" This is an idiom for the worst (cf. Isa. 14:15) or lowest places in the netherworld. They were violently slain in this world and humiliated in the next (cf. Ezek. 32:27, 32)!

Note the list of humiliated nations.

  1. Egypt, Ezek. 32:17-21,31
  2. Assyria, Ezek. 32:22-23
  3. Elam, Ezek. 32:24-25
  4. Meshech, Tubal (Anatolia), Ezek. 32:26-28
  5. Edom, Ezek. 32:29
  6. Princes of the north (i.e. Syrians or Armenians) and Sidon, Ezek. 32:30

Special Topic: Where Are the Dead?

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:26 "Meshech, Tubal"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:26 "Meshech, Tubal" These two nations/regions were located north of Israel/Judah (cf. Ezek. 39:2).

  1. Meshech (BDB 604, KB 646 II)
    1. north of the Black Sea
    2. central Anatolia
    3. see full note at Ezek. 38:2
  2. Tubal (BDB 1063, KB 1683) was a nation/region
    1. in eastern Anatolia (Asia Minor)
    2. in Cappadocia (Josephus)
    3. see fuller note at Ezek. 38:2
32:27
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta, REB, JPSOA  "uncircumcised"
LXX, NRSV, TEV, NJB  "long ago"

The phrases are spelled similarly in Hebrew

  1. MT, "from among the uncircumcised" מערלים
  2. LXX, "of old" םעולם

The second fits the context best (NET, p. 1514) because these people were part of the uncircumcised and the term is repeated in Ezek. 32:28. The UBS Text Project, p. 112, gives the LXX version a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

NASB, NKJV, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "their iniquity rested on
  their bones"
NRSV, TEV  "whose shields are upon
  their bones"
NJB  "their shields put under
  their bones"
REB  "their shields over their
  bones"

These men of Meshech, Tubal are honored even in death, but not so for the Egyptians!

The UBS Text Project, p. 113, gives "their iniquity" (BDB 730, KB 800) an "A" rating. However, many translations emend it to "shields" (BDB 857 III, KB 1037 II)

  1. better parallel to "weapons of war" and "swords" under their heads
  2. similar spelling of "iniquity"
    1. "their iniquity"  עונתם
    2. "their shields"  צנותם
