FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Ezekiel 12-24 explains YHWH's reason for His judgment on Judah.

  2. Ezekiel 25-32 is YHWH's judgments on the surrounding nations.

  3. Ezekiel 33-39 is the message to the exiles of YHWH's promised restoration.

  4. Ezekiel 33 is very similar to Ezekiel 18 in its emphasis on individual responsibility (cf. Deut. 24:16; Jer. 31:29-30). In this chapter the people admit their sin (cf. Ezek. 33:10). This theme of individual responsibility is one major truth of the book of Ezekiel and it begins in Ezek. 3:16-21.
    Special Topic: Covenant

  5. A footnote in the REB Oxford Study Bible, p. 893, asserts that this chapter repates themes given earlier in Ezekiel.
    1. 33:1-6 from 3:4-11
    2. 33:7-9 from 3:16-21
    3. 33:10-20 from 18:1-32
    4. 33:23-29 from 12:17-20

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:2 "Son of man" See full note at Ezek. 2:1.

Special Topic: Son of Man

▣"speak" As so many of Ezekiel's prophecies this one starts out with the command "speak" or "say" (BDB 180; KB 210, Piel IMPERATIVE).

▣ "to the sons of your people" This is found only in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 3:11; 33:2,12,17,30; 37:18) and mostly in this chapter.

Special Topic: Sons of. . .(OT)

▣ "If I bring a sword upon a land" This theme is amplified in chapter 21. The word was one of several items of judgment (sword, famine, plague, wild beasts, e.g. Ezek. 5:17). This would take the readers'/hearers' minds back to Leviticus 26 or Deuteronomy 27-28.

▣ "watchman" The world translated "watchman" is really a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE of the VERB "to look out," "look about" or "spy out" (BDB 859, KB 1044, cf. Ezek. 33:2,6 [twice],7). This is the man who stood on the wall (or in a watchtower) to give an early warning of coming danger (cf. Ezek. 3:16-21; Isa. 21:4-10; 56:10; Jer. 6:17; Hosea 9:8).

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:3 "he sees the sword coming"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:3 "he sees the sword coming" The sword is used as imagery for an invading army. In this case it refers to the army of Nebuchadnezzar II of Neo-Babylon.

Special Topic: Kings of Neo-Babylon

▣ "the trumpet" This refers to the sophar (BDB 1051) or ram's horn. It was used both for religious purposes and and military purposes (cf. Josh. 6:4; 2 Sam. 2:28; 18: 24,25; Ps. 81:3; Joel 2:15; Amos 3:6; Hab. 2:1).

Special Topic: Horns Used By Israel.

▣ "warns" This VERB (BDB 264, KB 265, Hiphil PERFECT with waw) means "to warn" or possibly from an Aramaic root, "to teach" (cf. Exod. 18:20). It is found in the VERB form only and predominately in Ezekiel in two forms.

  1. Hiphil, to warn or caution (cf. Ezek. 3:17,18 [twice],19,20,21 [twice]; 33:3,7,8,9)
  2. Niphal, to be warned (cf. Ezek. 3:21; 33:4,5 [twice],6)

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:4,6 "his blood will be on his own head. . .but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:4,6 "his blood will be on his own head. . .but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand" Ezekiel felt the pressure of speaking YHWH's word to a non-responsive people (as did Isaiah and Jeremiah). In a sense he is defending his message of judgment on Judah. If he had not spoken, the inhabitants could have blamed him or God for the destruction and death of the nation. But he did speak and they still did not respond (cf. Isa. 6:9-10).

 The word "blood" stands for a person's life (cf. Ezek. 18:13; Lev. 17:11,14).

Special Topic: Blood

▣ "watchman's hand" See Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:8 "you will surely die"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:8 "you will surely die" This is a Hebrew grammatical construction (i.e. INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB from the same root, here BDB 559, KB 562), which denotes emphasis or intensity (same phrase in Gen. 2:17).

  1. This one is repeated in Ezek. 33:14.
  2. Another related one (i.e. BDB 310, KB 309, "he will surely live") is found in Ezek. 33:13,15,16.

▣ "that wicked man shall die in his iniquity" This is the message of chapter 18. If one repents, YHWH will forgive. If one sins and refuses to repent, that one will bear his judgment.

Special Topic: Repentance (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:10 "say"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:10 "say" It is characteristic for an IMPERATIVE (BDB 55, KB 65, Qal IMPERATIVE) to designate the beginning of YHWH's new message through Ezekiel (i.e. Ezek. 33:10,11,12).

▣ "Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we are rotting away in them" In chapter 18 the people were blaming their forefathers for YHWH's judgments, but here in chapter 33 they acknowledge their personal and corporate rebellion.

The phrase "rotting away" is from the curses of Lev. 26:39-42. This phrase is found three times in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 4:17; 24:23; 33:10).

Special Topic: Biblical Faith Is Corporate

▣ "then can we survive" This is literally "live" (BDB 310, KB 309, Qal IMPERFECT). We must see the devastating mental and physical anguish that the destruction of Jerusalem caused to the covenant people. Ezekiel, in chapters 33-39 after the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, begins to reassure the covenant people that YHWH is still their Covenant God (cf. Isa. 49:14-15) and that He will forgive and restore them, physically and spiritually (cf. Ezek. 37:11-14).

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:11 "'As I live!' declares the Lord God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:11 "'As I live!' declares the Lord God" This is an oath related to the name of the Covenant God, YHWH, from the Hebrew VERB "to be." It is the ever-living, only-living God who swears by His own life (cf. Ezek. 5:11).

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

Special Topic: Life (zoē)

▣ "I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked" This is a repetition of Ezek. 18:23,32. The heart of God is love, not judgment (cf. Exod. 34:6-7; John 3:16; Matt. 11:28-30). God wants all human beings made in His image and likeness to turn and respond to Him (cf. John 3:16; 4:42; 1 Tim. 2:4; Titus 2:11; 2 Pet. 3:9; 1 John 2:1; 4:14) by repentance and faith (cf. Mark 1:15; Acts 2:38,41; 3:16,19; 20:21).

Special Topic: Characteristics of Israel's God (OT)

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

Special Topic: Seek the Lord

▣ "turn from his way and live. Turn back, turn back from your evil ways! Why will you die, Oh house of Israel" The VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERTAIVE) is repeated for emphasis (cf. Ezek. 3:19,20; 14:6 [thrice]; 18:21,23,24,26,27,28,30 [twice],32; 33:9,11 [twice],12,14,19). This is a choice humans must make (cf. Deut. 30:1,15,19). Repentance is a crucial spiritual requirement.

Repentance primarily is a turning from self and a turning to God. The Hebrew word (BDB 996) speaks of a change of action, while the Greek speaks of a change of mind. Both are involved (cf. Ezek. 18:31; Jer. 31:33; also note 2 Cor. 7:8-11).

Special Topic: Repentance (OT)

Special Topic: Repentance (NT)

▣ "house of Israel" Israel in this context refers specifically to Judah. Ezekiel uses this designation to foreshadow the coming unity of the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:12 "The righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in the day of his transgression"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:12 "The righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in the day of his transgression" This does not refer to cumulative guilt or acquired merit (cf. chapter 18), but lifestyle relational faith! What a terrible warning! What a wonderful invitation (cf. Ezek. 33:10)!

Special Topic: Righteousness.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:13 "and he will surely live"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:13 "and he will surely live" This is the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 310, KB 309, cf. Ezek. 33:15,16), which expresses intensity or emphasis (see note at Ezek. 33:8).

▣ "and he so trusts in his righteousness" This is always a danger of religious humanity. The believer must trust in God, not in oneself or one's performance. His/her trust (BDB 105) must issue from an initial faith and repentance to an ongoing faith and repentance. Biblical faith is a daily relationship! Obedience does make a difference (cf. Ezek. 33:16,31-32; Deut. 4:1; Hab. 2:4; Eph. 1:4; 2:8-10; James 2:14-26) and is the natural result of a dynamic faith.

Special Topic: Covenant

Special Topic: Keep

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:14 "practices justice and righteousness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:14 "practices justice and righteousness" Notice that there is no distinction in this context between secular and sacred because all belongs to God. This is a truth that moderns need to hear. All life and all relationships are sacred because of Gen. 1:26-27. We must not separate justification from sanctification.

Special Topic: Judge, Judgment, Justice

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:15 "restores a pledge"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:15 "restores a pledge" This term, "a pledge," (BDB 286, KB 285) basically means "to bind." When one borrows he is obligated to repay. To secure this repayment (without interest to a fellow Israelite) the creditor could take something of value and hold it.

  1. grinding stone, Ezek. 24:6
  2. garments, Ezek. 24:17; Exod. 22:25-27; Job 24:7,10
  3. ancestral land and houses, Neh. 5:3 (possibly Job 24:2)
  4. an essential animal, Job 24:3
  5. essential help, the children, Exod. 21:7; Lev. 25:39-43; 2 Kgs. 4:1; Job 24:9

Each of these items was a necessary part of daily agricultural existence. To remove any one of these jeopardized the family, even life itself. YHWH's compassion and care for Israel was to be emulated by those Israelites who had resources. God would bless them for their compassion. They would be given more so that they could share more (cf. Ezek. 33:13; 2 Cor. 9:6-10).

Special Topic: Wealth

▣ "pays back what he has taken by robbery" Robbery is discussed in Exod. 22:1-4; Lev. 6:4,5. The stolen items must be returned with a penalty.

Special Topic: Stealing

▣ "walks by the statutes" The VERB (BDB 229, KB 246, Qal PERFECT) is an idiom of lifestyle faith. Faith is personal and communal. The first can be seen and evaluated by how we treat others!

Notice that the statutes of God are meant to bestow life (another INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root, BDB 310, KB 309). God's laws were to protect humanity during this period of fallenness (i.e. Deut. 30:16).

Special Topic: Terms for God's Revelation

Special Topic: The Path, The Way

Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:16 "None of his sins that he has committed will be remembered against him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:16 "None of his sins that he has committed will be remembered against him" What a tremendous promise of the forgiveness of YHWH (cf. Ezek. 18:22; Ps. 103:12; Isa. 1:18; 38:17; 43:25; 44:22; Micah 7:18, 19)! When God forgives, God forgets!

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:17 "The way of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:17 "The way of the Lord" This speaks of lifestyle faith (i.e. Deut. 3:33; 8:6; 10:12; 11:22; 19:9; 26:17; 28:9; 30:16). The early church's title was "The Way" (cf. Acts 9:2; 18:25,26; 19:9,23; 22:4; 24:14,22).

Special Topic: The Path, The Way

▣ "right" This refers to a measuring standard (BDB 1067). It is used often in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 18:25 [twice], 29 [twice]; 33:17 [twice], 20). They were claiming that YHWH's justice was unfair (weighted falsely, cf. 1 Sam. 2:3; Prov. 16:2; 24:12), but the problem was human, willful rebellion (cf. Ezek. 18:25, 29).

Special Topic: Righteousness

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:17-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:17-20 This supposed dialogue between YHWH's spokesperson and the wicked is similar to the diatribe format found in Malachi, Paul's writings, and 1 John.

A statement of truth is made, then a supposed contemporary objector restates or challenges the first statement. In a concluding statement from the first speaker, God gives His answer to contemporary false views.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:20 "I will judge each of you according to his ways"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:20 "I will judge each of you according to his ways" Notice the individual emphasis continues (i.e. Deut. 24:16; Jer. 31:29-30; Ezek. 3:16-21; 18; 33). This is a recurrent biblical truth. We reap what we sow!

Note Job 34:11; Ps. 28:4; 62:12; Prov. 24:12; Eccl. 12:14; Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:6; 14:12; 1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7-10; 2 Tim. 4:14; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12!

Special Topic: Judge, Judgment, Justice

Special Topic: Judgment in the NT

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:21 "in the twelfth year of our exile"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:21 "in the twelfth year of our exile" The Syriac translation (Peshitta) has "eleventh." The Septuagint has "tenth." The exact date is uncertain.

This is one of several dates in Ezekiel that seem to mark the beginning of a new prophetic revelation from YHWH. If this is correct, then the next date is found in Ezek. 40:1, which implies Ezek. 33:21-39:29 is a unified literary unit. This section of Ezekiel emphasizes the promise of divine restoration of a segment of the seed of Abraham (see Special Topic: The Remnant [three senses]).

The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1107, identifies several separate oracles in this literary unit.

  1. 33:21-33
  2. 34:1-31
  3. 35:1-36:15
  4. 36:16-37:14
  5. 37:15-28
  6. 38:1-39:39

▣ "The city has been taken" Ezekiel had predicted this earlier, but this was the first eyewitness confirmation. This is a crucial point in Ezekiel's ministry. Once the predicted judgment of YHWH has struck (i.e. the destruction of Jerusalem), Ezekiel then begins to proclaim YHWH's messages of hope and restoration.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:22 "the hand of the Lord had been upon me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:22 "the hand of the Lord had been upon me" This is an idiomatic way of referring to YHWH's initiation of a revelatory message (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 3:14,22; 8:1; 37:1; 40:1). The phrase usually marks crucial transition points, but here and in chapter 3 it denotes an incoming message.

Special Topic: God Described As Human

Special Topic: Inspiration

▣ "He opened my mouth" Previously, Ezekiel had been forced to do dramatic actions because he could not speak, but now he was permitted to speak (cf. Ezek. 3:26, 27; 24:27).

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:24 "they who live in these waste places in the land of Israel are saying"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:24 "they who live in these waste places in the land of Israel are saying" Those who escaped the captivity and exile to Neo-Babylon (cf. Jeremiah 24), were asserting that YHWH had blessed them and had cursed the exiles, but this was simply not the case (cf. Ezek. 33:27; 11:1-27).

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:25 "You eat meat with blood in it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:25 "You eat meat with blood in it" This refers to

  1. the improper preparations of meat (cf. Lev. 3:17; 7:26-27; 17:10,12,14; 19:26; Deut. 12:16, 23; 15:23). In this context it probably refers to cultic meals at pagan altars.
  2. This may refer to Canaanite divination (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 721).

▣ "lift up your eyes" This is imagery for prayer. They were idolaters.

▣ "you shed blood" This refers to

  1. the killing of righteous people
  2. the killing of the poor
  3. the offering of their children to the Phoenician fertility god, Molech (see Special Topic: Molech)

▣ "Should you then possess the land" This question is very similar to Jeremiah's temple sermon of chapter 7, in particular Ezek. 33:9 and 10. YHWH's covenant with Abraham's seed was conditional. This is a crucial theolgocial point!

Special Topic: Covenant

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:26 "You rely on your sword"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:26 "You rely on your sword" They were trusting in their military power and walled cities (cf. Ezek. 33:28, "the pride of her power will cease").

▣ "you commit abominations and each of you defiles his neighbor's wife" This refers to the fertility rites of the Canaanite gods, Ba'al and Ashterah.

Special Topic: Fertility Worship of the ANE

Special Topic: Abomination (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:27-29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:27-29 These curses reflect Lev. 26:22,25.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:29 The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1108, says this verse summarizes the message of the whole book.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:30 Ezekiel's fellow exiles were talking about (his prophecies) what happened to Jerusalem and what would happen to the few who remained. In this context the prophet is commanded to address their concerns.

  1. come ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE PLURAL
  2. hear ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE PLURAL

YHWH still wants to speak to His people. The ones in exile are the people He will begin again with.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:31 "They come to you as people come, and they sit before you as My people but they do the lustful desires expressed by their mouth, and their heart goes afte
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:31 "They come to you as people come, and they sit before you as My people but they do the lustful desires expressed by their mouth, and their heart goes after their gain" There was outward, religious show, but no true piety. To them Ezekiel was the best show in town (cf. Ezek. 33:32), but they had no real desire to turn to YHWH (cf. Isa. 6:9-13; 29:13).

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:32 "for they hear your words but they do not practice them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:32 "for they hear your words but they do not practice them" They hear, but they do not do (i.e. the opposite of shema; see Special Topic: Listen/Hear [shema]). This is the condemnation of "religious people," cf. Matt. 7:24-27; James 1:23-25).

The exiles loved to come hear or observe Ezekiel's messages, but they did not really believe them. He was the only show in town. This would all change with the news brought by an exiled survivor of Jerusalem that indeed all that Ezekiel had predicted had occurred (cf. Ezek. 33:33).

Special Topic: Keep

33:33 The mark of a true prophet is that what they predict (unless repentance occurs, i.e. Jonah) comes to pass (cf. Ezek. 33:29; 13:6; Deut. 18:22; Jer. 28:9). Ezekiel had been right about Judah and Jerusalem and he would be right about the destruction of the nations! He would also be right about the forgiveness and restoration to come!

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What is the significance of chapters 18 and 33?
  2. What is the difference between the attitude of the people in chapters 18 and 33?
  3. Explain the spiritual relationship described in Ezek. 33:12, 13.
  4. What is repentance?

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:2 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

Special Topic: Son of Man

▣ "prophesy" This term (BDB 612, KB 659) is first used in Ezek. 4:7 (Niphal PERFECT, cf. Ezek. 37:7), but it appears often as a Niphal IMPERATIVE (cf. Ezek. 6:2; 11:4 [twice]; 13:2,17; 20:46; 21:2,9,14,28; 25:2; 28:21; 29:2; 30:2; 34:2 [twice]; 35:2; 36:1,3,6; 37:9 [twice],12; 38:2,14; 39:1).

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

▣ "the shepherds of Israel" "Shepherd" (BDB 944, KB 1258, Qal PARTICIPLE, cf. Ezek. 34:2 [6 times], 3, 5,7,8 [3 times],9,10,12,23 [twice]) refers to the leaders, both political (i.e. 2 Sam. 7:7) and religious (i.e. priests, cf. Isa. 56:11; prophets, cf. Jer. 23:1-4; both Jer. 23:9-10; Zech. 11:17; and king, cf. Ezekiel 22).

This VERB also occurs in

  1. Qal IMPERFECT, Ezek. 34:2, 3, 8,10,14 (twice),15,16,18,19,23 (twice)
  2. Qal PERFECT, Ezek. 34:8,12,13,23
  3. Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, Ezek. 34:10

The origin of this concept comes

  1. from the pastoral traditions of the Patriarchs (cf. Genesis 49:24)
  2. Moses was a shepherd (cf. Exod. 3:1)
  3. from David's early life as a family herdsman (i.e. 1 Samuel 16:11; Psalm 78:70-71)
  4. Ultimately YHWH is the "good shepherd" (cf. Ps. 23; 77:20; 78:52; 80:1; Isa. 40:11; Jer. 23:3; 31:10.
  5. The Davidic Messiah ‒ Jer. 23:5-6; Ezek. 34:20-24; Matt. 2:6; John 10:11,14-16; Heb. 13:20; 1 Pet. 2:25; 5:4; Rev. 7:17

Sheep are animals that need constant care and protection. Shepherding became a powerful image for this (i.e. Gen. 49:24 Psalm 23).

Zechariah also uses the concept of true and evil shepherds in an eschatological, apocalyptic setting (cf. Zechariah 11-13).

Special Topic: Titles for the Special Coming One

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:3 "the fat"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:3 "the fat" These CONSONANTS (חלב) can be revocalized as "milk" (LXX, Vulgate), referring to butter, cheese, or cream. The UBS Text Project, p. 117, gives "milk" a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:3-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:3-4 These false shepherds think more of their own well-being than they do of the people of YHWH (cf. Jer. 23:1-6; 50:6).

  1. feed (lit. pasturing) themselves, Ezek. 34:2,8,10
  2. eat the fat of the sheep, Ezek. 34:3,10 (possibly referring to milk products)
  3. take the wool, Ezek. 34:3
  4. do not feed the flock, Ezek. 34:3
  5. do not help the sick, Ezek. 34:4
  6. do not bind the broken, Ezek. 34:4
  7. do not seek the scattered, Ezek. 34:4
  8. treat the flock violently, Ezek. 34:4

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:4 "but with force and with severity you have dominated them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:4 "but with force and with severity you have dominated them" Note the three terms which denote the cruel treatment.

  1. with force, BDB 306, cf. Jdg. 4:3; 8:1; 2 Sam. 2:16
  2. with severity, BDB 827, cf. Exod. 1:13,14; Lev. 25:43,46,53
  3. dominated, BDB 921, KB 1109, Qal PERFECT, cf. Lev. 25:53; 26:17 (this is the same root used in Gen. 1:26,28)

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:5 "they are scattered for lack of a shepherd"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:5 "they are scattered for lack of a shepherd" Also refer to Num. 27:17; 1 Kgs. 22:17; and Matt. 9:36.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:5-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:5-6 As a result of the action, or lack of action, of leaders, the people of YHWH

  1. are scattered (cf. Jer. 23:1-2)
  2. are preyed on (cf. Ezek. 34:8,23; 14:15,21)
  3. wandered away and no one searched for them

Sheep usually stay together. For them to be scattered demonstrates a stressful, dangerous situation.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:6 "there was no one to search or seek for them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:6 "there was no one to search or seek for them" The term "search" (BDB 205, KB 233, Qal PARTICIPLE) is used several times in this chapter.

  1. Judah's leaders did not seek, Ezek. 34:6
  2. the shepherds did not seek (BDB 205, KB 233, Qal PERFECT), Ezek. 34:8
  3. YHWH will require (BDB 205, KB 233, Qal PERFECT with waw) His sheep, Ezek. 34:10
  4. YHWH, Himself will search (BDB 205, KB 233, Qal PERFECT with waw) for His sheep, Ezek. 34:11

The word "search" is parallel in this verse with "seek" (BDB 134, KB 152, Piel PARTICIPLE, cf. Jdg. 6:29; 1 Chr. 16:11; 2 Chr. 20:3-4; Job 10:6; Ps. 24:6; 38:12; 105:4; Jer. 29:13)

Special Topic: Seek the Lord

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:7-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:7-10 This surely is an example of individual responsibility and divine judgment. This individual aspect is characteristic of Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 18).

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:11-31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:11-31 Notice the number of FIRST PERSON MASCULINE SINGULAR statements! YHWH, Himself will act on behalf of His people. This is exactly the opposite of Ezek. 34:2-6.

  1. I Myself will search for My sheep, Ezek. 34:11
  2. I Myself will seek them out, Ezek. 34:11
  3. I will care for My sheep, Ezek. 34:12
  4. I will deliver them, Ezek. 34:12,22
  5. I will bring them out from the peoples, Ezek. 34:13 (cf. Ezek. 11:17; 20:41)
  6. I will gather them, Ezek. 34:13 (cf. Ezek. 11:17; 20:34.41; 28:25; 36:24; 37:21; 38:8; 39:27)
  7. I will feed them, Ezek. 34:13,14,15,18
  8. I will lead them to rest (lit. "cause to lie down"), Ezek. 34:15 (cf. Ps. 23:1,2)
  9. I will seek the lost, Ezek. 34:16
  10. I will bring back the scattered, Ezek. 34:16
  11. I will bind up the broken, Ezek. 34:16 (cf. Isa. 30:26)
  12. I will strengthen the sick, Ezek. 34:16 (cf. Ps. 147:3)
  13. I will feed them judgment, Ezek. 34:16
  14. I will judge between one sheep and another, Ezek. 34:17,22
  15. I will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep, Ezek. 34:20 (cf. Ezek. 34:16)
  16. I will set over them one shepherd, My servant David
  17. I will be their God, Ezek. 34:24
  18. I will make a covenant of peace with them, Ezek. 34:25
  19. I will eliminate harmful beasts, Ezek. 34:25
  20. I will make them and the places around My hill a blessing, Ezek. 34:26
  21. I will cause showers to come down in their season, Ezek. 34:26
  22. I have broken the bars of their yoke, Ezek. 34:27
  23. I have delivered them, Ezek. 34:27
  24. I will establish for them a renowned planting place, Ezek. 34:29

Here YHWH acts because of His faithless leaders, but in Ezek. 36:27-36 He acts because of His people's inability to be faithful and obedient to His Mosaic covenant. This default on the part of His people precipitates a new covenant based on God's actions and faithfulness (cf. Jer. 31:31-34)! Jesus is the Good Shepherd (cf. John 10; Heb. 13:20; 1 Pet. 2:25).

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:12 "when he is among the scattered sheep"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:12 "when he is among the scattered sheep" As a shepherd was present with his flock, so YHWH will be personally present (i.e. for blessing and protection) with His people.

▣ "on a cloudy and gloomy day" This is an idiom for judgment (cf. Ezek. 30:3; Ps. 97:2; Joel 2:2; Jer. 13:16; Zeph. 1:15), in this case Israel's (by Assyria) and Judah's (by Neo-Babylon) exile.

34:16
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, NAB  "but the fat and strong I will
  destroy"
NJB  "I shall watch over the fat
  and healthy"
LXX  "I will guard the strong"
Peshitta  "I will protect the fat and
  strong"

The MT has "I will destroy," BDB 1029, KB 1552, Hiphil IMPERFECT FIRST PERSON SINGULAR (שׁמד), but the ancient versions (LXX, Peshitta, and Vulgate) have "I will preserve" or "I will watch," BDB 1036, KB 1581 (שׁמר). The context supports both.

  1. "preserve" fits the immediate verses (vv. 11-16a)
  2. "destroy" fits
    1. Ezek. 34:16b-c
    2. the larger context (cf. vv. 17-22)

The UBS Text Project, p. 117, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:17 "As for you, My flock"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:17 "As for you, My flock" Ezekiel is making a comparison between the future condition of

  1. the current leadership
  2. the people

▣ "I will judge between one sheep and another, between the rams and the male goats" This refers to a judgment between the strong and the weak, between the greedy shepherds and the true shepherds (cf. Ezek. 34:22).

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:18 "Is it too slight a thing for you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:18 "Is it too slight a thing for you" This is an idiom of inappropriate actions (cf. Ezek. 16:20; Num. 16:9,13; Josh. 22:17; 2 Sam. 7:19; Isa. 7:13).

▣ Sheep do not like to feed in trampled pastures nor drink from muddied waters (cf. Psalm 23). The wealthy not only exploited the weak, poor, and socially ostracized, they made it such that they could not prosper and become free of their situation. This violates many passages in Leviticus and Deuteronomy about how the covenant people should treat each other.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:21 The leaders are described as aggressive male rams and goats that push and shove the people away.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:23 "one shepherd"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:23 "one shepherd" This probably refers to a united Israel (i.e. the children of Jacob, seed of Abraham). There will no longer be a divided monarchy as occurred in 922 B.C. (i.e. Israel and Judah).

The LXX has "another shepherd."

  1. one ‒ אחד
  2. another ‒ אחר

The UBS Text Project, p. 118, gives option #2 a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "My servant" This is an honorific title used first of the Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, cf. Deut. 9:27). It is used of Moses in Num. 12:7; Deut. 34:5; and Josh. 1:1,2,13,15; 8:31,33; 11:12,15; 12:6; 13:8; 14:7; 18:7; 22:2,4,5. It is also used of Joshua after his death (i.e. Josh. 24:29).

In Isaiah it becomes a way of referring to Israel collectively, but also to the special coming son of David (cf. Isaiah 40-56). You can clearly see this interplay between the corporate and individual in Isaiah 42. Note that Isa. 42:1 is quoted in the NT as referring to the Messiah (cf. Matt. 12:18-21), but Ezek. 34:19 obviously refers to the people of God (cf. Ezek. 41:8-10; 44:21). This interplay (i.e. collective or individual) occurs in several of the "Servant Songs" (cf. Ezek. 42:1-9; 49:1-7; 50:4-11; 52:13-53:12), which are unique to Isaiah.

Special Topic: My Servant

▣ "David" David became the ideal king (cf. Ezek. 34:24; 37:24; 2 Samuel 7; Ps. 18:50; 89; Isa. 9:6-7; 11:1-5; 16:5; 55:3-5; Jer. 23:5-6; 30:9; 33:15,17; Hosea 3:5; Micah 5:2-5). David was sinful (like all humans), but he had a heart for YHWH. He became a way of referring to the special coming king of righteousness (see E. W. Hengstenber, Christology of the Old Testament, pp. 687-690).

Special Topic: OT Titles for the Special Coming One

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:24 "I, the Lord, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:24 "I, the Lord, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them" These verses are (i.e. Ezek. 34:23-24) parallels of Ezek. 37:24-25. It is obviously Messianic. Note the typical covenant language! This is reunification of the covenant people under a Davidic monarch, as well as the fulfillment of YHWH's covenant blessings (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28. Also note the concluding phrase, which assures the fulfillment of this divine promise (cf. Amos 9:11-15).

Special Topic: Messiah

Special Topic: Messianic Era

Special Topic: Covenant

The questions related to these verses are

  1. when does it occur?
  2. who does it refer to?

Some try to relate this to the return under Zerubbabel (a prince of Judah, cf. Ezra 1:8; the exact relationship between Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel is disputed). Others note the continuing problems of the post-exilic period (see Haggai and Malachi) and assert that these ideal conditions must refer to the future.

It seems best to me to see it as an eschatological setting because of

  1. the nature of prophecy (see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks)
  2. the expansion of the NT into a universal gospel (i.e. Eph. 2:11-3:13)
  3. the symbolic nature of Ezek. 34-39, 40-41, which relates this to God's plans for a restored Israel in the Persian period. All prophecy is conditional, even this one. God wanted to restore Israel and would have if only Israel wanted to and would have been obedient.

Does the "everlasting covenant" of Ezek. 16:60 and 37:26 (cf. Isa. 55:3; 61:8) refer to a realized OT community or the NT human family? My presuppositional theology pushes me to option #2. For me as a historical-grammatical interpreter, the OT must stand on its own as the word of God. I must interpret it in light of the original inspired author's intent. However, progressive revelation (i.e. Jesus' life, actions, and teaching, plus NT authors) refocuses the message from a Jewish setting in Palestine to a universal gospel for all peoples (cf. Acts), thus fulfilling the concept of monotheism and the universal promise of Gen. 3:15. These prophecies must be analyzed through two lenses (i.e. the OT and the NT). Christianity is only true if the NT is the fulfillment of the OT and Jesus is the promised Messiah. The hope is wider than Israel. Genesis 3:15 is a promise to all the sons and daughters of Adam, not just Jews. There were no Jews in Genesis 3.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

Special Topic: The Gospel

▣ "I will be their God" The king of Israel was to be YHWH's representative (cf. 1 Samuel 8). This represents the ideal picture of a society where God is the true King and the righteous leader is His visible representative!

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:25 "I will make a covenant of peace"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:25 "I will make a covenant of peace" This term "peace" is the Hebrew Shalom (BDB 1022, cf. Ezek. 37:24-28; 39:25-29; Lev. 26:6. It must be remembered that all covenants have obligations. Free creatures have options!

Is this "covenant of peace" the same as "the new covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34? Ezekiel 36:22-36 (like these texts) describes a new way that YHWH will relate to His covenant people, a way characterized by (1) a new heart and a new mind and (2) YHWH's personal action on their behalf. A new covenant initially focuses on God's graciousness in redemption, but still desires a righteous people to draw "the nations" to Himself!

Special Topic: Peace (OT)

Special Topic: Covenant

▣ "eliminate harmful beasts from the land" As is so often the case, Ezekiel is influenced by Leviticus 26 (i.e. Ezek. 34:22) and Deuteronomy 28 (i.e. 32:24). The curses of disobedience are reversed into the blessing of covenant fidelity. The blessing was always YHWH's intent. He wanted to attract the nations to Himself by blessing Israel.

The prophecy of the new age is Isa. 11:6-9; 65:25, which includes animals and shows the original intent of Eden (i.e. a place of fellowship between God and humanity, and humanity and the animal kingdom). The Bible starts with an Edenic setting and also ends the same way (cf. Revelation 21-22). Heaven is depicted as a recreated Garden of Eden. Animals are part of this depiction!

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan)

▣ "so that they may live securely" This was part of the promises of Deuteronomy, which Ezekiel restates (cf. Ezek. 28:26; 34:27,28; 38:8,11,14; 39:26; Jer. 33:16). Their security is because of the presence of God!

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:26 "My hill"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:26 "My hill" This is a reference to Jerusalem and specifically the temple mount (cf. Ezek. 20:40-49). YHWH's hill is a contrast to the worship of the fertility gods of Canaan on both natural and manmade hills.

The prophecy, which is typical of the prophets, refers to a restored Jerusalem. Must this be taken literally? This is a central issue in dispensational theology. I have come to a different conclusion. For a good critique of dispensationalism see Steve Gregg's YouTube video, Deconstructing Dispensationalism

▣ "I will cause showers" Moisture at the appropriate time and in expected amounts was part of the covenant blessings of Lev. 26:4 and Deut. 28:12. These were agricultural people living in an arid climate. Society was based on the regular and expected cycles of the seasons! YHWH controls the cycle and the seasons (i.e. Lev. 25:21).

The phrase "showers of blessings" reflects the agricultural nature of God's promised blessings to obedient descendants of the Patriarchs (cf. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28).

Special Topic: Waters

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:27 "a tree of the field will yield its fruit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:27 "a tree of the field will yield its fruit" This refers to the covenant abundance (cf. Deuteronomy 27; Hosea 2:22; Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13, 14; Zech. 8:12).

▣ "I have broken the bars of their yoke" This is an idiom of oppression first used in Lev. 26:13. So much of Ezekiel's vocabulary and theology comes from Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29.

▣ "hand" See Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:28-29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:28-29 The nations will no longer dominate YHWH's people. This is the result of the original covenant coming into reality!

Special Topic: Covenant Promises to the Patriarchs

34:29
NASB  "a renowned planting"
NKJV  "a garden of renown"
NRSV, NJB  "a splendid vegetation"
TEV  "fertile fields"
JPSOA  "a planting of renown"
NIV  "a land of renown"
REB  "their crops renowned"
Peshitta  "a plantation of peace"
LXX  "a plant of peace"

The word "planting" (מטע, BDB 642) can mean the plant itself or where it is planted. So the text is referring to

  1. God's people's crops and herds being very productive (i.e. evidence covenant restored, which is the fruitfulness and safety described in Ezek. 34:25-27)
  2. God's people going back to Palestine (evidence covenant restored).

The LXX and Peshitta reverse two consonants in the PREPOSITION plus the NOUN "renown/name" (לשׁם, BDB 1027) and change it to "peace" (שׁלם, BDB 1023) to link up with Ezek. 34:25 (i.e. "I will make a covenant of peace").

This imagery goes back to Ezek. 17:22-24 and the opposite of Ezek. 19:10-14 (cf. Isa. 60:21; 61:3). One of the titles for the Messiah is "Branch" (cf. Isa. 4:2). There is a mixing of images here.

  1. the cosmic tree (i.e. Ezekiel 31)
  2. Israel as a plant (or planting place, which is parallel to Ezek. 34:26a)
  3. the Messiah as a shoot or branch from a stump (cf. Isa. 11:2,10; 53:2; Rom. 15:12)

Special Topic: Peace (shalom)

Special Topic: The Branch of the Lord

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:30 "I the Lord their God am with them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:30 "I the Lord their God am with them" These are Covenant terms which show that the Covenant has been restored in the midst of the destruction of the temple! There is no more significant statement than "I am with them" (i.e. Emmanuel, i.e. Isa. 7:14).

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:31 This covenant language about God as Shepherd (cf. John 10) and His people as sheep is also found in Psalm 23; 78:52; 80:1; Isa. 40:11; Jer. 31:10). This is such a wonderful metaphor of personal presence, care, protection, and provision!

▣ "you are men, and I am your God" This is not meant to be an emphasis on transcendence, but on the special creation of humanity (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; 2:7-8). The LXX omits "you are men" and it is followed by RSV, REB, NAB. Because "men" are mentioned in parallel texts in this literary unit of Ezekiel (i.e. Ezek. 36:37,38), it seems best to stay with the MT.

entries.title: Ezekiel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
EZEKIEL 35

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
    Oracles of Restoration
(33:1-39:29)		    
Prophecy Against Mount Seir Judgment on Mount Seir The Oracle Against Edom God's Punishment on Edom Against the Mountains of Edom
35:1-9 35:1-9 35:1-9 35:1-4 35:1-9
(3b-4) (3b-4) (3b-4) (3b-4)  
      35:5-9  
35:10-15 35:10-15 35:10-15 35:10-13 35:10-15
      35:13-15  

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:2 "set your face against"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:2 "set your face against" See note at Ezek. 1:3.

▣ "Mount Seir" This refers to the nation of Edom (Ezek. 25:12-14; 32:29; 36:5). No other nation is listed in this context. I am surprised that another judgment against Edom is included. She is already addressed in Ezek. 25:12-14. Edom must have a symbolic connotation. She

  1. mocks and attacks YHWH's people, Ezek. 35:5,11, cf. Ps. 137:7; Isa. 63:1-6; Obad. 1:8-19
  2. is prideful (cf. Ezek. 35:10-11), here
  3. has arrogant thoughts against YHWH and His people, Ezek. 35:12,13 (Edom had "everlasting enmity," Ezek. 35:5)

Moderns must admit that we do not know the reasons and procedures for the editing and compilation of OT books. It is possible that Edom stands for all anti-God human societies (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 957).

The concept of "mountain" may be the key to this text. The high plateau of Edom, of which they were so proud, will not save them. As judgment came to the mountains of Israel (i.e. chapter 6), so too, now to the mountains of Edom (cf. Ezek. 35:8,15). As judgment comes to arrogant Edom, blessing will return to the repentant covenant people (i.e. the mountains of Israel, cf. Ezek. 35:12).

Special Topic: Edom and Israel.

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:3 "Lord God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:3 "Lord God" This is literally "Adon YHWH."

Special Topic: Lord (adon and kurios)

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

▣ "I will stretch out My hand against you" This is an anthropomorphic idiom of YHWH's ability to act effectively (cf. Ezek. 25:7,13; Jer. 51:25).

Special Topic: Hand

Special Topic: God Described As Human (anthropomorphism)

▣ "a desolation and a waste" These two parallel terms (cf. Ezek. 35:7) sound alike (i.e. BDB 1031 and BDB 1031) and have the same consonants as "Shammah," a grandson of Edom (BDB 1031, cf. Gen. 36:13,17; 1 Chr. 1:37). Possible meanings are

  1. desolation, שׁממה, cf. Ezek. 35:4,7,9,14,15
  2. waste, משׁמה, cf. Ezek. 35:7; 6:14; 33:28,29
  3. a grandson of Edom, שׁמה

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:5 "everlasting enmity"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:5 "everlasting enmity" This is a good exaple where the Hebrew term 'olam (everlasting) cannot have an eternal meaning. Judah's judgment was necessary, deserved, complete, but not eternal.

Special Topic: Forever ('olam and aiōnios)

▣ "sons of Israel" This is usiing "Israel" in its collective sense. The context is primarily addressing Judah.

▣ "at the time of their calamity, at the time of the punishment of the end" Notice that these two phrases are parallel. The first obviously refers to the invasion of Judah by Neo-Babylon. The second must refer to the same time, which shows "the end" (BDB 893). Interpreters must be careful of not assigning one meaning to a word or phrase and then using it in every place the word appears. Context determines meaning, not one's systematic eschatology!

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:6 "as I live"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:6 "as I live" This is an oath based on the name of YHWH, the ever-living, only-living, I Am (cf. Exod. 3:14). This is a recurrent idiom in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 5:11; 14:16,18,20; 16:48; 17:16,19; 18:3; 20:3,31; 33:11; 34:8; 35:6,11).

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

▣ "blood" The term (BDB 196) can refer to one's "life force" and if it is spilt, to one's death. It is used four times in this verse.

  1. I will give you over to bloodshed
  2. bloodshed will pursue you
  3. you have not hated bloodshed (i.e. murder)
  4. therefore, bloodshed will pursue you (repeated)

We reap what we sow (cf. Ezek. 35:11,15).

Just a textual note, the LXX changes #3 to "you are guilty of blood," which is followed by RSV, NEB, REB, NJB, but this demands a change of several consonants. The MT makes sense.

The UBS Text project, p. 120, suggests that #3 uses "blood" as a reference to Edom's kinsmen, Judah. It, like the NASB, adds the negative "not," which is missing in the MT. It was not Edom's violence (cf. Jer. 49:7-22) but her disregard for kinship that caused YHWH's wrath.

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 35:7 Mount Seir is an idiom for all the inhabitants of Edom (i.e. v. 15).

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 35:9 Edom's destruction will be permanent (cf. Mal. 1:2-4, esp. Ezek. 35:4; Jer. 49:13). Edom's permanent destruction was because of her "everlasting enmity" (Ezek. 35:5; and Obadiah)!

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:10 Edom rejected its required brotherly love for Judah (and Israel, i.e. "two nations") and desired her lands for herself (cf. Ezek. 35:5, 10). The problem is that Judah's land belonged to YHWH (i.e. "the Lord was there"). It was only Judah's by a conditional covenant.

YHWH left Judah in chapter 10, but in Ezek. 48:35 the book of Ezekiel ends with "The YHWH is there" (cf. Ps. 132:13,14).

Special Topic: Edom and Israel

Special Topic: Covenant

35:12
NASB  "revilings"
NKJV, NJB, REB, LXX, Peshitta  "blasphemies"
NRSV  "abusive speech"
TEV  "with contempt"
JPSOA  "taunts"
NET  "insults"

The NOUN (BDB 611, KB 658) is found only here and Neh. 9:18. The revilings are against "the mountains of Israel," but clearly, in context, it is against Israel's God (cf. Ezek. 35:5,10-11,13). This is why Edom is often seen as a type of all anti-God nations!

entries.title: Ezekiel 35:14 "as all the earth rejoices"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:14 "as all the earth rejoices" This is hyperbolic imagery. The earth, as YHWH's creation, rejoices when His will is done. The earth is affected by humanity's sin (cf. Genesis 3; Rom. 8:19-22).

Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth (OT)

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:1 As usual Ezekiel starts a new vision with YHWH addressing him directly (i.e. "son of man"). This literary marker is usually accompanied by IMPERATIVES. In this chapter

  1. prophesy, BDB 612, KB 655, Niphal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 36:3,6 (Niphal PERFECT in Ezek. 4:7)
  2. say, BDB 55, KB 65, Qal PERFECT (often Qal IMPERATIVE in Ezek. 12:10,11,23,28; 17:9,12)
  3. hear, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal PERFECT, cf. Ezek. 13:2 where all three are used. This command is repeated in Ezek. 36:4; see Special Topic: Listen/Hear (shema) .

▣ "O mountains of Israel" Earlier in Ezekiel's prophecies (chapter 6) this same idiom (unique in Ezekiel) is negative (i.e. judgment).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

It must be remembered that these chapters fall into the major literary unit of Ezekiel 33-39, which are an emphasis on YHWH restoring His people and their land.

  1. Ezekiel 36 is a personification of the land with its renewed blessings (cf. Deuteronomy 27-28).

  2. Ezekiel 37 is imagery the national restoration amidst the death of exile.

  3. Both of these chapters are historical precursors of future events.
    1. post-exilic restoration under Zerubbbel
    2. Pentecost, where believing Jews received the Spirit (Heb. 8:6-13)
    3. eschatological setting

  4. Ezekiel 36:22-36 describes the "new covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34. This is a foreshadowing of the grace-based covenant in Christ (i.e. NT).

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:2 The arrogance of the surrounding nations over the demise of YHWH's people and their annexing her lands causes Him to act!

▣ "Aha" This INTERJECTION (BDB 210) expresses joy at another's demise (cf. Ps. 35:21,25; Ezek. 25:3; 26:2; 36:2).

▣ "the everlasting heights" Often the mountains are used as one of God's two permanent witnesses, but here they are used as a personification of Israel and the blessings to come. It is ironic that the same word "heights," bamoth (BDB 119), was used of the high places of Canaanite fertility worship (cf. Ezek. 20:29). This phrase may imply that the surrounding nations see Palestine as an especially blessed place (i.e. fruitful, cf. Deut. 11:11).

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:3 "therefore"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:3 "therefore" Notice that Ezek. 36:3,4,5,6, and 7 all start with the ADVERB "so" or "thus" (BDB 485), when used with a PREPOSITION it means "that being so" or "therefore" (e.g. Num. 16:11; Ezek. 11:4; 37:12; 38:14).

▣ "for good cause they have made you desolate" This is a confession and recognition of the sins of God's people that resulted in the exile.

Judah's condition is described in three INFINITIVES.

  1. desolate, BDB 1030, KB 1563, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT used in two senses
    1. be desolate, Ezek. 6:4; 20:26; 25:3; 29:12; 30:7,12,14; 32:15; 33:28; 36:4
    2. be appalled, Ezek. 3:15; 4:17; 26:16; 27:35; 28:19; 32:10
  2. crushed or trampled upon, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE, cf. Ps. 56:2; 57:4; 94:5; Isa. 3:15; Amos 2:7; 8:4
  3. become the possession ("possession," BDB 440, cf. Exod. 6:8; Ezek. 11:15; 25:10; 33:24; 36:2,5), BDB 224, KB 243, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

▣ "the talk and whisperings of the people" This refers to amazement of the reproach of those who live near or pass by (cf. Ezek. 36:15; 34:29; Deut. 28:57; Ps. 44:9-16; Jer. 18:16). The people speak of defeated Judah as they did of her God (cf. Ezek. 34:12-13).

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:4 YHWH addresses His devastated land (i.e. its covenant people). God's people had become exactly the opposite (i.e. a prey [BDB 103] and a derision [BDB 541]) of what He intended for them to be to the nations.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:5 This is a summary verse expressing YHWH's sorrow in judging His own covenant people (i.e. jealousy is a love word). But now He will judge those who

  1. took His people's land
  2. rejoiced over their downfall
  3. disrespected ("scorn of soul") them
  4. drove them out of the Promised Land

These surrounding nations are the very ones Ezekiel addresses (except Neo-Babylon) in Ezek. 25-32.

Special Topic: Jealousy, Zeal

▣ "My land" YHWH owns all lands by creation (cf. Exod. 19:5; Deut. 32:8 in LXX), but He uniquely claims a special ownership of Canaan (cf. Ezek. 38:16; Lev. 25:23; Isa. 14:25; Jer. 2:7; Joel 1:6; 3:2).

▣ "all Edom" See Special Topic: Edom and Israel

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:7 "I have sworn"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:7 "I have sworn" This is literally "lift up my hands," which was an idiomatic way of referring to an oath (cf. Ezek. 20:5,6,15,23,28,42; 44:12; 47:14). Often YHWH's oath is stated as "as I live, declares the Lord."

Special Topic: Hand

Special Topic: The Problems and Limitations of Human Language

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:8 "Oh mountains of Israel, you will put forth your branches and bear fruit for My people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:8 "Oh mountains of Israel, you will put forth your branches and bear fruit for My people" This is the opposite of what the mountains of Edom will do (cf. Ezek. 35:3, 7, 15). This is a fulfillment of Ezek. 17:23 and 34:26-29 (cf. Isaiah 4; 27:6).

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:10 "all the house of Israel, all of it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:10 "all the house of Israel, all of it" This speaks of the reuniting of the thirteen tribes of Israel (cf. Ezek. 37:21,22; Jer. 3:18; 50:4).

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:10-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:10-15 This reflects the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy 28. It implies that the covenant is renewed and is being obeyed! These blessings are for a repentant and obedient Israel!

  1. multiply men on you
  2. cities reinhabited
  3. waste places rebuilt
  4. multiply man and beast
  5. treat you better than at the first
  6. possess Canaan as an inheritance
  7. no loss of children
  8. no more insults from the surrounding nations
  9. no more stumbling on Israel's part

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:12 "you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:12 "you" This is a personification of the Promised Land (i.e. "the mountains of Israel" or "the everlasting heights"). YHWH has been addressing them in Ezek. 36:1 through Ezek. 36:15.

▣ "never again bereave them of children" This phrase may link back to the spies' report found in Num. 13:32 or YHWH's judgment from Jer. 15:7. If so, it refers to famine, plague, sword, and wild beasts.

The VERB "bereave" (BDB 1013, KB 1491, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is repeated in Ezek. 36:13 and possibly Ezek. 36:14 (MT notes Kethiv, ["written"], "shall not stumble," BDB 505, כשׁל, but Qere ["read"], "shall not bereave," שׁכל), possibly just the author using a wordplay. This threat was first used in Lev. 26:22 (cf. Deut. 32:25). Ezekiel often used Leviticus 26 as a source for his vocabulary. Children were seen as a gift from YHWH, but for covenant disobedience He takes them away. However, a new day has come and no longer will the children be taken!

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:16-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:16-21 YHWH reminds His people of their sins.

  1. they defiled YHWH's land
  2. they shed blood (murder or child sacrifice to Molech)
  3. they were idolatrous

Therefore, YHWH (recurrent themes in Ezekiel)

  1. poured out His wrath on them
  2. scattered them among the nations
  3. judged them according to their ways and deeds

Instead of revealing YHWH to the nations, they profaned His name (in the land and in exile). YHWH wanted to use Abraham's descendants to reveal Himself to all people (cf. Ezek. 36:32,36). National Israel failed to be a clear reflection of YHWH, as a matter of fact, they distorted His image. He has a universal redemptive plan that will not be thwarted! So, He Himself, will act to reveal Himself. The new action is "the new covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34 (i.e. the New Testament). This new covenant, based on YHWH's actions, is described in Ezek. 36:22-36.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:17 "like the uncleanness of a women in her impurity"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:17 "like the uncleanness of a women in her impurity" To covenant people all bodily excretions made one ceremonially unclean. See Lev. 15:19-30.

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:18 "the blood which they shed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:18 "the blood which they shed" This refers either to

  1. the murder of righteous people
  2. the murder of poor people
  3. child sacrifice to Molech

Special Topic: Blood

Special Topic: Molech

▣ "idols" See note at Ezek. 18:15.

Special Topic: Idolatry

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:19 "I scattered them among the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:19 "I scattered them among the nations" This is the covenant curse of Lev. 26:33 coming to fruition (cf. Ezek. 20:23). This judgment on Judah's covenant disobedience became an opportunity for YHWH to reveal Himself to the nations (cf. Ezek. 36:20-21,22-23).

▣ "and according to their ways and their deeds I have judged them" See note at Ezek. 33:20.

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:20 "they have profaned my holy name"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:20 "they have profaned my holy name" Remember that YHWH was linked to Israel and Judah and they were taken into captivity. YHWH was willing for His own name to be impugned that His people might turn back to Him. Israel and Judah profaned YHWH's name (i.e. reputation) in several ways.

  1. covenant disobedience
  2. Canaanite worship
  3. national defeat

YHWH is jealous for His holiness (cf. Ezek. 39:7).

Special Topic: Holy

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:21 "But I had concern for My holy name"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:21 "But I had concern for My holy name" YHWH is concerned (lit. "took pity," BDB 328, KB 328, Qal IMPERFECT, see the negative in Ezek. 5:11; 7:4,9; 8:18; 9:5,10) about His reputation (cf. Ezek. 20:39) because He is in the business of winning all humans made in His image and likeness (cf. Gen. 1:26-27) to faith and repentance in Himself (cf. Ezek. 36:14). His name stands for His person!

Special Topic: Call on His Name

Special Topic: "The Name" of YHWH

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:22-32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:22-32 Verse 22 captures the essence of the new covenant (cf. Luke 22:20; 1 Cor. 11:25; Galatians 3, 4; Heb. 8:6-13; 10:15-18)! Notice the things He will do to reestablish His reputation (cf. Ezek. 36:23).

  1. I will take you from the nations and bring you back to Canaan, Ezek. 36:24
  2. I will sprinkle clean water on you and cleanse you from filthiness and idolatry, Ezek. 36:25
  3. I will give you a new heart and a new spirit, Ezek. 36:26
  4. I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to obey My covenant, Ezek. 36:27
  5. I will be your God in the Promised Land, Ezek. 36:28
  6. I will forgive and restore covenant fruitfulness, Ezek. 36:29-30
  7. YHWH will do this to reveal Himself (Ezek. 36:32). His people will be grieved over their sin (Ezek. 36:31-32).

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:25 "sprinkle clean water on you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:25 "sprinkle clean water on you" Remember that Ezekiel was a trained priest who would be familiar with water as a symbol of spiritual cleansing (e.g. Exod. 29:4; 30:18-21; Lev. 1:9,13; 6:28; 8:6,21; 14:5,6, 8,9,51,52; 15:5,6,7,8,10,11,21,22,27; 16:4,24,26,28; 17:15; 22:6; Num. 5:17-27; 8:7; 19:7,8,9,13,17,18,19,20,21). Some commentators think this text, which links "water" and "Spirit," is the key OT background to John 3:5 (see F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 67-68).

Special Topic: Forgiveness in the OT

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:26 "I will give you a new heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:26 "I will give you a new heart" The balance is seen in Ezek. 18:31 (see full note there), where the Judeans are commanded to make themselves a new heart (cf. Ezek. 11:19; Jer. 31:31-34). God always comes in grace, but humans, empowered by YHWH's grace, must respond. The "heart" was the center of the intellect as the spirit was the source of life. When both are used together, it refers to the entire person.

Special Topic: Heart

Special Topic: Old Things. . .New Things

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:27 "I will put My Spirit within you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:27 "I will put My Spirit within you" This is setting the stage for the "Spirit" in chapter 37. He is the sign of the new age (cf. Ezek. 37:14; 39:29; Isa. 42:1; 44:3; 59:21; Joel 2:28, 29). This is rare text where the Spirit is personalized and internalized (cf. Ezek. 37:14; 39:29; Isa. 11:2; 32:15; 44:3; 59:21; Jer. 32:36-41; Joel 2:28-29; Acts 2). This is New Covenant terminology! This is a precursor to the concept of a Trinity which is so difficult to contemplate in connection with monotheism.

For good articles on the Spirit in the OT see

  1. Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 273-274
  2. Christian Theology, 2nd ed., by Millard J. Erickson, pp. 881-885

Special Topic: Spirit in the Bible

Special Topic: Monotheism

Special Topic: The Trinity

Special Topic: The Personhood of the Spirit

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:28 "my people, and I will be your God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:28 "my people, and I will be your God" These are covenant terms (cf. Ezek. 11:20; 14:11; 37:23,27), which show that YHWH has reestablished the previous covenants of the Patriarchs and Moses.

Special Topic: Covenant Promises to the Patriarchs

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:30 "I will multiply the fruit of the tree"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:30 "I will multiply the fruit of the tree" This refers to the covenant blessings (cf. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28).

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:31 "You will remember your evil ways and your deeds that were not good, and you will loathe yourselves"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:31 "You will remember your evil ways and your deeds that were not good, and you will loathe yourselves" This refers to the repentance of the covenant people (cf. Ezek. 6:9; 16:61,63; 20:43; Jer. 22:22; 31:19). Repentance, faith, obedience (cf. Deut. 30:1-3), and perseverance are covenant requirements of the OT and NT. Justification must not be separated from sanctification! Both are gifts from God in which believers must participate (cf. Ezek. 36:20).

Special Topic: Repentance (OT)

Special Topic: Believe, Faith or Trust

Special Topic: Keep

Special Topic: Perseverance

▣ "abominations" See Special Topic: Abomination (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:32 YHWH wants His people to acknowledge their sin. This verse has three commands.

  1. "let it be known," BDB 393, KB 390, Niphal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  2. "be ashamed," BDB 101, KB 116, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "be confounded," BDB 483, KB 480, Niphal IMPERATIVE

Verse 32 is a crucial theological message.

  1. YHWH is going to act for His name's sake, not based on His people's merit (Ezek. 36:22).
  2. Judah must repent. The new covenant is also conditional on repentance, faith, obedience, and perseverance (cf. Ezek. 6:9; 16:63; 20:43; Jer. 31:18).

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:33-36
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:33-36 This is a repeat of Ezek. 36:10-15.

▣ "Eden" See Special Topic: Eden

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:36 "the nations that are left round about you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:36 "the nations that are left round about you" What nations are these? Does it refer to the surrounding nations addressed in Ezekiel 25-32? If so, then the call to "take prophecy literally" must be questioned here. If it refers to future unnamed nations, what is the purpose of their "knowing that I am the Lord"? Are these Gentile nations just to recognize His blessing on Israel or to come to know her God also?

All of us who believe, honor, respect, and cherish God's Word struggle with the relationship between the Old and New Covenants. If the NT is the fulfillment of the OT and the specific fulfillment of Gen. 3:15, then the scope of God's love must be expanded to all nations because of Gen. 1:26-27; 3:15; and 12:3! This does not minimize national Israel, but recognizes that the biblical focus is on YHWH, not Israel. The focus of the gospel is not Israel, but the redemption and restoration of all mankind. Jesus, not Israel, is the key thrust of the NT. If He is Messiah and if the NT writers are inspired (esp. Paul and the author of Hebrews), then a new day has come, a universal offer has been made, a once-for-all sacrifice has been given! The original purpose of creation has been fulfilled, not in Israel, but in fellowship between God and His highest creation, mankind. Salvation is the restoration of the image of God in humanity damaged in the fall of Genesis 3.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

Special Topic: The Gospel

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:37 "I will let the house of Israel ask Me to do for them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:37 "I will let the house of Israel ask Me to do for them" YHWH reverses His unwillingness to hear Israel's prayers (cf. Ezek. 14:3; 20:3,31; Isa. 1:15; Jer. 11:11).

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 36:37-38
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:37-38 This is a reemphasis on Ezek. 36:10, 11.

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:1 "The hand of the Lord was upon me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:1 "The hand of the Lord was upon me" This has been a recurrent literary marker of a new revelation (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 3:14,22; 8:1; 33:22; 37:1; 40:1).

Special Topic: Hand

Special Topic: Ways of Revelation

▣ "by the Spirit of the Lord" The word "Spirit" in Ezek. 37:1, 14 and the word "breath" in Ezek. 37:5, 6, 8, 9 (twice), and 10 and the word "wind" in Ezek. 37:9 all relate to one Hebrew term, ruah (BDB 924), which can mean "wind, breath, or spirit." There is a play on this root throughout this chapter.

Special Topic: Spirit (pneuma) in the Bible

Special Topic: Breath, Wind, Spirit

▣ "the valley" This seems to refer to the place of slaughter (cf. Jer. 7:32-8:2). The place of idolatry and judgment (i.e. Jerusalem, the Valley of Topheth, Valley of the Sons of Hinnom, Gehenna) will become the very place of resurrection and restoration.

The real question is to whom does this refer?

  1. past idolatrous leaders and Israelites (cf. Jer. 7:37-8:2)
  2. current Judeans
  3. the righteous remnant (see Special Topic: The Remnant, Three Senses)
  4. future Jews
  5. symbol of God's people (cf. Ezek. 37:11)

but not previous idolaters. It seems to me in context that #3 fits best. It is texts like this that cause some to say all Jews will be saved, but this violates too many NT texts, even the Jews of Romans 9-11 (as well as those of Zech. 12:10) must be repentant believers (cf. Jer. 3:22-4:2). There is no biblical support for the restoration of unbelieving, unrepenting descendants of Abraham. Only the people of faith are his true seed (cf. Rom. 2:28-29; Gal. 6:16). Remember that chapter 36 (i.e. new heart, new spirit) sets the contextual stage for chapter 37.

The term "valley" in Ezek. 37:1 is BDB 132 (which can refer to a broad plain, LXX), while Jer. 7:32 is BDB 161. However, they may still relate to one another.
