READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This section of Ezekiel (i.e. Ezek. 33-39) is confusing to me because
    1. it is surprising that Edom is condemned again in Ezek. 35 after it was dealt with in Ezek. 25:12-14.
    2. it is surprising that after Israel's marvelous restoration she is attacked again by surrounding nations (i.e. Ezek. 38-39).

       This section sets the theological stage for John's vision in Revelation 19-20. As surprising as it is, the truth is clear. Spiritual restoration will be followed by conflict (cf. Dan. 9:24-27)! However, a time of temporary victory will be followed by a time of ultimate victory over evil (i.e. the new covenant's consummation). It is surely possible that Edom, as well as Gog, Magog, Meshech, and Tubal, are imagery for the pervasive evil which attacks God's people again and again.

  2. The final literary unit (Ezek. 40-48) is a way of showing that the spiritual apostasy of Ezek. 8-10 is over and YHWH's earthly throne is restored to its special place (i.e. the Ark). The last vision is one of ultimate, complete victory (i.e. symbolized lby a new temple).

  3. However, if it is true that one must interpret the OT through the eyes of the NT, then the book of Hebrews tells believers that Ezekiel was a partial, temporary divine revelation (cf. Heb. 1:1). Progressive revelation negates a new temple! Even 2 Thess. 2:4 must be seen as a Greek temple (i.e. "take his seat," there is no seat in a Jewish temple). A current popular theology (i.e. dispensationalism) focuses on Israel and Jerusalem, thereby reading the NT through the eyes of the OT. The NT must have priority! The focus of the gospel is Jesus and His death for all humans, not Israel! Please look at (Special Topic: Why are OT Covenant Promises so Different from NT Covenant Promises? and Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan). Who are the "covenant people" now? This is the question!!
     For a good video on this issue, see Steve Gregg's YouTube video, "Deconstructing Dispensationalism"

  4. There are several key terms repeated in this chapter.
    1. רוח (BDB 924, KB 1194-1201,  also used extensively in Ezek. 1,3,11,42; see Special Topic: Breath, Wind, Spirit)
      1. Spirit, Ezek. 37:1,14
      2. breath, Ezek. 37:5,6,8,9 (twice),10
      3. wind, Ezek. 37:9
    2. חיה (BDB 310, KB 309, also used extensively in Ezekiel 18, 33)
      1. live, Ezek. 37:3,9,14
      2. come to life, Ezek. 37:5,6,10
    3. ידע, know, Ezek. 37:3,6,13,14,28 (BDB 393, KB 309, used extensively in Ezekiel)
    4. כתב, write (BDB 507), Ezek. 37:16 (twice), 20 (cf. Ezek. 2:10; 13:9; 24:2; 43:11)
    5. נבא, prophesy, Ezek. 37:4,7 (twice), 9 (twice), 10,12 (BDB 612, KB 659); see Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)
  5. There may be a shift in imagery from a battlefield, full of the unburied, sun-bleached bones in Ezek. 37:1-11 (esp. Ezek. 37:10), to a graveyard in Ezek. 37:12. We must remember this is highly symbolic Hebrew poetic prophecy. Ezekiel is a precursor to the interbiblical apocalyptic literature. However, this chapter is not apocalyptic!

  6. Especially in a prophetic book like Ezekiel we must familiarize ourselves with the genre of prophecy. Three books have helped me navigate these turbulent waters!
    1. How to Read the Bible For All Its Worth by Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart (pp. 181-204)
    2. Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic by D. Brent Sandy
    3. Cracking Old Testament Codes by D. Brent Sandy and Ronald Giese
    4. Also note Introduction to Biblical Interpretation by Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard, pp. 292-312.

      Many personal and denominational dragons (i.e. presuppositions and biases) live in these waters!
      Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

  7. After thinking through this whole issue of a restored geographical Israel, it becomes obvious why dispensationalism wants to separate Israel and the church. This relatively new system of thought (see C. Bass, Backgrounds to Dispensationalism) takes seriously OT Scripture (cf. Matt. 5:17-19). If OT prophecy is literally true (and I am not sure this is true in light of genre studies, cf. Plowshares and Pruning Hooks; Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic by D. Brent Sandy. I think prophecies, for the most part, are conditional), there must be an end-time national Israel and we learn from Ezek. 38-39 that it will be invaded during a golden age of peace and security.
     The problem comes when this is not the theological agenda of the NT, which focuses on believers and unbelievers and depreciates the Jew-Gentile divide (cf. Eph. 2:11-3:13). At this point the theological options are difficult to make.
    1. OT Scripture has been fulfilled and superceded by the gospel (i.e. Matt. 5:17-19,21-48). This means that all the promises of YHWH to Israel concerning her restoration to Canaan must be seen as
      1. fulfilled in Jesus (the Davidic Messiah)
      2. abbrogated because of Israel's continued covenant violations
      3. Israel was surely an initial part of YHWH's revelatory plan, but not the ultimate goal.
    2. Israel is no longer the key to world evangelization
    3. the OT prophesies about national Israel must be rethought (neither Jesus nor any NT writer reaffirms a national promise to Israel)
    4. the whole theological system of dispensationalism which posits
      1. all prophecies must be literally fulfilled to national Israel (see Special Topic: Prophecy [OT])
      2. the church and Israel are totally separate
      3. there will be a secret rapture of the church so that OT prophecies can be literally fulfilled to Israel
      4. the millennium (and the book of Revelation) are primarily about Israel and not the church must be rejected as sincere and clever, but misguided! Its presuppositional grid is more logical than biblical!

See suggested video at C.

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:4 Notice that the Spirit (wind, breath) and the Word (note Ezek. 37:14) of the Lord are parallel (cf. Isa. 59:21). As God (i.e. Jesus, cf. John 1:3,10; Rom. 11:36; 1 Cor. 8:6; Col. 1:16; Heb. 1:2; 2:10) breathed into the newly formed human body (cf. Gen. 2:7) to create persons for fellowship, so He does again!

This emphasizes the power of the Word of God (cf. Ezek. 6:3; 13:2,6; 16:35; 20:47; 25:3; 34:7,9; 36:1; Isa. 45:23; 55:11; Matt. 24:35). This is a re-creation event!

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:5 This is parallel to Gen. 2:7 (notice Ezek. 37:8); there by God (i.e. Jesus) and here by His Spirit (cf. Ezek. 37:14). Only God can give and sustain life! Only He has life! Here the "life" is national restoration to the Promised Land. The reversal of exile (national death) by the renewal of the covenant promises (conditional on covenant obedience, cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28).

Special Topic: Covenant

Special Topic: Keep

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:6 This is a recurrent theme, usually connected to judgment (i.e. Ezek. 35:9; 38:23; 39:6), but here to symbolic resurrection of a whole people (i.e. Joel 2:27; 3:17). In Isaiah 49 this phrase is linked to the inclusion of the Gentiles (cf. Eph. 2:11-3:13). This has always been God's plan!

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan.

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:7 "a noise"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:7 "a noise" The term (BDB 876) can refer to

  1. a human voice (Ezek. 27:30; 33:32)
  2. a sound (cf. Gen. 3:8,9)
  3. the Lord's voice (Isa. 6:8)
  4. Cherubim wings (Ezek. 1:24; 3:13; 10:5)
  5. Seraphim's voice (Isa. 6:4)
  6. angel (Dan. 8:16)
  7. animals/chariots (Ezek. 3:13)
  8. musical instrument
  9. thunder
  10. lament (Ezek. 26:15; 31:16)

BDB (#2g) calls it an earthquake. However, the context implies it was the sound (i.e. rattling) of bones coming together. That these unburied bones could live again is amazing symbolism of restoration and forgiveness of the covenant people (both corporate and individual).

▣ "a rattling" In Ezek. 12:18 this same word (BDB 950) is used of fear and trembling. It can also refer to an earthquake (cf. 1 Kgs. 19:11,12; Isa. 29:6; Ezek. 38:19; Amos 1:11; Zech. 14:5). These bones made a lot of noise as they assembled themselves.

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:8 Apparently the bones were scattered on the ground. At Ezekiel's prophesying they came together as a complete skeleton, but still lying on the ground (cf. Ezek. 37:10b). This cannot be used as a proof-text that Israel will return to the Promised Land unconverted (i.e. The Prophecy of Ezekiel by Charles Lee Feinberg, p. 213. See YouTube video by Steve Gregg, "The Modern State of Israel."

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:9 "say to the breath"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:9 "say to the breath" This verse has five commands.

  1. "prophesy," BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVES directed to Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 37:12)
  2. "come," BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "breathe," BDB 655, KB 708, Qal IMPERATIVE directed to the breath/wind/spirit (see Special Topic: Breath, Wind, Spirit)
  4. "come to life," BDB 310, KB 309, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense to the newly formed bodies

This word "breath" can also be translated "wind," "spirit." Notice this breath is personified (see Special Topic: Breath, Wind, Spirit).

  1. It comes from the four corners of the earth (cf. Isa. 43:5).
  2. It breathes breath on the inanimate human bodies.
  3. It comes into the human bodies (Ezek. 37:10) and brings life.

This is all parallel to Genesis 2 (esp. Ezek. 37:7). This is new life before the Fall, a new chance at obedience with a new heart and a new spirit (i.e. Ezek. 36:22-36)!

▣ "from the four winds" This is imagery for all directions. The exiles will return from all directions; the Spirit is with them and will bring them home.

Note the enemies of chapters 38-39 are also from all directions. Evil is also pervasive!

Special Topic: Symbolic Numbers in Scripture, #2

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:10 "an exceedingly great army"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:10 "an exceedingly great army" Although this Hebrew term (BDB 298) can mean "army" (i.e. Ezek. 17:17; 27:10), it can be understood as a multitude (cf. NRSV, note Ezek. 37:11). The new Israel does not need a great army, they have a great God (this is why chapters 38-39 are so surprising)!

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:11 "these bones are the whole house of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:11 "these bones are the whole house of Israel" This is YHWH's promise that the northern and southern tribes, split since 922 B.C., will be reunited (cf. vv. 15-23; Jer. 3:18; 23:5-6; 50:4-5; Hosea 1:11) under a Davidic king.

▣ "we are completely cut off" There is a possible manuscript issue in this phrase.

NASB  "we are completely cut off"

NKJV  "we ourselves are completely cut off"

NRSV  "we are cut off completely"

LXX    "we are quite spent" or "we are lost"

Peshitta "we are completely gone"

JPSOA "we are doomed"

The Tyndale OT Commentary Series, Ezekiel, by John Taylor mentions that F. Perles redivides the phrase to "our thread-of-life has been cut off" (238), which fits the context better than "we have been cut off for us" (Niphal PERFECT).

This refers to the Judean's view of themselves in light of the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple and the exile of the Davidic King. There was no hope humanly speaking (cf. Ezek. 19:5)!

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:12 "Thus says the Lord God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:12 "Thus says the Lord God" This recurrent literary phrase introduces (list from NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 445)

  1. judgment against the surrounding nations (cf. Ezek. 25:3; 30:2)
  2. judgment against individuals (cf. Ezek. 28:2; 39:1)
  3. judgment against Judah (cf. Ezek. 5:8; 12:19)
    1. her mountains, Ezek. 6:3
    2. her false religious leaders, Ezek. 13:3,18
    3. her faithlessness, Ezek. 20:30
    4. her injustices, Ezek. 45:9
  4. call for Judah to repent (cf. Ezek. 14:6)
  5. message of restoration and forgiveness (cf. Ezek. 36:33; 37:12,21; 39:25)
  6. message of hope to Ezekiel himself (cf. Ezek. 2:4; 3:11)

▣ "I will open your graves and cause you to come up out of your graves" This refers to an image of Abraham's seed being restored to Canaan. This is not an OT reference to individual resurrection, though later rabbis tried to use it in this sense (i.e. Sanh. 10:1 and b.Sanh. 90b).

Special Topic: Ressurection, II.

Special Topic: Pharisees

▣ "the land of Israel" both Hebrew words for "land" are used in chapter 37.

  1. Adamah (BDB 9, KB 15), which is used for Canaan, vv. 12,14,21
  2. erets (BDB 75, KB 90) used in v. 25 where it is also used of Canaan

Special Topic: World (several terms)

Special Topic: Covenant Promises to the Patriarchs

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:12-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:12-14 These are covenant promises (i.e. the land, cf. Ezek. 37:12,14) and covenant title (i.e. "My people," Ezek. 37:12,13). The covenant is renewed! Destruction and exile have ceased.

Again one asks the question, when did or will this occur?

  1. post-exilic return under Zerubbabal (seed of David) and Joshua (seed of High Priest)
  2. some future time (see my new verse-by-verse commentary on the book of Revelation online at www.freebiblecommentary.org)

Because Israel was attacked again by Rome and the temple destroyed again (A.D. 70, cf. Dan. 9:24-27), many modern interpreters assert a future orientation. There are certainly eschatological elements in chapters 36-48! My focus is on the conditional nature of prophecy. This reflects what God wanted His people to be and do, as well as what He wanted to do for them, but Genesis 3 (the Fall; see Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind) got in the way. Mankind's fallen propensities can be dealt with only by the Messiah's work and the new age (new covenant). Chapter 36 surely reflects this, but what of chapters 38-39? Israel is attacked again by surrounding enemies. Security is challenged!

The question is, "Was the opposition caused by

  1. Israel's continuing sin
  2. evil's attack on God?"

Number 1 fits the post-exilic period (cf. Malachi).

The hard question is, "Must all prophecy be literally fulfilled to Israel?" I think not (i.e. Jonah, see Special Topic: Prophecy [OT])! The NT focuses on Jesus, not Israel. The NT widens the OT promises to all humans. The national and/or geographic promises to Israel are not repeated or mentioned by Jesus nor any of the Apostles or NT authors! This is very surprising, but true.

Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:16 This is a symbol of the reuniting of Israel's tribes that politically split in 922 B.C. under Solomon's son, Rehoboam (Judah, Benjamin, Simeon, and most of Levi) and the Emphraimatic labor leader, Jeroboam I, who took the Northern Ten Tribes.

Note the IMPERATIVES in this paragraph.

  1. "take," Ezek. 37:16, Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 542, KB 534)
  2. "write," Ezek. 37:16, Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 507, KB 503)
  3. "take," Ezek. 37:16, Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB542, KB 534)
  4. "write, Ezek. 37:16, Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB507, KB 503)
  5. "join," Ezek. 37:17, Piel IMPERATIVE (BDB 897, KB 1132)
  6. "say," Ezek. 37:19, Piel IMPERATIVE (BDB 180, KB 210)
  7. "say," Ezek. 37:21 Piel IMPERATIVE (BDB 180, KB 210)
▣
NASB, NKJV, TEV, NKB, Peshitta, JPSOA  "stick"
REB  "one leaf of a
  wooden tablet"
LXX  "rid"
NET  "branch"

The root, עצ (BDB 781, KB 863) has a wide semantic field connected to wooden objects.

  1. a tree, trees (Ps. 1:3)
  2. Tree of Life (Gen. 2:9,16; Prov. 3:18; 13:12; 15:4)
  3. wooden idol (Deut. 4:28; 28:36,64; Jer. 10:8)
  4. building material (Gen. 6:14; Deut. 10:3)
  5. piece of wood
  6. firewood (Deut. 19:5; Isa. 30:33; Ezek. 24:5)
  7. stake on which bodies are impaled (Gen. 49:10; Deut. 21:22-23; Josh. 8:29; 10:26,27)
  8. vine (Ezek. 15:2,6)
  9. fertility gods (Deut. 12:2; Ezek. 6:13; 20:28; Jer. 2:20; 3:9,13)
  10. figurative (i.e. Jdgs. 9:8; Isa. 10)

This context speaks of a figurative usage connected to the reunification of Israel and Judah.

  1. symbol of national Israel (if a vine)
  2. symbol of faithfulness (Ps. 1:3)
  3. symbol of ruling staff of Davidic monarch (Isa. 11)

Special Topic: Trees

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:17-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:17-22 The one God will have one people, with one leader, in one place! This sense of "oneness" is also found in Eph. 4:4-6. It only makes sense that the one God (i.e. monotheism) who made all humans in His image (Gen. 1:26-27) for fellowship, and who promised to redeem all humans in Gen. 3:15, would provide a way (i.e. Christ, cf. John 1:12; 3:16; 4:42) for all humans to come into this fellowship (cf. Eph. 2:11-3:13; 1 Tim. 2:4; 4:10; Titus 2:11; 2 Pet. 3:9; 1 John 2:1; 4:14; see Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan).

In this context the oneness refers to a reunification of Israel and Judah. The people of God will be united again.

This text is a foreshadowing of the NT oneness! Monotheism demands a universal fulfillment to those who believe, not to those who can document their lineage.

My biases are showing in this chapter! I pray they are biblically based!

Special Topic: Monotheism

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:18 Ezekiel has been asked and has responded to several questions by the exiled Israelite community (cf. Ezek. 12:9; 21:7; 24:19).

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:23 It is true that the exile cured God's people of idolatry, but unfortunately other sins returned as the book of Malachi and interbiblical history show.

YHWH does cleanse His people, but the pull of the fallen nature traps them again. They need a new nature which only comes with the new covenant (Ezek. 36:22-36; Jer. 31:31-34; Joel 2:28-32).

There is a manuscript variant in this verse.

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "dwelling places"
NRSV  "all their apostasies into
 which they have fallen"
TEV  "all the ways in which they
 sin and betray Me"
NJB  "the acts of infidelity
 which they have committed"
JPSOA  "in all their settlements"
LXX  "all their transgressions"

The MT has מושבתיהם, "their dwellings" (BDB 444), but many modern translations have משובתיהם, "their backslidings" (BDB 1000). This kind of reversal of letters is surely possible in hand-copied manuscripts over an extended period of time. The UBS Text Project, p. 125, gives the LXX a "C" rating.

Special Topic: Textual Criticism

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:24 "My servant David will be king over them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:24 "My servant David will be king over them" This is a Messianic title and shows the new-covenant focus of this context (cf. Ezek. 34:23-24; Isa. 55:3-5; Jer. 30:9; Hosea 3:5).

It is surely possible that a new Davidic ruler, with a heart towards YHWH, will be manifested in order to fulfill 2 Sam. 7:16; Psalm 89; and Gen. 49:10! This ideal, godly king became a rallying hope for a godly people and the fulfillment of the conditional covenant promises. David was sinful, yet forgiven, so too, Israel! Restoration and salvation are the work of God (i.e. new heart and new spirit), but the new covenant must be received and walked in!

Special Topic: My Servant

Special Topic: Messiah

Special Topic: Messianic Era

▣ "they will walk in My ordinances, and keep My statutes, and observe them" For the terms "ordinances" (BDB 1048) and "statutes" (BDB 349) see the Special Topic: Terms for God's Revelation.

The VERB "walk" (BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERFECT) denotes a lifestyle obedience, as do the next two VERBS (see Special Topic: The Path, The Way).

  1. "keep," BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal IMPERFECT
  2. "observe," BDB 793, KB 889, Qal PERFECT

God's covenant people will be an obedient, godly people. This does not denote sinlessness, but a heart for God and His word (cf. 1 John 3:6,9). By their fruits you shall know them (Matt. 7:15-23, i.e. false prophets).

Special Topic: Keep

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:25, 26 "forever. . .everlasting. . .forever"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:25, 26 "forever. . .everlasting. . .forever" This word (BDB 761) must be dealt with in context (cf. Ezek. 37:28) and it seems to imply the eternal kingdom, as in the book of Daniel (cf. Dan. 7:14). It seems inappropriate to use this for the return from the exile (i.e. post-exilic period) or for the millennium (Revelation 20; see Special Topic: Millennium).

Special Topic: Forever ('olam and aiōnios)

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:25 "Jacob My servant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:25 "Jacob My servant" See Special Topic: My Servant

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:26 "a covenant of peace"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:26 "a covenant of peace" This same period of restoration is discussed in chapts. 16 and 20 (also called "the eternal covenant," cf. Isa. 24:5; 55:3; 61:8; Jer. 32:40; 50:5; Ezek. 16:60).

The full phrase "covenant of peace" is mentioned in Ezek. 34:25. The covenant of peace is contingent on repentance, trust/faith/belief, obedience, and perseverance, as is the "new covenant" fully clarified in the NT. It is free from a sovereign God, but it has requirements (cf. Eph. 2:8-10)! The very concept of "covenant" implies responsibilities on both parties!

Special Topic: Covenant

Special Topic: Peace (shalom)

NASB  "And I will place them and multiply them"
NKJV  "I will establish them and multiply them"
NRSV  "and I will bless them and multiply them"
TEV  "I will establish them and increase their population"
NJB  "I will resettle them and make them grow"
LXX       ——omits——
Peshitta  "and I will multiply them"

The VERB "give" or "set" (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT with waw) is repeated twice. It seems that the LXX translators left out an entire phrase.

The MT has "set" or "establish," but NRSV changes the VERB to "bless." The UBS Hebrew OT Text Project gives "set" a B rating (some doubt).

▣ "an everlasting covenant" The NIV Study Bible, p. 1279, has a good footnote about this. The phrase is used sixteen times in the OT. Here are some examples.

  1. Noah, Gen. 9:16
  2. Abraham, Gen. 17:7,13,19 (cf. Ps. 105:9-10)
  3. David, 2 Sam. 23:5 (cf. Ezek. 7:12; Isa. 55:3)
  4. the "new covenant," Jer. 32:40 (cf. Ezek. 31:31-34; 50:5)
  5. earlier in Ezekiel, 16:60
  6. new Israel, Isa. 61:8

It is found most often in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 24:5; 55:3; 61:8).

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:26-27 "My sanctuary. . .My dwelling place"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:26-27 "My sanctuary. . .My dwelling place" This obviously refers to a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. The question is, "When do these verses become a reality?"

In context, this refers to the decree of Cyrus II in 538 B.C., which allowed all the exiled people groups, including the inhabitants of Israel and Judah, to return home and rebuild their national temples at the expense of the Persian government.

For Israel and mostly Judah, this is recorded in

  1. Ezra
  2. Nehemiah
  3. Malachi
  4. possibly Obadiah and Joel

Special Topic: Post Exilic Chart

entries.title: Ezekiel 37:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:28 God wants a righteous people who reflect His character to the nations. Israel was meant to be "a kingdom of priests" (cf. Exod. 19:5-6), but this wonderful call turned into an elitism! The goal of creation is not Israel, but the whole world in fellowship with its Creator. Monotheism cannot become a weapon of exclusivism. It must become a promise of inclusion!

▣ "I am the Lord who sanctifies Israel" YHWH transfers His holiness to His people (cf. Ezek. 20:12). They are holy because of their relationship to Him. Now this positional sanctification must become fleshed out.

Special Topic: Sanctification

▣ "when My sanctuary is in their midst forever" YHWH's sanctuary was abandoned by Him in chapters 8-10. Now Ezekiel asserts it will return to a sanctified, united Israel under a new Davidic ruler. Chapters 40-48 are a graphic symbol of this new day. This may be an allusion to Exod. 25:8.

However, as the temple was central in the OT, Jesus, the true temple, becomes central in the NT (cf. Matt. 26:61; 27:40; Mark 14:58; 15:29; John 2:19; Acts 6:14). You may say to yourself, why bring Jesus into Ezekiel? He is the fulfillment of the OT. It is no longer about Israel (cf. John 8:31-59). These OT symbols and prophecies have their ultimate fulfillment and expansion through Him!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How do Ezek. 36 and 37 relate to the people of Ezekiel's day?
  2. How do they relate to end-time events?
  3. Why are Deuteronomy 27 and 28 such important passages?
  4. Explain what Ezek. 36:27 means when it says, "I will put My Spirit within them."
  5. Summarize Ezek. 37 in one sentence in your own words.

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:1 "the word of the Lord came to me saying" See note at Ezek. 1:3.

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. In prophecy the historical setting and the literary unit are crucial in interpretation. In this case both are difficult.
    1. As far as history, to whom do these nations refer? Are they symbolic of evil in general or specific geographical nations (or directions)?
    2. As far as the literary unit, is Ezek. 33-39 one unit or several? Are they all related to the post-exilic period or beyond? Is there a temporal relation between Ezek. 36-37 and 38-39? Is restoration followed by a final attack (cf. Dan. 9:24-27)?

  2. These questions haunt me! I cannot come to a place of peace about them! To read many of the commentaries available one would think there are no problems in interpreting these texts. One's systematic theology answers all the contextual questions. Part of my dilemma is my own presuppositional systematic theology (see Special Topics at Ezek. 12:16 and 34:26). I guess when all is said and done, the teachings of Jesus, the writings of Paul, and the sharp contrast of the book of Hebrews have become priority for me! I read the OT through these filters! The NT is surprisingly similar and surprisingly different from the OT! A new day of a universal offer and consequence has arrived in Christ! The believing remnant has been expanded into the gospel offer (i.e. John 1:12; 3:16; Eph. 2:8-10). Abraham's seed are by faith, not descent (cf. Rom. 2:28-29; Galatians 3-4).
    Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from NT Covenant Promises?
    Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

  3. One thing is sure, history is teleological. There will be a final and decisive conflict between fallen mankind and its Creator! This invasion is not because of restored Israel's sin, but the greed of Gog and his followers. Evil was already defeated in Christ, but will one day be revealed and removed (i.e. isolated) from creation (i.e. hell, cf. Matt. 25:46; Dan. 12:1-2).
    Special Topic: Eternal Punishment

  4. This literary unit (i.e. Ezek. 38-39) is more about God's honor (cf. Ezek. 37:22-38) than Israel. National Israel (Israel and Judah) was exiled in shame, but restored Israel, faithful Israel, cannot be defeated because YHWH fights on her behalf. The hero of the OT is God, not Israel!
      The nations misunderstood the purpose of the exile (i.e. YHWH allowing, even instigating, His covenant people to be disciplined). They thought Israel's God was weak and unable to fulfill His covenant promises. Ezek. 38-39 show this is not the case!

  5. When all is said and done, I cannot be sure of the who and when of chapters 38-39, but I am confident to whom they do not refer to! Prophecy cannot be read beside the morning newspaper without the great danger of reading our day, our history into every event! Please take time to review my exegetical, verse-by-verse commentary on Matt. 24; 2 Thess. 2; and the book of Revelation (2024).

  6. John Taylor, in the Tyndale OT Commentary Series, makes a good point about the genre of the literary unit (i.e. chapters 38-39).
     "This is typical of Hebrew poetry and of the kind of semi-poetical writing which is used in these oracles. It is fond of repetition and delights to revert to previous statements and enlarge on them, even though the result is to destroy all sense of consecutive arrangement. Failure to appreciate this has led many western commentators to find doublets, contradictions and inconsistencies, and so to assume multiple authorship where this is quite unnecessary" (p. 247).

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:2 "Son of man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:2 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

Special Topic: Son of Man

▣ "set your face toward" See note at Ezek. 13:17.

▣ "prophesy" This is the second IMPERATIVE in verse 2. The VERB (BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE) is used often in several forms. For a discussion of Niphal and all the Hebrew VERBAL STEMS see the Introductory Articles or Special Topic: Hebrew Grammar

  1. Niphal PERFECT, 4:7; 37:7
  2. Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, 11:13; 37:7
  3. Niphal PARTICIPLE, 12:27; 13:2,16; 38:17
  4. Niphal IMPERATIVE, 6:2; 11:4 (twice); 13:2,17; 21:2,7,14,33; 25:2; 28:21; 29:2; 30:2; 34:2 (twice); 35:2; 36:1,3,6; 37:4,9 (twice),12; 38:2,14; 39:1
  5. Hithpael PARTICIPLE, 13:17; 37:10

It is often used in connection with "set your face" (i.e. judgment oracle). It denotes that the message Ezekiel delivers to Israel, Judah, and the nations is from YHWH, not the prophet.

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:2 "Gog"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:2 "Gog" This (BDB 155, KB 182) could refer to

  1. Gyges (Gugu in Ashurbanipal's records, ABD, vol. 2, p. 1056), seventh century king (670-652 B.C.) of Lydia, who lived several generations before Ezekiel (also spelled Giges or Gogo, Encyclopedia Judaica, vol. 7, p. 691 and The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1115)
  2. Gaga or Gagaia (Amarna Letters), used as a general name for northern people groups
  3. Gaga (Ras Shamra Texts), an Akkadian or Babylonian god (cf. Enuma Elish)
  4. Gagi, a ruler of the city of Sabi (ZPBE, vol. 2, p. 770)
  5. Gog or Gug, a Sumerian word for "darkness" and thereby imagery for evil (ABD, vol. 2, p. 1057, and W. F. Albright)
  6. leaders of the Scythians (Josephus, Antiq. 1.6.1, ZPBE, vol. 2, p. 770), a people who lived on the fringe of the Roman Empire and invaded it from the northeast
  7. Gasga, a name appearing in Hittite texts and referring to a rebellious area on the border of Armenia and Cappadocia (Introduction To the OT by R. K. Harrison, p. 842)

The key to understanding this term is not to identify the exact person to whom it refers, but to see its symbolic usage (cf. #5) as an/the evil enemy from the north. In Jeremiah "the north" represents "invasion" (cf. Jer. 1:13-15; 4:6). Because of the desert between Mesopotamia and Palestine, Assyria and Babylon invaded from the north. The word itself became a symbol of evil invasion. This is not meant to be a geographical direction, although Magog, Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal are probably located in modern Turkey (i.e. Asia Minor) or between Cappadocia and Media (ZPBF, vol. 2, p. 770).

Gog is "the" eschatological enemy from the north (cf. Rev. 20:8)! This would correspond to the "Man of Sin" of 2 Thessalonians 2 or the "Antichrist" of 1 John. Evil is personified as a personal enemy and attempted replacer of Christ (the Davidic seed, cf. Ezek. 34:24; 37:24-25).

A good source for possible geographical identifications is Edwin Yamauchi's Foes From the Northern Frontier.

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:2 "the land of Magog"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:2 "the land of Magog" The term in Akkadian means "place/land of Gog/Gyges" (Gen. 10:2). Here in Ezekiel it is a land, but in John's use of it in the book of Revelation, 20:8, it is another evil nation (cf. LXX). These terms are also found in the apocalyptic writings called the Sibylline Oracles 3:319, 512.

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

NASB, NKJV, REB  "the prince of Rosh"
NRSV, JPSOA  "the chief prince of"
TEV  "chief ruler"
NJB  "the paramount prince of"

The NRSV, TEV, and NJB translations take "Rosh" (BDB 910) as meaning "head" or "chief" (i.e. Exod. 18:25; Ezek. 39:1), following the Aramaic Targums, Vulgate, and Aquila translations. The NASB lists "Rosh" (BDB 912, IV) in a list of nations in Isa. 66:19, but it is not in the Hebrew text.

▣ "Meshech" KB 646 II (BDB 604) identifies it with the mountain dwellers of Asia Minor (cf. Herodotus 3:94; 7:72). It is always associated with "Tubal" (cf. Gen. 10:2; 1 Chr. 1:5; Ezek. 27:13; 32:26; 38:2-3; 39:1; Isa. 66:19). In the Assyrian documents Meshech is Mushku of central Anatolia and Tubal is Tabal of eastern Anatolia (cf. IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 723).

▣ "Tubal" The name's meaning is, like the others, uncertain. BDB (1063, KB 1683) thinks it is a territory related to Asia Minor or Cappadocia. KB (1694) lists several other options (i.e. craftsman tribe, possibly related to the Kenites).

All of these specific leaders are from the line of Japheth (cf. Genesis 10). Now at the end, all of the descendants of Japheth attack the descendants of Seth (cf. Gen. 4:25-26) and Shem (cf. Gen. 9:26-27)!

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:4 "I will turn you about"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:4 "I will turn you about" This VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Polel PERFECT with waw) is also used in Ezek. 39:2. It denotes YHWH's direct involvement (cf. Isa. 37:29). He is in complete control of world events for His own purpose (cf. Isa. 10:5-19; 55:9-11; Hab. 1:5-11). History is in His hand (cf. Rom. 8:28-30)!

▣ "put hooks into your jaws" This parallel phrase also denotes YHWH's direct actions.

  1. causing Israel to go to Egypt, 19:4
  2. causing Israel to go to Babylon, 19:9
  3. destroying Egypt, 29:4

Here, it denotes YHWH's control and manipulation of these foreign empires (cf. Ezek. 38:5; 29:4). YHWH will instigate the final conflict with evil (cf. Ezek. 29:3-5), so as to destroy it once and for all. This is the theme that John uses in Revelation 20. Evil must be destroyed (or permanently isolated) for the purpose of creation (i.e. fellowship between God and humanity) to reach its full potential and design.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ "buckler and shield" These two terms (BDB 857 and 171) refer to two kinds of shields.

  1. The first is a large shield used to protect the whole body as well as another person, usually an archer. These were usually used in siege warfare.
  2. The second is a smaller shield carried into battle by individuals.

When they are used together (cf. Ezek. 23:24; 38:4), they denote soldiers fully armed for conflict.

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:4-6 "all your army"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:4-6 "all your army" Notice the wide geographical aspect of this end-time army assembled against the people of God.

  1. Persia, Iran, and Afghanistan (old Assyria [it is surely possible that פתרוס has been confused with פרס, since Pathros is mentioned in Ezekiel as connected to Egypt, cf. Ezek. 29:14; 30:14, which is also like #3 in north Africa])
  2. Ethiopia (Cush)
    1. below Egypt (cf. Gen. 10:6-7) or
    2. in Mesopotamia (cf. Gen. 10:8)
  3. Put
    1. Libya (LXX, but note Nahum 3:8) or
    2. Somalia
  4. Gomer, a son of Japheth (cf. Gen. 10:2), probably Cimmerians, who occupied Asia Minor in 8th century B.C. (i.e. Herodotus, cf. ABD, vol. 2, p. 1074)
  5. Beth-togarmah, a son of Gomer (cf. Gen. 10:3). Josephus identified them as Phrygians because of Ezek. 27:14. However,
    1. an Assyrian inscription (i.e. Til-Garimmu) makes it a city in east Cappadocia (ZPBE, vol. 4, p. 766)
    2. a Hittite text locates it (i.e. Tegaramara) at the head waters of the Euphrates River (ABD, vol. 6, p. 595). (Possibly #a and #b are the same site)
    3. Jewish Study Bible (p. 1115) identifies it with Armenia.
    4. IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT) says it refers to the capital city (Kammanu) in central Anatolia, p. 723.

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:6 "from the remote parts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:6 "from the remote parts" This term (BDB 438) denotes the extreme north (cf. Ezek. 38:15; 39:2), which is also the site of YHWH's mountain (cf. Ps. 48:2; Isa. 14:13). This phrase may be parallel to "from the ends of the earth," used in Deut. 28:49 and Isa. 5:26. The nations from afar serve YHWH's purposes. As YHWH brought Old Babylon (cf. Isa. 13) and Assyria (cf. Isa. 10:5), so too, now Gog.

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:7 There are two IMPERATIVES that address this great army. Like Ezek. 38:4, YHWH is directing this pagan, evil army for His purposes (note NJB translation, "and hold yourself at my service," also note Ezek. 38:8).

  1. be prepared, BDB 465, KB 464, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  2. prepare yourself, same VERB, but in the Hiphil IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:8 This verse obviously refers to a restored and peaceful Palestine. It describes the results of the new heart and new spirit of Ezek. 36:22-36 and the restoration, gathering, and uniting of Ezekiel 37.

▣ "in the latter years" See Special Topic: The Last Days (NT)

▣ "living securely" This VERB (BDB 442, KB 444, Qal PERFECT) is repeated in Ezek. 36:28,33,35; 37:25 (thrice); 38:11 (twice); 12 (twice), 14; 39:6,9,26. They are back in the land of promise.

The term "securely" (BDB 105) is repeated in Ezek. 28:26 (twice); 34:25,27,28; 38:11; 39:26. God's people trust in Him to rovide protection. YHWH vindicates His power and honor by totally and completely defeating the multi-national army (like Assyria's, old Babylon's, and Neo-Babylon's). His people were not exiled because of His weakness or indifference, but because of their sin, which has now been forgiven.

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:10-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:10-13 YHWH allows the evil greed of fallen humanity to gain control of the leaders of this northern army.

Is this literal? Is this future? John uses this scenario in Revelation 20 for a rebellion at the close of "the golden age" (i.e. millennium). Does YHWH need to be vindicated in history beyond the Second Coming of Christ? My study of the genre of prophecy and apocalyptic and my NT understanding tends to relegate this type of OT passage to symbolism and imagery of God's total defeat of evil, accomplished at the cross, the empty tomb, and the second coming!

See my new Partial-Preterist commentary on Revelation (2024).

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:11 This verse describes restored national Israel, who does not need fortifications or military equipment because YHWH is with them. They need no further protection! They even burn all the captured military equipment in v. 9.

38:12
NASB, NRSV, REB, JPSOA, NET  "at the center of the world"
NKJV, LXX  "in the midst of the land"
TEV  "at the crossroads of the
  world"
Peshitta  "in the beauty of the land"
NJB, LXX  "at the navel of the world"

The Hebrew term translated "center" (BDB 371, KB 367) can mean "highest point" or "central." The second term "world" (BDB 75) can mean land or world. This refers either to

  1. Palestine's geographical position as the only land connection between the powers of the Nile and the Tigris/Euphrates (cf. Ezek. 5:5; TEV)
  2. the people living in the hill country (NKJV, Rotherham footnote)
  3. Palestine as the special location of God's covenant people who are so special to Him (NJB). In Summerian/Babylonian mythology the temple in Nippur was the site where Enlil cut the navel cord that united heaven and earth (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 333).

Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:13 "Sheba and Dedan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:13 "Sheba and Dedan" These were brothers listed in Gen. 10:7. They are connected to Arabia and the trade routes (cf. Ezek. 27:20; Isa. 21:13). That is why they are linked to Edom in Ezek. 25:13; Jer. 49:8.

▣ "Tarshish" See note at Ezek. 27:25.

Special Topic: Tarshish

38:14
NASB, NKJV  "will you not know it"
NRSV  "you will rouse yourself"
TEV, NJB  "you will set out"
REB  "will you not bestir yourself"
JPSOA, NET  "you will take note"
LXX  "will you not be roused?"
Peshitta  "you will know it"

The MT has "you not will know." The LXX has a different root, "wake up" or "set out."

  1. MT ‒ תדע, BDB 393, KB 390, Qal IMPERFECT
  2. LXX ‒ תער (BDB 735)

The UBS Text Project, p. 126, suggests the second option but with a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:16 Notice the purpose of God allowing this treacherous invasion. God will manifest Himself, His power, glory, and holiness for all to see (cf. Isa. 43:8-13)! This theme (i.e. "know Me") is recurrent! God wants His highest creations to return to Him (cf. Ezek. 36:23; 37:28; 38:23).

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ "in the last days" This phrase is used of a future period (cf. Isa. 2:2; Ezek. 38:16; Dan. 2:28; 10:14; Hosea 10:14; Micah 4:1). In the NT this phrase becomes the time between the first coming of the Messiah and His glorious return (i.e. the overlapping of the two ages).

Special Topic: The Last Days (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: This Age and the Age to Come

Special Topic: The Second Coming

▣ "My land" By creation all the earth is YHWH's (cf. Exod. 9:29; 19:5; Deut. 32:8), but Canaan/Palestine was uniquely His (cf. Lev. 25:23; 2 Chr. 7:20; Isa. 14:25; Jer. 2:7; Ezek. 36:5; Joel 1:6; 3:2). It was the special place for the manifestation of Himself to the world (cf. Rom. 9:4).

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:17 This may allude to Psalm 2 or 83, but more probably Isa. 34:1-6 and 63:1-6 (if Edom is a symbol of all rebellious nations; this would also explain Ezekiel 35). This same theme is also found in Joel 3:9-16 (which I think is early post-exilic).

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:18-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:18-23 Note the imagery of God's passion for His people and their enemies.

  1. My fury, Ezek. 38:18
  2. My anger, Ezek. 38:18
  3. My zeal, Ezek. 38:19
  4. My blazing wrath, Ezek. 38:19 (cf. Ezek. 22:21,31)
  5. the earth will shake at My presence, Ezek. 38:20
  6. a sword, Ezek. 38:21 (cf. Ezekiel 21; 32:33)

Also notice the other images.

  1. cosmic upheavels (as YHWH approaches)
    1. earthquake, Ezek. 38:19
    2. animals tremble, Ezek. 38:20
    3. mountains fall, Ezek. 38:20
    4. walls fall, Ezek. 38:20
    5. pestilence, Ezek. 38:22
    6. torrential rain, Ezek. 38:22 (cf. Ezek. 13:11,13)
    7. hailstones, Ezek. 38:22
    8. fire, Ezek. 38:22
    9. brimstone, Ezek. 38:22
  2. war motifs of a zealous (jealous) Covenant God, YHWH
    1. humans tremble, Ezek. 38:20
    2. a sword is loosed, Ezek. 38:21
    3. blood, Ezek. 38:22

Many of these will later be amplified into apocalyptic imagery and phrases. I still think this literary unit in Ezekiel is a precursor of apocalyptic language (cf. Cracking OT Codes, by Sandy and Geise, p. 190), not one of its first examples, as is 40-48 (i.e. no angel guides, no number symbolism, no use of colors, no secret messages).

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:20 "the mountains also will be thrown down"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:20 "the mountains also will be thrown down" This phrase can be seen in two ways.

  1. The convulsing of nature at the coming of its Creator (i.e. stars fall, sun darkened, moon turned to blood, cf. Isa. 24:23; 64:1,3; Joel 2:30-31).
  2. An allusion to the trembling of the pagan gods (cf. Zeph. 2:11). The gods of Mesopotamia (Enlil and Ashur) and Canaan (El and Ba'al) are mountain gods. This may explain the strange references of Ps. 48:2; Isa. 14:13; and Ezek. 28:14,16.

This may explain how YHWH is tied to Mt. Sinai/Horeb and Mt. Zion. The culmination of history is at a mountain (cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 11:9; 24:23; 25:6-12; 65:25; Micah 4:1-5).

▣ "the steep pathways will collapse, and every wall will fall to the ground" The key term in the first phrase "steep pathways" (BDB 201) in Song of Songs 2:14 means a secret, inaccessible hiding place. Therefore these two phrases are parallel and mean there will be no hiding places from YHWH's personal presence, no place for humans to seek refuge (cf. Rev. 6:15-16).

38:21
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "a sword"
TEV  "terrify"
REB  "universal terror"
LXX  "every fear"

The MT has "a sword" (BDB 352), which is followed by most English translations. The LXX has "terror" (BDB 353).

  1. sword ‒ חרב
  2. terror ‒ חרדה

The UBS Text Project, p. 127, gives the first option a "B" rating (some doubt).

▣ "Every man's sword will be against his brother" This is an interesting phrase. Judges 7:22 and 2 Chr. 20:23 describe an invading army destroying itself. 1 Samuel 14:20 describes a great confusion. But Haggai 2:22 describes an act of God whereby Israel's now post-exilic leaders (Zerubbabel and Joshua) are established. This may be the thrust of Ezekiel 38-39!

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:22 As God has fought on Israel's behalf (i.e. the Exodus, cf. Exod. 14:14; 15:3; Deut. 1:30 and the Conquest, cf. Deut. 3:22; Josh. 10:14,42) and used the forces of nature, so too, again. Israel is at peace and has no army (this surely does not fit modern Israel) or walled cities! God will act on their behalf (covenant promises). Now the "destroyed army" will not be Israel's (i.e, Ezekiel 37), but the pagan evil, unbelieving nations on the fringes of the Mediterranean world, who had no contact with God's people (or His word) before this time.

See Steve Gregg's "The Modern State of Israel"

entries.title: Ezekiel 38:23 "and make Myself known in the sight of many nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:23 "and make Myself known in the sight of many nations" This could be understood in two ways.

  1. YHWH's judgment on sinful nations (cf. Ps. 9:4,16; Isaiah 34; 43:8-13)
  2. YHWH's desire for the nations to know Him and come to Him (cf. Ezek. 37:28; 38:16; 39:27)

Israel was meant to be a "kingdom of priests" because all the world belongs to YHWH (Exod. 19:5-6). Abraham's call included a blessing for all the nations (cf. Gen. 12:3). The initial "good news" (cf. Gen. 3:15) was to humanity, not Israel. Even the Law of Moses mentions God's purpose of informing the nations (cf. Deut. 4:5-8). Also several passages in Isaiah address the nations being included (i.e. Isa. 42:6; 49:6; 51:4-8; 66:18-21).

Special Topic: Seek the Lord

Special Topic: Call on the Name

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:2 "from the remotest parts of the north"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:2 "from the remotest parts of the north" This term (BDB 438) is used in Isa. 14:13 (cf. Ps. 48:2) for the far north. It is used in that same sense here (cf. Ezek. 38:6,15). This term is used in Jeremiah to describe the invasion of Neo-Babylon (cf. Jer. 6:22; 25:32; 50:41). Another enemy is coming at YHWH's behest, but this one will not succeed, but be totally destroyed. This was a way to

  1. show YHWH's power
  2. vindicate YHWH's name (cf. Ezek. 39:7)
  3. reveal YHWH to the nations (cf. Ezek. 39:6,7)
  4. remove evil from God's creation

▣ "against the mountains of Israel" This is imagery for Canaan/Palestine (cf. Ezek. 17:22-24). Earlier in Ezekiel these mountains are judged (cf. Ezek. 6:2-7) but now in the context of a restored, forgiven, obedient Israel, they are defended by YHWH Himself.

This is another allusion to Isaiah 14 (esp. Ezek. 39:13-14). All of these world events are personally directed by YHWH for His revelatory and redemptive purposes (Isa. 14:26-27)!

Special Topic: Armageddon

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:2-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:2-6 Notice the VERBS which emphasize YHWH's actions (i.e. "for it is I who have spoken," Ezek. 39:5,8; 38:4,8) against Gog.

  1. I shall turn you around, Ezek. 39:2, BDB 996, KB 1427, Polel PERFECT with waw
  2. I shall drive you, Ezek. 39:2, BDB 1058, KB 1664, Piel PERFECT with waw (this word is found only here in the OT. KB says possibly, "lead along on a rope" or "lead a child")
  3. I shall take you up, Ezek. 39:2, BDB 748, KB 828, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
  4. I shall bring you against, Ezek. 39:2, BDB 97, KB 112, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
  5. I shall strike your bow, Ezek. 39:3, BDB 645, KB 697, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
  6. I shall dash down your arrows, Ezek. 39:3, BDB 656, KB 709, Hiphil IMPERFECT
  7. I shall give you as food, Ezek. 39:4, BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT

YHWH acts for Israel in Ezek. 36:22-36, but here against the northern enemy!

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:3 "hand. . .hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:3 "hand. . .hand" See Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:4 "You shall fall on the mountains of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:4 "You shall fall on the mountains of Israel" This is a recurrent theme.

  1. unfaithful Judah shall fall (cf. Ezek. 6:2-7; 33:28)
  2. Edom (Mt. Seir) shall fall (cf. Ezek. 35:2-3,12; 36:4-7)
  3. Egypt fell (cf. Ezek. 31:12; 32:5,6)
  4. Babylon fell (cf. Ezek. 28:16)
  5. and now another enemy from the north, Gog, will fall

▣ "I shall give you as food to every kind of predatory bird and beast of the field" This curse (cf. Ezek. 39:17-20) reflects the horror and carnage of ancient battle fields, where the number of dead is so large and complete that no one is left to bury them.

This curse is also directed toward

  1. Egypt, Ezek. 29:5; 32:4-5
  2. faithless Judah, Ezek. 33:27 (cf. Isa. 46:11)

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:7 This refers to Ezek. 36:22-23! YHWH wants His name (i.e. Himself) to be known to all the world.

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

Special Topic: "The Name" of YHWH

▣ "the Holy One in Israel" The title ("Holy One of Israel") for YHWH is used often in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 12:6; 43:3,14; 55:5; 60:9,14) and probably is derived from the vision of Isaiah 6. YHWH as "holy" goes back to Lev. 11:44-45; 19:2; 20:7,26. It is clearly stated in Josh 24:19. It speaks of His unique character (cf. 1 Sam. 2:2; Ps. 22:3; 99:3,5,9; 111:9). YHWH the Holy One is also the creator of Israel (cf. Isa. 43:15; 45:11).

Special Topic: The Holy One

Special Topic: Holy

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:8 The concept of a final day of reckoning was crystalized in Amos' "day of the YHWH."

Special Topic: That Day

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:9 This verse describes the huge number of the invading coalition army which was/will be totally defeated by YHWH (cf. Zechariah 12).

The number seven speaks of the symbolic nature of this context.

Notice that the weapons take seven years to burn and the bodies seven months (cf. Ezek. 39:12) to bury. It is only western literalism that demands that eastern prophetic texts be interpreted as literal history! This is prophetic symbolism. It certainly reveals truth, but modern interpreters must be genre-sensitive and cognizant of Jewish number symbolism! See

  1. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.
  2. John J. Davis, Biblical Numerology

Special Topic: Symbolic Numbers in Scripture, #4.

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:9 "I am for you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:9 "I am for you" The covenant will be restored. YHWH will be with and for His people again. The promises of Deuteronomy 28 will be actualized.

▣ "I will turn to you" As is so often the case, Ezekiel, being a priest, uses phrases from Leviticus 26. This phrase is in Lev. 26:9.

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:10 There is a series of VERBS followed by the PARTICIPLE of the same stem, which was a grammatical form of emphasis, certainty, or intensity.

  1. spoil, BDB 1021, KB 1531, Qal PERFECT with waw, Qal PARTICIPLE, Ezek. 39:10
  2. plunder, BDB 102, KB 117, Qal PERFECT with waw, Qal PARTICIPLE, Ezek. 39:10
  3. pass over, BDB 716, KB 778, Qal PERFECT with waw, Qal PARTICIPLE, Ezek. 39:15
  4. bury, BDB 868, KB 1064, Qal PERFECT, Qal PARTICIPLE, Ezek. 39:15 (also Ezek. 39:13,14)

Note the ironic reversal of the situation (so typical of the Bible). Those who came to gain spoils will be despoiled! Evil is overcome by the good God!

39:11
NASB, TEV  "a burial ground"
NKJV  "a burial place there"
NRSV, Peshitta  "a place for burial"
JPSOA  "a burial site there"
REB  "a burial ground"
LXX, Vulgate  "a noteworthy place as a tomb"

The MT is reflected in the NRSV and Peshitta. The UBS Text Project, p. 128, suggests a vowel change to "a famous place (lit. 'a place with a name') for burial." It gives this change a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

NASB, TEV  "of those who pass by"
NRSV, JPSOA  "of the Travelers"
TEV, MT  "Travelers' Valley"
NJB  "of the Obarim"
REB  "of the Abarim"
LXX  "of those who reach the sea"
Peshitta  "the great valley"

The UBS Text Project, p. 128, suggests the NRSV, JPSOA translation, but with only a "C" rating.

The NASB reflects the Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, "pass by" (BDB 716, KB 778), possibly from a Ugaritic idiom. It may denote the arrival of Gog's army with those already dead!

▣ "Hamon-gog" The Hebrew CONSTRUCT (BDB 242 and 155) means "the multitude of Gog" (cf. Ezek. 39:15-16, JPSOA). Earlier in the verse another CONSTRUCT (BDB 161 and 716) calls the same valley "the Valley of the Travelers" or "the Valley of those who pass by" (cf. Ezek. 39:14,15). It seems to be a wordplay (i.e. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1117) on "the valley of Abarim" (i.e. Vulgate), which is east of the Dead Sea and from whose peak (i.e. Mt. Nebo) Moses viewed the land of Canaan (cf. Num. 27:12; Deut. 32:49). Therefore, this refers to the Arnon River Valley.

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:14-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:14-15 Unburied bodies polluted the land making it Levitically unclean (i.e. Deut. 21:22-23). The new restored Israel wants to fully and completely observe God's laws.

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:16 "the name of the city will be Hamonah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:16 "the name of the city will be Hamonah" This means "multitude" (BDB 242) and apparently is a city located in this burial valley by the same name.

What a contrast to Ezek. 37!

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:17-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:17-20 This banquet for the birds of prey and carnivorous animals is symbolic of the judgment of God (cf. Isa. 18:6; 56:9; Jer. 12:9; Rev. 19:17-18). The unclean pagan soldiers are eaten by the unclean animals! The Deuteronomic curse, which threatened unfaithful Israel (cf. Lev. 26:22; Deut. 28:26) is now unleashed on Israel's enemies.

Notice the number of IMPERTAIVES in Ezek. 39:17 to the wild, carnivorous birds and animals.

  1. speak to, BDB 55, KB 65, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. assemble, BDB 867, KB 1062, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  3. come, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. gather, BDB 62, KB 74, Niphal IMPERATIVE

The Oxford Study Bible (REB), p. 900, has an interesting comment about this paragraph.

"17-20: an evil army other than God's, which has been buried, is slaughtered and then offered as sacrifices for wild beasts, thus reversing the usual practice of animal sacrifices offered by human beings. The significance of lthis is not clear."

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:21 "My hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:21 "My hand" See Special Topic: The Problems and Limitations of Human Language

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:21-24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:21-24 YHWH will reveal Himself! He was revealed by Israel, but in an inappropriate way (cf. Ezek. 36). His people were not exiled because of His lack of power or interest, but because of their covenant disobedience. Now He will reverse this misinformation (cf. Ezek. 38:22-23) by restoring His people (cf. Ezek. 39:25-29) and destroying all opposing human armies!

Israel was meant to be a light to the nations, a kingdom of priests, but they failed.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:23 "I hid My face from them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:23 "I hid My face from them" This is a figurative anthropomorphic way of asserting that YHWH would not hear their prayers (cf. Deut. 31:17-18; Isa. 1:15; 54:8; 57:17; 59:2). YHWH will reverse this in Ezek. 39:29. This phrase is an antithetical parallel to "I shall pour out My Spirit"! Prayer sent, received, and acted on was a concrete sign of the new covenant.

▣ "into the hand" See Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:25 "Jacob"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:25 "Jacob" This is the Patriarch from whom the name Israel comes (cf. Gen. 32:28). YHWH is promising to have mercy (BDB 933, KB 1216, Piel PERFECT with waw) on all the exiled people of God (i.e. the northern and southern kingdoms, cf. Ezek. 36:10; 37:21-22).

▣ "I shall be jealous for My holy name" The VERB (BDB 888, KB 1109, Piel PERFECT with waw) describes YHWH's special love and care for Israel (cf. Exod. 34:14; Deut. 4:23-24), through whom He will reveal Himself to the world. They failed (cf. Ezek. 36:22-23), but now through the new covenant (cf. Ezek. 36:22-28; Jer. 31:31-34; Joel 2:28-32), He will succeed!

Special Topic: Jealousy, Zeal

Special Topic: "The Name" of YHWH (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:25-29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:25-29 For those who see every prophecy as eschatological, this paragraph must refer to the post-exilic period introduced by Cyrus II, the king of Medo-Persia, in 538 B.C..

Prophecy characteristically takes a current situation (positive or negative) and projects it into a future setting. How God's people live today determines what future they will experience.

  1. To take prophecy "literally" misses the point.
  2. To take prophecy "unconditionally" misses the point.
  3. To take prophecy "as modern western prose" misses the point!

Special Topic: Kings of Persia

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:26 Israel will remember and be ashamed of her rebellion and sin (cf. Ezek. 6:9; 16:61,63; 20:43; 36:31-32).

There is some variation in the translations of Ezek. 39:26.

  1. "forget" (BDB 674, נשה), NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB, NIV, REB
  2. "bear" (BDB 669, נשא), Peshitta, NKJV, JPSOA, NET Bible

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:28 "I made them go into exile"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:28 "I made them go into exile" It was not the power of the pagan deities or the power of the national armies of the Ancient Near East, but YHWH's judgment (i.e. Jer. 29:4,7,14; Amos 5:27) and personal activity (i.e. He used Assyria, old Babylon, Neo-Babylon, and later Persia for His revelatory and redemptive purposes). This is "the" major theological issue in Ezekiel (i.e. God's holy name).

entries.title: Ezekiel 39:29 "I shall have poured out My Spirit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:29 "I shall have poured out My Spirit" The VERB (BDB 1049, KB 1629, Qal PERFECT) is used of YHWH's equipping presence

  1. for life, Ezek. 37:14
  2. for new covenant, Ezek. 11:19; 36:26-27; Joel 2:28 (all mankind)
  3. for fertility, Isa. 32:15; 44:3

In the OT God's Spirit is used in the sense of His power to accomplish His will in the world. The full NT Trinitarian sense does not clearly occur.

This is a sacrificial VERB (cf. Lev. 17:13; Deut. 12:16; 15:23). It is used of pagan practices in Ezek. 16:15; 23:8).

Just a balancing note about this VERB. It is also used of YHWH pouring out His wrath on the disobedient (cf. Isa. 42:25; Jer. 7:20; Lam. 2:4; Ezek. 21:31).

Special Topic: Poured Out

Special Topic: Personhood of the Spirit

Special Topic: The Trinity

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:1 "In the twenty-fifty year of our exile"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:1 "In the twenty-fifty year of our exile" This would be 573 B.C., dating from the exile of King Jehoiachin (i.e. 597 B.C., cf. 2 Kgs. 24:10-17).

▣ "at the beginning of the year" It is uncertain if the new year began in the autumn with the month Tishri (cf. Lev. 25:9), or with the month Nisan (cf. Exod. 12:2). No New Year feast is mentioned in the OT or NT or by Josephus or Philo.

Special Topic: ANE Calendars

▣ "after the city was taken" The VERB (BDB 645, KB 697, Hophal PERFECT, cf. Ezek. 33:21) means "to be attacked and captured" (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1-7).

▣ "the hand of the Lord was upon me" See note at Ezek. 33:22.

Special Topic: Anthropomorphic Language Used to Describe Deity

Special Topic: Hand

▣ "He brought me there" This VERB (BDB 97, KB 112, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw) speaks of a spiritual (i.e. "in visions," cf. Ezek. 1:1; 8:3; 40:2) transportation (this parallels Ezek. 8:3; 11:1,24) from exile in Babylon to the site of a high mountain (same VERB is Hiphil PERFECT in Ezek. 40:2). The Spirit does this to Ezekiel several times in chapter 40 (cf. Ezek. 40:2,3,4,17,28,32,35,48).

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

  1. First paragraph
  2. Second paragraph
  3. Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHT TO EZEKIEL 40-48

  1. Brief outline
    1. Ezek. 40-43 — the temple restored
    2. Ezek. 44-46 — the ritual restored
    3. Ezek. 47-48 — the land reallocated

      This obviously builds on the restoration vision of Ezek. 37.

  2. There is a series of special places where the God of Israel dwelt (i.e. the location of the Ark of the Covenant) and interacted with His people.
    1. the tabernacle
      1. description, Exodus 25-40
      2. procedures, Leviticus
    2. the temple of Solomon (based on a Phoenician pattern), 1 Kings 5-8; 1 Chr. 17;22;28;29; 2 Chr. 2-7
    3. the temple of Zerubbabel, Ezra; I Esdras; I Macc. 1:20-24; Josephus, Apion 1.22
    4. the temple of Herod, Josephus, Antiq. 15.11-12; Wars 5.5; Middoth in Mishna
    5. the temple of Ezekiel, Ezek. 40-48
    6. Jesus as the true temple, Hebrews (John 2:19-21; Hebrews 9-10 address this new covenant concept)

  3. Ezekiel was a trained priest of the line of Zadok. He was greatly concerned that the temple had become idolatrous (i.e. Ezek. 8-11) and that YHWH had left and moved east to be with the exiles in Babylon. The temple was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's army in 586 B.C. Ezek. 40-48 represents YHWH's return to His special place with His people. One wonders how much the prophecy of Jer. 31:38-40 affected Ezekiel; and how much Ezekiel affected Zechariah 2 and John's book of the Revelation. The imagery of the prophets reveal that
    1. they knew of each other's writing
    2. the Spirit used the same imagery again and again to tie God's promises together
      The details (cf. Ezek. 40:5-42:20) of
      1. steps
      2. their width
      3. along with the type of metal

        were symbolic of the levels of holiness as one approaches the most holy of places, the place where YHWH symbolically dwelt, the Holy of Holies and its Ark of the Covenant.
        Special Topic: Ark of the Covenant

  4. If taken literally, there is much disagreement between the procedures of Moses (Leviticus) and those of Ezekiel (chapters 40-48). Ezekiel knew Leviticus well. He alludes to it often. The Rabbi Hananiah bar Hezekiah attempted to reconcile them (cf. b. Shab 13b). Some rabbis assert that it must refer to a future Messianic temple (cf. Seder Olam 26; Rashi).

  5. Some possible interpretations
    1. It was never meant to be literally fulfilled, but was a literary way to reverse Ezek. 8-11. It was written to encourage the exiles.
    2. It was conditional prophecy to which the Jews did not respond appropriately (i.e. sin of the post-exilic period, cf. Ezra, Nehemiah, and Malachi).
    3. It was to be fulfilled in the return from the Exile under Zerubbabel (prince of Judah, seed of David) and Joshua (seed of the last high priest before the exile).
    4. It was fulfilled in Herod's temple.
    5. It will be fulfilled in an eschatological temple (Seder Olam 26).

  6. Personal problems interpreting this text
    1. Ezekiel, in sharp contrast to Isaiah, is very Israel-focused. Isaiah's universalism (God's love and inclusion of all the nations) is totally missing. The nations will know God through His judgment on them and blessings on Israel.
    2. Ezekiel focuses exclusively on national geographical Israel, which is so different from the NT (see Special Topic: OT Predictions of the Future vs. NT Predictions).
    3. Ezekiel, as a priest, takes seriously the curses and blessings of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29. He does predict an end-time Davidic seed and a restored sacrificial system (cf. Ezek. 34:23-24; 37:24-28).
    4. The NT
      1. specifically excludes an end-time sacrificial system in Hebrews 9 and 10 (see F. F. Bruce, Questions and Answers, pp. 32-33)
      2. includes Gentiles, while Ezekiel 40-48 is very nationalistic
      3. Jesus seems to have rejected the Jews as God's instrument of redemption in
        (1) the cursing of the fig tree (cf. Matt. 21:18-22; Mark 11:12-14)
        (2) the parable of the wicked tenants (cf. Matt. 21:33-46; Mark 12:1-12; Luke 20:9-19)
        (3) the "woes" of Matt. 23
        (4) see my new verse-by-verse commentary on the Olivet Discourse of Jesus (Matt. 23-24; 2 Thess. 2; Revelation [2024])
    5. I do believe that the Church is spiritual Israel (cf. Rom. 2:28-29; 9:6; Galatians 3-4; 6:15-16; Eph. 2:11-3:13; Phil. 3:3; 1 Pet. 2:8-9; Rev. 1:6). This has surely affected the way I understand Ezekiel. But before you say to yourself, "aha!" let me remind you that you, too, are presuppositional and historically and denominationally affected. We are all trying to understand the individual books of the Bible and then put them together into a perspective that embraces all of God's revelation. And, it is not easy! Quite often the problem is the ambiguity of Revelation itself.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:2 "God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:2 "God" This is Elohim (cf. Gen. 1:1; see Special Topic: Names for Deity, C.)

Why Elohim is used in v. 2 and YHWH (i.e. Lord, See Special Topic above, D.) is used in v. 1 is uncertain.

  1. Elohim ‒ God as creator, provider, and sustainer of all life
  2. YHWH ‒ God as savior, redeemer, and covenant-making God

Special Topic: Pentateuch Source Criticism

▣ "set me on a very high mountain" There are no "high" mountains in Israel. Because of Ezek. 17:27 and 20:40, this seems to refer to the temple on Mt. Moriah (cf. Isa. 2:2-3; Micah 4:1).

Special Topic: Moriah, Salem, Jebus, Jerusalem, Zion

NASB, NKJV  "on it to the south"
NRSV, REB, NET  "to the south"
TEV, NEB, RSV  "in front of me"
MT, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "on the south"
LXX  "opposite" or "before me"

The MT has "on the south" (BDB 616). The Septuagint has "opposite it" (see RSV, REB), which would refer to the

  1. Mount of Olives
  2. Mt. Zion

This change involves only one consonant in the Masoretic text ("south," בגנמ; "in front of," דגנמ). the UBS Text Project, p. 131, gives the MT a "B" rating (some doubt).

▣ "there was a structure like a city" This may relate to Ps. 48:2, but this is uncertain because of the description "in the far north" (cf. Isa. 14:13; see G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 224-225).

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:3 "a man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:3 "a man" This turns out to be an angelic guide (cf. Ezek. 40:3), so characteristic of apocalyptic literature.

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

▣ "line of flax and a measuring rod in his hand" The line of flax (BDB 833) was used to measure long distances (i.e. Zech. 2:9), while the measuring reed (i.e. river reed, BDB 889) was used to measure short distances and the "cubit" even shorter.

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:4 Ezekiel is given a series of commands.

  1. see, BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. hear, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. give attention (lit. "set your heart"), BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 44:5
  4. declare, BDB 616, KB 665, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

▣ "declare. . .all that you see" This is theologically similar to Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Jer. 26:2. Ezekiel must disclose everything that was communicated to him from YHWH to the people.

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:5 "there was a wall on the outside of the temple all around"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:5 "there was a wall on the outside of the temple all around" This begins the very detailed description of the new temple. This wall's length is measured in Ezek. 42:20.

▣ "a measuring rod of six cubits, each of which was a cubit and a handbreadth" There seem to have been two cubits:

  1. described in Deut. 3:11 and 2 Chr. 3:3 as the distance from a man's elbow to his longest finger, about 18 inches
  2. a longer cubit was used in both Babylon and Egypt, which was the regular distance plus the width of a man's hand, which made it about 21 inches (cf. Ezek. 43:13)

The Mishnah says that the measuring rod/reed was about 10 feet, 5 inches long.

Special Topic: Cubit

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:6 This is the gate from which YHWH left the temple (cf. Ezek. 11:1,22-23) and the direction from which He will return to the new temple (cf. Ezek. 43:1-5).

▣ "went up its steps" Throughout chapter 40 a series of steps is mentioned (Ezek. 40:6,22,26,31,34,37, and 39). These ascending steps and shrinking doorways seem to depict the levels of holiness as one approaches the Holy of Holies (cf. chapter 41:2-3).

40:9
NASB  "its side pillars"
NKJV  "the gateposts"
NRSV, REB  "its pilasters"
NJB  "its piers"
JPSOA  "its supports"
LXX, Peshitta  "its posts"

This rare Hebrew word (BDB 18 II, KB 40 III) means "door jamb" in 1 Kgs. 6:31, but here (cf. Ezek. 40:9, 10, 14 [twice], 16 [twice], 21, 24, 26, 29, 31, 34, 36, 37 [twice], 38, 48, 49; 41:1, 3) its meaning is uncertain. The NIV translates it as "projecting walls" and "jambs." The same consonants (איל) in BDB can mean

  1. ram, I
  2. leader III
  3. prominent tree (terebinth), IV
  4. strength (KB)
  5. deer (KB)
  6. projecting pillar, II

KB 40 III offers "pillar of an archway" as a possible meaning.

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 40:14 This verse is very difficult in the Masoretic text. Note the different translations available to you. Here is the JPSOA: "He made the vestibule ‒ 60 cubits ‒ and the gate next to the support on every side of the court."

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:16 "palm tree ornaments"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 40:16 "palm tree ornaments" These (BDB 1071, cf. Ezek. 40:22,26; 41:18) were also in Solomon's temple (cf. 1 Kgs. 6:29,32,35; 7:36; 2 Chr. 3:5), but not the tabernacle. Solomon elaborates the tabernacle's design and Ezekiel elaborates Solomon's design.

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:17 "pavement"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:17 "pavement" This (BDB 954) refers to some type of stone or mosaic floor covering.

  1. Xerxes' palace ("in the court of the garden of the king") in Susa, Esther 1:5-6
  2. Solomon's temple, 2 Chr. 7:3
  3. Ezekiel's temple (i.e. outer court), Ezek. 40:17,18; 42:3
40:43
NASB  "double hooks"
NKJV, Peshitta, Targums  "hooks"
NRSV  "pegs"
TEV  "ledges"
NJB  "runnels"
JPSOA  "shelves"
LXX  "hewn stone"

The Hebrew consonants (שׁפת) in the words "hooks" (BDB 1052 II) and "ledges" are the same. "Hooks" fits Ezek. 40:42 (i.e. sacrifice) and the last phrase of Ezek. 40:43 ("and on the tables was the flesh of the offering"). However, "ledges" are mentioned in the "Temple Scroll" of the Dead Sea Scrolls (30:13, see IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 725).

40:44
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA  "chambers for the singers in the
  inner court"
LXX, RSV, TEV, REB  "two chambers"
MT  "chambers for the singers"

The MT has "chambers for the singers." The Septuagint has "two chambers" (RSV, TEV, NJB, REB) and says these rooms were "for the sacrificing priests" in Ezek. 40:46. We can see the different functions of the Levite priests in Ezek. 40:45-46, therefore, "chambers" fits the immediate context better.

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:31 Food, especially for priests, must be handled in specific ways (i.e. how the blood and fat was dealth with, cf. Lev. 7:24; 17:15; 22:8). The Hebrews did not make a distinction between sinful and ceremonial acts.

Special Topic: Food Laws

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:46 "These are the sons of Zadok"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 40:46 "These are the sons of Zadok" This was the lineage of Ezekiel. Zadok served Solomon in his temple. Jeremiah was from the line of Abiathar, who rebelled against David and was exiled by Solomon from temple service. Verses 45-46 may reflect the forgiveness of the line of Abiathar. As Israel and Judah are reunited, so too, the two families of priests. However, the sons of Zadok still exclusively attend the altar (cf. Ezek. 43:19; 44:15-16).

entries.title: Ezekiel 40:49 "and the width eleven cubits"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:49 "and the width eleven cubits" The Septuagint has "twelve cubits," which seems to fit the overall structure better. But, the UBS Text Project, p. 148, thinks "eleven" is original.

▣ "at the stairway by which it was ascended" The Septuagint adds "ten steps."

▣ "the sacred pillars" This seems to refer to the two free-standing pillars in the front of Solomon's temple, which were called Jachin and Boaz (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:15-22,41; 2 Chr. 3:17).

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ezekiel 41:1 "he brought me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:1 "he brought me" Does the "he" refer to (cf. Ezek. 40:17,24,28,32,35,48)

  1. the hand of the Lord, Ezek. 40:1,2
  2. the Lord's Spirit
  3. the angel guide, Ezek. 40:45,47; 41:2,3,4,15

In context #3 fits best.

NASB, NRSV  "the nave"
NKJV, REB  "the sanctuary"
JPSOA  "the great hall"
TEV  "central room"
NJB  "the Hekal"
LXX  "the shrine"
Peshitta  "the temple"

This word (BDB 228, KB 244) can refer to

  1. palace/temple of God as the great king, 2 Kgs. 18:16; 23:4; 24:13; Jer. 7:4; 24:1; Ezek. 8:16?
  2. the holy place of Solomon's temple, 1 Kgs. 6:17; 7:50, and of Ezekiel's temple, 41:1, 4, 15, 21, 23?
  3. the heavenly temple of Isaiah, Isa. 6:1 (cf. Ps. 11:4; Micah 1:2; Hab. 2:20)?
  4. the second temple built during Zerubbabel's time, Hag. 2:15,18; Zech. 6:12,13,14,15; 8:9; Mal. 3:1?
